en: The Sūtra of the Array of the Basket of Qualities (Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha-sūtra).
Chapter 1: The Avadāna on the Benefits of Revering the Glorious Triple Gem.
Om! Homage to the glorious Three Jewels! Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
Having gone for refuge to that Protector, the glorious Śrīghana, the Great Buddha, the Victor, and Lord of all worlds, I shall proclaim the noble discourse of Lokeśvara.
Through the grace of devotion to her, the illustrious Bhagavatī Goddess, the sovereign mistress of all phenomena, I shall explain the means for attaining enlightenment.
I shall proclaim the accomplishment of all aims for that Lord of the World (Lokeśvara), by whom this entire world of the three realms has been protected;
namely, there was once a Great Being, Jinaśrīrāja, who possessed self-knowledge.
Having gone for refuge to the Triple Gem, he became an ascetic, an Arhat, and a son of the Conqueror.
At one time, that Arhat, having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening at the seat of enlightenment in the hermitage of the Victor, devoted himself to the welfare of the world.
Then, the great master of supernormal knowledge, the self-knowing ascetic Jayaśrī,
took his seat upon the throne in the assembly hall in order to teach the true Dharma.
Seeing him, all the disciples— the monks who were practitioners of the holy life—
approached and took refuge in him, in order to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Likewise, other bodhisattvas who had accomplished the vow for perfect enlightenment gathered at that assembly to drink the nectar of his well-spoken words.
Likewise, the bhikṣuṇīs and śrāmaṇeras, as well as the upāsakas and upāsikās,
and even those great beings who observe vows and practice with devotion toward the Perfectly Awakened One.
Brahmins and kṣatriyas as well, kings, ministers, and common people; counselors, guild-leaders, citizens, caravan leaders, and great folk.
Likewise, there were people from the countryside, from villages, from the mountains, and from the cities;
as well as other local folk who desired the qualities of the true Dharma.
Having all come together, they honored that Arhat Jayaśrī in due order, and having bowed down, they took their seats nearby.
With palms joined in reverence, they joyfully gazed upon the Teacher; desiring to drink that nectar of his true Dharma, they circumambulated him and sat down.
Then that Arhat Mahāsattva, the Bodhisattva born from the Conqueror,
O King Jinaśrī, beheld all the worlds gathered in the assembly.
Desiring to hear the greatness of the qualities of the Three Jewels,
he rose from his seat before Jayaśrī.
Wearing his upper garment and resting on his knees upon the ground,
he bowed with palms joined before the Lord’s lotus feet and made this request with great reverence.
Venerable One, I wish to hear the excellent discourse on the arising of the Three Jewels;
may the Blessed One, O Teacher, instruct me and awaken my understanding.
When he had thus made his request, the Teacher— Jayaśrī, who is endowed with the virtues of the glory of the Victors, and Sumati— beheld the assembly and commanded as follows:
Excellent! Listen with focused attention, O noble-minded Jinashriraja, to the detailed account of the qualities and the origin of the Three Jewels.
Just as it was instructed to me by my teacher Upagupta, a practitioner of the *jinakalpa* for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, so shall it be spoken by me.
For example, O Great King, there was once a universal monarch,
a ruler of men named Aśoka, a lord of kings who bore the welfare of all the world as his purpose.
Once, that great king, longing for the virtues of the True Dharma,
desired to hear about the majesty of the qualities of the Three Jewels for the benefit of the world.
Then that king, the lord of the earth, together with his ministers, countrymen, and citizens,
took up offerings for worship and, having celebrated with great festivities, [set out].
Filled with great joy, he proceeded to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery;
having arrived there, O King of kings, he entered it with a serene mind.
He beheld Upagupta, possessed of great supernormal powers, together with his community of monks;
having gazed upon that Arhat and bowed with joy and palms joined in reverence.
Having approached suddenly, one should worship according to the prescribed rite;
then, having circumambulated, one should prostrate at the lotus-feet.
With palms joined in reverence, she took her place before him to hear the sublime Dharma;
thereafter, all the people of the world also arrived one after another in due order.
Having bowed to that Arhat ascetic and circumambulated him,
King Aśoka, the lord of kings, then took his seat, having observed the people gathered in the assembly hall.
Rising from his seat, he approached the presence of the Teacher; wearing his upper robe over one shoulder, he knelt with both knees upon the ground.
Having bowed to that ascetic with palms joined in reverence, one should pray thus with devotion:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear the excellent discourse on the origin of the Three Jewels."
"What is that which is known as the Three Jewels? You should explain that to me.
When the king had thus entreated him, that wise Arhat, a son of the Jina, [replied].
Having gazed upon that lord of men, Upagupta spoke as follows.
Excellent! Listen, O Great King, with a concentrated mind for the welfare of the world.
Just as it was instructed by my Guru, so shall it be spoken by me to you:
namely, that which arises from the beginning is the very nature of the Dharmadhātu.
Born from the portions of the five Buddhas, he is the Lord of the World, the Tathāgata;
the Great Buddha, the Protector of the World, the Teacher of the World, and the Great Sovereign.
The King of Dharma, Lord of Sages, the Arhat, who maintains the Vairocana-samādhi;
the Omniscient One, the receptacle of all virtues, the Victor, sovereign of all vidyās.
The Sugata whose limbs are the form of Samantabhadra, the source of glorious bliss,
the great hero possessing the six superknowledges, the leader Vajrasattva.
The destroyer of Māra’s pride and delusion, the sun of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment—
this Blessed One is known in the world as the Jewel of the Buddha.
And those bodhisattvas who, having gone for refuge to this [teaching], maintain the vow of the conduct of awakening and practice the auspicious deeds for the welfare of the world;
Having conquered all the hosts of Māra, the Arhats, with their intentions free from stain,
attained perfect enlightenment and reached the state of a fully awakened Buddha.
All those Lords of the World, Tathāgatas, Sovereigns of Sages, Blessed Ones,
possessors of great super-knowledges, are known as the Jewels of the Buddha.
And the Blessed Goddess Śrī is Prajñā, the locus of all virtues.
She is the mother of all Buddhas, the sun of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
She who destroys the pride and delusion of Māra, who bestows the virtues of the True Dharma,
the sovereign of all vidyās, Lakṣmī, who brings auspiciousness to all sentient beings.
This gatherer of the true Dharma is known as Dharmaratna.
Furthermore, whatever other well-spoken Mahāyāna sūtras and so forth were taught by the Sugatas, those too are remembered as the Jewel of the Dharma;
and the Bodhisattva who has accumulated the True Dharma is the Lord of the World.
The Great Being, the Lord of the World, the Sovereign Master of all phenomena.
He is the destroyer of the darkness of wicked afflictions, the sun for the lotus of perfect enlightenment;
he possesses all forms and the great superknowledges, and he bears the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings.
The glorious Lord of all worlds, the King of Dharma, the Son of the Victor—
this Teacher is known as Lokeśvara, the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
And those other great beings who are Bodhisattvas with conquered senses,
Arhats whose selves are stainless, and who have accomplished the knowledge of perfect enlightenment.
Those who practice the conduct of the *Bhadracaryā*, who dwell in the four sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*),
and who belong to the community of the Perfectly Awakened One— they too are remembered by the Victors as the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
Those who, having gone for refuge to them, always and constantly worship them with minds composed by devotion and faith, even while recollecting them day and night.
Those great beings, bodhisattvas who are mines of virtue, have attained true glory and prosperity; they are a festival of benefit for all sentient beings.
Having observed the vow of the conduct of awakening and always performing what is auspicious in the world,
they enjoy only happiness at all times and finally go to Sukhāvatī.
Thus, considering the veneration of the Jewel of the Saṅgha to be the supreme merit,
those who seek its virtues go for refuge to it and venerate it.
With a self purified by this merit, he shall never fall into an evil rebirth;
always born only in fortunate states, he shall become a sovereign of the Dharma.
And those who, having always gone for refuge to the jewel of the Dharma, listen to this well-spoken teaching and honor it with faith and devotion;
Those noble great beings, the Bodhisattvas, are the locus of virtues;
they are the support for the bliss of the glory of perfect enlightenment and are devoted to the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having undertaken the conduct of enlightenment and always acting for the welfare of sentient beings,
and having enjoyed only true happiness, they finally go to the abode of the Sugatas.
Thus, having understood this excellent bull [of dharma] for the sake of honoring the jewel of the Dharma, those who seek what is auspicious should go for refuge and honor it.
One whose self is purified by this Dharma never goes to an evil rebirth;
born only in the good destinies, they eventually go to the abode of the Victors.
Having understood this, those mortals who desire the happiness of the true Dharma should go for refuge to the Three Jewels and always venerate them throughout existence.
By the power of this merit, men whose intentions are completely purified attain the mind of complete enlightenment and practice the vow of awakening.
Practicing the conduct of awakening, they gradually fulfill the perfections.
Having completely conquered the four Māras, free from afflictions and possessing pure intentions,
they shall attain Arhatship and reach the state of perfect enlightenment.
Having understood this, the mortal who desires the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha should first go for refuge and rely upon a true guru.
Having propitiated the true guru with devotion, having satisfied him and won his grace,
and having received his instruction, one should bathe at a sacred ford and observe the vow.
The lords of sages have declared that among all vows, the Poṣadha is the most excellent;
by the power of its merit, one attains supreme enlightenment.
Even the perfectly awakened ones of the past, through the power of this merit,
became Victors who, having conquered the Māras and attained perfect awakening, became Buddhas.
(Gkv 6)
And all those who currently abide [in this state] shall, through the power of this merit,
attain perfect enlightenment upon reaching arhatship and truly become Sugatas.
And all those future Bodhisattvas who resemble those bound by vows— they too, through the ripening of this merit, shall become lords of sages.
In this way, through the ripening of that merit, they will become lords of sages.
In this way, all other beings as well— whosoever observes this vow— all those great beings shall become partakers of enlightenment.
They are illustrious, repositories of excellent qualities, free from afflictions, and have conquered their senses;
they are dedicated to the welfare of all sentient beings and abide in the four divine abodes.
For they never go to an evil rebirth within the abode of existence.
Always born indeed in happy realms and endowed with true happiness,
the Bodhisattvas are wise and accomplish the virtues of the True Dharma.
Having gradually fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment and remaining in meditative concentration,
they shall attain the threefold enlightenment and reach the state of nirvana.
Thus, O wise ones, those mortals who desire the state of nirvāṇa,
having undertaken this vow, should proceed according to the prescribed rule.
For those purified by this merit do not go to an evil destiny;
always born in happy states, they eventually attain perfect nirvana.
Thus was it instructed to me by my guru, just as it was taught by the Lord of Sages;
so have I related it to you, O King—let it be well considered.
You too, O King, should always act in this way, if you do not desire an evil rebirth.
If you indeed desire liberation, you must always be born into a good rebirth.
O King, observe this vow called Poṣadha according to the prescribed rule;
with your self purified by this merit, you will surely attain perfect peace.
Having heard this instruction given by that Arhat Śaya,
King Aśoka desired to observe that vow.
Then that king, the lord of men, having approached with palms joined in reverence and bowed down to the Arhat Upagupta, made this request with joy:
"O venerable ones, having heard what has been commanded by you, it pleases my mind;
thus shall I observe this supreme vow of the Poṣadha."
Please explain the method for that practice and its specific fruit,
as well as the extensive fruit of merit arising from devotion to the Three Jewels.
When the king had thus made his request, that Teacher, the Arhat of noble mind, looked upon the great king Aśoka and instructed him as follows.
"Excellent! Listen with a concentrated mind, O Great King, to that which you desire;
I shall relate it to you exactly as it was told to me by my teacher."
For example, this person of serene mind, wishing to observe the vow,
first rises in the morning and bathes at a sacred ford according to the prescribed rite.
Enveloped in pure conduct, with a pure mind, and dwelling in the divine abodes (brahmavihāra),
he undertakes the Poṣadha vow endowed with the eightfold rules.
One should fashion the mandala of the glorious Lord of the World,
who is free from pride, adorned with five colors and accompanied by his retinue.

Having installed [the image] according to the prescribed rite, one who is pure in conduct and composed in mind should likewise avoid liquor, meat, and the like, as well as garlic and similar substances.
First, having worshipped the Guru according to the prescribed rite, one should prostrate;
then, having worshipped the Jewel, one should prostrate, having gone for refuge.
Then [he saw] Lokeśvara, the Lord of the World, known as Amoghapāśa.
Having meditated upon him and invoked him with the mind, one should respectfully offer water for the feet and the arghya offering.
Having established [the deity] there in the maṇḍala together with his retinue, being fully delighted and endowed with faith and devotion, he should worship according to the prescribed ritual.
One should worship and satisfy [the deity] completely with incense, perfumes, beautiful flowers, lamps, the five nectars, all ritual substances, and precious gems.
Having praised him with recitations, hymns, and the like, having performed many circumambulations,
and having bowed with the eight limbs while joining the palms in *añjali*, one should pray to Bhadrasaṃvara.
Then, standing with palms joined in reverence, he should perform the confession of his own misdeeds,
as well as the rejoicing in merit and the prayer for the long endurance [of the Dharma].
Thus, with a mind full of serene faith, having made this request for the vow of awakening, he should proceed.
Then, having made a request for forgiveness, one should dismiss that maṇḍala.

Then, during the third watch of that day, having partaken of the five nectars and other foods as desired, provided they are free from meat, one should practice while remaining composed in meditative concentration.
Having thus completed that vow and observing it with joy,
he should act for the welfare of all sentient beings, his mind set upon perfect enlightenment.
Having eaten this, his self is purified by merit; free from afflictions and with senses conquered, he is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who upholds the welfare of both himself and others.
Possessing glory, dwelling in excellent virtues, and maintaining the vow of the conduct of awakening,
he is always born in a happy rebirth and enjoys whatever food he desires.
Having attained the threefold enlightenment, one shall finally go to perfect nirvana.
In this very way, the exceedingly great fruit of merit arising from the two vows cannot be measured even by all the lords of sages.
The specific fruit of the merit gained from performing that worship is now being declared;
listen to it, O Great King, with a composed and attentive mind.
Those humans who, desiring merit, behold the Jewel among Men and go for refuge out of joy, become devoted to the Dharma, possessed of auspicious fortune, and delighted in the conduct of awakening.
Those who joyfully bathe the Triple Gem with the five nectars and the five fragrant waters shall bathe in the divine,
fragrant waters of the Mandākinī and rejoice in happiness in heaven.
And those who offer fragrant incense to the Three Jewels with joyful hearts, they become pure-minded, their limbs scented with purity; like jewels, they are endowed with glory and virtue.
Those whose minds are purified, who approach the bodies of the Three Jewels with the five fragrances,
become jewel-possessing sovereigns of the earth, desiring the welfare and benefit of all beings.
Those wise ones who joyfully offer excellent garments such as fine silk and brocade to the Lord of the Three Jewels,
their bodies adorned with silken robes and precious ornaments, become sovereigns of the Dharma.

And those who worship the Three Jewels with beautiful flowers grown on land as well as those born in water, they come to possess divine fortune, happiness, and enjoyments; they become endowed with glorious success and good luck.

Those who desire the Dharma and hang flower garlands upon the excellent images of the Three Jewels become kings of gods, endowed with supreme fortune, and, desiring perfect enlightenment, they become auspicious.
Those who scatter all fragrant flowers upon the images of the Three Jewels become lords of the gods when they go to heaven, and when they return to earth, they become sovereign kings of the land.
Those who arrange garlands of lamps before the Three Jewels, having destroyed the net of delusion,
become kings with beautiful forms, possessed of the jewels of virtue, their lotus-feet honored by sovereigns.
And those who offer lamps ignited with ghee or oil before the Three Jewels become pure-eyed, powerful, and rich in virtues; they shall become sovereigns of gods and lords of the earth.
Those who, endowed with devotion, offer excellent, delicious, and golden food to the Three Jewels,
become lords of the gods in heaven, as well as wise beings on earth.

Those people who offer this drink, rich with the excellent qualities of immortality, to the Three Jewels, become kings of the earth, free from disease, and most powerful; they even become lords of the three realms in heaven.
Those who offer vegetables, roots, and fruits to the Three Jewels,
having enjoyed them as they pleased and at their disposal, go forever to the abode of the Sugatas.
And those who, out of devotion, offer collections of wholesome medicines to the Three Jewels—
those lords of the earth, endowed with glorious prosperity, having enjoyed happiness, go to the abode of the Jinas.
Those who offer betel, areca nuts, and other elixirs to the Three Jewels become gods endowed with the excellence of beauty and virtue, delighting in divine physical splendor.
He who spreads a high canopy for the Triple Gem shall be honored by all kings;
he shall belong to a noble lineage, be virtuous, steadfast, and renowned for his great majesty.
Those who plant various colorful banners for the sake of a festival at a shrine of the Three Jewels become lords,
both in heaven and on earth, endowed with glory and prosperity, and delightful through their excellent virtues.

Those who are devoted to the Three Jewels and hang out glorious banners, being intent upon the [essence of] flavor, become lords of fortune who have conquered the hosts of the wicked; they become sovereigns both in heaven and on earth.
Those who offer parasols made of gold, or those fashioned from fine silk,
or with flowers of pure colors and jewels, to the Three Jewels;

Those kings of the earth, possessing supreme accomplishments, lords of fortune, whose bodies act for the benefit of all, who desire the true Dharma and are filled with the jewels of virtue, become venerable and endowed with preeminent supernatural powers.

With songs and instrumental music such as the muruja drums, the mukuṇḍa, ḍhakkā, and prāṇavaṇakas, as well as the maḍ, mṛdaṅga, paṭaha, and other instruments of enchanting sound, which are delightful to the ear and pleasing to the mind;
They offer worship to the Three Jewels with the sounding of kettledrums, ḍiṇḍimas, and jharjharas, with the beating of mardalas, and likewise with other auspicious sounds and musical instruments.

Those who delight the Three Jewels with the three types of musical performance, with auspicious and resonant conchs, and other instruments of pleasing sound, as well as with dances and other arts, are truly divine beings.
Possessing divine hearing and most pleasing sounds, their treasuries filled with the perfection of all wealth,
and delighting in merit conducive to the True Dharma, they move about in heaven after having enjoyed pleasures.
Those who, filled with joy, scatter parched grain, unbroken rice, and flowers toward the Three Jewels, never go to an evil rebirth; having gone to heaven, they, being fortunate, enjoy themselves.

Those wise ones who offer pure substances, jewels, and proper sacrificial fees to the Triple Gem obtain their desired aims and enjoy happiness; with all their faculties complete, they become truly fortunate.
Those who, having performed circumambulations with devotion, joyfully take refuge in the Triple Gem,
become pure in body and attain happiness, becoming gods or lords of men.
And those who honor the Three Jewels with pure praises, both in prose and in verse,
become lords of speech with abundant treasuries, protectors both in heaven and on earth.
And those who have gone for refuge to the Three Jewels and prostrate with devotion through the eight limbs of prostration,
they become lords of kings, filled with glory, virtues, and renown, and desirous of the true Dharma.
And those who, having constantly reflected with their minds, worship with devotion and have gone for refuge— they,
possessing pure bodies freed from evil and desiring the true Dharma, do not go to an evil rebirth.
And those who, having reflected upon the Triple Gem with their minds, constantly utter its name,
become pure in heart and stainless in nature, and take delight in the Dharma of the Perfectly Awakened One.
And those who, having seen the Three Jewels even from afar, bow with devotion and clear faith— they too, longing for the qualities of the True Dharma, become fortunate ones with pure three bodies.

Considering these and other such great merits, which are the means for attaining the auspicious virtues [of the Buddha] and arise from worshiping and venerating the Three Jewels, one should venerate Him who is the embodiment of the three qualities.

This has been declared by all the Sugatas: that merit arising from the service and devotion to the Three Jewels is so great that its equal is found nowhere, even throughout all the worlds; this is indeed the truth.
O King, if you desire awakening, understand that the Three Jewels possess such great merit— vast, supreme, boundless, and beyond calculation— and go for refuge to them.

(11) Those who have gone for refuge to the Triple Gem, who always worship it with devotion and clarity of mind— they shall all, delighting in the three virtues and desiring the true Dharma, become sons of the Sugata.
Having bestowed noble gifts upon those who seek them, those desiring perfect awakening should practice the excellent Dharma;
practicing the vow for awakening in due order, they shall attain awakening and become Victors. Then, perceiving the welfare of the world together with the Saṅgha, they shall teach the sublime Dharma.
Having completed all the Buddha's work throughout the three [times], they finally entered final nirvana.
Having understood this, if you desire to attain the bliss of nirvāṇa in this way,
always go for refuge to the Three Jewels and, with faith and clarity, constantly devote yourself to them.

O King, do not revile out of deluded contempt the Lord of the Three Realms, the bestower of auspiciousness, the Triple Gem; for the King of the True Dharma, the foremost in the world, is beyond reproach and is indeed worthy of veneration.

And those who, out of pride and arrogance, having reviled me, are born into wicked families with their self-composure shattered by unpleasantness; even they, upon seeing the Three Jewels—who always bestow the welfare of the three worlds—will praise them with clear minds.

All of them would be delighted by transgression, heedless, devoted to reviling the true Dharma, and corrupt; ruined by malice toward others, intoxication, and pride, they would be intent on the destruction of sentient beings.
Consequently, those who are afflicted by such misfortune, being fearless even regarding great evils,
might listen to all the well-spoken words on Dharma and Artha with apparent clarity, yet treat them with contemptuous derision.
Having thus committed many such terrible sins and constantly practicing them,
and further engaging even in extreme evils, they shall experience sufferings and go to hell.
Even after going there, their bodies submerged in the lower realms, tormented by the fire of hunger and utterly deluded,
they remain unsatisfied even after eating filth or drinking urine while parched with thirst.
Hungry and exceedingly thirsty, tormented and deluded by the fires of the afflictions,
afflicted by intense and extreme suffering, their fortitude utterly lost, they shall wander about, dwelling in delight within this prison.
Furthermore, even while being bound by this sin, they would not obtain the path of liberation;
thus, overcome by intense agony, they would remain there forever.

And those whose fortitude is corrupted by afflictions, who— driven by greed and even by force— seize, rob, or plunder the property of the Three Jewels, such as wealth, food, and so forth, and then consume it;
Those wicked beings, deeply attached to evil, having committed even the most terrible sins and having experienced intense suffering for a very long time, died with great difficulty and went to hell.
There too, their fortitude destroyed by afflictions, their limbs scorched by the fires of hunger and extreme thirst,
consuming excrement, urine, and the like, they shall wander and thus dwell in hell.

In the course of time, having regained their composure and reflecting upon their own evil deeds, they would remember the Triple Gem with a mind full of remorse; and with serene hearts, they would meditate and offer their prostrations.
Then, having been released from that body and having emerged from hell at some point,
they may attain human birth, yet they would be wretched, impoverished, and miserable.
There too, those wicked ones, attached to their evil ways and devoted to the misdeeds of slandering the True Dharma,
will again commit great sins and thus go once more into the hells.

Wandering thus in many ways through existence, having experienced sufferings for a long time while afflicted by disease, they— bound by the accumulation of their own sins— dwell in hell and shall not obtain even the slightest happiness.
Thus, the lords of sages have described the extremely terrible evil born from offenses against the Three Jewels;
considering this, O King, do not commit even the slightest offense here against the Triple Gem.
Having broken through [doubt] and become serene, go for refuge; always worship the Jewel alone.
By the ripening of this, having constantly performed virtuous deeds, may you go to the abode of the Sugatas.
Having heard this command of his, King Aśoka bowed to that Arhat,
his teacher, and spoke thus with palms joined in reverence:
"Venerable sir, having heard what you have taught, it pleases my mind;
accordingly, having gone for refuge to them, I shall honor them at all times."
O Teacher, I also desire to maintain the vow of these Three Jewels with constant reverence; therefore, you ought to instruct me accordingly.
In which month and on which lunar day (tithi) should one observe this vow?
Having explained this correctly, may you enlighten me.
Having heard this request made by the king, that arhat of great intelligence,
Upagupta, looked toward the lord of men and spoke as follows.
"Listen well, O Great King, if you desire this vow;
I shall explain it to you exactly as it was taught by my teacher."
"Just as one should practice throughout all months, especially on the five festival days, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, and on the full moon; so have the Jinas declared."
Among the months, Śrāvaṇa is the best, and Kārttika especially so; therein,
the ripening of performed actions is most extensive and its number is fixed.
Thinking thus, O Great King, remain composed for as long as you live; having gone for refuge to the Triple Gem, always observe this vow.
This is declared by all the Buddhas to be a most noble merit, bestowing the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, indeed inexhaustible and incomparable.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, the king was gladdened; and having mastered that instruction, he desired to perform that vow.
Then that king, the lord of men, together with his wife, sons, and kinsmen,
having performed the preparatory rites according to the rules, constantly observed this vow.
Having received that command from the king, all the ministers, as well as the servants,
the hosts of soldiers, the citizens, the villagers, the twice-born, and the rest, [acted accordingly].
Likewise, all the world, having gone for refuge to the Triple Gem with devotion,
always worshipped them with joy, honoring them with offerings and faith.
Then, in that place, the ever-auspicious and great enthusiasm proceeded on all sides without obstruction, due to the manifestation of this Dharma.
Thus it was told to me by my teacher, and thus have I heard and spoken it;
having rejoiced in this, you too should always practice this vow.
For those Arhats, purified by this merit and with the three spheres completely purified, being stainless in nature, shall attain perfect enlightenment.
Thus it was fully explained by the wise Jayaśrī;
having heard it, all those disciples were enlightened and rejoiced.
From that time forth, Jinaśrīrāja, with a serene mind and transcendent consciousness,
having gone for refuge to the Triple Gem, constantly practiced this vow.
The ascetics of that Saṅgha, practicing the four divine abodes,
having paid homage to the Three Jewels, always observed this vow.
Then all those practitioners, having purified the three spheres,
became Arhats with stainless selves, partakers of enlightenment.
And those mortals here who cause this Triple Gem, with its renowned multitude of virtues, to be heard by the world;
and those who, clear in their faith and devotion, listen with joyful minds.
All those bodhisattvas, endowed with every virtue, possessed of glorious prosperity, and deeply wise,
having enjoyed happiness forever, shall at last proceed to the realm of the One Possessing Ten Powers and dwell there in delight.
Having always enjoyed happiness, at the end they shall go to the realm of the One Possessing the Ten Powers and rejoice there.
Thus ends the first chapter, the *Avadāna on the Merits of Devotion to the Three Jewels*.
(Gkv 14) 2. The Chapter on the Glorious King of Dharma’s Awakening that Dries Up Avīci.
Then the wise Mahāsattva Jinaśrīrāja, the knower of self, [spoke].

Having bowed to the ascetic Jayaśrī with palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus: "Venerable sir, I desire to hear of the supreme qualities of greatness of the glorious Lokanātha, who possesses the excellent mind of the Jewel of the Saṅgha."
Therefore, for the benefit of the world, you ought to proclaim the greatness of the virtues of that glorious Lord Bodhisattva, the sovereign ruler of the three worlds.
Thus being entreated, that wise ascetic Jayaśrī,
beholding Jinaśrīrāja, spoke to him as follows:
"Excellent! Listen, O illustrious one, to that which was spoken by my preceptor;
I shall relate it to you in brief for the welfare of the world."
For instance, O Great King, that sovereign of men, Aśoka, once again proceeded to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery in order to hear the Dharma.
Having sat down there together with his ministers and the citizens,
he bowed down to the Arhat Upagupta and took his seat near him.
Having approached that arhat ascetic there with joy, he honored him,
bowed with palms joined in reverence, and made this request with great respect:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear of the greatness of the qualities of the True Dharma of Lokeśvara, the Lord of the World; you should deign to instruct me on that."
Thus entreated by that lord of the earth,
Sanmati Upagupta, upon beholding the protector of the land, gave him this instruction:
"Listen well, O Great King, to how it was heard by me from my Guru; thus shall I proclaim to you the majesty of the Lord of the three worlds."
Just as that great Buddha Śākyamuni, the teacher of the world,
the King of Dharma, possessed of great super-knowledges, the omniscient one, the Arhat, and the Lord of Sages;
The Blessed One, Śrīghana, the Teacher, the Tathāgata, the Guide,
the Conqueror of Māra, the Sugata, the Protector, the Lord of the three realms, the Victor.
Accompanied by the Saṅgha, he dwelt in the Jetakodyāna monastery of the illustrious Gṛhastha Mahāmati, the protector of the protectorless.
Then all those great beings, bodhisattvas, sons of the Conquerors, headed by Maitreya, came there to hear the true Dharma.
There, having seen that Śrīghana with a deeply serene disposition, they joyfully prostrated at his lotus feet and took their seats in his assembly.
All the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats who had assembled there bowed down to the Blessed One and took their places at one side.
The disciples, the monks, the ascetics, and those living the holy life,
having bowed down to that Teacher, took their seats in his assembly.
All the great beings, the ṛṣis who long for the true Dharma,
having seen Śrīghana approaching from afar, bowed down and came near.
Brahmā and the others, possessing great supernormal powers and illuminating all directions,
saw the Sugata from afar, bowed down, and approached him.
All the gods, Indra and the others, longing for the nectar of the Dharma,
beheld the Teacher from afar, bowed, and approached him.
Likewise, all the world-protectors, headed by Agni, being filled with joy,
approached and paid homage from afar upon beholding the Blessed One.
Likewise, all the Gandharvas, including Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others,
having gazed upon him from afar, suddenly approached while bowing down.
Virūḍhaka and all the others, as well as the Kumbhāṇḍas, were filled with joy;
seeing him from afar, they too approached suddenly while bowing down.
Virūpākṣa and the others, as well as all the lords of the nāgas,
having seen him from afar, also approached the Jina.
Vaiśravaṇa and the other yakṣas, all filled with joy,
seeing him from afar, bowed to that Sage and approached him.
All these lords of the planets, beginning with the Sun, have assembled here,
as well as all the hosts of stars and all the Vidyādharas.
The Siddhas, the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Vāyus, and the Maheśvaras—
all the lords of the desire realm, as well as those headed by Śrīpati.
All the lords of the Garuḍas, as well as Kiṃnara lords such as Drumā and others;
all the lords of the Daityas such as Vemacitra and others, and even the Rākṣasas.
The mahoragas and the nāgas, all those who move in the water,
all the sons of the gods, and all the hosts of apsarases;
All the daughters of the Gandharvas, all the daughters of the Kinnaras, the daughters of the Nāgas with divine limbs, and the auspicious daughters of the Rākṣasas.
There were innumerable daughters of yakṣas, as well as innumerable daughters of daityas,
and likewise innumerable, captivating daughters of vidyādharas.
Likewise, the daughters of the Siddhas and the daughters of the Sādhyas, who are exceedingly enchanting,
as well as the daughters of the gods and all other maidens, were filled with joy.
Having observed him shining brightly, they approached him near the assembly hall.
And likewise there were celibate students, nuns, and even those wearing rags; there were also laymen observing vows, as well as laywomen.
Likewise, other daughters of sages have come to hear the true Dharma,
as well as learned brahmins, heretics, and ascetics.
The kings, the kṣatriyas, and all the princes;
the ministers, the counselors, the guild-leaders, and the great men as well.
The soldiers, throngs of warriors, servants, and attendants as well;
householders, wealthy men, caravan leaders, and other groups of merchants.
Artisans and farmers as well, all householders,
all Vaiśyas and Śūdras, and likewise all other castes.
The citizens of the city, the townsmen, the people of the countryside, the merchants, the villagers, those dwelling in border regions, the pilgrims, and the mountaineers— (Gkv 17).
Thus all the worlds as well, their minds filled with devotion for the Perfectly Awakened One,
have come to drink the nectar of the greatness of the qualities of the Three Jewels.
There, all those worlds, beginning with Brahmā, approached;
beholding that Lord of Munis, they bowed down and stood before him.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite and having prostrated in due order,
he circumambulated [the deity] three times with joy, his hands joined in the añjali gesture.
Turning all around to drink that nectar of his true Dharma, they approached him,
placing him at their head, with focused minds, gazing upon him.
There, having seen that they had all taken refuge,
the Blessed One then entered the meditative absorption named "The Purification of All."
At that moment, radiant rays of light arrived there, illuminating all directions and shining forth.
Then, in that monastery touched by those rays,
all the pillars everywhere were beautifully adorned, consisting of gold and jewels.
And all the gabled pavilions were adorned with gold and jewels;
all the doors there were made of gold and silver.
All the stairs were made of gold and silver,
and all the windows were made of gold and precious gems.
All the doors were made of silver and jewels,
and likewise all the walls shone, being composed of gold and jewels.
The panels were made of gold and adorned with jewels;
all the railings there were likewise embellished with gold and precious gems.
All the archways as well were made of gold and jewels;
likewise, all the palaces were adorned with gold and precious gems.
All the grounds, too, shone forth— resembling lapis lazuli, level, pure, and soft.
Thus, the monastery in that Jātaka Grove,
adorned with the splendor of divine gold and jewels, shone forth beautifully.
And outside, all around the monastery in the Jeta Grove,
wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) have arisen, bestowing happiness upon all who seek it.
Rich with trunks and branches of gold, covered with leaves of silver,
and beautifully adorned with hanging divine garments and other ornaments.
They were hung with brilliantly shining, noble, and beautiful garlands of jewels;
they were hung with necklaces of pearls and other gems, as well as all kinds of ornaments.
And many flowering trees arose on all sides,
bearing clusters of flowers whose divine fragrances and scents were pervasive.
And many fruit trees have sprung up on all sides,
bearing fruits that are heavy with divine nectar-like flavor and are most wholesome.
And all medicinal herbs, endowed with taste, potency, and quality,
appeared everywhere as destroyers of all diseases.
And many beautiful lotus ponds, filled with pure water and abundant with flowers such as lotuses and water lilies, appeared.
In this way, all things there became adorned with excellence, prosperous with glory, and entirely serene on every side.
Thus, at that time, there proceeds a great enthusiasm, endowed with the qualities of the dharma of the bliss of great joy, which gladdens the minds of all sentient beings.
Having seen this great marvel, all the worlds, including the gods and others,
stood with their faces upturned, gazing on with hearts overcome by wonder.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, who possesses right-mindedness, seeing them, was filled with wonder.
Seeing all those seated in the assembly with minds agitated by wonder,
he gazed at that lord of sages and stood there, reflecting on its cause.
Then that Blessed One, the Teacher, being composed in meditation, sought to fully understand that great and wondrous cause which affected all the worlds, including even the asuras.
Having gone there and seen [it], he composed himself; then, having emerged from that meditative absorption,
he desired to teach the cause of that great wonder.
Then, having observed that, the wise Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, the son of the Conqueror, being accomplished, looked intently.
Rising up and approaching, resting his knees upon the surface of the ground,
wearing his upper robe over one shoulder, he joyfully joined his palms in reverence.
Beholding that Lord of the World, the Teacher, the Guru of the three worlds,
the Omniscient One, the Mass of Glory, he bowed and made this request with great devotion:
O Blessed One, I have attained supreme wonder upon beholding this:
from where have these rays of sublime merit come together here?
By whose meritorious self was this great domain of the True Dharma produced,
such power as this as we have never before seen?
Therefore, may your lordship— the Teacher of the Triple Elephant, the Omniscient Blessed One, the Victor—
having instructed us in this matter, deign to enlighten us.
Thus entreated, the Blessed One, the Victor and Lord of Dharma,
looked upon Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin and spoke to him.
He who is the glorious Āryāvalokiteśvara, possessed of the great superknowledges,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the sovereign lord of all the worlds.
Having received the command of the Victorious One Amitābha, he, whose nature is compassion,
has come to deliver the sentient beings of the world-realm Sukhāvatī.
Having now beheld the beings being tormented there in the Avīci hell, he has come, extending his hands, to deliver them.
That light, having touched everyone there in that hell, made them all endowed with happiness;
then, having uplifted them and illuminated everything on all sides, it departed.
These radiances have come here; they are the offspring of that Lokeśvara.
Thus this Great Being, possessing a vast abundance of merit,
has come even here to deliver sentient beings who are sinful.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, the wise Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, a son of the Sugata, was filled with wonder.
Having gazed upon that Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, with curiosity,
he spoke thus in order to inquire about the merit and majesty of Lokeśa:
"Blessed One, in the Avīci hell there is a great fire that is perpetually blazing;
because its flames are so immense, no interval between them can be discerned."
How then does that Great Being, the Lord of the World, endowed with compassion and the Teacher of the World, enter therein to deliver sentient beings?
Where the ground at the edge of the wall was made of iron,
there was a great pit of fire filled with blazing flames.
In that place stands a great cauldron filled with oil;
therein dwell wicked beings, most sinful and devoted to evil deeds,
immeasurable and innumerable, boiling day and night.
At the end of the day, those harsh creatures stand with their limbs shattered and exhausted.
Thus those wicked beings, afflicted by unbearable sensations,
remain tormented, experiencing the consequences of their own misdeeds.
Even there, how could that Great Being, the Lord of the World and Son of the Victor,
having entered, lift them up and send them elsewhere?
O Blessed One, Teacher of all things, having instructed us in all this in great detail, you should now awaken us further.
When that wise Bodhisattva had thus made his request,
the Blessed One, looking toward that Mahāsattva, spoke as follows.
Excellent! Listen attentively, O Great Being, if you so desire;
for the benefit of the world, I shall proclaim the majesty of the supernatural power of Lokeśvara.
For example, it is like a sovereign king, a universal monarch, a lord of men,
who is endowed with great royal power, prosperity, and great energy.
In the spring season, when all things were adorned with flowers,
he entered the delightful and magnificent great garden, filled with joy, in order to sport.
Likewise, that Lord of the Three Worlds, endowed with the splendor of the power of merit,
beholding that Avīci hell, enters it while illuminating it.
In his body there is no change whatsoever;
there is only bliss, great joy, great enthusiasm, and exultation.
When that Lord of the Three Worlds emits rays from his own body, he moves through the Avīci hell, illuminating it completely.
Then, at the outset, the Avīci hell, filled with great flames of fire,
becomes cool, full of great bliss, and a body of happiness in an instant.
Then, seeing this, the guardians of Yama, their minds agitated by agitation, became despondent, wondering, "What inauspicious omen has arisen here?"
"Which great hero among the gods, or which Daitya, has arrived here?
Having said this, they moved about everywhere to look for him.
There he beheld him seated, possessing a divine form and great radiance,
with a gentle appearance and beautiful limbs, adorned with celestial ornaments.
Adorned with a magnificent crest-jewel and graced by a crown of matted locks,
they behold him and stand there filled with wonder.
Then that Lord of All Protectors, Lokeśvara, the son of the Victorious One,
enters while looking about and illuminating [the place] with his pure splendors.
When that Bodhisattva, the Lord of the World, had entered there,
then a radiant great lotus appeared there.
There he remains, taking refuge upon that [lotus] made of the seven precious gems;
then the cauldron bursts asunder and that fire is extinguished.
There, in the midst of that pit of fire, a lake appeared;
then those sinful beings, through the touch of its rays, found refuge.
With the suffering of their sensations gone and endowed with great bliss,
they— filled with wonder and with minds perfectly serene— behold that Lord.
Having observed him, they approached suddenly with palms joined in reverence; having bowed at his lotus feet with joy and praised him, they worshipped him with devotion.
Then all those beings, having completely abandoned their transgressions,
with purified limbs and stainless souls, proceed to Sukhāvatī.
And they shall all gather together in Sukhāvatī, filled with joy,
forever having gone for refuge to Amitābha, the Lord of Munis.
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, they move about for the welfare of the world.
Then all those guardians of hell,
their minds agitated upon seeing that great marvel, were overwhelmed by astonishment and fear;
seizing their respective weapons, they fled swiftly from there.
Then, having gone quickly into the presence of Yama, the King of Death, they bowed down and reported this event in full detail.
Having heard what was reported by them, King Yama was greatly amazed;
summoning them before him, he questioned them with great respect.
"Why have you all come here with such distressed minds? From where has this fear arisen, and why have you been driven away?"
If you have devotion toward me, you ought to recount this entire account to me again and again in detail.
When King Yama had spoken thus, all those servants of Yama bowed down to King Yama and reported [the matter] in detail.
"Indeed, Your Majesty, you yourself are the Lord of the World; therefore, please understand that a great calamity has arisen there in Avīci, which is now being described."
First, a fragrant and cool breeze blows upon him;
thereafter, delightful splendors arrive and illuminate him.
Touched by its radiance, even that fire of the Avīci hell is extinguished;
consequently, the cauldron bursts open, shatters into pieces, and is ground to dust.
There too, in the midst of the pit of fire, a lake appeared;
then, within it, the Great Being was present, able to assume any form at will and exceedingly beautiful.
Of auspicious form and pure essence, adorned with a crown of matted locks, glorious, possessed of great supernatural power, steadfast, and embellished with divine ornaments.
Possessing the auspicious portions of compassion and mercy, radiant as the cool-rayed moon,
he enters [the world], illuminating it and beholding sentient beings who are sinful.
Then, at that place, a great lotus, radiant with the seven precious gems,
appeared; resting upon it, he remains, illuminating all.
Beholding him seated there, those sinners were filled with wonder;
approaching and seeking refuge, they honored him with great respect.
Then all those beings, with purified bodies and filled with joy, prostrate themselves at his lotus feet; having done so, they all pass away from there.
Thus this hell, Avīci, has been utterly destroyed;
therefore, O Lord, having observed this, you ought to deliberate upon it.
Having heard what was reported by them, King Yama was struck with wonder;
saying, "What is this marvelous thing that has occurred? he reflected thus.
"Who is this god who has arrived, possessing such a form and great supernatural power— is it Maheśvara, or Viṣṇu, or Brahmā, or the Lord of the Thirty-three?"
He was like a great submarine fire rising at the time of universal dissolution,
or like a Gandharva, or a lord of the gods, or a Kinnara, or even a Rākṣasa.
Has a great wind arisen, possessing extreme power and prowess? Or is it a yakṣa, a being of great strength, that Vajrapāṇi, the king of the Guhyakas?
The great hero Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, who vies with me;
or the great hero, the lord of Yakṣas, the king of kings, or anyone else.
Or is it Rudra, the Lord of Beings, the Sovereign, the Master of the Pramathas?
O Hero, Lord of the World, who else possesses such an abundance of power as this?
And for all of these as well, she possesses the power of great heroism.
Indeed, such power and majesty of heroic strength is not seen in anyone at all.
Or perhaps, O lord of men, he is some ascetic or even a seer,
endowed with great heroism and supernatural power through the strength of his perfected austerities.
Devoted to which god or which goddess, what accomplished practitioner,
having obtained a boon, has come here to even conquer me?
Where else is there another man of such great heroism to be found who would be able to extinguish the blazing fire of the Avīci hell?
A being such as this, of great majesty and endowed with the abundance of vast merit,
is not seen anywhere at all, even throughout the worlds of the three realms.
Having reflected thus, King Yama was terrified and greatly amazed;
with his divine eye, he beheld him there in the Avīci hell.
There, he is seated upon a noble lotus throne made of jewels;
he is divine, exceedingly beautiful, lovely, and adorned with celestial ornaments.
He possesses the physical form of Samantabhadra, adorned with matted locks, a crest-jewel, and a diadem;
he shines with gentle radiance, being auspicious and the locus of meritorious qualities.
Having beheld that glorious one, the Lord of the World, the son of the Jina,
and recognizing him as a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, he was filled with joy.
King Yama, rising suddenly and hurrying there, approached him;
having arrived, he bowed with palms joined and praised that son of the Jina in this way:
Homage to you, the Bodhisattva, the Mahāsattva, the Protector;
to the noble Avalokiteśvara, the Great Lord, the one of sublime glory.
Homage to you whose limbs are adorned with the glory of the lotus, who bestow the boon of the True Dharma;
homage to you, the founder of the lineage, who brings about the vision of the world.
And to the one who always bestows the boon of consolation upon the world,
who possesses hundreds of thousands of hands, and who has millions of auspicious marks.
Homage to you, whose forms are infinite and beyond number, who possesses every form;
homage to you, the primordial Lord, whose form is the self of all beings.
And to him whose face is the moon reaching as far as the mouth of the submarine fire, who conforms to all phenomena, who loves the Dharma, and who is the perfected one; to him, [I bow].
To the one who effects the great liberation of all sentient beings from suffering; to the one who provides consolation to creatures such as fish and aquatic beings;
to the one whose head is the supreme mass of wisdom; to the one who bestows the beloved fruits of the Dharma.
To him whose limbs are adorned with jewel-glory, and who bestows the glory of excellent virtues.
To the one who causes the drying up of all the realms of hell,
to the one who radiates the glory of wisdom, and to the one who bestows the fortune of wisdom.
To him who is fully honored by the worlds together with the gods and the lords of the asuras,
who is saluted with devotion, and who is worshipped— to him, let there be constant homage.
To the one who has bestowed the gift of fearlessness and who teaches the perfections.
To the one radiant with the light of the sun, and to the one who kindles the lamp of the Dharma.
To the one who possesses the forms of desire, who has the beautiful form of a gandharva, who is perfectly beautiful,
who is mounted upon the golden mountain, and who bears the yoga of the ultimate truth.
To him whose nature is as profound as the ocean, who reveals himself face-to-face,
who has attained all meditative concentrations, and who brings about his own supreme delight.
To him whose body is adorned with sacred knowledge, who possesses the form of the bull among sages,
and who effects the liberation of those bound by the fetters of execution;
To the one whose form is the means for all beings, who has fully accumulated the causes,
who is enriched by a vast retinue, and who possesses the form of the wish-fulfilling gem.
And to the one who bestows the vision of traversing the path to nirvāṇa,
and who causes the drying up of the abodes of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and others;
To the one who has become a parasol for the worlds of those dwelling in the three realms,
and who effects the complete liberation of all those afflicted by mental anguish and physical disease.
To the one who wears the serpent-king Nanda and Upananda as a sacred thread.
And for the manifestation of the form of the glorious Amoghapāśa,
who has attained mastery over the qualities of all mantras and possesses true virtues.
And to the one who causes the great yakṣa Vajrapāṇi to flee,
who assumes a terrifying form for the sake of the wicked beings of the three worlds.
To the one who causes fear to spirits, vetālas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, and the like;
to the one with beautiful eyes like blue lotuses, whose intellect is profound and steady.
To the sovereign lord of all vidyās, to the remover of all afflictions,
and to him who has accumulated the path to the perfect awakening of the manifold dharmas.
To him who has ascended the path to liberation, who upholds the powerful Dharma,
and who has accumulated the true mind of perfect awakening and the excellent path;
And salutations to those who bestow liberation from the afflictions of miserable rebirths such as the hungry ghosts, and who maintain concentrations as numerous as the atoms of the universe.
Homage to you, the Lord of the World, to you, the Bodhisattva at all times,
the Mahāsattva who bestows the perfection of the qualities of the True Dharma.
I bow to you, O Teacher of the World, always seeking refuge;
I worship you constantly with devotion—be gracious, O Lord of the World!
May my transgressions be forgiven, whatever wrong I may have committed;
from this day forth, O Teacher, may I always remain one who has taken refuge in you.
Bearing your command upon my head, I shall act for the welfare of the world;
I will do exactly as you direct me here.
Therefore, O Lord of the World, having looked upon me with favor, may you be gracious;
I shall perform whatever task is desired by you in this world.
Having thus praised him and offered his prayers with joy, that King of Dharma,
bowing again with palms joined in reverence, stands once more before him.
Then that Lord of the World, looking upon that King of Dharma,
respectfully instructed him to apply himself to the path of perfect enlightenment.
O Yama, you are the King of Dharma and the instructor of all worlds;
therefore, having gladdened sentient beings with those very riches, instruct them in the Dharma.
And even those living beings who are wicked, most sinful, and evil-minded—
having established them in the Dharma and awakened them through diligent effort— [he leads them to liberation].
And those who, with faith and devotion, have gone for refuge to the Three Jewels,
always and constantly worship them, desiring the dharma of perfect enlightenment.
Having observed all of them, you must always protect them.
Having awakened them and having observed them, they should always be protected.
Having awakened them all and having caused them to practice the auspicious vow,
and having established them on the path to enlightenment, they should be sent to Sukhāvatī.
And as for those who are sinful and wicked, you too should diligently awaken them by observing them, and always cause them to practice what is auspicious.
Having heard these words of mine, if you desire perfect enlightenment, then,
having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, proceed for the welfare of the world.
If you act thus in the world, practicing the dharma of compassion,
then your title "Dharmarāja" (King of Dharma) will become truly meaningful and fruitful.
Having heard this instruction from that Lord of the World, Dharmarāja understood it, saying, "So be it."
Then that King of Dharma, having beheld that Lord of the World, the son of the Jina,
bowed with palms joined in reverence and departed for his own abode.
Then that Lord of the World, overwhelmed with compassion,
set out once more to wander elsewhere in order to deliver sentient beings.
Thus ends the chapter on the drying up of the Avīci hell and the awakening of the King of Dharma.
3. The Chapter on the Deliverance of the Pretas from the Mountain with Needle-Mouth and Needle-Belly.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, the son of the Sugata, the Bodhisattva, beholding that Lord of Munis, spoke as follows:
O Blessed One, when will that Lord of the World, the Son of the Victor, the Bodhisattva Śāstṛ, come here? It would be fitting for you to instruct him on this matter.
Having heard what was thus spoken, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
looked upon the Bodhisattva and instructed him once more as follows.
O son of noble family, that glorious Great Being, wandering from there, goes to the abode of the pretas in order to deliver them from the world of pretas.
Having gone there to the abode of the pretas and seeing the pretas from afar,
he emitted cool rays and entered, illuminating them.
Her rays, shining brightly, illuminating everything on all sides,
make that entire realm of pretas endowed with coolness.
Then all those female spirits, endowed with cool rays,
stood there filled with wonder, reflecting, "What is this?"
When that Lord of the World entered there, illuminating all,
then the thunderbolt-storms on the earth were completely pacified on every side.
Beholding that marvel, the gatekeeper was struck with wonder;
looking about with bloodshot eyes, he reflected, "What is this?"
Rising up suddenly, he seized the great poison Kālakūṭa;
grasping a slingshot, a bow, and arrows, he trembled with rage.
There, beholding him seated upon that jewel-lotus, radiant with cool rays, even he, though possessed of a most fierce mind, was filled with wonder.
Touched by those rays, he attained a mind of compassion;
reflecting upon the karma that was the cause of his own suffering, he thought thus:
Fie on me, who, being so passionately attached to such a sinful means and wicked deed,
acts out evil deeds while serving as a gatekeeper here!
"Even for me, who protects such work, no auspiciousness shall come;
surely this is the great fruit of sin that has always been yours."
"How can such an action be right, when it is a cause for nothing but suffering?
Therefore, I shall not remain here; having said this, I will even go home."
Having reflected thus, that gatekeeper, overcome with great compassion,
bowed down before the Great Being and then departed from there.
There, seeing him approaching, radiant as the moon, all the female spirits ran swiftly toward him.
Having come before you, tormented by the fires of hunger and thirst,
they indeed stand surrounding you, begging for water.
Seeing those needle-mouthed goats and sheep, which were clinging to burnt pillars like skeletons held together by a mechanical frame, the Great Being was deeply moved.
Covered with their own hair and body-hair, emaciated in limb and distorted in face,
they are consumed by the fires of hunger and thirst, feeding upon feces, urine, and phlegm.
Beholding all such sinful and wicked pretas,
his soul overcome with extreme compassion, he offers water from his lotus-hand to them.
Even after drinking that water, all those deceased spirits were not satisfied;
desiring to drink even more, they stood before him.
Seeing that they were still unsatisfied, the Lord of the World, overcome with great compassion,
caused rivers to flow forth even from his ten fingers.
Beholding those flowing streams, all those hungry ghosts joyfully drank as much as they desired, yet they did not attain satisfaction at all.
Desiring to drink once more, they all approached him;
yet, beholding him in such a state, they wandered about, afflicted by thirst.
Seeing them wandering about, that Lord of the World, filled with great compassion,
caused other [fingers] to emerge even from his ten toes.
And seeing those great rivers, all those hungry ghosts approached with joy and drank, yet they did not attain satisfaction at all.
Seeing them thus distressed, that Lord of the World, filled with great compassion,
causes rivers to flow forth from all his pores.
And seeing them, all those preta-s, afflicted by thirst, suddenly approached and drank as much as they desired.
When all those hungry ghosts drink that water, which resembles nectar and is endowed with the eight excellent qualities, they drink it with delight and joy.
Then all of them, with their bodies restored, their throats wide,
and their faculties fully nourished, become satisfied and filled with joy.
Then that Great Being, seeing that they were satisfied with water, being compassionate by nature, desired once again to satisfy them.
There, that ocean of compassion, having raised clouds on all sides,
pours down a continuous rain of exquisite, delicious food.
Seeing those divine, delicious foods raining down from all sides,
all those female spirits were filled with wonder and joy.
Having observed this, they took [the food] at their own will and enjoyed it as they pleased;
thereafter, all those beings were satisfied by that food.
Then they were all satiated with foods and drinks comparable to nectar, and were filled with great bliss, happiness, and energy.

Then, being happy and speaking of the qualities of the true Dharma, they all, with completely pure intentions, speak thus after having reflected: (Gkv 30) "At that time, being happy and speaking of the virtues of the true Dharma, they all, with perfectly pure dispositions, speak even as follows after having reflected:"
Oh, how happy are those people of Jambudvīpa who,
having taken refuge in the cool shade, remain meditating upon the True Guru!
Happy are those people who, having always performed service for their mother and father according to their comfort, attend upon them with devotion.
Happy are those people who have drawn near to a true friend;
having always heard well-spoken words, they always practice what is virtuous.
Happy are those great beings who practice the vow of perfect enlightenment;
having brought about the welfare of all sentient beings, they always proceed in what is auspicious.
Blessed are those fortunate ones who, possessing excellent conduct and seeking what is auspicious,
observe the Poṣadha vow for the sake of benefiting both themselves and others.
Those noble beings of great fortune who attend upon the Saṅgha are always those who strike the gong of the Dharma at the proper time.
Those who, having established a monastery, have gone for refuge to the Three Jewels and practice while observing the vows of a lay follower— they too are partakers [of the merit].
Blessed are those great beings who, having repaired and re-established a dilapidated monastery, make it beautifully adorned;
and those who [repair] previous stūpas and images that have become shattered and cracked.
Having consecrated and established it, those fortunate ones partake of it.
Those who, having honored the preachers of the true Dharma,
attend upon them and listen to their well-spoken words, are fortunate and endowed with happiness.
Those who behold the various miracles of the Buddhas,
and those who behold their walking-places— all of them are likewise partakers [of the merit].
And those who behold the various miraculous transformations of the supernatural powers of the Pratyekabuddhas, as well as their walking meditations— they too are all possessed of great merit.
Those who behold the miracles and the walking-meditations of the Arhats are themselves fortunate and established in happiness, even as they move within the phenomena of saṃsāra.
And those who behold even the walking-places of the Bodhisattvas, as well as their miraculous displays— they too are fortunate and highly blessed.
Those who, having gone for refuge to the Buddha, always remember and honor him,
are indeed fortunate and blessed, attaining the qualities of the True Dharma.
And those who hear the true Dharma, honor it, and cause it to be heard— they too are all highly fortunate, partakers in the nature of perfect enlightenment.
Those who, having gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, honor and serve it, are all fortunate and blessed, and shall attain perfect awakening.
And those who, having given gifts and protected their possessions,
perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, they are the truly fortunate ones.
Those who have desisted from evil, whose three spheres are completely purified,
and who practice the eightfold vow— they are auspicious ones of noble cultivation.
And those who, having maintained the vow of patience, always possess a perfectly serene intention and act for the benefit of all sentient beings— they are the ones of sublime cultivation.
And those great beings who, while accomplishing the jewels of the true Dharma for the welfare of the world, always perform deeds for the benefit of the world; they are truly great people.
And those great beings who have reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge,
having performed auspicious deeds for the sake of sentient beings, they are truly fortunate.
And those who, with faith, have gone for refuge in the teaching of the Buddha and,
having undertaken the vows of renunciation, practice them, they become perfectly stainless.
And those who, with concentrated minds, constantly purify the Buddhist hermitage,
they possess limbs that are most beautiful and auspicious, and are endowed with the happiness of the True Dharma.
And those who are always affectionate toward one another and, having acted for each other's benefit, accomplish fame and dharma— they are fortunate and of noble character.
Those who always practice what is auspicious, having desisted from the ten evils, are blessed, pure-souled, and attainers of the happiness of true virtues.
Those who practice austerity in the forest, having renounced all possessions,
are truly auspicious and pure-souled, always treading the path of the virtuous.
Those who, having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, practice for the welfare of the world,
are great beings, men who shall attain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having addressed him in this way, they were all filled with joy;
bowing down to that Great Being, they made this request with great reverence.
O virtuous one, you are indeed our protector, refuge, master, friend, and lord;
there is truly no one else who thus bears the welfare and protection of those to be guarded.
Since you yourself, having perceived us sinners in great distress,
have come and protected us by satisfying us with the enjoyments of immortality.
Therefore, we have always gone for refuge to you alone;
now we desire to provide service with respectful offerings.
Therefore, you ought to join us in accomplishing our welfare;
whatever has been commanded by you, we shall certainly carry it out.
Having heard this prayer made by them all, that Lord of the World,
looking upon them with a compassionate gaze, commanded them once again.
Listen to that which has been declared by me for the sake of accomplishing your welfare;
practice it accordingly at all times, if you desire constant well-being.
Thus, first of all, go for refuge with joy to the Three Jewels;
always remembering them in your mind, honor them with deep respect.
Homage to the Buddha, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha—homage, homage!
Having thus paid homage to these three, go forth everywhere.
By the power of this merit, may there be auspiciousness everywhere;
may there always certainly be freedom from calamity and great enthusiasm.
Then, having gradually purified the three spheres and fully accomplished the thought of awakening, you shall desire to practice the vow.
By virtue of this merit, all of you, having passed away from here while maintaining mindfulness of the Three Jewels, shall go to Sukhāvatī.
There, having come for refuge to the Lord Amitābha and performing worship at all times, you shall practice great bliss.
Then, having gathered together and duly observed the supreme vow of the Poṣadha, you shall obtain right-mindedness through these merits.
Then, with pure souls and eager for the welfare of all sentient beings,
you shall uphold the vow of the conduct of awakening and practice for the benefit of the world.
Then, having fulfilled all the perfections in their proper sequence and having conquered all the hosts of wicked Māras, you shall become Arhats.
Then, free from desire for wandering through saṃsāra and having conquered the senses,
you will attain the threefold enlightenment and reach the state of nirvāṇa.
In this way, O beings, always going for refuge to the Three Jewels,
remember their names, recite them, and having bowed, devote yourselves to them until there is no further becoming.
Having heard this command from Lokeśvara,
they all replied, "So be it," and, filled with joy, rejoiced.
Then Lokeśvara, perceiving the purity of their minds, caused the well-spoken discourse of the *Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra* to be uttered.
Having heard those well-spoken words, they were all filled with joy;
they desired to accomplish the happiness born from the zeal of honoring the Three Jewels.
Then, all of them, filled with joy, went for refuge to the Three Jewels;
they cried out, "Homage to the Buddha, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha!"
Then all those beings, intent on the mindfulness of the Jewel of the Teacher,
become weary of the exertion of saṃsāra and long for the Dharma.
Then, having shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity with the sword of wisdom and cast off the body, they all proceed from there to Sukhāvatī.
There, having come for refuge to the Lord Amitābha and receiving his instruction upon their heads, they proceed joyfully toward what is auspicious.
Then they shall all become Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who abide in the four Brahma-vihāras and whose speech is directed toward their desired goal.
In this way, that Great Being, Lokeśvara, the son of the Victor,
having delivered all the pretas, sends them to Sukhāvatī.
Thus, this Lord of the Three Worlds, the accomplished one of great compassion,
having personally beheld the world with pity and protected it, causes it to enter [the path].
Whichever beings, having constantly remembered the name of that great-souled Lokeśvara and uttered it, worship him, having gone for refuge;
All of them, being free from evil, illustrious, and mines of excellent virtues,
always conduct themselves in what is auspicious, having performed what is beneficial for all sentient beings.
Having observed the vow of the conduct of awakening and enjoyed the happiness of the fame of the Dharma,
and having maintained enthusiasm for honoring the Three Jewels, may they go to Sukhāvatī.
None of them ever go to an evil rebirth;
always born in fortunate realms, they are the locus of auspicious glory and excellent virtues.
Those steadfast ones with purified faculties, who uphold the vow of the conduct of awakening,
shall go at the end to the abode of the Victors, having accomplished the welfare of both themselves and others.
Thus, that Great Being, who bears the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings,
is an ocean of the greatness of the qualities of compassion, pity, and the true Dharma.
Indeed, the immeasurable majesty of the merit of that Lord of the World cannot be measured even by all the lords of sages.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, that son of the Sugata,
the wise Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, spoke as follows:
"Blessed One, that Great Being does not come; when will he go?
I wish to behold him, the Lord of the Three Worlds."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
looked at Vikambhin and again instructed him in this way.
In this way, that Lord of the World (Lokeśvara), awakening those sons of noble family and sending them to Sukhāvatī, then departs from there.
Elsewhere as well, beholding with his eyes of compassion those sinners dwelling in hell so that he might deliver them, he moved along, illuminating everything.
Day after day, he would come and, illuminating them, behold all the wicked sinners submerged even within the various hells.
Having personally delivered all of them and brought them to happiness, awakening them and establishing them on the path to enlightenment, he shall send them forth to Sukhāvatī.
Thus ends the chapter on the deliverance of the hungry ghosts from the Sūcīmukhodara mountain in the glorious Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha.
4. The Chapter on the Manifestation of the Deities such as Śrī Maheśvara.
The Blessed One said: "In this way, that Mahāsattva Lokeśvara, the son of the Jina..."
Having personally rescued the world from the ocean of existence, he always protects it;
even those who are corrupt and most sinful, he diligently awakens,
establishes them on the path to enlightenment, and sends them to the abode of the Victors.
There is no being endowed with such qualities even within the three realms;
indeed, no one possesses such eloquence.
And among all the lords of sages, there is no such swift brilliance;
therefore, he is called by the name Bodhisattva Lokeśvara.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, Viṣkambhin, that son of the Sugata,
looked at the Blessed One and spoke as follows.
O Blessed One, by what cause is he called the Lord of All Worlds, the Sovereign, and the Lord of the World? Please explain this correctly.
How indeed could it be that even for all the Lords of Munis, that very thing which appears as such does not exist at all?
O All-Knowing One, explain this correctly; I wish to hear it, for all these members of the assembly are seated here with their minds intent on hearing its qualities.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
looked toward the highly wise Viṣkambhin and commanded him as follows.
Listen, noble son, to the power of this Lokeśvara;
out of affection for you, I shall fully proclaim it for the sake of awakening all sentient beings.
In the past, there was a Teacher, a Tathāgata, the Lord of Sages;
he was the Perfectly Awakened One named Vipaśyin, the Victor and sovereign of all sciences.
The omniscient one, the Arhat, the possessor of great super-knowledges, the King of Dharma, the Guide, the Blessed One,
the Lord of the World, who bears the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings.
At that time, noble sons, I was a merchant’s son named Sugandhasukhasaṃjñaka; I was as vigorous as a bull and yearned for the qualities of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having taken refuge in that teacher Vipaśyin, the perfectly awakened one and master of the world, they practiced the vow of awakening.
At that time, I heard the majesty of the qualities of Lokeśvara being fully proclaimed by that Lord of Sages, the omniscient Vipaśyin.
Just as that Teacher of the World, the Blessed One, the Victorious Vipaśyin,
sat down in the midst of the assembly to fully teach the True Dharma.
Then that Lord of the Three Worlds, the Sovereign of the World and Son of the Victorious One,
filled with compassion, beheld all sentient beings in order to deliver them.
Emitting rays of merit that illuminate all directions,
he gazes upon all sentient beings dwelling in the hells who are suffering.
Having rescued them with effort, having awakened them, and rejoicing in their merit;
having established them in taking refuge in the Three Jewels, and having caused them to practice the auspicious Dharma.
Having established them on the path to enlightenment and caused them to hear well-spoken words, he enjoined them to the Dharma that accomplishes perfect awakening, thereby bringing them relief.
Having performed auspicious rites everywhere, he conducted a great festival free from calamity,
proclaiming the majesty of the qualities of the Three Jewels.
Then, touched by those rays, the entire earth became beautifully adorned,
filled with pure auspiciousness, enthusiasm, and happiness.
Having observed that wondrous, great bliss, and great enthusiasm on all sides,
the Great Being, the wise son of the Conqueror, [reflected].
Overwhelmed with wonder, they reflected thus within themselves.
Aha! Whose radiant splendor is this that has arrived here, illuminating the entire world and purifying it with its beauty?
With his mind thus agitated by these thoughts, that Bodhisattva Mahāmati rose up, adjusted his upper robe over one shoulder, and went before him.
Placing his knees upon the ground and with palms joined in reverence, he joyfully bowed to Vipaśyin,
the Lord of Sages, and questioned him thus:
"Blessed One, whose power is this by which this radiance has arrived, illuminating the entire world, purifying it, and making it beautiful?"
Having seen this great marvel, everyone is utterly amazed; O Omniscient One, they wish to hear it—You ought to explain it.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, Vipaśyin, the Lord of Sages,
looked upon that Mahāmati Mahāsattva and instructed him as follows.
Mahāmati, listen now to this marvelous account of its origin;
I shall presently describe the power of its merit.
