I shall explain it fully to you, and having heard it, rejoice in it.
Whatever golden ground exists here in Jambudvīpa, in that [ground] dwell the Apramāṇābhas beings with their faces turned downwards.
Seeing all those sinful and wicked beings, that son of the Sugata,
Lokeśvara, has come here to rescue them and lead them to Sukhāvatī.
For the sake of purifying their sins, that treasury of compassion emits rays of merit, illuminating the worlds of living beings, and goes there.
Touched by its radiance, they were all endowed with sublime happiness;
wondering "What is this?", they remained with their minds filled with amazement.
Then, there, that Lord of the World, manifesting in the form of a rishi,
approached those beings who were all facing downward, looking upon them; and they, beholding that rishi approaching and radiating light, [were moved].
All those beings, though previously facing downward, now approach him face-to-face;
there, all those beings, having bowed with joy to that Sage, [remain].
Having established him upon the seat of faith, they entreated him with such reverence:
"O Great Sage, that you have come here is due to the power of our good fortune."
Therefore, out of compassion, you ought to tell us our destiny:
what terrible sin was committed by us in the past?
Because of which we have all become like this here, with our faces turned downward.
Having heard their request and having looked upon them— all those beings with their heads bowed— that great seer instructed them, awakening them to the truth.
Listen to how the deed was performed by you in the past;
I shall explain it here, and having heard it, let it be understood.
In the past, those who, casting aside the three ends [of existence], were intoxicated by pride, envy, and conceit, moved about with downcast faces, claiming that [the Buddha] was invisible.
Therefore, by the turn of fate, all of you now dwell here with faces cast downwards,
having experienced various sufferings.
Therefore, having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels with faith,
you should meditate upon them, recollect them, and invoke even their names, honoring them with devotion.
Having observed the poṣadha and the vows, and having practiced the four divine abodes,
always conduct yourselves in what is auspicious for the benefit of both yourselves and others.
Therefore, having always maintained the vow of enlightenment with the mind of awakening,
proceed for the welfare of the world through your zeal in honoring the Three Jewels.
Then, being free from stain, with the three spheres completely purified,
and devoid of afflictions, you shall attain awakening and obtain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Having heard what was thus commanded by him, they all, filled with joy,
bowed again at his feet and, standing before him, spoke as follows:
You are the Lord in the world of beings, the source of the bliss of the true Dharma;
therefore, comfort us who are blind and practitioners of evil.
For those whose vision is overwhelmed by darkness, who wander upon lost paths, who are without a protector, who are enemies to themselves, who are wretched, and whose minds are deluded.
For those who are devoid of protection and refuge, who are dull-witted, and who partake in suffering—
having fully kindled the lamp of Dharma, show them the path to nirvāṇa.
Having given [this], become a protector who possesses true happiness and prosperity, bearing auspicious wealth;
having given the means for acquiring merit, become a true friend endowed with right understanding.
Having provided the means for crossing over the miserable realms, be a refuge in the happy states of existence; having given the means for proceeding to those happy states, O Teacher, be our Guru.
Having warded off attachment to evil, be a protector who removes the afflictions;
having destroyed the torment of misconduct and the defilements, be a refuge for all beings.
Bestowing the zeal for accomplishing the true Dharma, be our guide;
bestowing the excellence of virtuous qualities and happiness, be our lord and good friend.
Having fully taught the True Dharma, lead us into excellent self-restraint;
having granted the means for achieving liberation, send us forth to nirvana.
Blessed and happy are those who, having always remained in refuge,
remember [the name], recite it aloud, and meditate upon it, honoring it at all times.
Such suffering as this shall never again come to you anywhere in the wandering of existence,
such as the suffering that we always experience here.
Those great beings are truly fortunate who always attend upon them and,
having heard the Dharma that is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end, indeed practice it.
We too, all of us, shall always remain in refuge to you;
having heard the Dharma, we desire to practice the auspicious vow.
Therefore, be gracious, O Great Sage; become our true guru.
Having fully taught the sublime Dharma, lead us into the excellent restraint.
Having heard this request made by them, that great seer, having addressed and looked upon all those who were thus propitiated, commanded as follows:
Listen with reverence, you who always desire what is auspicious;
for your benefit, I shall proclaim the means of awakening through the true Dharma.
Having thus instructed them and recited this well-spoken Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra,
he causes them to hear it and even joins them to the conduct of awakening.
Then all those city-dwellers, striving to accomplish the true Dharma,
paid homage to the Three Jewels and lived within the excellent vows.
Then those pure-souled ones, having purified the three spheres and undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, proceed for the welfare of the world.
All those great beings, the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power, become bringers of supreme happiness and are irreversible.
Thus the Lord of the Three Worlds, instructing them in the form of a rishi,
enjoins all of them to the conduct of awakening and causes them to practice it as well.
Having thus directed them all onto the path to enlightenment, that great seer then vanished and departed through the sky, blazing like a fire.
Seeing him situated in the sky, they were all utterly amazed; having prostrated, they moved about with great reverence, praising his virtues.
This auspicious and meritorious splendor of that Lord Lokeśvara,
having illuminated the world of living beings, has been extended even here.
Thus that Lord of the Three Worlds, Lokeśvara, the Son of the Victor,
having brought about the welfare of all sentient beings, moves everywhere.
Therefore, the lords of sages have declared that his mass of merit will be vast, most excellent, immeasurable, and incalculable, and so forth.
Having understood this, you should all always remember, meditate upon, and recite the name of this Lord of the World with devotion; it is fitting that you do so.
Those who, having gone for refuge to him, always remember him, meditate upon him, and even by uttering his name, worship him with faith and joy; (Gkv 78)
They do not go to an evil rebirth, but are always born in a good destination;
having enjoyed the excellence of the qualities of the glory of the Dharma, they go to Sukhāvatī.
Having heard these instructions given by the Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū,
all those people gathered in the assembly, being thus enlightened, rejoiced.
Thus have I heard the supreme power of merit of the Lord of the World, as it was taught by Viśvabhū, the King of Sages.
Having thus understood the greatness of the merit of the true guru, the Lord of the World, those who desire awakening should take refuge in him and worship him.
Those who, having gone to him for refuge, always revere him with faith,
shall enjoy the bliss of the qualities of the True Dharma and go to Sukhāvatī.
Having gone there, [one shall obtain] the supreme nectar of the true Dharma of Amitābha.
Having drunk [it] and attained perfect enlightenment, they reached final, complete nirvāṇa at the end.
Having heard this instruction given by the Lord of Sages, Śrīghana,
all those people gathered in the assembly, being thus enlightened, rejoiced.
Thus concludes the section on uplifting sentient beings who are face-downward.
8. The Chapter on the Four-Legged Earth Made of Form for the Rescue of Men:
Then the Blessed One, the Teacher, Śākyamuni, the Lord, having looked upon Viṣkambhin, again instructed him in this way.
Listen, noble son, to the greatness of the qualities of the true Dharma of this World-Wanderer, the True Teacher; having heard it myself, I shall now speak of it.
Then Gaganagañja, having bowed down to the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū, questioned him once more in this way:
O Blessed One, where else would that Lord of the World, the Son of the Conqueror who possesses great supernormal knowledge, go in order to further deliver sentient beings?
Furthermore, I desire to hear that which he, while transmigrating elsewhere, [attained].
Seeing sentient beings, you uplift them and then direct them toward the Dharma; teach that!
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
looked toward Gaganagañja and again instructed him in this way.
Listen, noble son, to this Lokeśa, the Lord of the World;
I shall proclaim his greatness of virtuous qualities, if you desire to hear it.
Just as that Great Being, Lokeśvara, the son of the Victor,
proceeds from there to the stage consisting of form, illuminating it completely.
There, having beheld sentient beings, humans, and four-footed cattle,
that Lokeśvara, possessing a divine form, approached and stood before them.
Beholding that divine form, they were all filled with wonder; approaching him from the front and bowing down, they joyfully made this request:
Oh, what great fortune is ours that you are seen here!
Therefore, looking upon us with compassion, it behooves you to deliver us from this state.
Thus entreated by them, that compassionate Lord of the World addressed them all, looked upon them, and commanded as follows:
O Blessed Ones, having composed yourselves here, listen with respect;
I shall speak that which is a great accomplishment, the means for achieving the nirvāṇa of the Dharma.
Just as follows: having recollected and gone for refuge to that which is the best in the world—the Three Jewels who bring about auspiciousness—serve them always with reverence.
Those who have gone for refuge to them do not go to an evil destiny;
always born in a good destiny, they conduct themselves within the vow of awakening.
By the power of this merit, may all those supreme persons,
the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, thus proceed for the welfare of the world.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order and having accomplished the welfare of all sentient beings, they will go to Sukhāvatī.
Having gone there, seated in the assembly of Amitābha, the Conqueror of Indra,
they shall enjoy the nectar of the true Dharma and rejoice in great festivals.
Thus, having enjoyed happiness and auspicious festivals there for a very long time,
they will finally attain the threefold enlightenment and proceed to nirvana.
Thinking thus, and remaining in refuge through faith in the Three Jewels,
one should worship with devotion by recollecting, meditating upon, and even pronouncing their names.
Then, with your limbs anointed by this merit, you shall become Bodhisattvas— pure in intention, masters of the senses, free from afflictions, and of stainless nature.
Then, for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, having exerted yourselves in the vow of the conduct of awakening and having established goodness everywhere, you shall go to Sukhāvatī.
There, having always drunk the nectar of the Dharma from the Lord Amitābha,
you shall delight in the excellent vow through your enthusiasm for the auspiciousness of the True Dharma.
Thus, having enjoyed happiness there for a long time through auspicious and great festivals,
you will finally attain perfect awakening and reach complete nirvana.
Thinking thus, they have always gone for refuge to the Jewel of the Buddha;
by recollecting, meditating upon, and even uttering his name out of fear of existence.
Even having heard the majesty of the jewel of the Dharma, those who abide in the refuges should remember it,
contemplate it, and recite its name, honoring it with devotion.
And thus, having attended upon the jewels of the Saṅgha with offerings,
by recollecting, meditating upon, and even uttering their names, you have transcended both existence and non-existence.
This merit is renowned as great, incalculable, and most excellent;
it is declared to be immeasurable by all the lords of sages.
Thinking thus, having taken refuge in the Three Jewels,
by recollecting, meditating upon, and even uttering their names, they became objects of service.
By the power of this merit, you shall all become free from stain,
devoid of afflictions, and pure in soul, and you will go to Sukhāvatī.
Having gone there, having taken refuge in Amitābha, the Lord of Sages,
and always drinking the nectar of the Dharma, you shall rejoice in auspicious festivals.
Thus, having enjoyed there for a long time the happiness consisting of great bliss,
you will finally attain perfect awakening and proceed to complete nirvana.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, all those men, filled with joy,
replied "So be it," and being delighted, spoke as follows.
O noble one, you have become the guide to the true path for us who were blind;
you are the protection for those without protection, and the refuge for those seeking refuge.
He is the father and mother of the helpless, the beloved lord and friend; he is the refuge for those without refuge, and the friend who removes their misfortune.
You are a great lamp for those whose path has been lost in darkness;
you are the teacher and the proclaimer of the true Dharma for the foolish and the heedless.
Therefore, we all shall always remain in your refuge;
having received your command, we will certainly proceed in the auspicious Dharma.
Fortunate are those who have taken refuge in you, O Blessed One;
having honored the Three Jewels, they always proceed toward what is auspicious.
They shall never experience such suffering as this great hardship that we are undergoing in existence.
Therefore, out of compassion for us, you ought to remain in this world after imparting the true Dharma, which is the means for attaining the bliss of liberation.
Having heard what they thus requested, that omniscient Bodhisattva,
looking upon them all who were awakened, spoke to them in this way.
I cannot remain here forever, for I have many duties to attend to;
therefore, always act by maintaining what has been explained to you here.
Having spoken thus, he who possesses the great superknowledges (mahābhijñā) instructed them in the well-spoken *Kāraṇḍavyūha-sūtra*, the means for attaining perfect awakening.
Having heard this, which is the most excellent and supreme among all Mahāyāna sūtras, all those in the city, being enlightened, rejoice.
Then all those people, respectfully holding that thread and taking refuge in the Three Jewels, moved about joyfully in auspiciousness.
By the power of this merit, they all become pure-minded Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who lead a life of celibacy.
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening and acting for the welfare of the world,
they become engaged in the practice of the true Dharma and are irreversible.
Thus all those persons, with the three spheres completely purified,
move about in great bliss through their zeal for the welfare of themselves and others.
Thus that Lord of the Three Worlds, Lokeśvara, the Son of the Victor,
instructs and awakens all those men, establishing them in the Dharma.
Then, elsewhere in that world, that Lord of Beings, eager to deliver sentient beings,
vanished and traveled through the sky like a blazing fire.
Having performed this, a great mass of merit— immeasurable and incalculable— for that Lord of the World has been proclaimed by the Lords of Sages.
Thinking thus, they have always taken refuge in him;
by merely recollecting his name, uttering it, or even meditating upon him, they worship and attain the state beyond becoming.
Those who, having taken refuge in him, attend upon him with faith—
whether by recollecting him, meditating on him, or even by uttering his name— truly worship him.
They never go to an evil rebirth anywhere in any state of existence;
always born in a good rebirth, they become practitioners of the Dharma.
Having enjoyed the true happiness of the virtues of the glory of Dharma, they go to Sukhāvatī;
having gone there, they take refuge in the protection of Amitābha.
Constantly drinking the nectar of the Dharma, they are intent on the welfare of themselves and others;
with the enthusiasm born of the bliss of great joy, they rejoice at their ease.
Having enjoyed that very state for a very long time, they shall wander for the welfare of the world; and finally, having attained awakening, they shall reach the state of nirvana.
Having thus fully understood this truth, if you desire awakening, then always throughout existence worship Lokeśa, the possessor of great super-knowledges.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū,
Gaganagañja, the noble son of the ṛṣis, rejoiced with eager anticipation.
Thus has this been taught by Viśvabhū, and it has been heard by me;
you too should always worship him with devotion in that same manner.
You too, having likewise enjoyed such happiness and always delighting in virtue,
endowed with the qualities of the glory of enlightenment, shall go to the abode of the Victors.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Munis, Śrīghana,
all those people belonging to the Saṅgha were enlightened and rejoiced.
Thus ends the section on the extraction of the defects regarding the four pillars consisting of form.
9. The Chapter on Bali’s Address and Introduction to the Path of Enlightenment.
Then, having been thus congratulated, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin bowed once more to Śrīghana and made this request with great reverence:
“O Blessed One, I wish to hear once more about the greatness of the qualities of the True Dharma of this Lord of the World. Having heard this, the Blessed One,
looking toward the Great Being Viṣkambhin, spoke as follows:
Then that Lord of the Three Worlds, Lokeśvara, the Son of the Victor,
seeing sentient beings, approached Pātāla in order to deliver them.
And there, upon the iron ground at the base of the ocean, where the abode of the gods is situated,
he— possessing great supernormal knowledge— approached, illuminating that place as well.
There dwells that Vāmana, along with his retinue of women, by whom even King Bali— the sovereign of all the Daityas— was bound.
Beholding him— who was difficult to subdue, possessed of great heroism, and a source of terror to the three worlds— as one to be uprooted, he entered there, illuminating everything.
There, having emitted a ray of light that illuminated everywhere,
he moved slowly, observing his surroundings, and approached the assembly hall of Bali.
Seeing him approaching from afar, radiant like a golden image,
Bali set aside his offerings and reflected thus:
Who is this who has arrived here, illuminating [the place] with divine splendor—
is it Maheśvara, or the sun, or the moon, or even the fire?
Who else possesses such glorious splendor— whether a god or even a dānava, a gandharva or a kinnara, a nāga or even a garuḍa?
Possessing such great supernatural power and glory, there is none even within the three realms.
Whether it be a bodhisattva, or an arhat, or the Lord of Sages who has arrived.
Thinking thus, Bali, together with the Vāmana-demons and all his attendants, approached him in order to see him.
Seeing him, that powerful king, upon observing the Son of the Conqueror—
the Lord of the World, the Great Being— recognized him and was filled with joy.
Approaching him suddenly with joy and palms joined in reverence,
he bowed at his lotus feet and, gazing upon him, spoke thus:
Today my birth has become fruitful through the arising of the sight of you;
now my vow and my heart's desire are fully accomplished.
My self is purified; I am liberated from all evil. Today I am freed from bondage and have attained the path of the Sugata.
That you have come here yourself, having perceived [my state], to deliver me—
this is indeed seen by me today as the ripening of my own merit.
Indeed, those meritorious men who behold you become endowed with glory and happiness, freed from all afflictions; those beings are happy in the world, utterly pure and stainless.
Those who have been liberated from wandering through existence are seen by you within existence;
by the mere sight of you, I am thus released from the bonds of existence,
and the afflictions and other defilements flee like serpents before Garuḍa.
You alone are the Lord of the World, the Teacher, the proclaimer of the True Dharma;
you are my protector, my sustainer, and my refuge—there is no other source of friendship for me.
Therefore, may you, having looked upon me with compassion, lift me up from the ocean of existence, establish me on the true path, and graciously protect me.
Having thus prayed, Bali, the lord of the Daityas, with palms joined in reverence,
bowed again to that Lord of the World and respectfully led him to his own city.
Having led him there to his own city with great festivals and celebrations,
he seated him upon a brilliant throne of gold and jewels within the inner apartments.
Having established it there, King Bali was filled with joy;
together with the members of his harem, he honored it according to the prescribed rites.
Having honored him with great royal wealth and hospitality, he worshipped him with joy;
then, bowing at his lotus feet, he made this request with great reverence.
O Blessed One, you are the Lord of the three realms; since you have come here yourself, it behoves you to look upon us all with compassion and deliver us from every danger.
No protector is found for us who wander through the ten directions,
who are terrified by old age and death, and whose selves are consumed by the fire of the afflictions.
For those exhausted by the toil of the ocean of existence, whose minds are perpetually anxious,
who are without a protector and without kin— be their mother, father, and friend.
For these beings who are bound by fetters, born blind, evil-minded,
deluded, and impure, may you become their refuge and the remover of their afflictions.
Be the protector, O Lord of the World; be the teacher who proclaims the True Dharma;
be the refuge, the true guru, the friend, the savior, the sustainer, and the one who bears the welfare of others.
Just as you, having turned the world away from the path of evil and established it upon the path of Dharma, protect it while keeping watch over it.
Likewise, having turned even us, the most sinful, away from the path of evil and having restrained us, it behoves you to protect us by looking upon us with compassion.
Out of compassion, having rescued us who are deeply attached from the ocean of existence, may he awaken us and enjoin us to the Dharma that accomplishes perfect enlightenment.
Having heard this prayer made by Bali, who desired auspiciousness,
and having looked upon Bali, Lokeśvara commanded him thus:
"Excellent! Listen with focused attention and respect, O Lord of Daityas;
for your benefit, I shall proclaim that Dharma which is the means to awakening."
If you desire to enjoy auspicious happiness at all times within saṃsāra,
recollect the Three Jewels and worship them constantly with a concentrated mind.
Those who, having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, always devote themselves to existence,
are completely liberated from the miserable realms and always go to a happy rebirth.
Born only into the happy realms, they are intent upon accomplishing the true Dharma; having enjoyed merit, glory, virtue, and sublime happiness, they go to the abode of the Victors.
The fruit of merit arising from honoring the Three Jewels is vast and great;
it is immeasurable and incalculable, and it is the means for accomplishing the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
Having understood this, O Lord of Daityas, if you desire awakening,
approach the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and constantly worship it with a concentrated mind.
Those who, having worshipped the Dharmadhātu, always revere it with devotion,
are all liberated from sins and go to the abode of the Jinas.
Having always heard the true Dharma with reverence, faith, and respect,
having honored it and taken refuge in it, worship it constantly with a concentrated mind.
Those who, having always heard the true Dharma, with reverence, faith, and respect,
go for refuge, pay homage, and worship it with great joy;
All those bodhisattvas, liberated from afflictions and pure in the three spheres,
possessing great supernormal powers, proceed to the abode of the Sugata.
Those who, having honored the jewels of the Saṅgha with faith and gone for refuge,
always joyfully attend upon them with respectful services.
Those great beings as well— freed from afflictions, pure in intention, and striving toward virtue— having experienced virtuous enthusiasm, go to Sukhāvatī.
The Victors have declared that for one who, with faith, offers even a single bowl of ground grain to an Arhat, the merit is incalculable and immeasurable.
I am able to describe the measure of all other merits,
but even the Jinas themselves are not able to describe the measure of this merit.
If all sentient beings born within the three realms were sons of the Sugata,
they too would not be able to measure the extent of this merit.
How much more so am I alone here; how then could I possibly describe this mass of merit, which cannot be described even by the Victors?
Even if one were to grind the entire earth into powder and reduce it all to atoms,
it would be possible for even all the Buddhas together to count every one of them.
But the mass of merit from honoring the Three Jewels can never be measured by all the Lords of Munis, nor even by me.
I am able to count, by means of the measurement of the number of drops, even all the waters of every ocean and river.
One might write out the complete syllable upon birch-barks as vast as Mount Meru;
I am able to count all those syllables.
In all the oceans and in all the rivers as well,
it is possible for me to count as many grains of sand as there are.
I am able to count the hairs growing on the bodies of all living beings dwelling within the four continents.
I am able to count the leaves of all trees, the plants growing on the earth of the four continents, and even the grains.
I am able to measure the number of drops from a single cloud raining incessantly among many clouds that are pouring down rain.
But as for the immeasurable mass of merit born from honoring the Three Jewels and giving alms-food and the like, it is not possible for me to measure it.
If all sentient beings were established on the ten stages, and were bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, and practitioners of the holy life;
Whatever great merit there is in their means for achieving the vehicle of perfect enlightenment,
even greater than that is the great merit born from making offerings to the Three Jewels.
What is the use of so much being said by all the lords of sages,
since it can never be numbered or measured?
How then could I alone be able to enumerate them here?
Let it be understood in this way: that it is immeasurable and incalculable.
This very [practice] is a great merit that is never exhausted;
it is the means for accomplishing the qualities of the True Dharma and for bestowing benefit upon all sentient beings.
It bestows the establishment in the excellence of auspicious glory and happiness;
it removes the torment of the fire of all afflictions; it is the means for achieving perfect awakening.
Realizing that the fruit is thus great, always remember the Three Jewels;
with a concentrated mind, worship them constantly by meditating upon them, praising them, and bowing down to them.
Those who always and constantly take refuge in the Three Jewels with faith,
and who— whether by recollecting, meditating, being satisfied, or prostrating— continue to worship them;
All of them were stainless in nature, with completely purified faculties and intentions;
free from afflictions, they were the repositories of excellent qualities and practitioners of the four divine abodes.
Those sons of the Conquerors, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, will possess the excellence of the qualities of the glory of Dharma, auspicious enthusiasm, and delight in happiness.
Then, having fulfilled all the perfections in due order,
and having conquered all the hosts of Māra, they became free from afflictions with stainless faculties.
The Arhats, worthy of worship by the three worlds, leaders endowed with the great superknowledges,
having attained the threefold enlightenment, shall reach the state of a Perfect Buddha.
Thus has the truth been fully proclaimed by all the lords of sages;
therefore, recognizing this, take refuge in the Three Jewels if you desire awakening.
Having heard this command issued by the Teacher of the World,
Bali, the lord of the Daityas, beholding it, was filled with wonder.
Then, reflecting upon his own past deeds such as sacrifices and gifts,
with tears streaming down his face as he gazed upon the Lord of the World, he spoke to him.
"Blessed One, what kind of deed was committed by me, a fool,
by which even here I have encountered this bondage along with my own kinsmen?"
"Alas! By me, of wicked intellect, a sacrifice was performed that is esteemed by heretics;
as the fruit of which I, along with my people, have been bound here below."
Oh, how wonderful is the merit resulting from that gift bestowed upon the Buddhists,
by which one enjoys auspicious prosperity in this world and finally attains nirvāṇa!
Alas! I have acted foolishly by following the teachings of the heretics, whereby I have encountered such great suffering here along with my own kin.
O Lord of the World, when I began my great festival, I gave gifts according to their desires to all seekers with due respect.
Then Vāmana, having arrived before me as a celibate student (brahmacārī),
standing only two paces in height, made a request upon the earth.
Having heard that, with my mind stained by greed for gifts and being excessively proud in my conceit,
I offered him a third footprint upon the surface of the earth.
Having taken what was given by me and uttering words of blessing,
that Vāmana assumed a massive form and stood before me.
That great being, possessing three feet, of terrifying form and great supernatural power,
assuming the triple-striding (Traivikrama) manifestation, looked at me and spoke thus:
"Give back to me that which was given by you; there is no place for me for this third step. Tell me, where shall I place it?"
One was placed by me in the sky, and the second upon the surface of the earth.
Tell me this: where would you place my third foot?
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, I was ashamed and my mind became despondent;
with a bewildered heart, I remained there, unable to say anything at all.
Then that Viṣṇu, having looked at me, spoke again:
"Wherever I shall establish [the image], there one should certainly install it."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, I then spoke in that manner.
Wherever it is established by you, there I shall establish it.
Having heard these words of truth spoken by me, he was greatly delighted;
then the valiant one, having stepped upon my head with his third foot, strode forward.
"He will place me here in the netherworld of Adhaspātāla, along with my harem, my kinsmen, and my followers, and cast us into bondage."
"Whatever extremely cruel sin was committed by me, merciless as I am, because of that I have met with this imprisonment here, along with the members of my harem."
Having given all kinds of requisites to all who requested them, as well as whatever substance they desired, such as elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles;
The fruit of whatever gift was given in a lowly field of merit is now experienced here;
alas, what have I done after hearing the teaching of the heretics?
Thus, I have never heard of such meritorious fruit arising from devotion to the Three Jewels anywhere; nor is such a supreme result ever known.
Alas! Having been corrupted by wicked heretics, I was enticed; though deceived, I was led away into false dharma and even here into bondage.
Such a fruitful merit for accomplishing the auspicious splendor of enlightenment,
born from giving on an excellent field, has never been heard of nor conceived by me before.
If such great merit, which bestows the auspicious glory of enlightenment,
had not been known, one would have always taken refuge in the Three Jewels.
Having heard this spoken by you, O Blessed One, I have understood it;
therefore, I shall always remain taking refuge in the Three Jewels and honor them.
Therefore, may your honor explain the method for taking refuge in the Three Jewels;
from this day forward, until the end of existence, I shall always practice in this way.
Thus, O Blessed One, I am established in the refuge of the Jewel of the Buddha.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, may I worship you at all times throughout existence.
And thus, having approached for refuge in the jewels of the Dharma,
may I always honor and practice them with devotion after hearing their secondary qualities.
Likewise, I always abide in refuge in the Jewel of the Saṅgha,
and I worship it with due honor, offering worthy food as well.
I shall indeed conduct myself exactly as you have instructed here;
it behoves you to fully teach the Dharma that accomplishes perfect awakening.
Having heard what was thus spoken, that omniscient Lord of the World,
perceiving that the lord of the Daityas had been awakened, commanded him in this manner.
"O virtuous one, Bala, you are the lord of the asuras; listen to this with a concentrated mind.
I shall speak for your benefit if you desire the true Dharma."
First, having desisted from evil deeds, one should keep far away from wicked friends.
Having relied upon a true friend, O auspicious one, conduct yourself with concentrated mindfulness.
Therefore, O steadfast one, with a mind of faith and abiding in the four divine abodes,
having paid homage to the Three Jewels, practice the vow of the conduct of awakening.
With joy and reverence, out of faith toward the followers of the Sugata and those who seek [the Dharma],
perform your desired giving with the aspiration for perfect enlightenment.
Whatever decline has been made through faith by means of the vow for perfect enlightenment,
its fruit is indeed established as great, accomplishing the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Therefore, any other gift that is naturally given with joy and through aspiration might bestow great prosperity and happiness for a time, but it can never bestow the bliss of the Sugata.
Therefore, recollecting those Three Jewels and fixing your intention upon perfect enlightenment,
give gifts with faith if you desire the state of a Buddha.
Having thus constantly given gifts, with the mind set on awakening and senses subdued,
practice the Poṣadha vow with pure conduct and observance of the precepts.
Without the vow, even the three bodies of the Great Ones would not be purified;
therefore, through the aspiration for enlightenment, practice the vow of the Sugatas.
Always maintaining this vow and upholding the four divine abodes,
practice the vow of patience through the aspiration for perfect enlightenment.
That merit acquired through giving for the sake of the Three Jewels over thousands of eons,
the wicked world, provoked by the afflictions, destroys in a single instant through anger.
Conquering those enemies— the afflictions of the world— which are rooted in anger and corrupt the world,
practice the vow of patience toward sentient beings through the aspiration for perfect enlightenment.
The vow of awakening is not accomplished through mere forbearance alone;
it is perfected only through the exertion and enthusiasm of vigor.
Therefore, casting aside that anger and fixing your intention upon perfect enlightenment,
maintain your courageous exertion and proceed toward the accomplishment of the auspicious goal.
For even for those of great intelligence, no task is accomplished without diligence;
therefore, having applied diligence and resolved upon perfect enlightenment, [one should proceed].
Accumulate the jewel of the true Dharma, which brings about the welfare of both oneself and others;
for the great enthusiasm and vigor of one with corrupt intellect do not accomplish what is auspicious.
One should always act for the benefit of oneself and others, like an enemy;
maintaining that fortitude and excellent intelligence, one should be established in the meditation on perfect enlightenment.
Accumulate the jewel of the true Dharma for the sake of bringing benefit to all sentient beings;
for one devoid of wisdom does not achieve success even if established in meditative concentration.
Therefore, accumulate that great jewel of true wisdom for the welfare of the three worlds.
Having understood this as the supreme means for accomplishing the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, you should always practice the noble vow for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
Then you would be a bodhisattva, bearing the welfare of all sentient beings—
a practitioner of the auspicious conduct, possessed of great supernormal knowledges, a great being, and a son of the Conqueror.
Thus, if you desire to attain the state of a Buddha for the welfare of the world,
worship the Three Jewels in order to obtain the great jewel of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).
Through the power of the jewel of merit arising from honoring the Three Jewels,
one will attain the great jewel of the mind of awakening for the benefit of the world.
Having heard this instruction from the Teacher of the World,
Bali was awakened and desired the vow of the conduct of awakening.
Then Bali, beholding that Lord of the World, the Son of the Conqueror,
joined his palms in reverence, prostrated himself, and made this request with great devotion:
O Blessed One, you alone are the Lord of the three worlds and the Teacher of the universe; you are my savior, my well-wisher, and my friend—there is truly no other for me.
Having taken your command upon my head with a concentrated mind,
I shall practice the excellent restraint, having performed devotion to the Three Jewels.
In order to attain that jewel of the mind, I go for refuge at all times to all the Buddhas, the lords of sages, as well as to the Jewel of the Dharma and the Sangha.
Approaching them with faith, I shall perform worship for them;
and having heard the Dharma from the Saṅghas, I shall give food as is appropriate.
From this day forward, I shall always be a lay follower of those lords of sages; having undertaken the vow according to the rule, I will act for the welfare of the world.
In order to grasp the jewel of my own mind, I perform this perfect worship of the Tathāgatas,
as well as of the stainless Jewel of the True Dharma and of the Sons of the Buddha, who are mines of virtue.
As many flowers and fruits as there are, and whatever varieties of medicinal herbs exist;
as many jewels as there are in the world, and waters that are clear and delightful;
There were mountains composed of jewels, as well as other forest regions delightful for their solitude;
there were creepers radiant with the ornaments of beautiful flowers, and trees whose branches were bowed down by excellent fruit.
And in the worlds of the gods and others, there are perfumes and incenses, wish-fulfilling trees, and trees made of jewels;
there are lakes adorned with lotuses and rendered exceedingly enchanting by the cries of swans.
And all these various kinds of crops that grow without being ploughed, or other objects worthy of worship and adornment, extending as far as the reaches of space— all these too are without ownership.
Taking this with my intellect, I offer it to the bulls among sages together with their sons;
may they, who are most worthy of offerings and possess great compassion, accept it from me out of pity for me.
I am devoid of merit and greatly impoverished; I have nothing else for the sake of worship.
Therefore, O Protectors, considering my welfare and the welfare of others, please accept this offering according to my own capacity.
I give myself entirely and in every way to the Victors and likewise to their sons; O Supreme Beings, accept me as your own; through devotion, I enter into the state of servitude unto you.
Through your grace, I am free from fear in this existence and work for the welfare of sentient beings;
I transcend my former evil and shall not commit further sin again.
May rains of flowers, jewels, and other offerings fall continuously upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as upon the reliquaries and images.
Just as the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, worship the Victors,
so do I worship all those Lords of Sages together with their sons.
I praise those oceans of virtue with hymns that are like oceans of melodic branches;
and from these, clouds of musical eulogies arise in no other way.
I prostrate with as many bows as there are atoms in all the kṣetras,
before all the Buddhas of the three times, together with their supreme Dharma and assemblies.
I pay homage to all caityas, as well as those that are the abodes of Bodhisattvas;
I likewise bow down to my preceptors and to the ascetics who are worthy of veneration.
I go for refuge to the Buddha until the attainment of enlightenment;
I go for refuge to the Dharma and likewise to the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
With palms joined in reverence, I address the perfectly awakened Buddhas who reside in all directions, as well as the Bodhisattvas endowed with great compassion.
Whatever sin has been committed or caused to be committed by me, like a beast, throughout beginningless transmigratory existence or even in this very birth;
And whatever was approved by me, deluded as I was, for the sake of my own destruction— that transgression I confess here, tormented by remorse.
Whatever harm I have done to the Three Jewels, or to my mother and father,
or to other gurus and others, through the impairment of body, speech, and mind;
Whatever terrible sin has been committed by me, a wicked person corrupted by many faults and deluded by ignorance, all of that I now confess.
And how may I escape from this, for I am now constantly anxious?
May death not come to me before my accumulation of evil deeds has been exhausted.
This death, which destroys trust and examines what has been done and left undone, cannot be relied upon by the healthy or the sick; it is a great thunderbolt that strikes at once.
"Out of attachment to the pleasant and aversion to the unpleasant, I have committed evil in many ways;
that I must depart, leaving everything behind, was not known by me in such a manner."
Those who are unpleasant shall not exist, nor shall those who are dear to me exist;
I myself shall not exist, and everything shall not exist.
Whatever object is experienced becomes a mere memory;
like everything experienced in a dream, once it has passed, it is never seen again.
While I remain right here, many things pleasant and unpleasant have already passed;
the evil I committed on their account stands before me now.
Thus, I do not regard myself as a mere newcomer;
rather, through delusion, attachment, and aversion, I have committed manifold evils.
Day and night, without ceasing, the expenditure of life increases; there is no acquisition of even a fraction of it—how can I not die?
Even here, while lying on my bed and standing in the midst of my kinsmen,
I alone must endure the agonizing pain of the severing of my vital organs and other such torments.
When one has been seized by the messengers of Yama, where are relatives, friends, or companions?
At that time, merit alone is protection; it is that which I have accumulated right here.
Not knowing such fear as this— attachment to a life that is impermanent—
I, being heedless and blinded by intoxication, have accumulated much evil.
Even when being led away for the purpose of having his limbs severed, another person withers away;
parched with thirst and with a wretched gaze, he perceives the world as something entirely different.
Why is he presided over by wicked messengers of Yama with terrifying forms,
seized by a mass of great terror, and enveloped in the discharge of excrement?
With trembling eyes darting in all directions in search of protection, [he thought:
"Who here might be a virtuous savior for me from this great terror?"
Seeing all directions devoid of protection, I fell once again into utter confusion;
what shall I do then in that place of great terror?
Now, indeed, I go for refuge to the Jinas, the lords of the world, possessed of great power,
who are intent upon protecting the world and who remove all fear.
I take refuge with devotion in the Dharma realized by them, which destroys the fear of saṃsāra, and likewise in the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
Overwhelmed by fear, I offer myself to Samantabhadra;
terrified, I cry out with a piteous voice—may he swiftly destroy my fear.
In this matter, to think "I shall transgress the word of the Lord of the Omniscient One, who removes all sins"— shame on me, utterly deluded!
I remain exceedingly vigilant even when others have departed;
how much more so, then, when facing a precipice a thousand yojanas deep that extends for a long period of time?
Death may come this very day; it is not fitting for me to dwell in ease. I shall certainly cease to exist; why then is my mind so complacent?
What essence remains for me from those things previously experienced that have perished,
through my attachment to which I transgressed the words of my gurus?
Leaving behind this world of the living, as well as my kinsmen and acquaintances, I shall go somewhere all alone; what use have I for all these things, pleasant or unpleasant?
But this alone is my constant thought, day and night:
"How may I certainly emerge from this impurity, which is inevitably suffering?"
Whatever evil was previously committed by me, wicked and deluded,
I now confess it before the Protectors,
with palms joined, fearing suffering, and prostrating again and again.
May the Leaders accept this transgression as a transgression;
O Protectors, I shall never again commit what is unwholesome.
I rejoice with great joy in the merit performed by all sentient beings, which provides rest from the suffering of the miserable realms; may those who are suffering abide in happiness.
I rejoice in the liberation from suffering for embodied beings within saṃsāra, and I rejoice in the state of a bodhisattva and the state of buddhahood for the Protectors.
And I rejoice in the oceans of the generation of the mind of enlightenment belonging to the Teachers, which bring happiness to all sentient beings and establish the welfare of all sentient beings.
With palms joined in reverence, I entreat all the Buddhas residing in every direction:
may they provide the lamp of Dharma for those who have fallen into suffering through delusion.
And to those Victors who desire to enter parinirvāṇa, I entreat them with great reverence:
may you remain for no small number of eons, lest this world become blind.
When this was said by that Bali, the Lord of the World (Lokeśvara), having heard it again and again, expressed his approval with "Excellent! Excellent! and spoke thus to Bali:
This attainment of the opportune moment is extremely difficult to find; it is the means for accomplishing the goals of human life.
If one does not contemplate what is beneficial now, how will such a convergence ever occur again?
Just as in the thick darkness of night a flash of lightning momentarily reveals light,
so too, through the power of the Buddhas, the mind of the world may for a moment turn toward meritorious deeds.
Therefore, virtue is always weak, while the power of evil is great and most terrible;
how then could that [evil] be conquered by any virtue unless it were indeed the mind of complete enlightenment?
This very benefit has been perceived by the lords of sages who have reflected for many eons;
for it is through happiness alone that happiness, when increased, carries across immeasurable multitudes of people.
Those who wish to cross over hundreds of worldly sufferings, those who wish to remove the calamities of sentient beings,
and those who wish to enjoy hundreds of manifold pleasures must never, indeed, abandon the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
Who is the best among those bound in the prison of existence? One is called a son of the Sugatas in an instant;
from this very moment, upon the arising of the thought of awakening, one becomes worthy of veneration by the world of humans and gods.
Having taken this image of impurity, one fashions from it an image of the jewel-like Jina that is beyond price;
therefore, take hold of the exceedingly piercing and very firm jewel of the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), which is like an alchemical elixir.

May those whose nature is to wander away from the city of the [liberated] states firmly grasp the jewel of the spirit of enlightenment (bodhicitta)— a treasure thoroughly examined by those of immeasurable wisdom and of great value, as proclaimed by the sole caravan-leaders of the world.
Like a plantain tree, everything else indeed perishes once its fruit is gone;
however, the tree of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) constantly bears fruit, never perishes, and indeed continues to produce further fruit.
Even after committing most terrible sins, one crosses over them in an instant by taking refuge in him;
just as one escapes great dangers by taking refuge with a hero, why is he not sought for refuge by ignorant beings?
It consumes great sins in an instant, like the fire at the end of an eon;
the wise Lord Maitreya described its immeasurable benefits to Sudhana.
That bodhicitta should be understood, in brief, as being of two kinds:
the mind of aspiration for enlightenment and the mind of setting out toward enlightenment.
Just as a distinction is perceived between one who desires to go and one who is going,
so too should the distinction between these two be understood by the wise according to their respective order.
The mind of the vow for enlightenment yields great fruit even within saṃsāra;
however, it does not possess uninterrupted merit in the same way as the mind of application.
From the moment he generates that mind with an irreversible resolve for the sake of liberating the boundless realm of sentient beings.
From that time forward, even while he was asleep or heedless,
continuous streams of merit flowed forth like the sky in their vastness.
How indeed can the merit of the jewel of the mind be measured— that seed of the world's bliss and the medicine for the world's suffering?
The worship of the Buddha is distinguished even by the mere wish for the welfare [of others];
how much more so by the exertion for the sake of the complete happiness of all sentient beings!
(98) Driven by the desire for escape from suffering, they rush headlong into suffering itself;
through delusion and the mere longing for pleasure, they destroy their own happiness like an enemy.
Whoever would satisfy those who are repeatedly afflicted by the pains of the Sukharankas with all forms of happiness, and who would sever all their afflictions— [that person shall attain this state].
He even destroys delusion; how could anyone be equal to such a virtuous person?
Where is there such a friend, or where is there such merit?
Even one who returns a favor for a service rendered is praised;
how much more so, then, is a virtuous Bodhisattva who acts without being prompted?
The Lord has said that whoever, while these two sons of the Conqueror are thus conversing, creates defilement within his own heart,
shall remain in the hells for as many eons as there are moments of the arising of that defilement.
Now, for one whose mind attains serenity, there shall arise from that an even greater fruit.
Therefore, having firmly grasped the thought of awakening, the son of the Conqueror should always strive, without indolence, not to transgress the training.
And as for you, why do you remain indifferent in this matter according to your ability?
If you do not exert effort today, you shall go from the surface to the very depths by means of the surface.
And if, having made such a vow, you do not accomplish it through action,
what will be your destiny after deceiving all these people?
"But that man who, having thought of it in his mind, does not give it again—even regarding an object of very little value—he becomes a preta; so it has been said by the Blessed One."
How much more so for one who, having loudly proclaimed with sincere devotion the unsurpassed bliss,
brings about the ruin of the welfare of all sentient beings by falling away from it?
Furthermore, whoever else shall create an obstacle to his merit for even a single moment—
that destroyer of the welfare of sentient beings shall have no end other than the miserable realms.
For by neglecting the welfare of even a single sentient being, one would be ruined;
how much more so for all embodied beings dwelling as far as the unexhausted reaches of space?
Immeasurable Buddhas have come, seeking after all sentient beings;
yet you, through your own fault, have fallen beyond the range of their healing.
Indeed, by conduct such as this, a good rebirth cannot be attained again;
when a good rebirth is not attained, how can there be any merit, for there is only evil?
When you, though capable of virtue, do not perform virtuous deeds, O you who are deluded by the suffering of the lower realms, what will you do then for the sake of the auspicious?
For one who fails to practice skillful means and accumulates only evil,
even the very term "good rebirth" is destroyed for hundreds of millions of eons.
Some, due to a sin committed in a single moment, remain in Avīci for an aeon.
Given the evil accumulated since beginningless time, what talk can there be of a happy rebirth?
If, having obtained such a moment as this, you again falter, deluded,
you will grieve for a long time once more, driven on by the messengers of Yama.
The unbearable fire of hell will burn your body for a long time;
and the fire of remorse will long burn the mind of one who failed to train.
The enemies of craving, hatred, and so forth lack hands, feet, and other limbs; they are neither brave nor wise. How is it that you have been made their slave?
Remaining within your very consciousness, they strike you down while remaining well-established;
herein you possess no awareness, like one deluded by mantras.
Even if all the gods and humans were to become your enemies,
they would not be capable of producing the fire of the Avīci hell.
All things are conducive to welfare when practiced in accordance with what is suitable;
yet these afflictions, when indulged in, cause even greater suffering.
These guardians of the prison of existence are executioners even within the hells and other realms;
if they dwell within the chamber of your intellect, luring you with greed, how can there be happiness for you?
Even those wounded by enemies without cause carry them upon their bodies as ornaments;
why then should sufferings be an obstacle to you, who are striving for the accomplishment of a great purpose?

Fishermen, outcastes, farmers, and others whose minds are bound solely to their own livelihood endure the hardships of cold, heat, and so forth; why then do you not endure them for the sake of the welfare of the world?
Those such as the devotees of Durgā and Karṇa endure in vain the pains of burning, cutting, and so forth for the sake of liberation; why then are you so cowardly?
And for you who seek liberation, it is fitting to abandon the bonds of greed and worldly honor;
how can you harbor hatred toward those who release you from bondage?
Even when touched by warm water, you, being so delicate, are tormented;
yet, having committed deeds that lead to hell, why do you remain so at ease?
There is no object whatsoever that is difficult to master through repeated practice;
therefore, by practicing with regard to slight pain, even great pain can be endured.
O evil-minded one, you do not desire suffering, yet you desire the cause of suffering;
since suffering has arisen from your own transgression, why is it blamed elsewhere?
Having abandoned the supreme delight in the Dharma, which is a continuum of infinite bliss,
how can you find pleasure in laughter and the like, which are causes of suffering?
Even when touched by merely warm water, you, being so delicate, suffer in agony; yet, having committed deeds that lead to hell, why do you remain so composed?
There is no object whatsoever that is difficult for practice to accomplish;
therefore, by practicing with mild pain, even great pain can be endured.
O evil-minded one, you do not desire suffering, yet you desire the cause of suffering;
since suffering has arisen from your own transgression, why is it blamed elsewhere?
Having abandoned the supreme delight in the Dharma, which is a succession of infinite bliss, how can you find pleasure in laughter and the like, which are causes of suffering and destroyers of joy?
Because you were previously separated from the aspiration for awakening, such misfortune has now arisen; therefore, strive to accomplish awakening.
Since physical suffering arises from evil in the mind through false conceptualization,
one should therefore cultivate a desire for the wholesome with such earnestness.
O Blessed One, you have not attained the joy of the great festival of worship;
you have performed no service for the Teaching, nor have you fulfilled the hopes of the poor.
Fearlessness was not granted to those who were afraid, nor were the afflicted made happy;
you performed sacrifices and gave gifts solely for the sake of your own personal pleasure.
And for those who commit evil deeds, there arise the frustration of their desires,
as well as sufferings, mental distresses, and various kinds of fears.
Wherever a doer of evil who desires happiness goes,
right there he is struck by the weapons of suffering produced by those very evils.
Wherever the desire of those who perform virtuous deeds goes,
there too they are honored for the sake of its fruit by the value of that merit.
Seated within the centers of vast, fragrant, and cool lotuses,
their radiance was enhanced by feeding upon the sweet voice of the Jina.
Go forth, O sons of the Sugata, who have emerged with excellent bodies; through your wholesome deeds, you become sons of the Sugata before the Sugata, awakened by the hand of the Sage.
With all its bark stripped away by the servants of Yama, crying out in agony,
its body drenched as if poured with molten copper from the heat of fire;
With the flesh of his limbs repeatedly hacked away by hundreds of blows from flaming swords and spears, he falls many times onto the intensely heated iron ground due to his own evil deeds.
That same habit persists even in another birth; through evil, suffering increases.
Furthermore, whatever task is undertaken is accomplished poorly, both in its execution and its timing.
If your mind is weak, even a minor misfortune afflicts it; indeed, when one is rendered motionless by despondency, misfortunes become easy to overcome.
Even when emerged from meditative absorption and acting in the world, he is difficult to defeat even by the great;
therefore, this pride must be borne: "For I am the son of the Lion of the Victors."
Those wretches who have been conquered by the pride of enjoyment are not truly proud;
for it is pride that brings one under the power of the enemy, whereas they have instead fallen under the power of the enemy that is pride.
Led to miserable rebirths by pride, these fools are ill-favored, emaciated, hopeless, and humiliated; even in human form, their joy has been destroyed.
They alone are truly proud and victorious, they alone are heroes, who carry pride for the sake of conquering the enemy that is pride;
who, having struck down that foe of pride even while it is surging, bestow upon people at will the fruit of victory.
There is no satisfaction with sensual desires in saṃsāra, which are like honey on the edge of a razor;
how then could there be satisfaction with the nectar of merit, which is auspicious and sweet in its ripening?
For whom could there be affection for things that are impermanent,
when one shall not behold a loved one again for thousands of births?
He certainly finds no steadfastness and does not abide in meditative concentration;
nor is he satisfied even upon seeing [the object], for he is oppressed by thirst as before.
He does not see things as they truly are; through agitation he falls away, and is overcome by that grief and the longing for union with what is dear.
Through constant worry about that [wealth], one's short life passes away in vain again and again;
and through such impermanent friends, eternal Dharma is lost.

One who practices in common with fools will certainly go to a miserable rebirth; one who does not desire to be of the same class as them—what could possibly be gained from associating with the powerful?
In one moment they become friends, and in another moment they become enemies;
ordinary people are difficult to please and become angry even when there is cause for satisfaction.
When addressed with beneficial advice, they become angry and ward off that benefit;
yet if their words are not heeded, being enraged, they go to a miserable rebirth.
Envy arises from one who is superior; rivalry from one who is equal; pride from praise when one's self is lowly; and resentment from disparagement—when, then, could there ever be benefit for a fool?
Self-exaltation, disparagement of others, and talk of delight in cyclic existence—
such unwholesome things inevitably arise in every way from association with the foolish.
Therefore, a wise person should not desire that [wealth], for from desire fear is born;
beings with diverse inclinations were not satisfied even by the Victors.
Many became gainful and many became renowned; yet, along with their gains and fame, they were known by him [only] as to where they have gone.
For sensual desires produce misfortune both in this world and in the next:
in this world through the desire for imprisonment and execution, and in the next through rebirth in the hells and other such realms.
For whose sake messengers and female messengers were saluted in many ways,
and for whose sake neither sin nor ill-repute was reckoned with previously;
I have cast myself into danger and squandered my wealth;
yet, by embracing these very things, I attained the highest bliss.
Why does one not attain peace by embracing at will those very same bones— neither other than oneself, nor belonging to another, and now under one's own control?
From a single morsel of food, both saliva and impurity are produced for them;
since the impurity among these is undesirable to you, how can the drinking of saliva be dear to you?
If you have no passion for the impure, why do you embrace another—
a cage of bones bound together by sinews and smeared with the mud of flesh?
Because it is small and born of impurity, you do not desire an unclean worm;
yet you desire this body, which is composed of much impurity and born from impurity.
One sees other bodies as well, which are terrifying in the charnel ground;
how is it that, even knowing this, one feels pleasure in being born right there again?
For the sake of honor, fools, deceived by desire, enter into servitude;
they are burned, cut, and struck down with spears.

Know that wealth is endless through its acquisition and protection, yet it leads to despair; for those whose minds are preoccupied with the excellence of riches, there is no opportunity for liberation from the suffering of existence.
Examine this: from where does all that which is created by illusion and that which is created by causes come, and where does it go?
The realms of existence are like dreams; when investigated, they are like plantain trees.
In reality, there is no distinction between those who have attained nirvāṇa and those who have not.
Thus, when all things are empty, what could be gained and what could be lost?
Who, by whom, would be honored or insulted, and who could possibly come into being?
Whence comes pleasure or pain, what is dear or what is not dear?
What is craving, and where is that craving when sought by way of its intrinsic nature?
Upon reflection, in this world of living beings, who indeed here shall die?
Who will come to be, who has been, who is a kinsman, and who is whose friend?
Grasp all things as being like space; they are thus. They become enraged or delighted by causes for quarrel and celebration.
Desiring their own happiness through sinful deeds, they pass their time with great difficulty amidst grief, exhaustion, and despondency, as well as mutual cutting and piercing.
Having died, they fall into miserable states of long and intense suffering;
yet, having repeatedly returned to happy rebirths and having become accustomed to happiness, they [again fall].
In existence there are many precipices, and therein such is the reality;
therein there is mutual contradiction, and not much of such reality exists.
And therein lie incomparable, intense, and endless oceans of suffering;
therein lies such weakness of power, and even therein, the brevity of life.
Even there, one is beset by the concerns for life and health, by hunger, fatigue, and toil, by sleep, by disturbances from children, and likewise by fruitless associations with the virtuous.
Life passes away quickly and in vain, yet discernment is extremely difficult to attain; even if it is attained, whence comes the capacity to ward off the distractions one has long practiced?
Even there, Māra strives to cast one down into the great abyss of the miserable realms;
for there, the paths that are not the true path are numerous, and doubt is difficult to overcome.
Furthermore, there is the frailty of the moment, the appearance of a Buddha is extremely rare,
and the flood of afflictions is difficult to restrain— alas, what a succession of sufferings!
Alas! How truly pitiable are these beings wandering in a flood of suffering, for even while being so intensely tormented, they do not perceive their own miserable condition.
Just as someone, having bathed again and again, might repeatedly enter the fire,
so too do those who are in extreme distress fail to perceive their own well-being.
For those who dwell thus, possessing a morality that is as if ageless and deathless,
terrible calamities shall come, having placed death at their very forefront.
Thus, for the sake of the peace of those tormented by suffering, practice the vow of awakening;
the vow of awakening is a great merit and the means for attaining the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
With your own provisions for happiness produced from clouds of merit,
teach emptiness at all times to those who hold the view of apprehending true existence.
Practice the accumulation of merit through conventional non-apprehension;
therefore, just as you wish to protect yourself from pain, grief, and the like, [protect others].
Therefore, one should practice the mind of protection and the mind of compassion toward the world;
do not turn back from these difficult tasks due to the power of habituation,
for it is precisely through hearing of them that fear arises, and without them, there is no delight.
He who desires to quickly protect both himself and others should practice the supreme secret: behaving toward others as one behaves toward oneself.
Since one feels even the slightest fear out of excessive attachment toward that self, who would not hate that self which brings fear like an enemy? One should not hate it.
He who kills birds, fish, or deer with the desire to counteract hunger, thirst, and other such needs, and he who stands as an obstacle on the path; [these are both considered hunters].
One who, driven by the desire for gain, honor,
and fame, would even kill his own parents or seize the property of the Three Jewels, shall become fuel for the Avīci hell.
What wise person would desire, protect, or worship that self? Who would not regard it as an enemy, and who indeed would honor it in such a way?
"If I give, what will I have to eat?"— this is the state of a *piśāca* for one's own sake; "If I eat, what shall I give?"— this is the state of a king of gods for the sake of others.
Having oppressed others for one's own sake, one is cooked in the hells and other realms;
but by oppressing oneself for the sake of others, all perfections are attained.
Just as one might desire for oneself high status, happiness, and freedom from misfortune, so too,
by transferring that very same aspiration to another, one attains a good rebirth, honor, and wisdom.
Having commanded others for one's own sake, one experiences servitude and the like;
having commanded oneself for the sake of others, one experiences lordship and the like.
Whoever is suffering in the world, all do so out of a desire for their own happiness;
whoever is happy in the world, all do so out of a desire for the happiness of others.
What is the use of saying more here? Behold this difference between the fool who seeks his own interest and the sage who acts for the sake of others.
Buddhahood cannot be achieved by name alone; how, then, could there be happiness within cyclic existence for one who does not effect an exchange of their own happiness for the suffering of others?
Let alone the next world; even in this visible world, one's purpose is not accomplished:
a servant who does not perform his work, and a master who does not pay his wages.
Having abandoned the production of mutual happiness and seeing instead the festival of happiness— both seen and unseen—
deluded beings take up terrible suffering through their mutual disparagement.
Whatever calamities occur in the world, and however many sufferings and fears there may be—all these arise from the grasping at a self; so why do you grasp at your own self?
Without abandoning the self, suffering cannot be abandoned;
just as without abandoning fire, burning cannot be abandoned.
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying your own suffering and for the sake of pacifying the suffering of others,
give yourself away to others and take others as yourself.
O Saṃmata, resolve with certainty: "I belong to others.
Having renounced everything for the sake of sentient beings, you should now think of nothing else.
All this well-performed conduct, generosity, and worship of the Sugatas that has been practiced throughout thousands of eons— anger destroys it all.
There is no evil equal to hatred, and no austerity equal to patience; therefore,
one should cultivate patience with diligent effort through various methods.
When the thorn of hatred remains in the heart, the mind finds no tranquility, nor does it experience joy or happiness; it finds neither sleep nor steadfastness.
Even those who have taken refuge in him honor him with wealth and respect;
yet, because they are ill-favored by hatred toward their master, they also desire to kill him.
Even friends are repelled by him if he gives; yet if he does not give, he is not served.
In short, there is nothing at all by which an angry man may remain well-established.
Evil people, who are like the sky, do not go to destruction merely by being hated;
however, when the mind of anger is slain, all enemies perish.
Indeed, a living being, ignited by the fire of anger fueled by conceptual constructions, first burns himself; whether he will burn others or not is uncertain.
Old age for the beautiful, anger even for those with sight, and the destruction of virtue, wealth, and pleasure— therefore, one should restrain anger.
He who, through persistent effort, destroys anger born from the occurrence of the undesirable and the obstruction of the desirable, is happy both in this world and in the next.
Even upon reaching the ultimate limit of misfortune, you must not let your joy be disturbed;
even in the midst of mental distress, there is no lack of what is desired, for your virtue does not diminish.
If there is indeed a remedy, what is the use of despondency in that case?
But if there is no remedy, what is the use of despondency in that case?
Furthermore, another quality of suffering is that through its agitation, one’s intoxication falls away;
there arises compassion for those in cyclic existence, fear of evil, and a longing for the Victorious One.
Whatever offenses there may be, and various kinds of evils—all that arises through the power of conditions; nothing exists independently.
Therefore, whether you see a friend or an enemy acting unjustly, remain happy by reflecting: "Such are the ways of this person."
Impelled by your own karma alone, they have been born as your wrongdoers; for surely it was by you that they were slain, such that they shall go to the hells.
Relying upon these, your sins are destroyed and your forbearance becomes great;
but by relying upon you, they go to hells of long-lasting suffering.
You alone are the wrongdoer toward these people, and they are the wrongdoers toward you; they are provoked by delusion and other such states, while others, likewise deluded, become angry.
Having understood this, maintain patience toward sentient beings and practice what is wholesome,
so that all may come to possess minds of mutual loving-kindness.
Praise, fame, wealth, and honor do not lead to merit for those who possess wisdom;
they are neither for the sake of strength, nor for health, nor for the pleasure of the body.
Furthermore, such things as praise and the like destroy one's security and spiritual urgency.
They harbor envy even toward those who possess virtues, and they display anger toward prosperity.
Therefore, those who have arisen against you to destroy your praise and so forth, are actually engaged in protecting you from falling into the lower realms; they are your benefactors.
How can there be hatred toward those who have become like door-bolts for one wishing to enter into suffering, [bolts] which have arisen through the empowerment of the Buddha?
Who would not consider it appropriate to say that an obstacle has been placed against merit by this person?
Yet there is no austerity equal to patience; and this [obstacle] has not actually arisen for him.
But if, due to your own fault, you do not practice forbearance here,
then the obstacle has been created by you alone when the cause for merit had presented itself.
No obstacle to giving was created by the suppliant who arrived at the proper time; nor is it said that an obstacle to renunciation occurred when the one seeking ordination arrived.
Beggars are easy to find in this world, but those who do harm are rare;
for no one commits an offense against one who has committed no offense against them.
Therefore, it is like a treasure discovered in one's home that has been acquired through diligent effort.
Because he is a companion in the conduct of awakening, an enemy is always to be envied;
if one who harbors the intent to do harm is not honored, he is a far more formidable foe.
Otherwise, how could you have patience toward one who strives for the welfare of his patients?
Therefore, patience arises precisely in dependence upon that very evil intention;
thus, he alone is the cause of patience, and he should always be honored like the Dharma itself.
Therefore, the Sage has declared that the field of sentient beings is the field of the Victors,
for by honoring these [beings], many have reached the further shore of prosperity.
Since the attainment of the Buddha-dharmas is equal from both sentient beings and the Victors,
what is the logic behind having reverence for the Victors but not for sentient beings?
That one is worthy of worship because of a disposition of loving-kindness is simply the greatness of sentient beings;
that which arises from faith in the Buddha is simply the greatness of the Buddha.

Insofar as they possess a portion of the Buddha's teachings, sentient beings are equal to the Victors; however, no one is equal to the Buddhas in terms of their infinite qualities, which are like a vast ocean of attributes.
If even a minute quality is seen in someone who is a singular mass of the essence of virtues, the three worlds together are not sufficient for the purpose of honoring that person.
And a portion of the arising of the Buddha-dharma exists within sentient beings;
in accordance with that portion, worship of the Buddha is performed.
Moreover, for those who are sincere friends and immeasurable benefactors,
what other recompense could there be than the act of pleasing sentient beings?

Those in whose happiness the Lords of Sages find joy, and in whose suffering they enter into grief—it is by pleasing them that all the Lords of Sages are pleased; therein, any injury done to them is an injury done to the Munis themselves.
Just as one whose body is ablaze on all sides finds no joy even through all sensual pleasures,
so too for those composed of compassion, there is a means to find no pleasure even when sentient beings suffer.
This entire world has indeed been made their own by those whose very nature is compassion; of this there is no doubt.
These beings who appear before us are surely the Protectors themselves—why, then, show them such disregard?
This alone is the propitiation of the Tathāgatas; this alone is the accomplishment of one's own welfare;
this alone is the remover of the world's suffering; therefore, let this alone be your vow.
Let alone the future Buddhahood that arises from pleasing sentient beings;
do you not see the good fortune, fame, and well-being right here in this very life?
One who is patient, while wandering through cyclic existence, attains a pleasing appearance, health, joy, long life, and the abundant happiness of a universal monarch.
Thus, being patient, one should cultivate vigor, for awakening is established upon vigor;
indeed, without vigor there is no merit, just as there is no movement without wind.
For diligence is indeed the storehouse for all the jewels of virtue; by means of the great raft of diligence, one crosses over all calamities.
When one reflects upon it, there is no object whatsoever in this world that cannot be attained by one who has mounted the chariot of diligence.

In battles filled with elephants, horses, and foot soldiers, and crowded with iron arrows, javelins, and battle-axes, they slay their enemies and attain unsurpassed victory; that is indeed the great heroism of Viṣṇu, the Conqueror.

Having crossed, by their own prowess, as if they were mere puddles in a cow’s hoofprint, the oceans— which are terrifying with the breaking of towering and tumultuous waves churned by swarms of sea-monsters— heroes acquire wealth in the form of jewels of priceless virtue.
Having suppressed the fierce-bodied serpents of passion and the like, those endowed with fortitude should adopt right conduct,
which is the most pure mind of the virtuous.
Endowed with valor, mortals rejoice for a long time upon the most lovely slopes of Mount Meru, embraced by the noose-like vine-arms of celestial beauties.
That the gods dwelling in celestial palaces in the sky experience such joy, free from all dualities,
is the splendor resulting from the firm application of vigor performed for the sake of producing an exceedingly vast fruit.
Having overcome the host of enemies that are the afflictions, the steadfast attain the state of the glory of perfect enlightenment;
