they bestow the gift of the factors of awakening upon the virtuous, for they proclaim meditative concentration to be the cause therein.
Having torn asunder all the multitudes of defects such as those of kings, which serve as the sole cause for the continuity of birth,
men whose minds are equal to space— who regard a clod of earth and gold as the same— become the very causes of virtue.
The form of a man devoid of the wealth of wisdom is like a painting, lacking substance within;
for one endowed with intelligence, the desired fruit arises from vigor, yet vigor devoid of intelligence is an enemy leading to one's own destruction.
In the world of mortals, the Buddha, having shattered the great mass of defilements and darkness,
creates the light of wisdom and constantly strikes down the multitude of faults in men.
And he knows the supreme minds of others beyond the range of the senses in all their modes;
they proclaim that even there, wisdom—which is the constant mother of the most excellent auspiciousness—is the cause.
Even when deeply submerged in an ocean of difficulties or in the midst of battle, eminent men attain victory through the power of wisdom; therefore, wisdom is indeed the cause of auspiciousness.
Therefore, let wisdom alone be cultivated, for it is that which accomplishes all virtues and goals;
men devoid of wisdom do not shine, like lamps without oil.
These six perfections alone are the repositories of the jewels of qualities leading to heaven and liberation for men on this earth;
having understood this, be intent upon accomplishing their welfare, and therefore always exert yourself in what is virtuous.
One should not afflict this body, which is the means for accomplishing the true Dharma, for the sake of other ends;
for by understanding this, one shall swiftly fulfill the hopes of sentient beings.
The conduct of bodhisattvas is said to be immeasurable;
for now, practice that conduct which purifies the mind with constancy.
Whatever states one enters, whether by one's own volition or under the power of another,
one should diligently train in those very instructions appropriate for each of those states.
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever that is not to be learned by the sons of the Conquerors;
nor is there any merit that does not accrue to one who dwells in this manner.
Always act for the sake of sentient beings, whether directly or through a lineage;
and for the very benefit of sentient beings, dedicate everything toward awakening.
Never abandon a true spiritual friend, even for the sake of your life—
one who upholds the vows of a bodhisattva and is skilled in the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
Having heard this command thus given by the Lord of the World,
Bali, his face parched with tears, wept and spoke as follows.
"O Lord, what improper sacrifice, approved by the heretics, have I performed,
the fruit of which I now experience here while dwelling together with these people?"
Save me, O Blessed One, for I am a sinner with a deluded mind;
O Teacher, I, along with my kinsmen, always go to you for refuge.
Homage be to you, O Bodhisattva, who holds the auspicious lotus;
whose limbs are adorned with the glory of the lotus, and who wears a crown of matted locks.
To him who is crowned by the King of Jinas, who grants consolation to sentient beings,
who has compassion for the lowly and the wretched, and who possesses the excellent eye of the Sun-maker.
To Pṛthivīvaranetra and Bhaiṣajyarāja,
the lords of perfectly pure beings, who maintain the supreme yoga.
To the one whose supreme dharma is liberation, who shows the path to liberation,
who possesses the radiance of the wish-fulfilling gem, and who guards the treasury of the Dharma.
To the one who provides instruction in the six perfections,
who teaches the path to awakening, and who brings about virtuous intention;
Having thus praised that Lord, the Master of the World, the lord of the Daityas,
joyful and with palms joined in reverence, bowed down and spoke again as follows:
Protect me, O Lord, who am of evil mind; deliver me from the ocean of existence!
Having established me on the path to enlightenment, enjoin me to the auspicious Dharma.
From this day forth, O Protector, having always gone for refuge to the Triple Gem and having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, may I proceed for the welfare of the world.
Always remembering the Protectors dwelling in all directions— the Perfectly Awakened Ones and the Lords of Sages— I stand in refuge, bowing with palms joined in reverence.
And whatever Dharma has been taught by all the Victors for the welfare of the world,
I shall uphold that True Dharma and always conduct myself in virtue.
Always mindful of all the lords and protectors of the world, the Bodhisattvas who are sons of the Victors, I too remain established in refuge and honor them.
Having thus performed that devotion, by whatever merit has been accomplished by me,
may I become the pacifier of all the sufferings of all sentient beings.
May I be the medicine for those who are sick, and may I be the physician and their attendant as well,
for as long as there is sickness in existence.
May I dispel the suffering of hunger and thirst by raining down food and drink;
during the intermediate kalpas of famine, may I become food and drink myself.
May I become an inexhaustible treasure for sentient beings who are destitute,
and may I stand before them in the form of various useful articles.
I relinquish my own bodies, as well as enjoyments and all merit belonging to the three times, without regard for myself, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings.
Nirvana consists in the relinquishment of everything, and my mind seeks nirvana;
if I must relinquish all things, it is better that they be given to sentient beings.
I shall act so as to make myself happy; let those who are victorious strike me, revile me constantly, or scatter dust upon me.
Let them play with my body, laugh, and sport;
I have given my body to them—why should I worry otherwise?
And let them perform whatever actions bring them happiness;
may no misfortune ever befall anyone by taking me as their object of refuge.
For those whose minds become either angry or serene by taking me as their object,
I alone shall be the cause for the perpetual accomplishment of all their aims.
Those who would revile me, and others who do me harm, as well as those who mock me—
may they all partake in enlightenment.
I am the protector of the protectorless, the caravan leader for those traveling,
the boat for those desiring to reach the further shore, and both the bridge and the causeway.
May I be a lamp for those seeking a lamp, a bed for those seeking a bed,
and a servant for all embodied beings who seek a servant.
May I become for embodied beings a wish-fulfilling gem, a vessel of fortune, a perfected spell, a great medicinal herb, a kalpa-tree, and a cow of plenty.
The elements, beginning with earth, serve as various kinds of enjoyments for immeasurable beings dwelling throughout the entirety of space.
In this way, for the realm of sentient beings who abide in space, may I be their source of sustenance in manifold ways until all have attained nirvana.
Just as the Bodhicitta was previously taken up by the Sugatas of old,
so too do those [disciples] abide in the stages of the Bodhisattva training in due succession.
In that same way, I generate this bodhicitta for the welfare of the world;
and in that very same way, I shall train in those precepts in due order.
Today my birth has become fruitful; the wealth of the essence has been well-attained.
Today I am born into the family of the Buddhas; I am now a son of the Buddha.
Therefore, I must now act in a manner befitting my own family,
so that no stain may fall upon this stainless lineage.
Just as a blind man might obtain a jewel from among deadly *kalakūṭa* poisons,
so too has this bodhicitta arisen within me from some unknown source.
This elixir has arisen for the destruction of death in the world;
it is an inexhaustible treasure that pacifies the poverty of the world.
This is the supreme medicine that pacifies the diseases of the world;
it is the tree of rest for the world weary from wandering in the ocean of existence.
He is a common bridge for all sinners to cross over from miserable rebirths;
he is the risen moon of the mind that cools the fever of the world's afflictions.
It is the great sun that dispels the darkness of ignorance in the world;
it has arisen as the fresh butter produced from churning the milk of the true Dharma.
For this caravan of people wandering in the ocean of existence, who are hungry for the enjoyment of happiness,
this vessel of bliss has indeed arrived to satisfy all beings who have come as guests.
Today I have invited the world with the state of a Sugata and with happiness in the interim;
indeed, before all the Protectors, may the gods, asuras, and others rejoice!
Therefore, whatever suffering I have caused to those of great compassion by bringing grief to living beings, I now confess that sin; may those sages forgive me for having troubled them.
Today, for the sake of propitiating the Tathāgatas, I enter the world as a slave unto all beings;
let the multitudes of people place their feet upon my head or even strike me down—may the Lord of the World be pleased.
I go for refuge to you alone, the sage, the sole kinsman of all living beings even at the cost of their own lives, the one friend, the sole teacher, the singular guru,
and the protector of those creatures who have wandered into the cavernous depths of the three worlds' afflictions.
The teacher, the sovereign lord of reality, regarding the subject of the ultimate truth.
I believe my very being has now been purified by the waters of merit arising from prostration to the Teacher— waters as stainless as the mass of moonlight from the full-orbed moon.
Who are you, who, having bowed down to one whose heart is gladdened by profound compassion?
Having crossed over the river of intense misfortune, which causes despair, one has not yet reached the cessation of suffering.
Therefore, I declare my own intention: I would rather endure to dwell even in this entire cycle of existence, though it be terrifying and fearsome, yet adorned by the Lord of the World;
but I would never, for even a single moment, remain in a world devoid of a Perfectly Awakened One, even if it were the city of the gods.
In which the festivals of merit were plundered by hordes of Rākṣasas whose conduct was characterized by upsurging violence.

Therefore, as long as this entire world has not yet fallen into the pit of negligence— which is opened wide by the vows of false views— while the sun of the teachings of the Omniscient One has not yet set, one should partake of the elixir of his words.
Since even minds defiled by the habituation to evil attain purity— like waters at the end of the rainy season— by relying on spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*),
one should therefore always resort to the festive joy of meeting with true friends.
Those who desire the glorious perfection of faultless virtues must serve holy beings;
having thus resolved, I shall exert effort for the sake of practicing the training as it has been taught.
For how can there be health for one who is curable by medicine yet deviates from the physician’s instruction?
Having heard what was thus related by that lord of the asuras,
the Lord of the World looked at Bali and spoke as follows.
Excellent, excellent, Great King! If you thus desire the vow, then compose your mind and guard the training with diligent effort.
One who wishes to guard the training should strive to guard the mind;
for one who does not guard the flickering mind, it is impossible to guard the training.
Untamed rutting elephants do not cause such agony here as that which the elephant of the mind causes once it is unleashed in the Avīci hell and other realms.
If the elephant of the mind is bound on all sides with the rope of mindfulness,
all fear has come to an end and all that is auspicious has arrived.
Tigers, lions, elephants, bears, snakes, and all enemies;
all the guardians of hell, as well as ḍākinīs and rākṣasas.
All these become bound through the binding of the single mind;
likewise, all become tamed through the taming of the single mind.
For it has been declared by all the lords of sages that all fears and even various kinds of sufferings arise from the mind alone.
Therefore, having concentrated the mind and being mindful, one should protect it with effort;
for from the mind alone do fear and well-being arise in every circumstance.
By whom were the weapons in hell diligently fashioned?
By whom was the floor of glowing iron made, and from where did those women arise?
The Victors have declared that all this arises from a sinful mind;
therefore, there is nothing more terrifying in the three worlds than the mind.
If the perfection of generosity were accomplished by the former Protectors, why is the world still impoverished even today? (Gkv 115)
When the mind of all beings intends the relinquishment of one's entire possession together with its fruit, that is declared the perfection of giving; therefore, it is indeed the mind itself.
Where could fish and other creatures be taken so that they would not kill those who are bowed down [in surrender]?
But when the mind of non-violence is attained, it is considered the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
How many wicked people, who are like the sky, shall I slay?
When the mind of anger is slain, all enemies are slain.
Where would there be enough leather to cover the entire earth? By merely the leather of a sandal, the whole world is covered.
All external phenomena likewise cannot be prevented anywhere;
having restrained one's own mind alone, what is the use of restraining other things?
Or rather, even with both bodies and wealth, the fruit of that is inferior conduct;
whereas for even a single sharp mind, there is the state of Brahmahood and so forth.
The All-Knowing One has declared that all recitations and austerities, even those performed over a long period of time, are in vain if performed with a distracted or dull mind.
Those who have not cultivated this secret of the mind— the entire essence of the Dharma— wander in vain through the sky, seeking to destroy suffering and attain happiness.
Therefore, one's own mind should always be well-established and carefully guarded;
apart from the vow of guarding the mind, what is the use of many other vows?
Just as one standing among the fickle protects a wound with care,
so should one standing among the wicked always protect the wound of the mind.
May your gains perish at will, as may honor, body, and life;
may all other merit perish, but never your mind.
For one whose mind lacks clear comprehension, that which has been heard, reflected upon,
and cultivated does not remain in memory, like water in a leaking jar.
Even many who are learned, and even those devoted to faith and diligence,
become defiled by transgressions due to the fault of lack of clear comprehension.
Those who follow the thief of non-attention and the theft of mindfulness,
even after having accumulated merits, are robbed and go to an evil rebirth.
This host of thieves that are the afflictions seeks an opportunity for entry;
once it finds an opening, it robs and destroys the life of the good rebirth.
Therefore, mindfulness should never be removed from the gateway of the mind;
even if it has departed, it should be reinstated by recollecting the suffering caused by evil deeds.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess unimpeded power in all respects;
everything is foremost for them, and I too stand before them.
Having meditated thus and remaining in that state, endowed with modesty and reverence,
may the recollection of the Buddha also arise within you again and again.
Clear comprehension arises then, and having arisen, it does not depart again,
when mindfulness stands guard at the gateway of the mind for the sake of protection.
Thus, O Great King, practice the vow of the conduct of awakening;
having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, worship them, constantly recollecting them.
By the ripening of this merit, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva will certainly become one who has purified the three spheres and possesses great supernormal knowledge.
Then, having fulfilled all the perfections in due order and having utterly conquered the wicked Māras, may you become a sovereign of the qualities of the true Dharma.
A vessel for the virtues and glory of the True Dharma, upholding the welfare of all sentient beings,
may you become prosperous upon attaining the Great Vidyā of the Six Syllables.
Then, having conquered all the hosts of Māra, the wise one, who had mastered his senses as an Arhat, attained perfect enlightenment and reached the state of a fully awakened Buddha.
Then you will be the Tathāgata, the Jina, named Asurendraśrī—
the King of Dharma, the Lord of the World, the Omniscient One, the Arhat, and the Sovereign of Sages.
You shall become the sovereign of all sciences, the Teacher, the possessor of great supernormal knowledge, the Guide, the glorious Samantabhadra, and a mine of virtues.
All these gods there, those disciples who have conquered their senses,
shall become free from afflictions, pure in soul, and doers of good.
Then, throughout your Buddha-field, O Lord of Munis,
the active manifestation of the afflictions shall never occur at any time.
Having understood this, O Lord of Asuras, compose yourself;
having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, proceed for the welfare of the world.
The merit born from the conduct of awakening is never exhausted;
it always yields its fruit until the attainment of perfect enlightenment and nirvana.
The merit arising from the conduct of awakening cannot be measured even by all the lords of sages;
how indeed could it be measured by me alone?
Therefore, with every effort, having desisted from association with the afflictions and having rendered service to the Three Jewels, practice the vow of the conduct of awakening.
If you practice in this way, O King, you shall never fall into an unfortunate rebirth;
always born into a fortunate state, you will be a prosperous Bodhisattva.
Having accomplished the welfare of yourself and others, may you always enjoy happiness,
rejoicing in the true bliss attained through the virtues and glory of the sublime Dharma.
Having gone before the Lord of Jinas, Amitābha, in Sukhāvatī,
you shall behold him, go for refuge, and worship him with constant devotion.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, he— becoming an abode of the glorious qualities of a Perfectly Awakened One—
will attain the state of a Perfectly Awakened One and reach perfect nirvana.

Having heard these instructions from the Lord of the World, who possesses a virtuous mind, as taught in the scripture for the world, even that lord of the asuras rejoiced in the accomplishment of awakening.
Then Bali, the lord of the Daityas, being filled with joy, honored that sovereign lord of the worlds with the magnificent riches and hospitality of a great king.
Then, having bowed at his lotus feet with palms joined in reverence and being fully propitiated,
he made a vow for supreme enlightenment and spoke again as follows:
Oh, what a field composed of virtues, entirely free from all defects!
For the seed sown here today bears fruit this very day.
As long as all living beings have not yet become Bodhisattvas,
so long shall I practice the vow of enlightenment for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
O Protector, for the welfare of the world, I generate the mind set on supreme enlightenment;
I invite all the world and shall liberate it from poverty.
From this day forward, until I attain nirvāṇa, I shall no longer harbor a mind of malice, nor any wicked intent characterized by envy, stinginess, or ill-will.
I shall practice the holy life; I shall cast off evil bodily actions.
I will train myself in accordance with the Buddhas in the restraint and discipline of ethical conduct.
I do not strive to attain awakening in a hurried manner;
rather, for the sake of sentient beings, I wish to remain until the very end of existence.
I shall purify immeasurable fields in every direction,
and I shall make my name renowned throughout the ten directions.
I shall purify my actions of body, speech, and mind in every way;
having established them upon the path to enlightenment, I shall cause the world to practice what is wholesome.
Having made offerings to the Three Jewels until I have attained nirvāṇa,
and having maintained the vow of the conduct of awakening, I shall bring about the welfare of the world.
"O Teacher, this is my firm resolve; may you therefore be well-pleased with me.
Having obtained your grace, I am now truly a bodhisattva."
Having heard what was thus spoken, the Lord of the World was pleased;
seeing that Bali had been awakened, he instructed him once more as follows.
If your mind is thus firmly resolved upon the vow of the conduct of awakening, I shall speak for the sake of your welfare; listen to that with a concentrated mind.
He who has a desire for merit should always worship the Victors;
by that, he acquires the merit that accomplishes the qualities of perfect enlightenment.
He who has a longing for knowledge should listen to this supreme yoga;
from that, he attains the knowledge that accomplishes the state of perfect awakening.
Whoever has a desire for a particular enjoyment should perform the desired gift;
from that, the wished-for object of enjoyment, endowed with prosperity and virtues, is obtained.
He who has a desire for heaven should maintain virtuous conduct;
from that, he obtains divine and great happiness, which is the abode of glorious qualities.
One who desires eloquence must also show reverence toward the guru;
by that means, one will surely attain even greater eloquence.
Even by one who seeks to maintain [the body], selflessness should be cultivated;
through that, liberation is attained from the bonds of wandering in existence.
One who seeks happiness must abandon the inclination toward sinful deeds;
by doing so, one attains a most auspicious happiness free from affliction.
One who desires the welfare of sentient beings should also maintain the mind set on enlightenment;
by thus accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, supreme enlightenment is attained.
One who desires a beautiful voice must indeed speak only the truth;
by that, one becomes a speaker of truth with a beautiful voice and right understanding.
Even one who seeks pure qualities should serve a true spiritual teacher;
through that, one becomes enriched with the glory of the perfection of excellent virtues.
Therefore, one who delights in calm abiding (śamatha) should practice associating with the virtuous;
likewise, even one who seeks insight (vipaśyanā) should contemplate the emptiness of the self.
For in this way, there would be the complete pacification of all defects within existence.
Even by one who seeks the world of Brahmā, the state of abiding as Brahmā must be maintained; having attained that through it, the supreme goal is reached.
Even by one who seeks the glory of a king among men, the ten forms of skillful means (daśakauśalya) must be maintained;
through them, the splendor of the sovereignty of the lord of gods is certainly attained.
Even by one who seeks complete nirvāṇa, the application of knowledge must be performed;
for by that very means, having conquered all Māras, one shall attain perfect enlightenment.
One who seeks the qualities of enlightenment should also serve the Three Jewels;
by doing so, having attained the mind of enlightenment, one shall reach the state of nirvana.

Having understood this, O Lord of Daityas, which is the means for achieving the happiness of the true Dharma, I have declared what is for your benefit; having comprehended it, you may choose whether you wish to uphold it.
Having desisted from association with non-Buddhist sectarians, take refuge in the Three Jewels;
having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, proceed for the welfare of the world.
By doing thus, O Lord of Asuras, you shall become a Bodhisattva, a son of the Victors, a Mahāsattva, one possessing great supernormal knowledges, and the sovereign of all worlds.
Thus, he who practices here with a mind untroubled by afflictions will not wander upon the wrong path, attached to the qualities of Māra’s conduct.
Then, having excessively afflicted himself and being addicted to the ten unwholesome actions, he will act again without hesitation in terrible, extreme transgressions.
Then that person of extremely wicked nature, tormented by the heat of dreadful suffering,
with his limbs scorched by the fire of unbearable afflictions and passion, suffers intensely.
At that time, there will not be even a single good friend or protector for him;
thus, afflicted by a very long illness, he will die with great suffering.
Then, having been bound and threatened by a messenger of Yama, he will be led away;
there, he shall see all the wicked and terrifying beings everywhere.
He would see trees terrifying with garlands of blazing flames,
and the fearsome river Vaitaraṇī, filled with pus and blood.
Seeing them, he became terrified, distressed, and dejected in mind;
bewildered and despondent, he stood there, afflicted by fear and despair.
Then those messengers of Yama, having bound him with the nooses of Time,
would forcibly and swiftly lead him along a path as sharp as the edge of a razor.
Crows, vultures, owls, and other birds, as well as dogs and jackals, would devour the flesh torn from his feet and even drink his blood.
Furthermore, having been born again in this way, he will be shattered;
thus he shall experience great agony in hell.
Then, having brought him down and bound him once more, those servants of Yama would make him traverse here and there along a path covered with sharp thorns.
On each of his soles, five hundred extremely sharp thorns shall pierce him from every side.
There, unable to walk and tormented by intense pain, he cried out as he paced back and forth, "What sin have I committed? and wept aloud.
Having heard that, those messengers of Yama— red-eyed and with terrifying faces—
then brought that wicked man down and spoke thus in his presence:
O sinner, why do you grieve thus now?
For whatever action has been performed must necessarily be experienced as its fruit.
Indeed, you are experiencing here the fruit of that evil deed which was committed by you;
for if no evil deed had been committed, you would not experience its fruit here.
Dharma does not exist for you at all, nor is there anyone here to protect you;
Dharma alone is the friend and protector of all who wander through existence.
Since you, being stained by passion, have transgressed the words of the true guru and committed many sins out of affection for evil friends.
Even after killing many living beings, you have eaten with delight;
and having taken it by force, you have consumed property that was not given.
Afflicted by the disease of delighting in unrighteousness, they have even enjoyed the wives of others;
for the sake of fame, life, and wealth, they have uttered false speech.
Through your slanderous speech, you have caused a rift among friends; by your divisive prattle, you have instigated a state of enmity and conflict in the world.
Having reviled them with harsh words, even the virtuous were insulted by you;
out of greed for the property of others, your mind was afflicted by craving.
Even malice conceived toward virtuous ones and Arhats,
or any harm done to oneself or others through wrong view or negligence, [is abandoned].
Thus, by you— who are conceited on account of various kinds of afflictions—
having enjoyed yourself as you pleased and wandered about according to your desire,
only evil has been accomplished; not a single thing of dharma has been achieved.
Having merely enjoyed objects of pleasure at will with delight,
you have thus acquired the cause of suffering, like a beast that has played.
Your mind was never encouraged toward the practice of the true Dharma;
therefore, O evil-souled one, you have experienced such great suffering right here.
Nor have you given any desired wealth to those who sought it;
even upon seeing the bodies of others, your mind was defiled by anger.
You possess no moral discipline whatsoever, nor do you have any self-restraint;
you have not cultivated patience, even toward suffering beings.
No festival of honor and devotion was performed for the Buddha’s teaching;
nor, having recollected the Three Jewels, was meditation practiced for the benefit of the world.
Even though you have cultivated wisdom, it has not served to accomplish the qualities of the True Dharma;
nor did you rejoice even upon seeing the stupas and images of the Three Jewels,
and you performed no act of honor or veneration whatsoever.
Even though they have performed circumambulations, offered prostrations,
remembered [the name], or even uttered it, no auspicious merit has been accomplished.
Never at any time have you heard the preaching of the True Dharma anywhere,
nor have you ever performed an act of honor toward the Saṅgha.
And you have never heard the sound of the Dharma-gong;
your mind has never at any time yearned for even the slightest bit of the Dharma.
Therefore, you have certainly now experienced this terrible suffering;
for whatever action is performed by whomsoever, its fruit is experienced by that very person.
Having heard what they had said, that sinner was deeply distressed;
weeping before them, he spoke thus while sighing slowly.
At that time, I lacked faith in the Dharma and was indifferent to the virtues of the Three Jewels; through the instruction of evil friends, I was constantly engaged in evil deeds.
Therefore, you should forgive my offenses out of compassion;
I must be protected by you in every way, even though I am but a mother.
Having heard that request of his, all those servants of Yama shall bind him and lead him suddenly before King Yama.
Seeing him brought before him, King Yama,
beholding all those kinnaras, would suddenly instruct them thus:
Why has this most wicked and evil-minded man been brought here before me?
For I do not wish even to look upon the face of this sinner.
Go, and even after having bound him thus, display your own skill;
lead him quickly to that place where the fruit of his actions is to be experienced.
Having heard this command from the king, those Yama-kinnaras bound him and led him away abruptly to the most dreadful Kālasūtra hell.
Having hurled hundreds of spears, they would strike his body in many ways.
Thus, even though he was pierced in many ways by hundreds of spears,
he endured unbearable agony but did not give up his life while still alive.
Nevertheless, seeing that great villain still alive, they shall bind him, cast him into the midst of a pit of fire, and cause him to be consumed by flames.
Nevertheless, that sinner would not give up his life;
even though all his limbs were scorched, he remained there, gasping and bewildered.
Nevertheless, seeing him still not released from darkness, those servants of Yama would cast a red-hot iron ball into his mouth for him to consume.
By that [fire], his face, lips, tongue, teeth, throat, heart, mantras, and qualities are burned; even his entire body is consumed.
Then, his body consumed by fire, that sinner will abandon that physical basis and,
having obtained birth in another hell, shall experience suffering in this manner.
In the same way, O Great King, all those who practice the ten unwholesome deeds—
those sinful and wicked ones— experience agony in hell.
At that time, there is no savior whatsoever for them there in hell;
as long as their karma is not exhausted, so long shall they experience suffering on all sides.
Merit alone is the friend and protector for one wandering through all states of existence;
the sinful dwell in hell, while the meritorious indeed dwell in heaven.
Therefore, O King, having understood this, those who desire the welfare of cyclic existence must indeed perform meritorious deeds alone, in order to destroy suffering and attain happiness.
Through merit one is born somewhere, never at all in an evil state;
always born in a good rebirth, they become abodes of glory and virtue.
He shall be meritorious, possessed of fortune, illustrious, virtuous, intelligent, and accomplished;
he shall be proficient in all sciences and arts, and a sustainer of the welfare of all sentient beings.
One who is virtuous, self-controlled, steadfast, patient, energetic, powerful,
endowed with the qualities of meditative concentration, and wise, shall become the sovereign of all phenomena.
Having attained the thought of awakening, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, who bears the welfare of all sentient beings,
accomplishes the qualities of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, one should proceed for the welfare of the world.
Then that compassionate one, whose nature is mercy, having purified the three spheres,
being free from afflictions and an Arhat, shall attain the threefold awakening and reach nirvana.
Having understood this, O Indra among kings, if you desire perfect awakening,
desist from association with heretics and practice the vow of the conduct of awakening.
Having brought benefit to all sentient beings and maintained the four divine abodes,
and having rendered worship to the Three Jewels, accomplish the sublime jewel of merit.
If merit is accomplished in this way, you will indeed become one possessed of great supernatural power;
having attained the jewel of the True Dharma, you shall become the sovereign of the three worlds.
Having heard this instruction from Lokeśvara, Bali, being thus enlightened, replied "So be it" and rejoiced.
Then that lord of the Daityas, being delighted, honored his preceptor— the sovereign of the three worlds— with great royal splendor and hospitable offerings.
One should present as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) necklaces of pearls, gems, and other ornaments, which are radiant with divine jewels and adorned with crowns and earrings.
Then, having performed circumambulations with palms joined in reverence and filled with great joy,
he bowed at his lotus-like feet, gazed upon him, and spoke as follows.
O Blessed One, Sovereign Lord of the World, by the grace of your compassion,
my very self has now certainly become purified.
O Lord of the World, from this day forth I take refuge in you;
having honored the Three Jewels, I shall proceed within the vow of awakening.
Therefore, bestowing your grace upon me, you ought to look upon me always in this way;
having forgiven my transgression, protect me like a son.
Having relied upon this very [teaching], you have perfectly taught the True Dharma;
having bestowed your favor upon us, you ought to be victorious forever.
When he had thus petitioned him, the Lord of the World, the Great Being, the Master of the Universe, looked at that powerful one and commanded him as follows:
(I shall not remain here forever, for I have much work to do; therefore,
I am in the Jetavana park, in the monastery, the hermitage of the Sugata.)
There may even be gatherings of the worlds including the gods and asuras.
There, I wish to see that Lord of the Three Worlds, the Sage of the Universe, the Fully Awakened One; therefore, I shall go there now.
Having acted in accordance with reality as it has been fully understood, and remaining composed, uphold the vow of the conduct of awakening and always proceed happily in virtue.
Having heard this instruction given by the Teacher, Bali respectfully replied,
"So be it," and rejoiced in that Lord.
Thus that Lord of the Three Worlds, Lokeśvara, the Son of the Victor,
having instructed Bali, departed from there, illuminating the world.
Seeing him approaching, that lord of the asuras, together with his attendants,
bowed with palms joined from afar and, gazing [at him], went toward his own abode.
From that time forth, this lord of the asuras, undertaking the vow of the conduct of awakening and honoring the Three Jewels, has always acted for the welfare of the world.
All his people, too, were devoted to honoring the Three Jewels;
likewise, having undertaken the vow of awakening, they always practiced what was auspicious.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, all those present in the assembly, desiring the true Dharma and being thus awakened, rejoiced greatly.
Thus ends the chapter on the introduction to the path of enlightenment through the awakening of Bali.
10. The Chapter on Awakening the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas of the Ground of Darkness and Leading Them into the True Dharma.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, the son of the Sugata, having bowed again to the Blessed One with palms joined, spoke thus:
O Blessed One, when will that Lord of the World, the son of the Conquerors who possesses great supernormal knowledge, arrive here? And how shall he be beheld by me?
O Teacher, even after drinking the nectar of your virtues, I am not yet satisfied;
for I desire to see you directly— when will he [the Buddha] appear in this world?
That Lord of the Sovereigns of the Three Worlds, having awakened even the Dānavas who were difficult to subdue through his exertion, established them upon the path to enlightenment.
Indeed, such great power belongs to him alone; for no one else possesses it, not even by all the Lords of Sages, which cannot be measured at all.
Furthermore, I desire to drink once more that supreme nectar of his virtues;
therefore, may you, being satisfied, deign to instruct me within.
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
looked toward Viṣkambhin and instructed him once again as follows:
Listen, O virtuous one of great being, to the great qualities of Lokeśvara;
I shall further explain them to you for the sake of all that is auspicious.
Then, having emerged from the palace of the lord of the Daityas, that son of the Jina proceeded elsewhere,
gladdening beings as he rescued them.
Then that Lord of the World, possessing great supernormal knowledge, emitted various rays born of his own merit and illuminated the world of living beings.
The rays of that [light], having illuminated the worlds of the universe,
were extended and stood before Viśvabhū, the Lord of Sages, in the Jetavana grove.
Then, in that Jeta Grove, there appeared lakes filled with water endowed with the eight qualities, enchanting to the mind.
They were beautifully adorned, filled with divine golden lotuses and the like;
there were many wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa) hung with all kinds of ornaments,
and beautified by hanging necklaces of jewels, gems, pearls, and other precious things.
They were draped with garments and ornaments such as Kāśika silk, fine cloth, and woven fabrics; their pillars were red like coral, and they were adorned with plates of gold and silver.
Numerous flowering trees, fruit-bearing trees, and so forth,
as well as all the great medicinal herbs, appeared everywhere on every side.
Then, fragrant flowers and divine golden blossoms fell from the sky upon that grove and monastery.
Thus, having beheld that great and wonderful omen arisen from that auspiciousness, they all stood there filled with amazement.
Then the bodhisattva named Gaganagañja, filled with wonder,
arose to inquire about that great and auspicious miracle.
Standing before the Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū,
he prostrated at his lotus feet and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke thus.
"Lord, whose radiance of merit is this that has come?
From where has it appeared here, performing such a beautiful and wonderful marvel?"
Therefore, you ought to instruct all these people gathered in this assembly,
enlightening the world regarding the Dharma and bringing them joy.
When he had thus made his earnest request, the Blessed One, the Victorious Viśvabhū,
looked toward Gaganagañja and spoke to him once more as follows:
Emerging from that palace of Bali, this Lord of the World proceeds forth to protect sentient beings in the realm of blinding darkness.
This Puṇyaraśmi of that Lokeśvara has illuminated the world everywhere and has been extended here as well.
Therefore, O noble son, this auspicious rite arises;
having rescued sentient beings therein, that Lord of the World shall come forth.
Then, O son of noble family, having beheld that Lord of the Sovereigns of the Three Worlds who has arrived here, bow down and propitiate him with reverence.
Having heard these instructions given by the Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū,
Gaganagañja looked at that sage and spoke as follows.
How does that Blessed One travel upon that earth of blinding darkness,
where the radiance of the sun and moon is nowhere perceived?
Even there, he goes to uplift those living beings who are to be saved;
having observed how and for what purpose they dwell, where does the Son of the Conqueror abide?
When he had spoken thus, the Teacher Viśvabhū, that Lord of Sages,
looked toward Gaganagañja and instructed him once more as follows:
In that place as well, noble sons, there is a virtuous one named Varada,
a great jewel like a wish-fulfilling gem, possessing glorious splendor like the sun.
There, many thousands of yakṣas and even rākṣasas dwell,
moving about at their own will and enjoying pleasures according to their desires.
Seeing those wicked ones who were arrogant due to their afflictions, that treasury of compassion exerted effort to awaken them and cause them to practice excellent restraint.
Emitting the rays of his own merit and illuminating all directions,
he enters like the full moon, gladdening the world.
Touched by those rays, all those yakṣas and rākṣasas,
having attained great bliss, remained filled with wonder.
Then, seeing him approaching, radiant with glorious splendor, they were all filled with joy and came before him;
bowing with palms joined in reverence, they delightedly prostrated at his lotus-like feet.
Approaching before him, they questioned him thus with great respect.
O Blessed One, may you not be weary or exhausted in body;
is all well everywhere, and have you been away for a long time?
Having heard what was thus spoken by them, that son of the Conqueror, the Lord of the World,
looked upon all those who were seated nearby and spoke as follows.
I have many tasks to accomplish for the sake of achieving the welfare of sentient beings;
therefore, it is only now, after a very long time, that I have come here.
Indeed, my own person was not brought to fulfillment for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of a single being alone;
rather, it was perfected for the sake of accomplishing the true Dharma for all beings in the world.
Having beheld all sentient beings and awakened them through diligent effort,
I shall establish them on the path to enlightenment and send them to Sukhāvatī.
Therefore, I have now come here after a very long time;
my physical form is not intended for the accomplishment of the purpose of a single being alone.
For indeed, having observed all sentient beings, I have diligently brought them to enlightenment so that they might accomplish the true Dharma for the sake of the world and its beings.
Having established them on the path to enlightenment, they should be sent to Sukhāvatī.
Therefore, consider this: even after a very long time, I shall come to you for the sake of accomplishing your welfare once I have found the proper means; it shall not be otherwise.
Having heard this instruction given by that Lord of the World in the form of the *Jagacchāstra*,
they all joyfully spoke thus in his very presence.
May victory be yours always; may your desired aim be accomplished.
Looking upon us all with compassion, you ought to protect us forever in this way.
Having spoken thus, they all, with serene eyes, established him— the lord of the three qualities— upon a seat of gold and jewels, and bowing low, made this request:
O Blessed One, Lord of the World, you who accomplish the qualities of true happiness,
it behoves you to graciously teach us the Dharma for our benefit.
When they had thus made their request, that Lord of the World, the son of the Jina,
looked upon all those yakṣas and rākṣasas and commanded them as follows:
Excellent! Composing your minds, listen with reverence;
for your benefit, I shall speak the noble *Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra*.
Those who shall joyfully hear this king of Mahāyāna sūtras,
and having heard it, those who shall always uphold and recite it;
And those who shall master it, as well as those who shall write it down,
and those who shall cause it to be written, and those who shall always cultivate it.
And those who shall set it forth and cause others to hear it,
who, having always rejoiced in it and remembered it with mindfulness, also pay homage and devote themselves to it.
And those who shall always worship with faith at all times,
and those who shall always honor them with respect and due reverence;
Their merit is incalculable, immeasurable, and exceedingly great;
it is the means for accomplishing the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha, which possesses the glory of true virtues and supreme bliss.
All the Sugatas, who are omniscient, and even all the Lords of Munis at all times,
would not be able to measure the extent of this merit.
Furthermore, suppose that even all the young men dwelling in the four continents were each to erect a stupa made of gold and jewels.
All those men dwelling in the four continents would deposit precious relics within all those stupas.
Whatever great mass of merit, most noble and supreme, they may possess,
the merit born from the Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra is indeed even greater than that.
Just as the great rivers, carrying full waters, flow toward the ocean with their thousandfold retinues; so do they proceed.
In this very way, the great merit born from the Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra always flows forth abundantly through hearing, worship, and other such acts.
Knowing this to be a source of great merit, if you so desire,
all of you should abandon evil thoughts and listen to this well-spoken teaching.
Having heard, rejoiced in, honored, and respected [this] with constant devotion,
you shall indeed become sons of the Victors, anointed by this merit.
Having heard this instruction given by him, the Teacher of the World, they—
All those rākṣasas and yakṣas, being delighted, spoke as follows.
And as for those who have this king of Mahāyāna sūtras copied, O Light of the World— tell me, what merit would they possess?
When they had spoken thus, that Bodhisattva Lokeśa, the son of the Conqueror,
perceiving them all to be joyful, looked upon them and commanded this:
Noble sons, immeasurable merit arises for those who write this king of sutras themselves, as well as for those who cause others to write it.
If one were to have all eighty-four thousand aggregates of the true Dharma written down by them, the merit of those [who write them] would be even greater.
They will become kings, lords of men, universal monarchs (cakravartins);
they will be most righteous, sustainers of the world, radiant, steadfast, and wise.
And those who, having constantly recollected the name of this king of Mahāyāna sūtras, devote themselves to it with serene faith;
They were all liberated from the sufferings of existence, possessing pure intentions; free from afflictions, with perfect limbs, and their mouths fragrant with incense.
Their limbs shall be fragrant with sandalwood, and they shall possess excellent vigor, strength, and speed;
remembering their past lives, devoted to the Dharma, they shall become the abode of glory and virtue.
Thinking thus of this great merit, if you desire these qualities, then,
having desisted from the attachments of the afflictions, remain joyful with a completely pure intention.
Always, having recollected the name of this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of sutras, venerate it with faith and respect.
Then, liberated from the extreme suffering of the afflictions of existence, you—
free from defilements and pure in nature— shall go to Sukhāvatī.
There, having always drunk the nectar of the Dharma from the Lord Amitābha and having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, you shall become sons of the Victors.
Then, being the locus of the excellence of glory that brings about the welfare of sentient beings and the foundation of true virtues,
and having accomplished the benefit of all sentient beings, you shall attain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having thus fully understood this truth, those of pure intention and conquered senses,
having rendered service to the Three Jewels, should likewise honor these well-spoken words.
Having heard what was thus spoken, all those yakṣas and rākṣasas,
awakened by great enthusiasm, moved about with such reverence.
Then, some become followers by faith and followers by dharma;
others are stream-enterers, and still others are once-returners.
Others who were non-returners became engaged in the accomplishment of awakening;
consequently, all those yakṣas and rākṣasas were filled with joy.
Having attained what was taught by him, they become practitioners of celibacy;
and having performed what is beneficial for others, they always proceed toward auspiciousness.
Then, all of them, being delighted, bowed again to that Lord of the Three Qualities with palms joined in reverence and made this request with great respect:
O Blessed One, having awakened us, please fully teach the True Dharma;
dwell forever right here and do not go elsewhere.
"Having constructed a stūpa made of gold and jewels, we shall offer it to you here;
and we shall perform a chariot procession for the Lord of the World."
Always remaining in your refuge and joyfully drinking the nectar of the Dharma,
we shall practice the means of accomplishing the true Dharma and dwell in happiness and purity.
Having heard this request made by all of them, that Lord of the World then looked upon all those rākṣasas and yakṣas and commanded them thus:
I shall not remain here forever, but practicing likewise even here,
I will awaken other beings and establish them in the excellent restraint.
Therefore, all of you, having maintained this as it has been taught by me,
and having always practiced the Dharma, remain free from worldly existence.
Having heard this instruction from the Teacher, those yakṣas and rākṣasas,
afflicted by the intense suffering of separation from him, spoke thus to one another:
"Sirs, this Lord of the World, the Master of the universe, will depart;
therefore, we shall all be deprived of the True Dharma."
Having spoken thus, they all prostrated at the lotus-feet of that Lord of the Three Realms and remained there, taking refuge.
Then that Lord of the Three Worlds, the Sovereign of the World and Son of the Victor,
having addressed them all, set out and proceeded from there.
There, all those rākṣasas and yakṣas, weeping and afflicted by the passion of affection, followed behind as attendants of that Lord of the World.
Seeing that they had all arrived, that compassionate Lord of the World,
observing them from afar as they came along the path, spoke thus:
"You have come from very far; return to your own abodes.
Do not follow me; I shall go to the Śuddhāvāsa, the celestial realm."
When thus commanded by the Teacher of the World, all those yakṣas and rākṣasas bowed at the lotus feet of the Lord of the World and departed for their own abodes.
There, those rākṣasas and yakṣas, having received the command of the Lord of the Three Worlds,
practiced devotion to the Triple Gem and dwelt in the four sublime abodes.
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening and having fixed their aspirations upon perfect enlightenment,
they always move toward what is virtuous, acting for one another's benefit.
In this way, that Lord of the Three Worlds, having even appointed the yakṣas and rākṣasas who are difficult to understand,
causes them to practice the true Dharma by awakening them.
Thus that Lord of the Three Worlds, awakening all sentient beings and establishing them on the path to enlightenment, protects them forever within existence.
Therefore, the exceedingly great mass of merit of this Lord of the Three Worlds is immeasurable; it cannot be measured even by all the Victors.
Therefore, having remembered the name of that Sustainer of the World at all times,
and having uttered it and bowed down, one should perform worship with joy.
Those who always joyfully take refuge in him, even by uttering his name alone, do not go to an evil rebirth; they shall proceed to Sukhāvatī.
There, having taken refuge in the Protector Amitābha and always drinking the nectar of the Dharma, they shall proceed in perfect self-restraint.
Then, having maintained the vow of awakening and having moved about for the welfare of the world, they shall attain the threefold awakening and reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard this instruction given by the Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū,
all those people seated in the assembly, being thus enlightened, rejoiced.
Having heard this instruction given by the Lord of Sages, Śrīghana,
all those people, together with their assemblies, were repeatedly awakened.
Thus ends the chapter on "Awakening the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas of the Ground of Blinding Darkness and Leading Them into the True Dharma."
11. The Chapter on the Rescue of the Śuddhāvāsika Devaputra Sukuṇḍala.
Then that Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, with palms joined in reverence, bowed to Viśvabhū, the Lord of Munis, and spoke again as follows:
Blessed One, when will that great being, the Lord of the World and son of the Conqueror, arrive here? And how may he be seen by me?
Therefore, where has he gone to rescue those who are suffering? It behooves you to instruct us all so that we may be awakened.
When he had thus made his request together with Gaganagañja,
Viśvabhū, the king of sages, looked at him and commanded as follows:
Then, like the fire within a fire-drill that has vanished, he goes forth illuminating the sky and proceeds to the world of the Śuddhāvāsa deities.
There, assuming the form of a brahmin and looking all around,
he behaved like a wretched man among those hosts of gods.
There, a son of the gods named Sukuṇḍala was impoverished;
he was suffering, his self pierced by afflictions, unfortunate, and dejected in mind.
Perceiving this and desiring to rescue him with a mind cultivated through similarity [to his own],
he slowly approached and stood at the door of his house.
Seeing him standing at the gate, Sukuṇḍala asked him: "Who are you, and for what purpose have you come?"
When he had thus questioned him, that Brahmin, desiring wealth and feeling deeply distressed,
sighed and spoke slowly before him while looking at him.
"I am a Brahmin, O illustrious one, who has come here from a distant land;
I am tormented by hunger and thirst, so let food be given to me."
Thus entreated by him, that son of a god, adorned with beautiful earrings,
looking up at him with a piteous voice and weeping, spoke as follows while bowing low.
"O Brahmin, what object will you give? There is nothing at all in my house. Therefore, forgive my offense; I pray that you go elsewhere from here."
Having heard what was said by him, that twice-born man spoke thus to him:
"Something must be given to me, for I am exhausted by hunger and thirst;
if not even a little is given here, I shall meet my death."
Having heard what was thus spoken, the prince Sukuṇḍala entered his house to look for some object and looked about while sighing.
Then, by the power of the compassionate glance of that Sustainer of the World,
great riches of sovereign prosperity arose in that house.
Then, in his house there, within the wood-sheds on all sides,
there were vessels filled with various jewels and all kinds of minerals.
With foods, meals, and substances, even with divine nectars,
and with divine robes, garments, and all manner of ornaments and decorations;
Seeing them filled on all sides with fragrant substances and flowers, his mind was overwhelmed with great wonder.
"Aha! What is this wonder that I behold, or is it a dream?"—thus reflecting, he looked again and pondered in this way.
"Surely this man of great supernormal powers has come to my house;
for by the mere sight of him, such prosperity as this has arisen for me."
Having thus resolved in his mind, that son of the gods was filled with joy;
approaching the brahmin suddenly, he spoke to him with such respect:
Salutations to you, O best of Brahmins! Is there any well-being in your body? Please enter this house of ours; it behoves you to show us favor.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that brahmin was filled with faith;
rising up suddenly, he entered his house, looking all around.
There, that son of the gods, Sukuṇḍala,
with a very serene mind, having established the brahmin upon his own seat, honored him with joy.
Having clothed him in robes of fine silk, cotton, and other soft fabrics,
and having adorned his entire body with all kinds of ornaments and decorations.
With the utmost respect, he feeds [them] with foods that possess the finest divine essences, which are most delicious, like the highest nectar, and sublime in color, fragrance, and taste.
Having observed that hospitality, the brahmin was pleased;
having eaten as much as he desired, he bestowed upon him auspicious blessings.
May there be well-being and auspiciousness for you at all times and in every respect;
may Lakṣmī, who accomplishes the true Dharma, ever abide in your home.
May your mind always be pure and yearning for the true Dharma;
may your aspirations be fulfilled and the accomplishment of worldly activities be attained.

Having always enjoyed this happiness of the attainment of glorious prosperity, which brings about welfare, and having performed worship to the Three Jewels, remain and act with joy in what is auspicious.
I am going to the Sugata’s hermitage in the grove of the sage Jeta;
I long to behold and pay homage to Viśvabhū, the Lord of Sages.
Having heard what was thus spoken, that son of a god was struck with wonder;
looking intently at the brahmin, he questioned him with great respect in this manner.
"O twice-born one, tell me: what is that great garden, the hermitage of the Sugata and the sage Jeta like? And what is that delightful ground like?"
When the son of the gods had thus questioned him,
the brahmin, having heard him and looked upon him, spoke in this way with reverence:
That delightful garden of the sage Jeta was a hermitage of the Sugata,
adorned with various ornaments such as divine gold and jewels.
There, the wish-fulfilling trees produced from a single seed were such that all their flowering trees bore every kind of flower, and all their fruit-bearing branches bore every kind of fruit.
There were also many beautiful lotus ponds, filled with water and endowed with the eight excellent qualities, adorned with various lotuses such as the *padma* and *utpala*.
Therein were Arhats, pure-souled monks, celibate practitioners,
of pure morality, possessing great supernormal powers, worthy of offerings, and wise.
The disciples of the Lord of Munis, Viśvabhū, were practitioners of the path to enlightenment;
they were many bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas possessed of great supernatural powers.
The nuns were celibate, pure in virtue, and had conquered their senses;
there were also those observing the vow of wearing rags, as well as others belonging to the Saṅgha.
The laymen and laywomen were devoted to honoring the Three Jewels;
they had taken refuge in the teaching of Viśvabhū, the Lord of Sages.
Having always drunk the nectar of the Dharma, they dwell in meditative concentration;
so too do other people in the world, as well as brahmins and even those of other sects.
Kings and kṣatriyas, along with their ministers, country-folk, and citizens; guild-leaders, caravan-merchants, and great assemblies of people seeking auspicious merit.
Having come there and taken refuge, and having heard the true Dharma with reverence,
they honor the Triple Gem and always dwell in what is auspicious.
Likewise, the gods, the Daityas, the Gandharvas, and the Kinnaras;
the Yakṣas, the Nāga kings, the Garuḍas, and the Mahoragas.
The Siddhas, the Vidyādharas, and all the lords of the worlds also always assemble there before Viśvabhū, the Teacher of the World.
Having honored and venerated the true Dharma and heard it, they remain with respect.
Thus, the Lord of Munis, Viśvabhū, remaining there while displaying miracles and teaching the sublime Dharma, abides.
Thus, that delightful Jetavana monastery, a field of merit,
was frequented and governed by all the lords of the world.
Therefore, at this time, all the worlds, even the lords of the gods, have come here to hear the True Dharma and remain seated within that assembly.
If you also have the desire, go there from this place with equanimity;
behold the assembly of Viśvabhū, the Lord of Sages, and afterwards hear the Bull [of Dharma].
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma and set your aspiration upon perfect enlightenment,
pay homage to the Three Jewels and practice the vow of the conduct of awakening.
With a self purified by this merit and with the three spheres completely purified,
you shall attain the threefold awakening and reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Thinking thus and having composed yourself, listen to the true Dharma with reverence; having paid homage to the Triple Gem, remain always established in what is virtuous.
Having heard what was thus commanded by him, Sukuṇḍala,
being awakened to the truth, said "So be it," and questioned that brahmin in this manner.
"O twice-born one, you ought to tell me the truth before me:
are you a god, or a human being, or perhaps a lord of the Daityas possessed of great supernatural power?"
No one else possesses such power of compassion and virtue as you do, who, seeing me here, would protect me in this way. Who else could do so?
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that brahmin was moved to faith;
looking toward that son of a god, he spoke these words for the sake of awakening:
I am neither a god, nor a human, nor even a lord of the Daityas;
I am a Bodhisattva, one who accumulates [merit] for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, seeing sentient beings who are deeply suffering,
one should awaken them through effort and establish them in the excellent restraint.
Thus, throughout all worlds, having awakened even those who are suffering and sinful, and seeing for myself, I shall always engage them in what is auspicious.
Thus, having personally beheld them and awakened all sentient beings,
and having established them on the path to enlightenment, I shall go to that hermitage of the Victors.
Having heard what was thus commanded by him, he was filled with joy;
having given him a gift of jewels, he spoke to him in this manner:
Oh, what a field composed of virtues and free from all defects!
Wherein the seed sown today bears fruit this very day.
Blessed are all those people who possess true devotion to the Three Jewels;
having constantly drunk the nectar of the Dharma, they move about for the welfare of the world.
I too shall go to the Jeta Grove, the hermitage of the Victor,
desiring to see that Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū, together with his community of monks.
Therefore, I am eager to go there together with you;
thus, you ought to take me and show me that Lord of Sages.
When he had thus made his request, that brahmin, beholding the son of a god adorned with beautiful earrings, replied in order to instruct him.
Even while seeing and awakening sentient beings elsewhere in the world,
and having established them upon the path to enlightenment, I shall then proceed to that hermitage.
Go first yourself to that Jeta grove forest and show me that lord of sages, seated in his monastery together with his assembly.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma and set your intention upon perfect enlightenment,
and having paid homage to the Three Jewels, always proceed in what is auspicious.
Having spoken thus, that Great Being, the brahmin, departed from there;
in an instant he vanished like fire entering the sky.
Having seen that, the son of a god, his heart filled with joy and wonder,
bowed down and, looking repeatedly toward the sky, returned to his home after a long time.
There, seated in the abode of beings, they remember that Brahmin;
having applied what was taught by him, they remain and move about in auspiciousness.
Having made offerings to the Three Jewels, they always move about in auspiciousness.
Thus that Lord of the Three Worlds, Lokeśvara, the Son of the Conqueror,
having diligently awakened even the gods and gladdened them,
establishes them on the path to enlightenment and conducts himself in this way for the welfare of the world.
Thus, the mass of merit of that Lord of the World has been described by the lords of sages as exceedingly great, immeasurable, and incalculable.
In this regard, those who desire awakening should always worship this Lord of the Three Worlds by recollecting his name, meditating upon him, and prostrating before him.
Those who joyfully take refuge in him do not go to an evil rebirth;
always born in fortunate realms, they eventually go to Sukhāvatī.
There, having always drunk the nectar of the Dharma from the Lord Amitābha and having maintained the vow of the conduct of awakening, they shall go to the abode of the Victors.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, all those present in the assembly, being thus enlightened, replied "So be it" and rejoiced.
Thus ends the chapter on the rescue of the divine son Sukuṇḍala from the Pure Abodes.
12. The Chapter on Awakening and Rescuing the Rākṣasīs of Siṃhaladvīpa.
Then that Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, the son of the Victor, bowed once more to the Lord of Munis, Viśvabhū, and spoke as follows:
Even now, O Blessed One, that Great Being has not arrived here; when will he come? Where is he going at present?
When he had thus questioned him, Viśvabhū, that ocean of nectar,
looked toward Gaganagañja and instructed him further as follows:
Then, illuminating the world, that Lord of the World set forth;
having beheld the island of Siṃhala, the Lord of the World approached the rākṣasīs.
Assuming a divine and exceedingly beautiful form at will, he moves there, illuminating the place and gladdening the hearts of the rākṣasīs.
Upon seeing him arrive, exceedingly handsome and full of mature passion,
a lustful desire arose within all the rākṣasīs.
Then all those women, agitated by passion for the Rākṣasa,
possessed limbs lovely with fresh youth and were exceedingly beautiful like the goddess Rati herself.
Having appeared and beheld him, they approached his presence;
bowing at his lotus-like feet, they spoke thus with great reverence.
Welcome to you; we hope that you are well in every respect.
Beholding us, please satisfy us and deign to show us favor.
Among us young women, there is not even one who ever possesses a master, a husband, a lord, or a protector.
Then may you be our master, supporter, husband, lord, and friend; may you also be our refuge, protector, island, and ultimate resort,
as well as the eternal sanctuary in this world and the guide upon the path of the righteous.
Always remaining in your refuge, we shall all conduct ourselves with joy, maintaining exactly as you have instructed us.
There are various objects of enjoyment here, consisting of the most excellent flavors of divine nectar,
as well as diverse garments and various ornaments.
There were delightful ponds, pleasure gardens, and groves;
as well as charming palaces and beautiful, enchanting oblong lakes.
There are all kinds of substances, various jewels as well,
all types of utensils and articles, and even medicines that are very wholesome.
All these things are always at your disposal;
therefore, having considered them, you ought to grant them as you wish.
Having enjoyed happiness according to his desire, always delighting with us,
moving about as he pleases, may he remain and dwell right here forever.
Having taken refuge in your power, we shall all together fulfill our intentions and conduct ourselves according to our pleasure.
Therefore, you, having become our lord, ought to remain here forever, taking delight in this very place, protecting us who are deeply distressed like a king.
Having made you our vessel, we shall accomplish our desired aim;
therefore, let her remain with her very body here, and let her not go elsewhere anywhere.
Having heard what was thus related by them, the Lord of the World,
beholding all those women, spoke again as follows in their presence.
If you indeed act according to what I have instructed,
then I shall remain under your control and conduct myself here at all times accordingly.
Having enjoyed happiness at your pleasure and always delighting with you,
I shall certainly fulfill all your desires.
Having heard what was thus commanded by him, all those women, upon beholding that beloved man, spoke as follows.
Having heard what you have commanded, how could we not act? Remaining necessarily under your control, we shall do exactly as you have said.
Therefore, having heard our words and having eaten together with us in comfort,
enjoy yourself here as you desire and wander about according to your will.
Having heard what was thus related by them, the Lord of the World,
beholding all those rākṣasīs, spoke as follows to awaken them:
If you will all practice while holding fast to what I have declared, then listen with focused attention; I shall teach you that which is for your benefit.
Having desisted from the ten evils, having maintained the abodes of Brahma,
and having rendered service to the Triple Gem, practice the Poṣadha vow.
If you both always observe this vow with devotion,
then I shall remain here sporting, staying under your control.
Having heard this command given by him, all those women replied, "So be it," and performed exactly so in his presence.
"O Lord, we shall act exactly as you have commanded;
therefore, you ought to instruct us in this very procedure."
Having observed this prayer made by them, that son of the Conqueror,
perceiving that they were all awakened, looked upon them and spoke thus.
Listen, if you always desire this true happiness;
I shall teach you in detail the procedure for the King of Vows.
First, having maintained enthusiasm for merit and happiness with a pure intention and joy,
she bathed at a sacred ford until her limbs were purified, and donned clean robes.
Having honored the true guru and bowed down, they took refuge in the Three Jewels;
having meditated upon the glorious Lokeśvara and worshipped him according to the ritual procedure.
Then, having offered the water for honor (*argha*) and so forth, and having praised [the deity] with words of hymn,
one should bow respectfully with the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*) or perform circumambulations (*pradakṣiṇā*).
Having joyfully presented offerings such as relics, substances, and jewels with faith and reverence,
and having gazed [upon them] with palms joined in prayer, they were filled with delight.
Having confessed misdeeds, having maintained rejoicing in merit,
and having maintained the aspiration for perfect enlightenment, one should pray for the welfare of the world.
Having thus observed this vow constantly on the third day of the fortnight,
and having eaten food that is free from meat, perform the observance of the vow.
Thus, always maintaining meditative concentration and constantly observing this vow,
having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, proceed for the welfare of the world.
By the power of this merit, may those whose three spheres are completely purified always be born in the happy realms, possessing the splendor and virtues of the true Dharma.
Having always enjoyed the six pleasures, free from afflictions and with senses conquered,
and having established goodness everywhere, you shall go to Sukhāvatī.
There, by always drinking the nectar of the Dharma from the Lord Amitābha,
you shall attain the threefold awakening and reach the state of perfect buddhahood.
Knowing thus that great merit arises from the vow of the *poṣadha*,
if you desire constant well-being, then always observe that vow.
Having heard this command of his, all those women—
the Rākṣasīs— were delighted and desired to observe that vow.
Then all those women, even the rākṣasīs, being awakened,
prepared themselves according to the rule and observed the poṣadha vow.
By the power of this merit, may they all become pure in intention,
liberated from the passion of desire, and practitioners of the holy life.
At that time, the minds of all those rākṣasīs were never again afflicted by the afflictions or by the sufferings that snatch them away.
Among them, a mind of malice never arises at any time;
nor does attachment to the ten unwholesome actions arise in anyone.
All those who follow through faith become followers of the Dharma in accomplishing the qualities of the True Dharma;
likewise, those who follow through the Dharma become so once they have attained the vows.
Some attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths through scripture and reached the fourfold path;
others were awakened and attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Likewise, others had attained the fruit of once-returning, and some were engaged in the practice of the true Dharma.

Some had not yet attained arhatship, yet their three spheres were completely purified; others were intent upon the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, while some longed for perfect, complete enlightenment.
Thus, having received that instruction, all those women as well became devoted to the true Dharma, auspicious, and possessed of the mind set on enlightenment.
Thus, through the grace of that Lord of the World, those women were gladdened;
having attained the vows of training, they act for the welfare of the world.
Then, all of them, being delighted, approached that Teacher; bowing with palms joined in reverence, they made this request with great earnestness.
O True Guru, since you yourself have perceived that we are all far astray, you awaken us and enjoin us to the Dharma.
Therefore, you are our teacher, our well-wisher, our friend, and our true guru; having fully taught the sublime Dharma, it is right that you remain here with us.
We all abide in your refuge and follow your instructions;
whatever you have commanded us to do, we shall perform exactly so.
We shall never again adopt the conduct of a rākṣasī;
having undertaken the restraint of the precepts, we shall always practice the vow.
Just as mortals in Jambūdvīpa, having desisted from the ten non-virtues,
live devoted to excellent qualities while enjoying the happiness of conventional reality.
Likewise, having desisted here from the path of the ten unwholesome actions, may we live devoted to virtuous qualities, enjoying the happiness of righteous conduct.
Having always undertaken this vow, devoted to honoring the Three Jewels and having performed every act for the benefit of sentient beings, we shall proceed in virtue.
Therefore, looking upon us with compassion and always bestowing such favor,
please remain here after teaching the True Dharma, and do not depart elsewhere.
Having heard this prayer made by all of them, that son of the Jina,
Lokeśvara, looked at them and spoke again.
I would not remain with my body even for a moment, seeing that living beings everywhere are deeply suffering; rather, I shall act to deliver them myself.
Therefore, having maintained this restraint and being thus composed,
perform worship to the Three Jewels and remain established after enjoying happiness.
Coming at each successive occasion for the sake of accomplishing your welfare,
I shall teach the realization of the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha through the True Dharma.
Having thus exhorted all those rākṣasīs, that rākṣasa,
the great being who is the Lord of the World, then departed swiftly.
Then, having vanished and gone into the sky, illuminating like the moon and gladdening the world of beings, he wanders, eager for the welfare of sentient beings.
Seeing him gone into the sky, radiant and resplendent, all those rākṣasīs stood there, filled with wonder and rejoicing.
From that time forward, all those rākṣasīs,
being composed and having undertaken those precepts and vows, always conduct themselves in virtue.
Thus that Lord of the Three Worlds, even while awakening the rākṣasīs and establishing them on the path to enlightenment, always causes them to practice what is virtuous.
Thus, the mass of merit of that Lord of the World has been described by the lords of sages as exceedingly great and immeasurable in number.
Therefore, having taken refuge in that one who is the pit of the three worlds,
you should worship Bhava by meditating upon him, uttering his name, or even merely remembering him.
Those who, with faith, have taken refuge in that Lord of the three worlds,
and who always worship Him by meditating upon Him, uttering His name, or even merely remembering Him.
They always go to a good rebirth and never at any time fail to do so; they also become endowed with the excellence of auspiciousness, glory, and virtuous qualities.
Always intent on bringing about the welfare of sentient beings and delighting in the practice of the true Dharma,
they venerated the Three Jewels and proceeded to Sukhāvatī.
There, having always drunk the nectar of the Dharma from the Lord Amitābha,
the Arhats, having attained awakening, shall reach the state of a Perfect Buddha.
Having heard this command given by the Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū,
all the people gathered in the assembly, being thus enlightened, rejoiced.
Thus ends the section on the awakening and deliverance of the rākṣasīs of Siṃhaladvīpa.
13. Vārāṇasī: The Section on the Rescue of Worms and Insects.
Then that Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, with palms joined in reverence, bowed to Viśvabhū, the Lord of Sages, and spoke as follows:
"Blessed One, that Mahāsattva, the Lord of the World, the Son of the Victor, has not yet arrived here; when will he come? Please instruct us."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, Viśvabhū, that lord of sages,
looked toward Gaganagañja and spoke to him once more as follows.
Then, having set out and looking about, that Lord of the World proceeded toward Vārāṇasī to deliver sentient beings.
Having seen those many, countless beings in extreme suffering, clinging to excrement, urine, and mud, he remains standing there, reflecting thus:
Alas, what a sin! How could I, while awakening them, extract these thousands upon thousands of worms that are submerged in feces and urine?
There, reflecting and considering [the situation], he looked upon sentient beings with compassion;
assuming the form of a bee, he moved about attending to them.
Having uttered the sweet sound, "Homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha," he wanders, moving through the sky.
Seeing him wandering in the sky and hearing his piercing cry, all those living beings also became anxious and thought thus:
"Aha! This happy bird wanders through the sky according to its every desire;
what merit has it performed that it enjoys such happiness?"
"What sin have we committed that we are now dependent upon this impurity?"—
thinking thus, all those worms became desirous of that very happiness.
Having heard that [sound] vibrating, they remain with their faces turned toward it.
In that way, all those worms, conditioned by the recollection of his name,
remained with their minds fixed upon the homage to those Three Jewels.
And so, having thus uttered the names of the Three Jewels, and having remembered them with a focused mind and paid homage, they remain joyfully at the three jewels.
Anointed with this merit, they all developed wings;
