then, flying up, they fell into the Gaṅgā and gave up their lives.
Then those pure-souled ones, having set out for Sukhāvatī,
all become bodhisattvas named Sugandhamukha.
Having there constantly drunk the nectar of the Dharma from Amitābha,
and having attained the threefold enlightenment, they shall reach the state of final nirvana.
In this way, that Great Being, the Lord of the World, having diligently rescued even the worms, sends them to Sukhāvatī.
Likewise, the mass of merit of that Teacher of the World is declared by the Lords of Sages to be exceedingly great, immeasurable, and incalculable.
And those who, with faith, abide in the refuge of this Lord of the World,
who always worship him by meditating upon him, recollecting him, and uttering his name.
Always born in fortunate rebirths and never in miserable states,
having attained the glory and happiness of the True Dharma, they shall go to Sukhāvatī.
There, having always drunk the nectar of the Dharma from the Lord Amitābha,
and having attained the threefold awakening, they shall reach the abode of the Victors.
Thinking thus, those who always desire auspicious happiness within existence should take refuge in and worship this Lord of the Three Worlds.
Having heard these instructions given by the Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū,
all those people took refuge [in him] and, being awakened, rejoiced greatly.
Thus ends the chapter on the rescue of the worms and insects of Vārāṇasī.
14. The Chapter on Awakening and Delivering the Beings of Magadha.
Then that Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, filled with joy, bowed down to Viśvabhū, the Lord of Sages, and spoke as follows:
O Blessed One, when will that one of great supernormal knowledge appear here? Where has he gone now? It behoves you to explain this.
When he had thus made his request, Viśvabhū, the lord of sages,
looked toward that Bodhisattva and the assembly, and spoke as follows:
Then that Lord of the Three Worlds, departing from Vārāṇasī,
has now arrived in Magadha, seeing sentient beings in order to deliver them.
There, having taken refuge among those afflicted by famine,
he saw them even eating human flesh and drinking blood as well.
Observing those wicked ones, who were committing great sins, fighting with one another, and tormented by the fires of affliction, he questioned them.
Why have you come here, having fought one another and yet remained unharmed,
even after eating human flesh and drinking human blood?
Those whose selves are consumed by the fire of the afflictions and who wander in great transgressions are like elemental yakṣas with razor-sharp horses and chariots in this most inauspicious world.
Thus, upon seeing him questioned in this manner, even all those wicked people,
touched by the rays of his merit, became subdued in their hearts.
Then they all gathered before him;
beholding that Great Being, they reported his conduct to him.
"O virtuous one, since this great calamity of famine is occurring here,
there is no food, drink, or sustenance whatsoever to be found here."
Since he was born twenty years ago, this burning has continued;
scorched by the fires of hunger and thirst, we have all been excessively tormented.
Since they are thus tormented by afflictions, afflicted by unbearable sensations,
devoid of affection, merciless, cruel, and engaged in the livelihood of outcasts;
Having fought day and night, even killing one another,
they ate human flesh and drank human blood as well.
Having committed most cruel deeds and acting as perpetrators of great sins,
we wander about protecting ourselves alone and satisfying our own selves.
"A wilderness twenty years in extent lies here;
even by eating things that are unfit to be eaten, we shall preserve our own lives."
Therefore, if you are able to pacify the famine here,
you ought to become our savior by bringing about an abundance of food for us.
Having heard what they said, that Bodhisattva, endowed with supernatural powers,
went into the sky and rained down various kinds of goods everywhere.
The first rain of water fell everywhere;
seeing that, all those people were filled with wonder and their hearts were gladdened.
Having drunk that nectar of death, they rejoice according to their desire;
fully satisfied and content, they become delighted in their very being.
Then, possessing great supernormal knowledge, he causes various kinds of edible foods,
such as well-ground flour and other delicacies, to rain down on all sides.
Having seen them, they all gathered them up according to their desire;
having eaten them and attained happiness, they remained filled with wonder.
When they were all fully satisfied by that food and thoroughly gladdened,
he then caused all kinds of grain and rice crops to rain down.
And various garments, as well as various kinds of goods—
all the minerals and gems, and all the ornaments.
Raining there everywhere, he makes them all rejoice;
seeing that, all the people become filled with wonder.
Having seen all those things, they all take them as they desire;
having filled their houses and storehouses, they become greatly rejoiced.
When the intention of all of them was fulfilled,
they were all delighted and, having gathered together, retired to a secluded place.
Beholding one another with hearts filled with wonder and joy, they stood together and said, "Aha! Whose power is this? and remained there in worshipful attendance.
Then that Teacher of the Three Worlds, having gazed intently with a steady vision upon a certain aged man, dispatched him to his presence.
Moving about there, an old man— worn out, hunched, and decrepit—
leaning upon a staff, walked slowly and sat down behind him.
There, having sat down in the midst of them, that elder looked upon all those people gathered around him and spoke thus with humility.
"What do you think, sirs? By whose power has this auspicious event occurred?
Indeed, no one even within the three realms possesses such majestic power."
For this is the power of Jñānāloka, the Lord of the World and Master of the Universe;
listen, for his majesty shall now be described by me here.
The Bodhisattva named Lokeśvara, the son of the Victor,
a Mahāsattva possessing great superknowledges, is the sovereign lord of the three realms.
He is the protector of all, the lord, the teacher, the bearer of the aim of welfare,
the master of the excellence of the glory of Dharma and its virtues, the teacher, and the sovereign.
Like a lamp, he shows the true path even to the blind;
like the moon, he becomes a protective umbrella for those scorched by the heat of the sun and other afflictions.
He is a river for the thirsty, a celestial tree for the hungry,
a physician who extracts the thorn of disease for the sick, and both mother and father for those in distress.
He is the deliverer of those reborn in the hells and the bestower of nirvāṇa;
he is the provider for the poor and the refuge for those seeking refuge.
He is the refuge for those without refuge, a kinsman and friend, and the ultimate resort for the elephant-like [world];
what need is there for much speaking? He is indeed the sovereign lord of all dharmas.
Fortunate are they, blessed and auspicious, who have obtained the true Dharma—
those who, having recollected this Lord of the Three Realms, always revere him.
They too are fortunate and high-souled, having attained the virtues of the True Dharma,
who always revere him with faith after uttering his name.
Those who, being free from the suffering of existence, undefiled, and pure in intention,
worship with devotion and reverence using the various articles of offering, shall attain liberation.
And those who, having constructed his entire mandala and worshipped it according to the ritual rules,
take refuge in him and devote themselves through recitation, hymns of praise, prostrations, and so forth;
They become great kings, sovereigns of men and universal monarchs (cakravartins),
endowed with the splendor of Dharma, virtuous qualities, excellent fame, and the seven jewels.
Gentle, with fragrant bodies, their limbs complete and their faculties auspicious;
remembering their past births, possessing excellent portions of goodness, they were achievers of the virtues of the True Dharma.
How can the virtuous qualities of that Protector of the World be described,
when they have been declared by the Lords of Sages to be immeasurable and innumerable?
Thus, having understood that his mass of great merit is most excellent and even greater,
you should always worship him by recollecting even his name.
And those who, with constant faith, having recollected and meditated upon him with concentrated minds, take refuge in him and worship him while even uttering his name;
They never, at any time or in any place, go to an evil rebirth;
always born in a good realm, they become the abode of glory and virtue.
Having performed what is beneficial for sentient beings and having always enjoyed happiness,
and having maintained the vow of the conduct of awakening, they go at last to Sukhāvatī.
There, having always drunk the nectar of the Dharma from the Teacher Amitaruci,
they shall attain the threefold enlightenment and reach the state of nirvāṇa.
Having heard what was thus commanded by him, all those people,
responding with "So be it," then departed for their own homes.
That elderly man, having fully explained the extensive qualities of the True Dharma, rose up and departed for his own abode.
Then all those people of Magadha were awakened;
recollecting the Lord, they always worship him with joy.
From that time forth, there was always an abundance of food there;
all beings, having eaten according to their desire, lived righteously under the excellent bull.
All those pure-souled ones, abiding in the four divine abodes,
having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, always move within the auspicious.
Thus is he the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Sovereign of the World, the Son of the Victor,
the Master of all phenomena, the Teacher, the Bodhisattva, and the Treasury of Compassion.
Having personally observed even sinful and wicked beings,
he diligently awakens them and causes them to practice virtuous vows.
Thus, the mass of merit of that Lord of the World is said even by the Jinas to be exceedingly great, immeasurable, and incalculable.
Therefore, he is the Lord of the three worlds, the sovereign of the entire triple realm,
the one who fully realizes all dharmas, and the bearer of the jewels of the qualities of the glory of awakening.
He is praised and extolled by all the lords of sages,
and is constantly remembered and saluted by all the sovereigns of the world.
Thus, having understood this supreme greatness of the qualities of the true Dharma, those who desire awakening should maintain mindfulness and devote themselves to it.
Those who, having taken refuge in him, always honor him by remembering him, meditating upon him with their minds, uttering his name, prostrating before him, and praising him.
They never, at any time or place, go to an evil destiny;
always born into a good destiny, they are practitioners of the path to awakening.
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, striving for the welfare of all sentient beings,
and endowed with the qualities of the glory of awakening, they proceed to Sukhāvatī.
There, having always drunk the nectar of the Dharma from the Teacher Amitaruci,
and having attained the threefold enlightenment, they shall reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Thus, you too, having known and remembered Him, the Lord of the three qualities,
and having meditated upon, remembered, and saluted Him, worship Him always with devotion.
Having heard this instruction given by the Lord of Sages,
Viśvabhū, all those people said, "So be it," and being thus enlightened, they rejoiced.
Thus ends the chapter on the awakening and liberation of the beings of Magadha.
15. The Chapter on the Joyful Welcome to Śrī Jetārāma Viśvabhū and Sukhāvatī.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, that son of the Jina, having bowed with palms joined to Śrīghana and gazed upon him, spoke as follows:
O Blessed One, as that Mahāsattva Lokeśvara wanders from there, tell us: where has he gone now to deliver sentient beings?
Having heard what was thus spoken, that venerable lord of sages looked toward the assembly and Viṣkambhin, and commanded as follows:
Then, having vanished from that place as well, Lokeśvara ascended into the sky;
illuminating the world of living beings, he stood there and reflected thus:
Today, in the Jetārāma monastery, all the worlds, including the gods, asuras, and others, have gathered together and taken their seats in the assembly hall to hear the true Dharma.
I too shall go at once to pay homage to that Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū, the Teacher of the World, and to hear his Dharma.
Having meditated thus, that Lord of the World, illuminating all around and gladdening the world of beings, approached Jetārāma.
Having sat down there and beholding that lord of sages,
he approached while illuminating that entire assembly with his presence.
Seeing him approaching, Gaganagañja rose;
having approached that Sage and bowed with palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus.
"Blessed One, which son of the Sugata has arrived here?
Which Bodhisattva has come, illuminating the world of living beings?"
Having observed that which was asked, the Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū,
seeing that this Lord of the World had arrived, spoke to him.
Having approached that place, the Bodhisattva Lokeśvara, looking about and circumambulating three times the World-Teacher Viśvabhū,
joined his palms in salutation, prostrated himself, and took his seat on the left side.
"Is it well with your body? Are you not weary or exhausted? Having thus inquired after his welfare, the Blessed One asked him again:
"Noble son, how many sentient beings have been rescued by you from the lower realms?
And having awakened them, how many have you established and settled in the auspicious state?"
Thus questioned by the Lord of Sages, that Lord of the World (Lokeśvara) related from the beginning in detail, right there before the Lord of Sages, as follows:
Those beings in the realms of the hungry ghosts, such as the needle-mouthed pretas and others—
all of them have been rescued by me and sent to Sukhāvatī.
And all those who were submerged in the Avīci hell have been rescued by me.
Those beings who are in Kālasūtra, and those who have resorted to Raurava, and those who are in Hāhava and Tapana, and those who abide in Śītodaka;
And those beings who were being cut with swords, as well as those who remained in confinement—
likewise, they were situated similarly everywhere else throughout all the hells.
I have also rescued all of them and sent them to Sukhāvatī.
And even those who were sinful and wicked, having been awakened by me with great effort and established [in the path], have been set upon the way to enlightenment.
Likewise, even those beings on the golden ground who were facing downward,
I have all been diligently established by me upon the path to enlightenment.
Likewise, the beings and individuals on the earth made of form were also by me, through diligent effort, established upon the path to enlightenment.
And then, those Daityas led by Bali— who were difficult to subdue and arrogant with pride— resided in Pātāla upon the ground made of iron.
I too have diligently enlightened them all and inspired them with faith; having established them on the path to awakening, I have set them to work for the welfare of the world.
And those beings who are yakṣas and rākṣasas in the realm of blinding darkness—
all of them were awakened and established upon the paths to enlightenment.
In the celestial realm of Śuddhāvāsa, the immortals such as Sukuṇḍala and others were diligently awakened and established upon the path to enlightenment.
Then, on the island of Siṃhala, I also diligently awakened the rākṣasīs and established them all upon the path to enlightenment.
And even those worms in Vārāṇasī who were submerged in filth—
I have rescued them all and dispatched them to Sukhāvatī.
Then, even those wicked people of Magadha were diligently awakened by me and established upon the path to enlightenment; thus were they protected.
In this same way, other beings as well— those who were wicked and even those guilty of transgressions—
all have been rescued by me and sent to Sukhāvatī.
Likewise, the bhūtas, piśācas, pretas, and night-stalkers—
all those sinners who were submerged in all the hells—
have been rescued by me and sent to Sukhāvatī.
Even all the animals have been established by me in a happy rebirth;
having rescued them as well, I have sent them forth to Sukhāvatī.
In this way, the nāgas, daityas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras,
as well as the kumbhāṇḍas and rākṣasas, were wicked and arrogant with pride.
All of them have also been urged by me with diligence upon the path to enlightenment.
And thus, even those humans who are wicked and most sinful have been diligently purified, observed, and established upon the path to enlightenment.
In this way, having diligently awakened even the gods who were unattached to celestial pleasures,
I have established them all upon the path to enlightenment.
In this way, all sentient beings dwelling within the three realms should also be established upon the path to enlightenment and dispatched to Sukhāvatī.
Having thus surveyed everyone and rescued them from all sides,
I have now come here to grant you my vision.
Having obtained your vision, my exertion has become fruitful;
O Blessed One, Teacher, from here I shall go to Sukhāvatī.
May you, relying upon this existence here, illuminating the world with your meritorious splendor and always teaching the true Dharma, dwell for the welfare of the world.
Having heard what was thus related by him, Gaganagañja was greatly delighted; looking toward Lokeśvara, he spoke as follows.
Aha! Such great supernormal knowledge has never been seen or heard of by anyone;
it does not exist among the fully enlightened Buddhas—so whose could it belong to otherwise?
Having spoken thus, that Mahāsattva Gaganagañja rose and stood before Lokeśvara with his palms joined in reverence.
"Are you not weary, O Lord of the World? Is there well-being in your body? Having asked this, he bowed at his lotus-feet and remained gazing [at him].
When he had thus questioned him, Lokeśvara, having heard those words and looked toward Gaganagañja, spoke as follows with a smile:
I shall not walk among you here, even if I am weary or afflicted;
by the mere sight of you, my skill is perfected in every respect.
Having heard what was thus commanded by him, Gaganagañja was filled with joy; looking toward that Lokeśvara, he spoke:
O Teacher of compassionate mind, always dwell here for our benefit;
having drunk the nectar of your Dharma, we shall work for the welfare of the world.
Having heard what was thus spoken, the Lord of the World, the Son of the Jina,
looked toward Gaganagañja and spoke to him once more as follows.
I shall not remain with this body; indeed, I shall wander everywhere, for I must accomplish that benefit for the world which was vowed by me.
Having beheld all sentient beings and awakened them through diligent effort,
I shall establish them on the path to enlightenment and send them to Sukhāvatī.
Having rescued those beings, purified them, awakened them,
and established them on the path to enlightenment, I shall go to Sukhāvatī.
Therefore, always remaining thus within, having taken refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One and undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, may they dwell for the welfare of the world.
May there always be auspiciousness for you in the endeavor to accomplish perfect enlightenment;
may the glory of the means for accomplishing the welfare of the world be successfully achieved and flourish.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of the World, Gaganagañja was filled with joy;
looking at him, he spoke as follows:
May your undertakings also succeed for the benefit of the three worlds;
may there always be auspiciousness, and may the glory of perfect enlightenment flourish.
Thus, having inquired after each other's well-being, those two great beings gave one another auspicious blessings and remained silent.
Then the Blessed One, the Teacher Viśvabhū, having surveyed all those people gathered in the assembly, taught the True Dharma.
Listen, sons of good family, to this True Dharma which I have proclaimed as the means for attaining the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, and which brings about the welfare of sentient beings.
First, for the sake of accomplishing the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, a bodhisattva,
having made the vow for perfect enlightenment, should practice the desired giving.
Then, having diligently desisted from even those ten evils and having established pure ethical discipline, one should practice with perfect restraint.
Then, having completely conquered the afflictions and abiding in the four divine abodes,
one should always maintain the vow of patience and act for the welfare of the world.
Therefore, maintaining great enthusiasm for the Dharma in order to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings,
one should abandon aversion toward evil friends and cultivate that which possesses great virtue.
Then, having abandoned malicious intent and becoming dispassionate toward sensual enjoyments,
one should fix the mind with great steadiness and meditate upon that which is for the welfare of the three worlds.

Therefore, having abandoned attachment to enemies, one who is devoted to perfect enlightenment should strive to obtain the supreme jewel of awakening within the ocean of wisdom for the welfare of the world.
Having fulfilled these six perfections in their proper sequence and having conquered all the hosts of Māra, he shall attain the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
Thus, through such great supernormal knowledges, the perfection of glory, vigor, and excellent qualities,
having brought about the welfare of all sentient beings, one shall attain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Thus, having fully understood this, if you desire the state of perfect buddhahood,
fulfill all the perfections in their proper sequence.
Having maintained the vow for perfect enlightenment and practicing the four sublime abodes,
and having rendered service to the Three Jewels, proceed for the welfare of the world.
By the power of this merit, may you all become masters of your senses,
and having attained the state of an Arhat, you shall reach the stage of perfect enlightenment.
Having heard this command given by the Lord of Sages, Viśvabhū,
all those seated in the assembly approved, saying, "So be it."
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence to that Lord of the World of Tantra, the Sovereign of Sages who is the source of all existence, they departed for their respective abodes with joy.
Then Lokeśvara, having gone forth blazing like a mass of fire in the sky,
and gladdening the world of beings, quickly departed for Sukhāvatī.
Thus have I heard from Viśvabhū the great instruction concerning the Great-Souled Lord of the World, the Protector of the Three Realms, who possesses the great superknowledges.
Moreover, I have personally witnessed the power of the great supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of that Lord of the World, the Master of the Universe; I shall now describe it to you.
Thus, recognizing his great supernormal powers, you should with reverence meditate upon him, recollect him, and utter even his name; by so doing, worship him and be free from worldly existence.
Those who, having taken refuge in him, always meditate upon him, remember him,
and even utter his name, worship with a mind set on awakening.
They never go to an evil rebirth anywhere in any state of existence;
always born into a good rebirth, they accomplish the qualities of the true Dharma.
Possessing the attainment of the excellence of auspicious glory, virtues, prosperity, and accomplishments,
they shall always perform what is wholesome in the world and, at the end, go to Sukhāvatī.
There, having always drunk the nectar of the Dharma from the Lord Amitābha,
and having attained the threefold awakening, they shall reach the state of perfect buddhahood.
Having heard this instruction given by the Lord of Sages, Śrīghana,
all those people seated in the assembly were enlightened and rejoiced.
Thus ends the chapter on the Joyful Welcome to Sukhāvatī upon Seeing the Victorious Viśvabhū.
16. The Chapter on the Rescue of the Merchant Leader Siṃhala.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, that son of the Victor, having bowed once more to Śrīghana with palms joined in reverence, spoke thus:
Blessed One, this glorious Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Āryāvalokiteśvara is the sovereign lord of the three realms.
Personally beholding all sentient beings even within the worlds of the three realms,
he delivers them, leads them to perfect awakening, and sends them to Sukhāvatī.
Having perceived even the sinful, he himself uplifts them and awakens them;
having established them on the path to enlightenment, he causes them to maintain their vows.
How then does that Mahāsattva, having rescued them and purified them, make all their faculties pure and send them to Sukhāvatī?
By what means does he awaken even the most wicked and evil ones,
enjoin them to the path of enlightenment, and cause them to practice as he himself proceeds?
How does he make all those who are deeply suffering endowed with true happiness; how does he make the poor, the unfortunate, and the wretched wealthy, fortunate, and virtuous?
Having established even the Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Rākṣasīs— who are difficult to subdue—
upon the path to enlightenment, how does he practice his vow?
In order to explain that means which accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings—
the means by which he causes them all to partake in enlightenment— [he spoke].
When Viṣkambhin, who is possessed of noble qualities, had thus made his request,
the Blessed One looked at him and the assembly and commanded them as follows:
O son of the Kuru clan, where is that Lokeśa, who knows the application of great skillful means,
by whom sentient beings are uplifted and made partakers of enlightenment?
For that wise one, meditative absorption is a great means for the welfare of the world;
by means of it, having suddenly uplifted the world, he establishes it in what is auspicious.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, his heart filled with wonder, Viskambhin respectfully entreated the Blessed One in this manner.
The Blessed One should deign to teach me that samādhi by which he suddenly uplifts and leads the world toward what is auspicious.
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
looked toward Viṣkambhin and commanded him once again as follows:
Noble son, he possesses many samādhis,
by means of which he delivers sentient beings and sends them to Sukhāvatī.
That Lord of the World has entered into meditative absorptions that are immeasurable, innumerable, and characterized by the "performer of all forms" and other such qualities.
Endowed with thousands of supreme dhāraṇīs and vidyās,
immeasurable and incalculable, he shines forth in perfect absorption.
By means of their majestic powers, he has rescued them from the ocean of existence,
established them on the path to enlightenment, and protects the three worlds.
By the power of this merit, that Lord of the World, possessing great supernatural might,
having purified the beings of the world, causes them to practice the excellent restraint.
Thus, the mass of merit of that protector of the world is declared by the lords of sages to be exceedingly great, immeasurable, and incalculable.
Therefore, he is called the Teacher of the three worlds, the Lord of the entire triple realm,
the Sovereign of all phenomena, the Protector, and the Savior of the world.
Therefore, protection is never provided for him against fear or suffering;
rather, protection is always extended to all living beings everywhere.
Having rescued them by means of various skillful methods and awakening them,
he bestows the vow of the conduct of enlightenment and leads them to Sukhāvatī.
Thus this great being, the Bodhisattva of great supernatural power,
having brought about the welfare of all sentient beings, wanders everywhere.
In the past, I too was protected by him from a great danger;
listen now as I relate what happened to me long ago.
For example, in the capital city of Siṃhakalpā,
there was a caravan leader named Siṃha, a lord of merchants, who had a son called Siṃhala.
Even in his childhood, that Great Being was intent on the welfare of all sentient beings;
he was divine and exceedingly beautiful, lovely, and captivating to the hearts of all beings.
Even in his youth, he had reached the perfection of all branches of knowledge;
having acted for the welfare of all beings, he took delight in the company of his friends and companions.
Having given to those in need according to their desire, having constantly listened to well-spoken words,
and having performed service for his teachers, he remained devoted to the family dharma.
He worshipped all the gods, beginning with the deity of his own lineage;
he honored all the worlds and gratified his servants and slaves.
Delighting his kinsmen, relatives, friends, and ministers,
and enjoying pleasures as he desired, he took his delight with the permission of his parents.
Then, in his fresh youth, he became mature, with well-developed limbs,
skillful, brave, steadfast, full of energy, and expert in worldly affairs.
Intelligent, devoted to excellent virtues, and proficient in all branches of knowledge,
he who knows the self is honored by the Yadus; he upholds truth, righteousness, fame, and wealth.
Having taken the appropriate price and given the goods to all the merchants, he disciplined and established them under his own authority, and then gave them leave to depart.
Expert in the examination of all kinds of jewels,
he instructed all the caravan leaders and merchant chiefs as well.
Thus, having conquered all the worlds through his righteousness, glory, virtues, and valor, he shone as he moved about, like a king ruling with sound policy.
Seeing this perfection of his virtues, a merchant of envious mind and wicked intellect approached him in secret and spoke thus, like a friend:
"O virtuous one, you are blessed, a true son, and a delight to all the world; practicing the conduct inherited from your lineage, strive to acquire both merit and wealth."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that wise Siṃhala said: "Who is this Kulārjitasaṃvṛtti? You ought to tell me about him."
Having heard what was said by him, his mind agitated by envy,
he looked at Siṃhala and spoke only to instruct him:
O highly fortunate one, Janaka is a caravan leader and lord of merchants;
having gone constantly to the Mine of Jewels, he draws forth abundant prosperity.
Blessed indeed are those true sons who practice the dharma of their lineage;
others are merely kimpuruṣas, for they live as householders only after having consumed [their parents' wealth].
Having taken your father’s wealth and given it to supplicants, you have gained no fruit;
one should give only what has been earned by oneself for the sake of achieving fame, dharma, and prosperity.
O Śrīguṇotsāha, maintaining the conduct acquired through your lineage and the true reality,
go to the ocean, the mine of jewels, and procure precious gems.
Then, having returned home and given to those who ask whatever they desire,
enjoy happiness according to your wish and move about endowed with fame.
Thus, endowed with glory, virtuous qualities, fame, righteousness, and happiness,
always delight in the great enthusiasm for the activities and livelihoods of your own family.
Having thus heard what was said, that Siṃhala was awakened; increasing his resolve to go to the ocean, he proceeded with joy.
Then Siṃhala, eager to set out on a sea voyage,
addressed all the sons of the merchant-leader and spoke thus:
"Gentlemen, I desire to go now to the Treasure-Store;
if you also have the wish, please come along with me."
Having heard what he said, all those sons of merchants joyfully replied, "So be it," and spoke thus.
"O caravan leader, we wish to go to the ocean of jewels;
since you are our guide, it behoves you to lead us there."
Having thus conversed with them, Siṃhala, his mind uplifted,
bowed at the lotus-feet of his father and spoke thus with palms joined in reverence.
Therefore, I wish to go to the great ocean, the mine of jewels;
may you, O Sudṛśa, deign to grant me permission for this.
Having heard what was thus spoken by his son, that lion, the caravan-leader and father,
looked at his own son and, deeply troubled, spoke as follows.
"Son, listen to these beneficial words spoken by me, my child:
since you are so very delicate, how can you go out into the ocean?"
"I possess this great wealth acquired through hardships;
it is all now at your disposal, so enjoy it as you wish."
"O son, as long as I live, remain at home enjoying happiness;
having enjoyed yourself according to your desire, conduct yourself in this way as you wish."
And do not go anywhere else in that very great ocean;
even after I have died, you must never go there to that sea.
As long as the house is full of wealth, do not go anywhere at all;
when the house is depleted of wealth, even then, acquire it within your own home.
"O son, you should never have the desire to go across the great oceans so difficult to cross; indeed, if you have such a desire, [you must refrain]."
(163) What is the use of many material things when they give rise only to affliction? For one who is afflicted there is constant suffering in saṃsāra; whence can there be happiness?
For those who possess many possessions, there is constant affliction, suffering, and great fear;
since those many possessions are useless, do not exert yourself in their acquisition.
"My son, as much wealth as has been acquired and is present in the house—all of this is at your disposal; for what purpose, then, do you seek to acquire more?"
Taking all of this and giving it to those in need according to their desire,
and having eaten yourself as much as you wish, live happily for as long as you live.
Having heard what was thus commanded by his father, Siṃhala, the son of Atnaja,
looked at his father and addressed him once more in this way:
What you have commanded is indeed true; nevertheless, let my intention be heard. Having heard it, O father, may it be understood.
Impelled by destiny, wherever one is born, one shines only through the excellence of dharma, learning, virtues, and wealth, achieved by means of the livelihood appropriate to that birth.
Even a man endowed with all these things— righteousness, learning, virtues, and so forth— which have been acquired otherwise than through improper means, does not shine.
Since I was born by my own karma into a family of caravan leaders, I am eager to conduct myself in accordance with the customs and livelihood of that family.
Therefore, bearing the pride of the vigor and energy of my own family tradition,
I am eager to go even to the ocean, the mine of jewels, in order to acquire gems.
Having given away wealth acquired by my own efforts to those in need according to their desires, and having myself enjoyed it, I am able to support my own people and kinsmen as well.
Thus, having beheld me, your own son, who accomplishes family custom, livelihood, and the goals of dharma, you ought to rejoice.
"No obstruction should be placed here by you in my accomplishment of the goal of dharma;
I, your son, am to be gladdened by the granting of your permission."
If, by fate, misfortune should occur while I am in the ocean, the lord of all sacred fords,
I shall cast myself down, renounce everything, and proceed to the abode of the gods.
"Nevertheless, my great merit and fame shall purify my lineage;
knowing this, dear father, you ought to grant me your permission."
Even in our home, there may indeed be calamity through the turn of fate;
or perhaps those things that are inevitable must surely occur from every side.
Thus, having cast off the poison of doubt and possessing a mind mindful of the true Dharma,
one should always act with great enthusiasm in accomplishing the purpose of the Dharma.
Then, having attained skill in forgiveness and being free from affliction,
I returned joyfully to my own home, endowed with the happiness of jewel-like glory.
Then what is called happiness, accompanied by the festivals of fame and dharma?
Having given to those who ask according to their desire, and having enjoyed [the fruits], let us practice virtue.
Then those born of our lineage, endowed with righteous conduct,
having given to supplicants according to their desire and having eaten, would go to the abode of the gods.
Knowing this to be the truth, if you desire my welfare,
please show me favor with a gracious glance and grant me your permission.
If you grant me permission, there will certainly be no separation between us;
for death is always present before all living beings everywhere.
Having heard what was spoken by his son, the lion father was awakened;
looking at that son, he spoke thus to the lion:
If this is your firm resolve, my son, and you wish to go to the ocean,
it is impossible to restrain your persistent determination.
Therefore, go with your companions; for great dangers exist on the road, in the wilderness, in the forest, and upon the ocean—having observed these on all sides.
Enduring even those sufferings such as cold, wind, and heat that are difficult to bear,
proceed slowly while maintaining fortitude and looking about you.
May your voyage be successful; may there be auspiciousness everywhere.
Having taken the goods as desired, may you return without obstacle.
When his father had thus given him permission, Siṃhala was filled with joy;
having bowed at the feet of his parents, he immediately began to depart.
Then his mother, embracing her beloved son Siṃhala,
her face drenched with weeping tears and lamenting, spoke thus:
"Alas, my son! How can you wish to depart, abandoning me?
I have no other; you alone are my only child."
Alas! You are the delight of my life, for you alone are my beloved and no other.
Alas, O Prāṇa! How is it that you have no affection for your own mother?
From the moment you entered my womb,
I have always welcomed you with devotion and protected you with great care.
Even as you were being born, you were seen by me and joyfully protected; and even in your childhood, having constantly looked after you, you have been nurtured.
Having been propitiated even during your childhood, you were nurtured with joy; now, having reached maturity, you have attained full youth under my protection.
Now that you have become a youth, how can you wish to abandon me?
A son should indeed protect his own aged mother; he must never forsake her.
Now, how can you behave so heartlessly toward me?
Alas, my son! How could anyone bear to abandon me, who am so worn out by age?
"As long as I live, my son, do not go anywhere else;
enjoying happiness according to your desire, move about within the home, taking your delight."
"O son, when I have died, go wherever you desire and, as you wish, accomplish the means for achieving dharma and artha."
Having heard what was thus spoken by his mother, that Siṃhala was consoled;
and having comforted his lamenting mother, he spoke to her as follows:
Do not weep; why this despondency? Relying on fortitude, do not grieve.
Impelled by destiny, one's course must necessarily lead wherever it may be.
Whatever is destined to be, that shall always occur everywhere;
if it is to be such, it will indeed be so, and could never be otherwise.
For things that are necessarily destined to occur do indeed come to pass, and not otherwise.
Of all living beings wandering through existence within the six realms of rebirth.
For all living beings everywhere, death stands before them;
both prosperity and adversity follow from the influence of their respective destinies.
Having understood this, why fear the suffering of separation from one's mother?
For separation is inevitable for all who wander within the cycle of existence.
Thus, in this matter of my great task which accomplishes the purpose of my family's dharma,
you ought not to create an obstacle by weeping and trying to dissuade me.
If you have affection for me, look upon me with a kind eye;
having bestowed upon me auspicious blessings, you should grant me your permission.
Remembering the deity for my sake and praying for great auspiciousness,
dwell happily in the house with your father, enjoying pleasures and protecting the home.
"I shall return before long; remembering this, do not grieve for me. Cast off your despondency and be comforted, for I am indeed departing."
Having spoken thus to comfort his mother, the Great Being released her from her firm embrace, and after bowing down, he departed.
Then he caused a proclamation by the ringing of bells throughout that city, saying:
"The merchant-scarer Siṃhala shall go to the ocean, the mine of jewels."
Having heard the sound of that bell, the five merchants also desired to go with him to Ratnākara.
Then all those merchants, having gathered together suddenly with their coins, went before Siṃhala and, bowing low, made this request:
"O Caravan Leader, we are all indeed the sons of a caravan leader;
we truly wish to go together with you to the Mine of Jewels."
Since you are the leader of all merchants and the son of a caravan leader, it behooves you to show favor and consider this matter.
When they had all thus entreated him, that high-minded Siṃhala addressed them all and, looking upon them, spoke as follows:
"O honorable ones, if you desire to come with me, then take all your merchandise and come along; let us go."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, they were all greatly delighted;
they went immediately to their respective homes and gladdened all their kinsmen.
Having obtained permission from their father and mother and joyfully performed rites for prosperity,
they all set out together, taking their merchandise and conducting themselves accordingly.
That great being, having joyfully secured his safe passage and bowed at the feet of his parents, set out taking his merchandise with him.
There, having seen all those merchants and approached them, he consulted with them,
reached an agreement, and set out, proceeding with joy.
There, having observed all his kinsmen, friends, and well-wishers who had followed him, he exhorted them, turned them back, and made them desist.
Then, traveling along, he was accompanied by five hundred merchants and many pack animals, including donkeys, oxen, and camels.
Setting out slowly with his load of maritime merchandise, he passed in due course through villages,
forests, groves, gardens, market towns, and ports.
Wandering through Nagara, Rājya, Saurāṣṭra, Rājadhānī, Pyūra, and other such places, he beheld them and proceeded with great enthusiasm.
Then, traveling slowly through other regions, he passed through forests, wildernesses, and mountain ranges, and eventually reached a very distant forest.
Having arrived there, they were all despondent, overcome by terror and grief;
with their enthusiasm shattered, they proceeded slowly and beheld the ocean from afar.
Having seen the ocean, they were all greatly delighted; filled with enthusiasm and vigor, they reached the shore of the great sea.
Having approached him there, they all, with hearts full of joy,
bowed down to that Great Ocean and remained gazing upon him.
Then all those merchants, having gazed upon that great ocean,
stood there with their faces pale from terror, their energy extinguished by their love for life.
Then Siṃhala, seeing that they were all terrified in their hearts,
addressed the helmsman and spoke thus before him:
O illustrious helmsman, we have come here desiring all prosperity to go upon the ocean, the mine of jewels.
Therefore, may you, our true friend and leader who shows us the direction toward our welfare, deign to look upon us with favor and deliver us.
Having heard this prayer made by everyone,
the helmsman looked at all those merchants, addressed them, and spoke thus:
Sirs, if you desire to go to the ocean which is the abode of jewels, then,
having called upon the deity of fortitude, remain firmly established upon your ship.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, all those merchants bowed, boarded the ship, and remained there with composed minds.
Then that helmsman, having called upon his family deity and performed a prostration with palms joined in reverence, made this petition to the ocean:
O Great Ocean, you are the sustainer of the world and a mine of jewels and nectar;
therefore, all these merchants have come to take refuge in you.
Therefore, out of compassion, you ought to take all these seekers of wealth and deliver them to Subhadra at Ratnākara.
Having thus prayed and bowed to that ocean and to that boat,
the sailor boarded it and steered it forward slowly and by degrees.
Then that boat, constantly impelled by its movement,
being carried along in due course, reached an island in the middle of the ocean.
There, the ship was indeed wandering about, struck by the winds;
seeing that, the helmsman spoke thus to Siṃhala:
O caravan leader, you should recognize that there is great danger here;
for this ship, struck by mighty winds, is tossing about repeatedly.
Where do you intend to go? The winds blow with great speed; having remembered the deities of your own lineage and having entreated them for protection, [cross] the ocean.
Maintaining fortitude in all circumstances, remain composed and concentrated.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, they all, their hearts filled with terror,
called to mind their respective tutelary deities and prayed thus to the ocean:
O Great Ocean, Sustainer of the World, we have taken refuge in you;
therefore, holding us with compassion, you ought to deliver us.
Thus praying, they all called to mind their own deities;
and having summoned their courage, though terrified, they remained there as a mass of living beings.
Then the helmsman, having offered prayers to that great ocean and called upon his family deity, stood there having lost all hope for life;
the merchant leader Siṃhala also, having prayed for protection from the sea, remained there.
Having recollected the Three Jewels, he remained there, composed and steadfast.
Then those winds subsided and the ship moved forward by degrees;
seeing this, all the merchants stood with their hearts filled with joy.
There in the ocean, the rākṣasīs dwelling on Tāmradvīpa beheld that boat, which had come there and was occupied by the merchant.
Then, having quickly assembled, those rākṣasīs released tempestuous winds; these dark, stormy gales blew directly toward their ship.

Struck swiftly by them, that ship was whirled around and tossed about; battered by waves of intense and extreme velocity, it was shattered. Then all those merchants, their hearts overwhelmed by terror, [fell into despair].
Crying out, "Alas, O Fate!", they stood there, having lost all hope for their lives.
Then Siṃhala, seeing that ship shattered and observing all his friends terrified, spoke as follows.
Sirs, what is the use of despondency? Destiny alone shall be our refuge; therefore, maintain mindfulness of the Three Jewels and remain steadfast with fortitude.
If by fate there should be a disaster here in this ocean, the lord of sacred fords,
we would all have fallen along with our wealth and met our destruction.
May we be liberated from all misdeeds, with the three spheres completely purified;
born into a good rebirth and a noble family, may we become the abode of glorious virtues.
Having been addressed thus by him, all those lay followers of the non-Buddhists could not,
in any way, believe in the preservation of the recollection of the Three Jewels.
That very Siṃhala, having recollected the Three Jewels and gone for refuge,
meditated, uttered the name, and remained with his mind fixed on perfect enlightenment.
Even then, by the power of fate, their boat was struck by a black whirlwind and, overwhelmed by the tossing of the waves, was shattered into a hundred pieces.
All those merchants as well, their hopes shattered and utterly bewildered,
fell there into the great ocean and were submerged along with their goods.
There, all those merchants, although submerged,
by the power of fate and solely through the strength of their own arms, reached the vicinity of the shore.
Seeing all those merchants gathered near the shore,
the rākṣasīs dwelling on Tāmradvīpa were filled with joy.
Assuming the forms of divine maidens, they all arrived together;
standing on the bank and having brought them all ashore, they spoke to them thus:
"Do not fear; summoning your courage, come together beneath the tree.
Taking refuge in its shade, stay for a moment to rest everywhere."
Having heard what was thus spoken by them, those merchants then went and took shelter in the shade of a campaka tree.
Having rested there, they all looked at one another;
remembering their kinsmen and grieving, they sighed and spoke thus.
Alas, O Fate! How can such a calamity befall us? Who here at present would be a protector, seeking our welfare, and lead us to a happy state?
Having heard what they said, that caravan leader Siṃhala,
comforting all of them whose hearts were shattered by terror, spoke thus:
We have no protector here; who is a well-wishing friend or a source of refuge? Only the Dharma can be our protector and a source of refuge in every situation.
Inevitable events occur even for the great;
they happen to all living beings everywhere, and not otherwise.
Therefore, in this matter, may you all, with faith, being composed in mind, remember, recite the names, and even meditate upon the Three Jewels, and worship them with humility.
This alone is declared to be the root of Dharma within saṃsāra;
for Dharma itself is everywhere the protector, the sustainer, the friend, and the refuge.
Having understood this, all [beings], being composed in mind, should remember, recite the names of, meditate upon, and worship the Three Jewels with devotion.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, all those heretics and disciples were awakened; they no longer wished even to remember the Triple Gem.
That very Siṃhala, composed and mindful of the Three Jewels,
meditated, uttered their names, and remained with his mind fixed on perfect enlightenment.
Then those lovely women, charming young maidens,
seeing all those merchants standing before them, spoke as follows:
Why this despondency even here? For suffering is not to be contemplated;
having enjoyed happiness as you desire, wander according to your will.
Our master has no destination whatsoever, nor does he have any refuge;
he has neither a protector nor a dear friend.
Therefore, you are our masters,
our goals, our ultimate refuge, our supporters, our husbands, our lords, our friends, and our beloveds.
Here there are delightful houses and various objects of enjoyment,
as well as delicious drinks and diverse garments.
All substances, all jewels, and even all ornaments;
as well as delightful gardens and groves filled with the fruits and flowers of every season.
There are also lotus ponds here, filled with water of divine fragrance.
Therefore, what cause for despondency is there here?
Rejoice as you desire; having enjoyed happiness according to your pleasure, wander about filled with delight.
Having heard what was thus spoken by them,
all those merchants looked upon them and were filled with wonder.
Then all those women, perceiving them to be deluded by passion,
took each man individually and led him to their own respective homes.
Among them, an elderly woman who was beautiful, seeing him, approached;
taking that Siṃhala, she settled him in her own home.
Then all those women, having joyfully established each of their respective husbands in their own dwellings, gratified them with divine enjoyments.
Then, those women began to satisfy all of them, who were already satiated with worldly enjoyments, by means of the full enjoyment of the pleasures of secret dalliance.
Thus all those merchants, having eaten as much food as they desired,
and having sported according to their pleasure, wandered about filled with joy.
Having thus eaten and enjoyed themselves as they pleased day and night,
they spent seven days entirely absorbed in the bliss of great joy.
Then, on another night, that Siṃhala remained absorbed in meditation, maintaining mindfulness of the Three Jewels.
Then, while the rakshasi was asleep in that dwelling, a lamp, blazing with great brilliance, shone forth as he laughed aloud, illuminating everything.
Seeing him laughing while ablaze, his mind filled with extreme wonder,
he gazed at him for a very long time and, having reflected thus, thought:
"Aha! How strange! For what purpose is this lamp being laughed at?
Indeed, such a laughing lamp has never been seen, nor even heard of."
Having meditated thus and gazed for a long time, Siṃhala rose up;
approaching him and bowing with palms joined in reverence, he asked this:
For what reason do you laugh, O lamp? Explain this to me; for I do not know who it is that has entered here into you, sir.
When he had thus questioned him, that lamp, blazing brightly,
addressed Siṃhala and spoke as follows with a laugh:
"O Siṃhala, do you not know that she is a rākṣasī and not a human? Even after sporting with you as she pleases, she will undoubtedly devour you."
All those lovely women are Rākṣasīs and not human beings;
they will undoubtedly devour all of them along with your companions.
Having heard this account known as "The Lamp," that Siṃhala was terrified and asked him, "Is this truly so?"
"This is surely a *rākṣasī*, not a human being—this is my conviction.
How do you know this? Please instruct me on this truth."
When he had thus entreated him, that lamp-bearer, laughing once more,
addressed the caravan leader Siṃhala and commanded him as follows:
This which I have declared is true; if you do not believe it, go yourself to the great forest in the south and see for yourself.
In that great and inaccessible wilderness, within a high iron fortress,
hundreds of thousands of merchants were indeed cast and confined.
Some were living, some were dead, and some had been devoured;
their bones were scattered everywhere on all sides.
Having gone there and observed all this that I have described—
whether it be true or untrue— one should then place faith in my words.
Having heard this account related in such a manner, he was awakened;
eager to see all of this for himself, he went there to behold it.
Having rendered the Rākṣasī fast asleep, her senses shrouded by the sleep of the net of delusion,
he took up the sword Candraprabha and set out swiftly.
Then, traveling alone at night while looking about him,
he entered a vast and inaccessible forest in the south.
There, in that exceedingly lofty place, was a world-constructed city enclosed by a great wall made of bricks, provided with windows, gates, and ornamental turrets.
Having seen him, he approached and wandered all around;
hearing that which causes the world’s despair and exhaustion, he was overwhelmed with wonder.
Having climbed to the top of a campaka tree there, he took his place;
yet, despite making a great noise with shouts and cries, he did not summon those who dwelt therein.
"Sirs, who are you? How many have been cast in here? Upon whom do you depend?
Having eaten what do you dwell here? You ought to tell me all of that."
Having heard what he said, those merchants standing there,
upon seeing him perched on the tip of a tree branch, spoke thus:
"Who are you, sir? How do you come to be here? From where have you arrived?
You ought to explain this entire account in detail."
Having heard what was thus spoken, that merchant Siṃhala addressed all the people present there and spoke as follows.
"I am Siṃhala, a caravan leader who has come here from Jambūdvīpa,
together with five hundred merchants, to go to the ocean, the mine of jewels."
In the midst of the ocean, a ship was shattered by great winds;
all those on board fell into the water and crossed over the wind with their arms.
Having reached the shore and taken refuge in the shade of a tree,
we sat down in despondency, grieving for our own country.
There, all those charming young maidens, exceedingly beautiful and captivating,
gathered before us and spoke as follows.
"Do not fear, nor do despair; remain firm in courage.
For indeed, among all of us, there is no master whatsoever."
Therefore, having become the masters of us, enjoy yourselves as you desire;
having sported here according to your pleasure, always move about in happiness.
Having observed us all thus utterly deluded,
they each took one of us as their master and established him in their respective abodes.
There, having fed us according to our desire, they gladdened us exceedingly; and even after sporting as they pleased, they always caused us to experience happiness.
Having thus enjoyed such a great wonder of happiness, I was utterly amazed;
I came here to see what had occurred in this place.
Having heard what he related in this manner, all those merchants also told him their own stories and consoled him.
Since you are indeed a caravan leader, know those to be rākṣasīs;
do not remain here, impassioned by pleasure with them, but go quickly to your own city.
In the same way, we too, having fallen into the ocean and being in such a state of distress,
were rescued by the rākṣasīs and settled in their respective homes.
Having fed them according to their desire, having delighted them as they wished, having entertained them and established them under one's own control, they are always made to dwell in happiness.
When you arrived here, we were quickly brought by them all to this fortress and cast into the prison.
Having seized us with these rākṣasīs, they constantly devour men day and night, wandering about as they please.
You too will undoubtedly be seized here at will by these rākṣasīs and cast down to be devoured.
Having understood this, you must certainly act immediately by summoning all the caravans and returning quickly to your own country.
If you all depart from here immediately and suddenly, it may yet be well; otherwise, if you do not, you will all perish.
Having heard what was thus spoken, that awakened Siṃhala descended quickly from the tree and went suddenly to his own dwelling.
There, beholding that radiant lamp which produced delight,
he joined his palms in reverence, prostrated himself, and took his place before it.
Beholding him standing before him, that lamp, blazing brightly, asked him thus: "O virtuous one, have you seen the truth?"
Having heard what was spoken by the lamp, he, filled with wonder, spoke again:
"Everything is true, exactly as it has been described by you."
Is there some means here by which we may suddenly go back from this place to Jambūdvīpa? You should instruct us in that.
When he had thus entreated him, that lamp, blazing brightly,
laughed and, having comforted him, instructed him once more in this way:
There is a means for this as well, by which you may go quickly from here back to Jambūdvīpa; if you wish to do so, listen to it.
On this shore of the great ocean, on a place of golden sand,
there exists a great horse named Bālāha, whose nature is compassion.
Having consumed those white medicinal herbs, and having turned over and over, he would rise up,
shake his own body, and speak thus:
"Whoever among you wishes to cross this ocean and go to their own country once more, let them mount my back and stand firmly there."
If you have the desire to go back from here to Jambudvīpa,
then having gone there and bowed to that king of horses, make your request with earnest devotion.
"We desire to go back from here to Jambūdvīpa;
therefore, out of compassion, you ought to bring us all there."
Then that horse, possessing great supernormal knowledge, will swiftly carry all of you upon his back from here and bring you to the far shore of the ocean.
Having thus instructed him, that lamp vanished;
he too, having ascended to his bed, lay down with the rākṣasī.
Then, having touched the coolness of his limbs, that night-stalker awoke and asked him, "How is it that your body is so cold?"
Having heard that, the caravan leader Siṃhala, his mind filled with fear,
spoke thus to awaken his beloved woman:
"Beloved, I had gone out from the house to discharge urine;
having returned, I lay down, and by that my body was cooled."
Thus, although he had awakened that beloved woman with a falsehood, Siṃhala remained apprehensive; dejected in spirit, he stayed awake, turning his back on sleep.
Then, having risen in the morning, he summoned all those merchant-men and, having gone outside the city, took to his vehicle; likewise,
all those merchants also took their places there with him.
Having addressed one another, they stood there, filled with joy.
There, having observed all those merchants to be free from fear and full of joy, Siṃhala addressed them and spoke thus:
Sirs, I wish to ask you: speak the truth and not otherwise. With what kind of affectionate attentions do your beloveds honor you?
(Gkv 177) Having heard what was thus spoken,

then, taking this son of mine, I have slowly come here.
Having asked [her name], I went to the house of the caravan leader and took up residence there;
yet I was abandoned by my parents and forcibly driven out from their home.
Therefore, O King, I have come to you for refuge;
it behooves you to ask the citizens of Siṃhala for forgiveness on my behalf.
Having heard what she said and having looked at her, the king comforted her,
summoned his ministers, and spoke thus:
"O ministers, go at once, summon that caravan leader Siṃhala, the delight of the lion, and bring him here immediately."
Having heard this command of the king, those ministers quickly summoned Siṃhala and brought him before the monarch.
Seeing that Siṃhala approaching, the lord of men honored him respectfully and, having observed him closely, commanded thus:
"O Siṃhala, why has this princess been abandoned by you as a wife? Forgive her and, taking her along with her son, protect them within your home."
Having heard these instructions from the lord of men, the merchant Siṃhala bowed with joined palms to the king, looked upon him, and spoke as follows.
"O King, this is not the king's daughter, nor am I her husband;
this is a Rākṣasī, a devourer of men, who has come here from Tāmradvīpa."
Having heard this told by him, that king, deluded by passion,
looked at Siṃhala and her again and commanded thus:
All women are indeed Rākṣasīs; therefore, you ought to forgive this. Whichever among them is not desired by you, let her be released and given to me by you.
Having heard this spoken by the king, that wise merchant Siṃhala looked at the monarch and addressed him once more as follows.
"O Great King, this is a Rākṣasī; I shall neither give her away nor prevent you from doing so.
You yourself, having reflected thoroughly, should act in whatever way is for your own benefit."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that king, though steadfast, being deluded by passion,
said this and then departed from the lion toward his home.
Maintaining mindfulness of the Three Jewels, he remained steadfast and composed;
then, with joy, he caused his beloved wife and their son to enter his inner apartments.
Then that lovely woman, delighting the infatuated king with pleasures according to his desires, captivated him and brought him under her control.
Passionately attached to her alone, that king, delighted by sensual pleasures,
enjoyed happiness according to his desire and wandered about sporting at his own will.
Thus, having constantly delighted that king according to her desire and having brought him under her control, that Rākṣasī led him about at her own will.
Then that Rākṣasī, at night, caused all the people residing in the royal palace, headed by the king himself, to fall into a deep sleep.
Having caused them all to fall into a deep sleep, stupefied by the *prāsvāpana* spell,
she then joyfully traveled from the sky to Tāmradvīpa.
Thereupon, she suddenly approached all those rākṣasīs, summoned them before her, and having looked at them, spoke thus:
"Sisters, what is one Siṃhala of yours to King Siṃhakeśarin in the city named Siṃhakalpa?"
All the people, headed by the king, including those residing in the inner apartments,
were put to sleep by me, rendered unconscious through the *prāsvāpana* spell.
"Come with me at once; let us go there together. We shall now devour all those people, headed by the king."
Having heard what she said, all the rākṣasīs suddenly went through the air and joyfully assumed the form of lions.
Then, having approached all at once, they joyfully struck everyone present in the royal palace, from the king on down, with *khadira* wood.
All those people, including the king and others, were devoured by those rākṣasīs; even at dawn, the gate of the royal palace was not opened.
In the morning, vultures and other carrion-eating birds were seen wandering and shrieking above the royal palace.
Then, having arrived there in the morning, the ministers, counselors, and people,
seeing the birds wandering about, all stood there in amazement.
"How is it that the palace gate is not yet opened?
Many birds are wandering about," they said, and stood with their faces turned upward.
Upon hearing that account, Siṃhala rose up suddenly;
taking his sharpened sword, he proceeded there with great haste.
There, seeing that multitude, Siṃhala approached them;
with his face smeared by falling tears, he spoke thus in their presence.
"Sirs, since these birds that feed on corpses are wandering here,
it is certain that the king and all the people have been devoured by the rākṣasī."
Having heard that statement, "It was said thus," all the ministers and people asked him with respect, "How was this known by you?"
Having heard that, Siṃhala, looking at all those ministers and people, stood before him and spoke these words spontaneously:
"Gentlemen, let a long ladder be brought here at once;
having climbed it and gone to the top, I shall look all around."
Having heard what the minister said, the people quickly brought a ladder and immediately placed it against the edge of the palace.
Seeing them, Siṃhala took up his sword, climbed up,
and standing atop the palace, he terrified those night-stalkers.
Seeing that Siṃhala standing atop the palace with sword in hand,
all those rākṣasīs became terrified and fled in every direction.
Some of them grasped his head, some his feet, and others his arms;
all those rākṣasīs then fled swiftly from that place.
Then Siṃhala, seeing that they had all fled,
quickly descended from the palace and opened the gate.
Then those ministers, counselors, and all the soldiers went and, seeing that the king and everyone else had been eaten, they wailed aloud.
Having lamented for a very long time, all those ministers,
people, counselors, soldiers, and citizens wandered about with their hearts filled with terror.
Then Siṃhala, having seen all those ministers, people, counselors, soldiers, and citizens, addressed them and spoke as follows:
"Sirs, do not wander about here; there is no night-stalker woman here at all.
Therefore, let everyone sit down together and look once more in every direction."
Then those ministers and counselors, having looked all around,
thoroughly purified the entire royal household, both inside and out.
Then those ministers and counselors, having assembled the great people, beginning with the Brahmins, as well as the subjects, spoke thus in a conciliatory manner:
"Sirs, the king here has died and his lineage does not exist; therefore, whom shall we appoint here as king? Speak on this matter."
Having heard what was thus spoken by those ministers, those Brahmins and others,
as well as the great multitude and all the subjects, made this representation.
He who is wise, sattvic, heroic, and skilled in the treatises on ethics, whose nature is auspicious with compassion and kindness, and who upholds the welfare and purpose of all dharmas.
Having consecrated him here according to the prescribed rite and established him upon the royal throne,
having made him the sovereign of the entire kingdom, let everyone always acknowledge his authority.
Having heard what was said by them, certain wise men of great standing spoke thus in the presence of all those ministers:
This caravan leader Siṃhala is courageous, knowledgeable in ethics, and skillful; his nature is auspicious with compassion and pity, and he bears the welfare of all sentient beings as his purpose.
There is no great person whatsoever who possesses such heroism, great wisdom, and a mind endowed with compassion and mercy, nor who is a vessel for the glory of loving-kindness and excellent virtues.
Therefore, having consecrated this heroic Siṃhala upon the royal throne and having established him as king, you shall fulfill the desires of everyone together.
Having heard what was thus spoken by them, all those ministers, counselors, and people gave their consent and began to act accordingly.
Then those ministers, counselors, brahmins, and great men addressed Siṃhala, who was seated before them, and spoke as follows.
O Siṃhala, since this is also the consensus of our subjects,
you ought to rejoice in it and become the king here in this kingdom.
Having heard this request made by all those ministers, counselors, virtuous men, and brahmins, Siṃhala, intent upon that very purpose, spoke as follows.
"Gentlemen, I subsist by the profession and business of a merchant;
how then could I possibly be capable of bearing the burden of a kingdom?"
This is appropriate for me; may you forgive my inability to do otherwise.
Indeed, the ministers should employ each person in that very task for which they are suitable.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, all those ministers, counselors, and people looked at Siṃhala, consulted together, and spoke as follows.
There is no one else to be found who is like you— possessing right understanding, heroic, compassionate, skillful, virtuous, and world-renowned.
Furthermore, since there is no one at all remaining in the lineage of this king,
you ought to rule this kingdom here.
Having heard this request made by all those ministers,
Siṃhala looked at all his ministers and spoke as follows.
"Gentlemen, if you all desire to make me king,
I do not wish to rule the kingdom at this time."
Having heard what was spoken by him, all those ministers and people, looking upon that one of great supernormal knowledge, spoke thus:
Just as this agreement has been declared by you,
so indeed shall we all, being concentrated, practice with a unified mind.
Having heard that excellent speech, Siṃhala was fully awakened;
looking toward all those ministers and counselors, he spoke thus:
If you all desire to practice [the dharma] by taking this as true,
then I too am willing to bear the burden of sovereignty here.
Therefore, may you all, upholding my words here and pursuing the Dharma,
honor the Three Jewels and always practice what is virtuous.
Having taken this instruction to heart, you who have me as your companion in the Dharma ought to practice the Dharma that brings about the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, all the ministers,
the people, the counselors, the brahmins, and the citizens replied, "So be it."
Then those ministers, counselors, people, brahmins, and great men,
having all reached a consensus, began to appoint him as king.
Then, having thoroughly cleansed this city on all sides, they adorned it completely with ornaments such as banners, parasols, and other decorations.
Then, having purified him according to the prescribed rites, they enthroned him as the sovereign of the world, King Siṃhala, with great enthusiasm.
Having installed him upon the royal throne, all the people together with their ministers attended upon that great king of Siṃhala with great respect.
Then King Siṃhala, gladdening all the people and establishing them each in their own duty, ruled over them as if they were his own children.
Having received his instruction, all the people, beginning with the twice-born,
practiced devotion to the Three Jewels and always gathered together in auspiciousness.
Then, throughout his lord's kingdom and in all its territories,
an auspicious era free from calamities proceeded continuously.
Thus, attended by virtuous ministers who were experts in policy and dharma,
that great wise king shone like the lord of the gods.
There, having conquered all those kings on Jambūdvīpa, that monarch summoned his ministers and counselors and commanded them as follows:
"Let the fourfold army be quickly readied here;
I shall go to Tāmradvīpa to conquer even those rākṣasīs."
Having heard that command, all the ministers and people immediately mobilized the fourfold army in this manner.
Then, having equipped himself with the fourfold forces, that lord of the earth set forth with great enthusiasm and reached the shore of the great ocean.
There, having embarked all those fourfold armies upon ships, he set out upon the ocean, traveling with joy.
There, crossing over with all his fourfold army,
he safely reached the opposite shore of the great ocean.
Then, on that island of Tāmradvīpa, the great banner of the rākṣasīs,
situated in the marketplace, began to flutter and tremble, portending fear.
Seeing him trembling, all the rākṣasīs, alarmed by fear,
gathered together in one place and spoke thus among themselves:
"O lady, this banner standing in the marketplace is now trembling;
surely the kings of Jambudvīpa have come here to fight with us."
"Having prepared ourselves, we must now remain right here," they said;
having thus conversed, they approached the shore of the ocean to see it.
Remaining there, they all beheld those various kings, such as Siṃhala and others, who had crossed over to the shore and arrived with great enthusiasm to fight.
Seeing them approaching, those rākṣasīs were overcome with fear;
some fled in terror, while others resolved to fight.
Some went forth to fight, while others stood gazing at them in the sky.
Seeing them approaching, the army of Siṃhala quickly advanced,
filled with Vidyādharīs and illuminated by the weapons of the heroes.
The remaining women, having been addressed by the lordly King Siṃhala,
bowed at his feet with palms joined in reverence and spoke thus:
"Forgive us, O Great King; we go to you for refuge.
Therefore, it does not behoove a Kṣatriya to slay us—women and children."
Having heard what they thus requested, that lord Siṃhala,
perceiving that their lives would come to an end according to the agreement, spoke to them.
Having heard that, all those women bowed again with palms joined toward that lord of the Kṣatriyas from Siṃhala, and looking at him, spoke thus:
Whatever agreement you have declared to us,
we shall all indeed observe it at all times accordingly.
Having heard what was thus related by them, that wise king,
beholding all those rākṣasīs, spoke again in this manner:
"If you all abandon this city and dwell elsewhere,
provided that you do not commit any offense against anyone within my realm."
Then I shall indeed hold you all accountable for your offense;
if it is done otherwise, I shall undoubtedly slay you all.
Having heard what was thus related by him, they all bowed to that Siṃhala, and looking at him, spoke as follows:
"O Lord, we shall do exactly as you have commanded;
therefore, it behoves you to protect us, who are like children, through this woman."
Having thus entreated him, all those rākṣasīs were awakened to reason;
they abandoned that region and, having departed, took refuge in another forest.
There, King Siṃhala, together with his ministers, counselors, and people, remained established, and having empowered the world, he governed them each according to their own duty.
There, all those people, having accepted his royal command and having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, practiced their respective duties.
Then, through the power of this Dharma, there arose everywhere an abundance of food, freedom from calamity, and an enthusiastic celebration of the auspiciousness of the True Dharma.
Having conquered it himself and settled it, King Siṃhala caused it to be known as the Island of Siṃhala (Siṃhaladvīpa).
I was indeed that King Siṃhala at that time;
he who was King Siṃhakeśarin was my eldest elder brother.
She who was that rākṣasī at that time is indeed this very Anupamā;
and he who was Valāha, the king of horses, is this very Avalokiteśvara.
Even then, that Lord of the World, the Bodhisattva, having looked upon me in this way,
became a horse and rescued me from such great terror in the midst of the ocean.
Thus that Lord of the Three Worlds, the Bodhisattva himself, having constantly looked upon all sentient beings, delivered them from fear.
Therefore, there is no dharma equal to this for anyone anywhere;
it does not exist even for the Buddhas themselves, so how could it exist for others within the three realms?
Thus this Great Being, the sovereign lord of all worlds,
the master of all phenomena, the Teacher, shines forth as the supreme king of great supernormal knowledges.
Therefore, all the lords of the world, even the lords of the three realms,
take refuge in him and always honor him with devotion.
Those who, having taken refuge in him, always revere him with devotion, do not go to an evil rebirth; they proceed to Sukhāvatī.
Having gone there, they take refuge with Amitābha, the Lord of Sages;
and having constantly drunk the nectar of the Dharma, they act for the welfare of the world.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order,
they shall become free from afflictions, attain awakening, and reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Thus understanding this, those beings who truly desire the state of a Victor should take refuge in and devote themselves to that Lord of the World.
Having heard this instruction from the Teacher, all those present in the assembly, being thus enlightened, responded,
"So be it," and rejoiced.
Thus ends the chapter on the rescue of the merchant leader Siṃhala.

17. The Section on the Instruction of the Prophecy of Perfect Enlightenment for the Goddess Maheśvaromā, Concerning the Lifting-up of All Beings and Establishing Them on the Path to Perfect Enlightenment.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, that son of the Victor, having bowed once more to the Blessed One with palms joined, spoke as follows:
O Blessed One, how many dharmas exist within the body of you, the Lord, the Sovereign of the World, the Sustainer of the Three Realms? Please instruct us regarding them.
Having heard this prayer thus offered by Viṣkambhin,
the Blessed One looked upon that Great Being and commanded him as follows:
O sons of noble family, within the body of this Protector who dwells in the triple world, all the true dharmas are fully present and established.
Just as there are heroes within the pores of his body, I shall describe them briefly; listen to me with respect.
Just as many thousands of Gandharvas dwell in great happiness within a single pore of a hair, so too do they dwell there.
They are not afflicted by the afflictions, nor even by the sufferings of saṃsāra;
being dispassionate toward evil conduct, their supreme faculties are utterly purified.
They were devoted to the practice of the true Dharma, dwelt in the four divine abodes,
maintained pure ethical discipline, and always observed the eightfold *poṣadha* vow.
There, the glorious great jewel, radiant as a wish-fulfilling gem,
having arisen of its own accord for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, remained present.
