When those Gandharvas worship the jewel and pray for their desired object, then everything of theirs is likewise fully accomplished.
Thus, having enjoyed such auspicious happiness, those gandharvas were filled with joy;
having paid homage to the Three Jewels, they moved about established in virtue.
Even this great Dharma resides within a single pore of his hair;
by means of it, he, the Lord of the Three Worlds, shines forth as the Dharmakāya.
Furthermore, in another hair-pore of the Lord of the World called Kṛṣṇa,
hundreds of thousands of millions of great sages also dwell.
Some possess one supernormal knowledge, some two, and some even three;
some possess four supernormal knowledges, and some possess five.
All those wise sages, upholders of the specific vows of their respective lineages,
were seated upon paved terraces on the slopes of the golden mountains.
Some are situated on the flanks of mountains consisting of gold,
and some are on the flanks of mountains consisting of ruby.
Some, resting on paved floors, were on sides made of sapphire;
some were on sides made of diamond; and some were situated on sides made of jewels.
Some had floors of vaidūrya, others were made of aśmagarbha;
some had sides made of beryl, and others even of the seven precious gems.
And on all sides of all the jewels, as well as in the lakes,
in some gardens, in groves, and in forests;
Even though they were adorned with all kinds of trees such as those bearing fruit and flowers,
some [trees] were sandalwood trees and others were agalloch trees.
Some [were made] from tamāla trees, some from campaka trees,
and others from aśvattha, vaṭa, and other kinds of trees.
Likewise, others dwell with concentrated minds, taking refuge in leaf-huts at the foot of wish-fulfilling trees that grant all desired objects.
Some, having taken refuge in lakes filled with water pure in its eight qualities and adorned with divine lotuses, blue lilies, and other such flowers, remained absorbed in meditative concentration.
Possessing pure conduct, with purified limbs, pure intentions, and conquered senses,
they remain composed, having undertaken various ascetic observances and vows.
And there are many wish-fulfilling trees with leaves of gold and silver,
having red stalks and hung with all kinds of ornaments.
There, at the foot of each such wish-fulfilling tree,
a hundred gandharvas stand, constantly recollecting the Three Jewels and paying them homage.
When, having reflected upon the various sufferings of wandering through existence, they become weary of themselves, they even utter this:
Alas! For all living beings wandering perpetually in saṃsāra, there is the state of suffering, agitated by the afflictions of birth, old age, and disease.
Those humans of Jambudvīpa, their mental continuums scorched by the fire of the afflictions,
wander about practicing evil conduct after having experienced various kinds of sufferings.
How is it that those young men, having seen that life is as fragile as a bubble, do not perform worship of the Three Jewels and practice for the welfare of the world?
Having made offerings to the Three Jewels, those who act for the welfare of the world.
Indeed, every intention of theirs shall be accomplished here as well.
In the next life, they will be conveyed to the world-system of Sukhāvatī and will take their stand in the refuge of Amitābha, the Lord of Jinas.
Having always performed worship and joyfully drunk the nectar of the Dharma,
and having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, one should proceed for the welfare of the world.
Then those Bodhisattvas, sons of the Conquerors, being pure in soul,
having attained the threefold awakening, shall reach the state of a Perfect Buddha.
Having heard what was thus related by them, the birds, beasts,
and other animals— even those who were but creatures— became deeply agitated and reflected thus in their minds:
Alas, what suffering there is even for humans wandering in saṃsāra;
what then can be said of us, who belong to the species of animals and beasts?
When, having abandoned this sinful body and attained a human birth once again in a future existence, shall we always practice the Dharma?
Blessed are those people in the world who have gone for refuge to the Three Jewels;
remembering, meditating upon, and honoring them, they move about for the welfare of the world.
Having reflected thus, all those birds, wild animals, and others,
recollecting the Triple Gem and meditating upon it, venerated them with devotion.
Then the intention of all of them is fulfilled,
and all divine objects of enjoyment and the like come into being.
Having seen that, all those birds, wild animals, and others became very joyful; having performed worship to the Three Jewels, they continued to roam about while paying homage.
In this way, those sages, gandharvas, and creatures such as birds and beasts—
all of them remain joyful, filled with auspicious enthusiasm.
Thus, within the hair-pores of the body of the Lord of the World named Kṛṣṇa,
there are great beings such as ṛṣis and others, who practice the Dharma with great supernatural powers.
Thus, all virtues reside within the body of that Sustainer of the World;
therefore, he is the Lord of the three worlds, the sovereign master of all phenomena.
Thinking thus, may all who desire awakening take refuge in him with faith; having pronounced even his name or merely remembered him, may they worship him.
Those who, having taken refuge in him, always recite even his name, and who,
with true devotion and a serene mind, worship him by meditating upon and remembering him;
They do not go to an evil rebirth; they will proceed to Sukhāvatī, having come to take refuge there in the Protector Amitābha.
Having always drunk the nectar of the Dharma and purified the three spheres,
they shall attain the threefold awakening and reach the state of perfect buddhahood.
Having heard these instructions given by the Lord of Sages, all those seated in the assembly,
headed by Viṣkambhin, were enlightened and offered their joyful praise.
Then the Blessed One, having respectfully addressed Viṣkambhin, that son of the Jina, gazed upon him with such reverence and spoke as follows.
Noble son, furthermore, within a single pore of the body of that Lokeśvara, the Lord of the Three Realms, there is a jeweled earring.
There, many hundreds of thousands of millions, indeed many millions of gandharva maidens, always dwell in constant joy.
All those divine maidens possessed celestial forms that were enchanting;
they were gentle, exceedingly beautiful, lovely, with auspicious nourishment, senses, and dispositions.
They are not afflicted by the defilements, nor even by human sufferings;
they rejoice, being endowed with the happiness of the excellence of the glory and virtues of the true Dharma.
All of them, composed in meditation at the four junctions of the day, honor that Lord with reverence, having meditated upon him, uttered his name, and called him to mind.
All their objects, substances, and ornaments appear and are accomplished exactly as they have been desired.
Thus, endowed with happiness and abiding in the four divine abodes, they maintained the vow of the conduct of awakening and proceeded for the welfare of the world.
Having made offerings to the Three Jewels, with their aspirations fixed upon perfect enlightenment and devoted to the true Dharma, they remain filled with great joy.
Thus, his body—the Lord of the World—is an abode of merit;
by that [body], he, the Lord of the three worlds, Dharmarāja, shines resplendent.
Then, in another pore of that hair of the Lord of the three worlds, [there was a city].
Hundreds of thousands of millions dwell there, subsisting on the food of immortality.
All those immortals were steadfast, with their intentions fixed upon perfect enlightenment;
they were bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who dwelt in the four divine abodes.
Some reside on the first stage, some on the second stage,
some on the third stage, and some on the fourth stage.
Some belong to the fifth stage, some to the sixth stage;
some belong to the seventh stage, and some to the eighth stage.
Some are on the ninth stage, and some are on the tenth stage.
All of them, practicing the vow of awakening to bring about the welfare of all sentient beings, move through the world for its benefit after having paid homage to the Three Jewels.
And within that cleft are mountains made of gold and silver,
rising sixty thousand yojanas high and exceedingly vast.
All those hundred-peaked mountains are radiant, composed of the seven precious gems;
on all their sides dwell bodhisattvas, great beings, yogins who remain absorbed in meditation, beginning with those on the first level.
And there were also hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gandharvas.
They rejoice in palaces made of jewels with great festivals,
accompanied by the sounds of songs and musical instruments, and with celebrations for the vows of the Mahāyāna.
Having made offerings to the Three Jewels, they move about for the welfare of the world.
Then, having rested, they all took refuge in celestial palaces;
engaging in discourse on the sublime Dharma, they dwelt together in great joy.
Then, at the place for walking meditation, there were lotus ponds filled with auspicious waters endowed with the eight qualities, and covered with lotuses.
In that riverside dwelling, which was covered with flowers such as lotuses and water-lilies,
it was adorned with ornaments and decorations made of gold, silver, and other precious gems.
Adorned with wish-fulfilling trees having leaves of gold and silver, with pillars red as coral and hung with every kind of ornament,
they all spent that night there walking back and forth, meditating with concentrated minds.
They are free from longing for wandering through existence in the six realms of rebirth and desire only for nirvana.
Free from afflictions, pure in nature, and abiding in the four divine abodes,
they have taken refuge [in the Buddha] after joyfully undertaking the vow of the Mahāyāna and enjoying happiness;
thus, all of them remain constantly composed in meditative absorption during the four junctions of the day.
Having performed the propitiation of the Three Jewels, they dwell there while remaining devoted.
Thus, the body of this Lord of the World is the locus of the qualities of the Dharma;
therefore, that Lord of the Three Worlds shines forth as the Dharmakāya.
Furthermore, in another fissure there called Vajramukha,
there are many thousands of millions of crores of mountains.
Some are made of gold, some of silver or even of diamond;
some are made of sapphire, and some even of ruby.
Some are made of jewels, some likewise of emerald;
others are of beryl, of crystal, and even of the seven precious gems.
Upon all those mountains, there were kalpa-trees of great height,
as well as coral trees and sandalwood trees.
All fragrant trees, all flowering trees,
and all fruit-bearing trees of every season were found there, beautifully adorned.
There are also thousands of lotus ponds, filled with divine nectar and brimming with fragrant flowers such as lotuses and water lilies.
Indeed, there are also many thousands of celestial palaces,
and they are composed of gold, silver, divine gems, and other such precious materials.
In those divine palaces, hundreds of thousands of lakhs of virtuous kinnaras dwell amidst celestial festivities.
All those divine kinnaras were adorned with ornaments of celestial jewels;
agitated by the fear of wandering through existence, they practiced the four divine abodes.
They were givers, of virtuous conduct, compassionate, and noble-minded;
they were established in the concentration of yoga and were distinguished by their pure wisdom.
Having rested within those celestial palaces, all those who have conquered their senses,
having paid homage to the Three Jewels, move about for the welfare of the world.
Then all of them, having taken their seats in those celestial palaces,
engaged in a discourse concerning the Dharma of all the perfections.
Then, in that place for walking meditation, delightful with its gabled pavilions,
beneath the wish-fulfilling trees whose leaves were of gold and silver—
Wearing all their ornaments and carrying their spears and quivers,
they all paced about there and then sat down to rest.
Experiencing the various sufferings of wandering through existence in the six realms of rebirth,
they have become disenchanted with the course of worldly existence and possess an inclination that delights in the true Dharma.
Maintaining mindfulness of the Three Jewels, they remain composed in meditative concentration;
then, for all of them, [visions] appeared from every direction.
All articles of enjoyment, including precious gems and all types of utensils, [should be offered].
Thus all those kinnaras, endowed with the joy of the glory of the true Dharma,
having performed worship to the Three Jewels, remain with their minds set on awakening.
Thus, the body of that Lord of the World rests upon the great bull;
by means of it, he, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds, shines resplendent within the Dharmakāya.
Then, in another hole from the Sun-ray [hole],
there are once again twelve hundred thousand golden mountains.
Then, each one of them had ten hundred times a hundred peaks.
There, each side consists of one hundred million [leaves];
on each of those sides, they are radiant, composed of the seven precious gems.
The gardens were diverse and adorned with celestial trees.
There were also many lotus ponds, completely filled with fragrant water possessing the eight excellent qualities, as well as with lotuses and other flowers.
There were also hundreds of thousands of gabled palaces made of gold and jewels,
adorned with various divine gems and ornaments.
Among them, the great jewel Sāradakoṣidha is supreme;
it is a wish-fulfilling gem that brings welfare to the world and fulfills all intended purposes.
Upon all of them dwell innumerable bodhisattvas;
having paid homage to the Three Jewels, they reside there in meditative composure.
When those bodhisattvas have approached that wish-fulfilling gem and, having honored it, make their requests according to their desire for the welfare of the world.
Then he fulfills all their aims exactly as they desire.
In this way, the sons of the Victorious Ones abide, endowed with glorious happiness.
When those bodhisattvas of pure intention are established therein,
they recite the great vidyā-mantra, the six-syllable one, while remaining mindful.
Then they all behold that Jina Amitābha, the Lord and Sovereign of all worlds, residing in Sukhāvatī.
They behold all the Buddhas, who have taken their place among all the kṣatriyas, as well as the bodhisattvas— beings of perfect equanimity— and all those who are mines of virtuous qualities.
Thus, having joyfully satisfied all the Jinas and Bodhisattvas,
they all likewise went forth and wandered about as they desired.
Some were in gardens made of jewels, even on the banks of lotus ponds; some were on the slopes of mountains, even at the foot of wish-fulfilling trees.
There, having assumed the cross-legged posture, with the three spheres completely purified,
the yogins remain meditating with bodies straight and mindfulness present.
Thus, the body of that Lord of the World is the refuge of all virtues;
by this, the Lord of the Three Worlds shines as the Dharmakāya.
Furthermore, in another pore named Indrarāja, there is again—
And there were eighty thousand mountains made of gold and jewels.
Upon these, O steadfast one, the irreversible Bodhisattvas rely.
These great beings possess hundreds of thousands of millions of great supernormal powers.
There, having worshipped that great wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) arisen in the center, they all together request whatever they desire.
Then that wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) always fulfills the intention and every desire of them all.
For them, no suffering whatsoever will ever arise;
nor are they ever afflicted by afflictions, diseases, or the like.
Always abiding in the four divine abodes, those great beings,
having honored the Three Jewels, move throughout the world for its welfare.

Thus, there they abide, possessing great supernormal knowledges, never turning back from the conduct of awakening, having dedicated their very selves to perfect enlightenment, and remaining in meditative concentration.
Furthermore, in another cave there called Mahauṣadhī,
there are also nine thousand nine hundred mountains.
Some were made of gold, some of silver, and even some of diamond; some were made of sapphire, and even some of ruby.
Furthermore, there are mountains there made of emerald, some even of crystal, and others consisting of every kind of jewel.
There, many thousands who have first set out upon the path of awakening,
having performed worship of the Three Jewels, move about for the welfare of the world.
They are all never oppressed by afflictions or sufferings;
endowed with the excellence of auspicious virtues, they are free from disease.
Those of virtuous conduct and pure self, who dwell in the four divine abodes,
having made the vow for perfect enlightenment, proceed within the excellent restraint.
Upon those mountain peaks and on all their sides,
many thousands of gandharvas dwell.
All of them were fully concentrated in the vows and conduct of the Mahāyāna;
they were wise ones of purified intention, whose aspirations were fixed upon perfect enlightenment.
Constantly engaged in the great festivals of the communal chanting of the Dharma,
they maintain mindfulness of Lokeśvara and always proceed toward what is auspicious.
All those who practice for awakening, having reflected upon the three kinds of liberation, cultivate perfect peace through this great enthusiasm for the Dharma.
Then, experiencing pleasure, pain, and other states throughout the course of existence,
they make the vow for perfect enlightenment and abide in meditative absorptions.
Then, in another hole called Lomnacitrarāja,
there were once again hundreds of millions and billions of Pratyekabuddhas.
On the sides and even in the caves of the mountain composed of the seven jewels,
they abide in meditative absorptions, having established mindfulness through contemplation.
All of them, possessing great supernormal powers and great miraculous abilities, being wise and stationed in the sky, display various kinds of miracles.
Then, having taken refuge upon the ridges composed of the seven precious gems,
they remain there, delighted, engaging in various discourses on the Dharma.
Then, having taken refuge in the shade of the wish-fulfilling trees,
they remain there with composed minds, their selves absorbed in meditative concentration.

Then, having respectfully requested from the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa) all objects of enjoyment along with precious gems and wealth, they enjoy them themselves and give them away to those in need.
Thus, there abide Pratyekabuddhas who have attained great supernormal powers.
Having meditated and performed what is beneficial for sentient beings, they move everywhere.
In this same way, within all the other [pores] and even within the pores of the body hair,
there are Brahmā and the other lords of sages, as well as Śakra and the other immortals.
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, Sādhyas, Rudras, lords of the Gaṇas,
all the Bhairavas and Mātṛkās, and even the hosts of Mahākāla;
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas and others,
as well as nāgas, garuḍas, and daityas, all follow their respective dharmas.
Brahmins, Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas, yogins, celibate students, Nirgranthas, other sectarians, ascetics, and those who practice austerities— (Gkv 213) all these [are included].
Kings, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and all human beings— indeed,
all living creatures whatsoever who wander within the cycle of existence.
Devoted to the vows and conduct of their respective lineages and practicing righteousness,
they all took refuge in every pore of that Lord of the World.
When, having meditated upon and recollected that Lord of the World with great reverence,
they also pay homage to the Triple Gem while remaining composed in concentration;
Then, for all of them, every intended accomplishment of the qualities of the Dharma-glory will be fully realized exactly as desired.
Thus, the body of that Teacher of the World is the abode of all virtues;
by means of it, he, the Lord of the three worlds and King of Dharma, shines forth.
At the tip of that hair-pore, at the top of the banner, and at the very rear,
there are eighty thousand peaks made of jewels.
There exist hundreds of millions of wish-fulfilling trees,
as well as trees bearing sandalwood, agallochum, fragrant flowers, and fruits.
The entire ground was composed of vajra, radiant with the luster of moonlight,
and contained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gabled palaces.
In all of those [palaces], which were composed of gold and the seven precious gems,
the staircases and other features were likewise composed of gold and the seven precious gems.
In all those gabled pavilions, Tathāgatas are stationed,
teaching the Dharma that accomplishes perfect enlightenment for the welfare of the world.
In this way, all those Sugatas also constantly teach all the perfections to human beings here in Jambudvīpa.
Thus, at all times, having performed various teachings of the Dharma for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, they remain established in meditative concentration.
Thus, the body of that Teacher of the World is the refuge of all virtues;
by means of it, he, the Teacher of the three worlds, shines forth as the Dharmakāya.
(Gkv 214) Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, that son of the Victor,
having gazed upon the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, spoke thus:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, there are other pores of the skin as well;
O Teacher, you should explain them all to me."
Having heard what was thus spoken, that Blessed Lord of Sages [replied].
Having beheld Viṣkambhin, he commanded him once again in this manner:
Noble son, beyond that point,
on the big toe of the Lord of the World, the four oceans revolve to the right.
When it emerges from his thumb and falls into the Vāḍava fire,
then all that water will be reduced to ashes.
Thus, the body of that Lord of the World is the abode of all dharmas;
by means of it, this King of Dharma, the Lord of the three worlds, shines forth.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, that son of the Victor,
having gazed upon the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, spoke thus:
O Blessed One, having now heard the majesty of the Lord of the three worlds as instructed by you, I have indeed attained a state of supreme wonder.
Having heard that, the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Guru of the World,
looked toward Viṣkambhin and questioned him thus with great respect:
"Noble son, for what reason have you attained such supreme wonder?
You ought to tell me this truth here in its entirety."
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, that son of the Jina,
Viṣkambhin, looked toward the Blessed One and spoke as follows.
Since that Blessed One, the Protector, the refuge of all phenomena,
the sovereign lord of the three realms, the King of Dharma, shines forth in splendor;
Those who, having gone to him for refuge, attend upon him with faith;
and those who, having meditated and recollected him, even by uttering his name, worship him.
Then, for those who strive to accomplish the qualities of the true Dharma,
even all the excellence of auspicious glory and happiness is fully realized.
Blessed and happy are they all, who with faith and joy listen to the discourse on the qualities of the True Dharma of the Lord of the three realms.
And those who, out of praise for its virtues, would write this *Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra* or cause it to be written, or read it or cause it to be read;
Having heard it, one should constantly contemplate it with the mind at all times with devotion,
and one should explain its meaning in detail to others.
That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also blessed, possessing virtuous intentions;
he is free from evil, pure in self, and pure in his faculties.
Nor is he oppressed by afflictions or by the sufferings that wander through existence;
nor is he born into low families or even in the miserable realms.
In his body, the eight fevers, diseases such as leprosy and others,
and all various ailments shall never arise at any time.
He was neither deficient in his faculties nor was he in a wretched state with evil intentions;
rather, he was strong, with well-nourished limbs, pure in his senses, happy, and wise.
Zealous in accomplishing the true Dharma and longing for the qualities of a Perfect Buddha, one should honor the Three Jewels and proceed for the welfare of the world.
With their selves purified by this merit, their faculties completely cleansed,
and being accomplished, they shall attain the threefold awakening and reach the state of a Perfect Buddha.
Having heard what was thus related by him, the Blessed One, with joy,
looked upon Viṣambhin and instructed him once again as follows.
Excellent, excellent, O Mahāsattva! You possess such eloquence that you proclaim the majesty arising from the qualities of Lokeśvara.
Having heard this and other such instructions from the Lord of Munis, that son of the Sugata was filled with joy; looking toward the Lord of Munis, he spoke as follows.
O Blessed One, that I may speak this excellent discourse on the qualities of Lokeśvara here in the midst of this assembly is due to your majestic power.
O Blessed One, when I speak here of this well-composed discourse on the World-Protector, then all these worlds will have their intentions offered with faith.
Having heard that praise of its benefits, all those present in the assembly—
headed by Brahmā, Indra, the Asuras, and the Nāga kings— rejoiced.
Always established in refuge in this Lord of the Three Worlds,
they now constantly desire to propitiate him through meditation.
When he had thus spoken, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
looked toward Viṣkambhin and commanded him once again.
Excellent, excellent! You are a true friend of the wise, in that you repeatedly encourage these people and bring them all to enlightenment.
Therefore, I am pleased with you because all of you, gathered here in my assembly, have gladdened me by encouraging the Dharma of this Lord of the Three Worlds.
Having been thus instructed by the Lord of Sages, Viṣkambhin, filled with joy,
bowed down to the Blessed One and made this request with great reverence:
"O Blessed One, I wish to see those pores of the Lord who sustains the three worlds; therefore, O Teacher, you ought to show them to me."
When Viṣkambhin had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the All-Knowing, looked upon that Great Being and commanded him as follows.
O son of good family, the hair-pores of the Lord of the World are ungraspable;
they are indeed untouchable and invisible, just like space.
Within them, Bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra and others, the sons of the Victors,
all wandered about in agitation on every side for twelve years.
Indeed, all those pores were seen by him alone;
even the Buddhas do not see them, despite being situated right within them.
What need is there for other bodhisattvas, arhats, celibate practitioners, yogins, or even sages? They are not seen by anyone at all.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, that son of the Sugata,
Viṣkambhin, looked toward the Blessed One and spoke as follows.
And those things which are not seen even by Samantabhadra as he wanders about,
nor are they seen by the Buddhas even though they are stationed right there.
"O Blessed One, how indeed could I possibly be able to behold them?
Alas, my birth is in vain, for that Lord of the World has not been seen by me."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
looked toward Viṣkambhin and again commanded him in this way.
O sons of good family, even as I have long been intently observing his pores from every side, they are now visible to me.
O son of good family, that Lokeśa is illusory and possesses a subtle form;
even when appearing as formless, he is without shape and untainted.
Then he was embodied, of great form, possessing universal forms and a vast body; he had eleven heads and a hundred thousand hands.
He has a hundred thousand crores of eyes, possesses a divine form, and is most beautiful;
he is a great yogin, possessed of great wisdom, and the protector of the yoga of ultimate reality.
The Bodhisattva is of noble mind, possessed of great higher knowledge,
the Lord of the world, of high lineage, the Sustainer of the three worlds, and the Sovereign Lord of all phenomena.
The deliverer of all sentient beings, the one who ferries them across the ocean of saṃsāra,
the Great Being, the teacher of the Mahāyāna Dharma, the Guru of the World.
The Lord of the world in the three realms, who bears the very nature of the dharmadhātu;
the omniscient one, the support of the three qualities, free from afflictions, and possessing stainless faculties.
He is an Arhat, established on the path to perfect enlightenment, who bears the welfare of all sentient beings as his purpose.
He is like a shadow to all auspicious dharmas, undisturbed,
fulfilling the equipment for the qualities of perfect enlightenment, and a mine of glorious virtues.
A celibate practitioner of pure soul, the bringer of auspiciousness to all worlds,
the upholder of all perfections, and the sovereign leader of the entire Saṅgha.
Thus is the glorious Mahāsattva, the noble Avalokiteśvara,
the Bodhisattva of great supernormal knowledges, the foremost bearer of all samādhis.
This one, the locus consisting of all phenomena, is not seen by anyone;
for he is inconceivable and beyond scrutiny, yet he assumes the form of every emanation.
Having gazed upon all sentient beings with diligence, he rescues them from miserable states of existence and,
awakening them, establishes them in the auspicious Dharma.
Even observing those who are difficult to subdue, he displays miracles and,
having awakened them through diligent effort, establishes them in the excellent restraint.
Bringing the bodhisattvas, the great beings, to maturity and establishing them on the path to enlightenment, he protects them as if they were his own children.
Thus, that Lord of the Three Worlds, awakening the entire world and establishing it on the path to enlightenment, shall depart for Sukhāvatī.
Having taken refuge in the Lord of Munis in Sukhāvatī and always upholding his instruction, they move about for the welfare of the world.
Always drinking the nectar of the Dharma from that Lord Amitābha,
he remains steadfast, having undertaken the vow to establish the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, that son of the Jina,
Viṣkambhin, gazed upon the Blessed One and spoke as follows:
"Blessed One, by what means, where, when, and how may I behold that Āryāvalokiteśvara, the Lord of the World?"
O Blessed One, that Lord of the World by whatever means is initiated— may you, my Guru, deign to instruct me in that method.
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the Knower of All,
looked toward Viṣkambhin and again gave this instruction:
O son of good family, that Lokeśa, having rescued sentient beings from all quarters,
shall first arrive here in this assembly for an audience with me.
Having heard what was thus instructed by the Teacher, that son of the Sugata,
Viṣkambhin, looked toward the Blessed One and spoke as follows.
"I authorize him, O Teacher; let that Protector come here. When will he, the Lord of the World, arrive? Please instruct me on this."
Having heard what he had said, the Blessed One looked toward that son of the Jina, Viṣkambhin, and instructed him once again in this way.
Having gazed upon him, O son of good family, he further instructed him in this way:
Noble son, when every sentient being is established on the path to awakening,
that great being may here first undertake [the practice].
Having heard what was thus declared by the Teacher, Viṣkambhin was overcome with despondency;
resting his cheek upon his hand, he reflected thus in his mind.
Alas! What sin have I committed, that I shall not obtain a vision of this Lord of the three worlds, the sovereign master of all dharmas?
What is the use of this body of mine, or of a very long life,
if I am without the sight of the Teacher of the World here in this world?
When shall I behold the moon-like face of that Protector?
Stricken by the heat of the afflictions, I shall obtain great bliss that brings refreshing delight.
When shall I, having approached his lotus feet as my refuge and having prostrated, obtain the glorious qualities that grant the welfare of all sentient beings?
When, having performed worship of him and constantly drunk the nectar of Dharma,
shall I move about for the welfare of the world with the enthusiasm of great bliss and happiness?
Having upheld his teaching and always performed what is beneficial for all,
may I go to Sukhāvatī to attain the bliss of the glory of perfect enlightenment.
When shall I go to Sukhāvatī, behold the Lord of Sages Amitābha, and having taken refuge in him, worship him always with joy?
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma and having made the world consist of Dharma,
when shall I attain the state of a Perfect Buddha and go to Nirvana?
Having thus meditated in his mind, Viṣkambhin went before him;
bowing once more to the Blessed One, he made this request with great reverence.
O Blessed One, when will that Lord of the World appear?
For I truly desire to see that Protector anywhere at all.
By whatever means that Protector may be clearly perceived by me,
it behoves you to instruct me thoroughly in that very method.
Having heard that request of his, the Blessed One, though smiling,
looked toward Viṣkambhin and commanded him once again.
"Noble son, the time for Lokeśvara has not yet arrived;
for it is only when the proper moment comes that he, possessing great supernormal knowledge, will necessarily act here."
O sons of noble family, the sight of this Lord within the three realms is difficult to obtain;
indeed, it is only at some time, by someone, and in some way that one finally attains it.
Since he is the lord of all worlds, the sovereign master of all phenomena,
the gatherer of the qualities of the true Dharma, and the locus of the excellence of auspicious glory.
For all sentient beings wandering through existence in the six realms,
[he] is the protector, the sustainer, the father, the mother, the true friend, the true guru, and the refuge.
The worthy refuge, the ultimate resort, the island, the friend, the kinsman, the bestower of welfare;
the deliverer from the ocean of existence, the nectar that extinguishes the fire of afflictions.
He is the destroyer of all Māras, the remover of the fear of all the wicked,
the instructor of the path to perfect enlightenment, and the teacher of the state of nirvāṇa.
Thus he is the one of great authority, the sovereign lord of all worlds,
the chief of the Bodhisattvas, the Teacher, and the leader of the entire Saṅgha.
In saṃsāra, even hearing the true Dharma is difficult for him to obtain;
even the grasping of its name, and even its recollection, are difficult to obtain.
Those who, having taken refuge in him, always meditate upon and remember him,
and having uttered his name, worship him with concentrated minds.
By the power of experiencing this merit, they all possess stainless faculties;
free from afflictions and pure in nature, they become practitioners of the path to enlightenment.
Then those of auspicious conduct, dwelling in the four [meditative] abodes, having observed the poṣadha vow, wandered about with concentrated minds.
By the power of this merit, may those whose three spheres are completely purified,
through their zeal in honoring the Three Jewels, move about for the welfare of the world.
Then those great beings, the Bodhisattvas born from the Conqueror,
shall attain the six-syllable Great Vidyā, the Queen of Vidyās.
When those sons of the Victors, having obtained the six-syllable vidyā,
always recite it with faith, having meditated upon it, remembered it, and uttered it;
Then, within the pore-hairs of that Lord of the World, which is the refuge consisting of all dharmas, all those sons of the Sugata would be born.
Then they might at some point wander again within that very cycle of existence;
born within the pores of his very skin, they would roam there until the end of worldly existence.
Arising right there, they should remain composed, having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening, which is the means for accomplishing the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
Remaining right there, even without difficult practices, they shall easily attain perfect enlightenment and reach the state of nirvana.
Having heard this which was thus taught in the scripture, that son of the Sugata,
Viṣkambhin, looked toward the King of Munis and spoke as follows.
"O Blessed One, I desire to obtain the six-syllabled vidyā; therefore, you ought to grant me this vidyā."
Having heard that request of his, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages,
looked at Viṣkambhin and again commanded him thus:
O son of noble family, this six-syllable queen of vidyās is difficult to obtain;
even the Buddhas do not know it, let alone other sons of the Conquerors.
Having been thus instructed by the Lord of Sages, Viṣkambhin was overcome with despondency;
looking toward the Blessed One, he addressed him once more as follows.
"O Blessed One, since all the Buddhas and sons of the Victors do not know this, how shall I obtain this vidyā? Please instruct me in that."
Having heard what was thus spoken, the Blessed One, the Conqueror who knows all,
looked toward Viṣkambhin and again commanded him in this way.
"O sons of noble family, this vidyā of this Lokeśvara, the Lord of the World,
is declared by all the Buddhas to be the supreme heart-mantra (paramahṛdaya)."
This knowledge is difficult to obtain; it is the leader of all knowledges.
He who knows this knowledge truly understands the ultimate reality.
When the Lord of Sages had thus instructed him, Viṣkambhin, the son of the Jina,
gazed upon the Blessed One and questioned him with great reverence as follows.
O Blessed One, that great being exists even within the abode of existence;
he who knows this spell ought to reveal himself.
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, looking toward the great-minded Viṣkambhin, instructed him once again as follows:
"O son of good family, does anyone here know that six-syllable great vidyā of theirs, which is renowned throughout all the three realms?"
This is the most supreme knowledge, which brings all yogas to their end;
it is not even known by all the Buddhas or by any of the sons of the Victors.
Even all the Buddhas, the Victors, and the Bodhisattvas, desiring this very knowledge, wander everywhere throughout the ten directions.
It is not obtained from anywhere at all, even by those Buddhas who have passed away, nor by all those Bodhisattvas; thus, it is extremely difficult to find.
This may be attained by someone wandering here for a very long time,
through the power of much merit and by the grace of Lokeśvara.
Blessed are they, possessing a great flood of merit, who have attained the qualities of the glory of enlightenment,
and who constantly recite this Heart of Lokeśvara with joy.
Whenever and wherever one recites this six-syllable vidyā, at that time all the Buddhas likewise take refuge in its presence.
And all the Bodhisattvas, the Great Beings of great supernatural power,
having assembled and drawn near, shall protect that Great Being.
All six perfections depend upon his door;
may they grant the accomplishment of the means for achieving perfect enlightenment for the welfare of the world.
And all thirty-two sons, together with their retinues,
having beheld that speaker, would protect him even when he is beset by calamity.
And the four great kings, together with their armies, ministers, and retinues,
stationed in the ten directions, shall provide protection for him.
And all the lords of the nāgas, dwelling upon the earth,
seeing him, would grant a great jewel for the purpose of providing his protection.
All the terrestrial yakṣas as well, having taken refuge and being thoroughly pacified,
will provide protection for him and move about on all sides.
And many Buddhas, residing within the pores of his body, being well-pleased, would utter the word of praise "Excellent! and thus describe him.
Blessed are you, noble son, since you have obtained such a treasury of glorious virtues, a great jewel like a wish-fulfilling gem; well done, O one of excellent resolve!
And may all those twenty-seven lineages, with their three spheres completely purified,
free from afflictions and stainless in nature, attain the state of nirvāṇa.
Moreover, all the multitudes of living beings dwelling within your womb shall indeed become Bodhisattvas, Great Beings, who are irreversible.
Thus, the lords of sages have declared that the merit of this six-syllable vidyā is supreme, immeasurable, and incalculable.
And whoever, being composed, should bind this six-syllabled Great Queen of Knowledge at the crown of the head, the throat, or even the arm, and wear it;
Freed from all evils, with the three spheres completely purified,
and with a self free from afflictions and utterly pure, he shall certainly become a vajra-body.
Like a stupa containing a jewel of the Buddha-nature, it is a support consisting of the Dharma;
it is a glorious repository of excellent qualities, a mass of the finest jewels of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
He who upholds the qualities of the Tathāgata, an ocean of the qualities of the true Dharma,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva possessed of great prosperity.
And whoever, having joyfully received this great vidyā according to the ritual rules,
meditates upon the glorious Lokeśvara and recites it daily with a concentrated mind;
Freed from all transgressions and with the three spheres completely purified,
he shall become one whose intellect is steeped in the true Dharma and who possesses inexhaustible eloquence.
The Teacher is the sovereign of all phenomena, possessed of the perfection of the mass of gnosis;
he is one whose conduct is auspicious and who dwells in the four sublime abodes.
The sovereign lord of all kings of vidyās, a universal monarch and a mine of virtues,
shall daily fulfill the six perfections day after day.
And those who are touched by his breaths shall also become stainless;
they shall become Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, who are irreversible.
And even those who touch his garments become stainless;
they shall indeed be steadfast Bodhisattvas in their final existence.
And those who even behold him while he is reciting [the mantra] shall also become stainless;
they shall all become sons of the Sugata in their final existence.
Whether they be birds, beasts, or any other living beings,
all those who behold one reciting the mantra shall become sons of the Victorious One.
Thus it is: for one of noble mind who recites this great vidyā, the Victors have proclaimed the impelling of the perfection of merit, glory, and virtues.
Having heard what was thus instructed by the Teacher, that son of the Conqueror,
Viṣkambhin, looked toward the Blessed One and spoke as follows:
"O Blessed One, I desire to attain the six-syllable Great Vidyā; from where and how shall I obtain it? You should deign to instruct me."
Whoever would give me this vidyā, the sovereign mistress of all vidyās,
the pinnacle of all yogic qualities, and the bestower of the fruits of all meditative virtues;
She brings about the accumulation of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, shows the path to nirvāṇa,
is the foundation for overcoming afflictions and ignorance, is auspicious, and shines with the true Dharma.
It extinguishes the fire of the afflictions and the suffering of wandering through the cycle of existence in the six realms;
it gathers the accumulations for awakening and bestows the wisdom of omniscience.
Therefore, I truly desire to bestow these four continents, filled with the seven precious jewels; this which I have spoken is the truth.
For he is my mother and my father, the one who shows me the way through saṃsāra;
he is the true friend among friends and the true teacher among teachers.
Having upheld his teaching, I shall always take refuge in it;
free from conceptual construction and composed in meditative absorption, may I move everywhere with joy.
"O Blessed One, these words of mine are indeed true and not otherwise;
therefore, send me quickly to where that true guru resides."
In all ten directions, throughout the entire triple-world system,
wherever that Teacher resides, there too I am eager to go.
Thus, there is indeed no weariness in my mind nor even in my body;
you know all of this, so may you be gracious toward me for its sake.
You alone are the Teacher of the world, the bearer of the welfare and benefit of all phenomena;
therefore, having bestowed your grace upon me, may you fulfill my heart's desire.
Having heard this which had been spoken, the Blessed One, the guide for all caravans, looked toward Viṣkambhin and instructed him once again as follows:
"Noble son, in the past, I too was filled with zeal and wandered through all the world-systems in order to accomplish this vidyā."
Having wandered for a very long time through all the Buddha-fields,
I did not obtain this great vidyā from any sage.
Then, moving with joy in the world-system named Ratnottamā, he practiced.
There, walking before the Perfectly Awakened One named Ratnottama, he approached in his presence with palms joined in reverence.
Having bowed at his feet, their faces smeared with tears, they gazed upon him and spoke thus.
O Blessed One, I now come for refuge to you;
therefore, you ought to grant me the great six-syllable vidyā.
Having heard what I had thus spoken, that omniscient Ratnottama,
the Fully Awakened One, looked at me with my face smeared with tears and gave this instruction.
"Noble son, do not shed tears; that for which you have come here is certainly not found by me. Therefore, pray to others for it."
If you indeed have the desire to attain the six-syllable vidyā,
O Mahāmati, go to the world-system named Padmottama.
There, the Tathāgata named Padmottama, the Lord of Sages, dwells for the welfare of the world, having fully taught the sublime Dharma.
He alone understands this great six-syllable vidyā.
Therefore, having propitiated him, entreat that Lord of Munis;
he is your teacher, the Jina, possessed of great super-knowledge and sovereign over all dharmas.
One should bestow this great vidyā, the six-syllabled one, for the welfare of the world.
Having heard what was thus instructed by him, I was filled with serene joy; thereafter, I proceeded with delight to the world-realm named Padmottama.
There, having beheld from afar the Perfectly Awakened One named Padmottama seated in his assembly, I approached him immediately.
Having gone there before that true guru Padmottama,
I bowed with palms joined at his lotus-feet and made this request with great reverence:
"Blessed One, having wandered through all the worlds and Buddha-fields,
I practice here desiring to attain the Great Knowledge of the six syllables."
For the sake of her, by whose mere recollection those who have purified the three spheres may attain the enlightenment that is so difficult to find, I go forth.
May that purpose for which I have wandered through countless world-systems and now come here to take refuge in you be fulfilled for me.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that all-knowing Padmottama, being perfectly enlightened, beheld me in my state of affliction and commanded as follows.
You are fortunate, O son of good family, that for this purpose you have come here, wandering through all the Buddha-fields with an untiring mind.
For that purpose, O Great Being, I shall fulfill [your wish] for the benefit of the world;
I will speak of the majesty of the qualities of that merit—listen with a concentrated mind.
For example, noble sons, the supreme merit of this vidyā has been declared by the Lords of Sages to be immeasurable and incalculable.
Even if one were to turn all stationary objects into atoms, it would be possible to count them;
however, the merit of reciting the great six-syllable mantra cannot be measured.
It is possible to count the number of grains of sand in all the oceans,
and the number of rice stalks grown upon the entire surface of the earth can also be known.
The number of drops in the waters of all the oceans is known,
and the number of drops in the waters of all the rivers is also known.
The number of leaves on all grasses and trees exists,
and the number of hairs on all living beings also exists.
And even the number of drops of water from constant rain exists.
Even if all sentient beings were established on the ten stages,
the great merit belonging to them would be far surpassed by this [merit].
Among all meritorious pilgrimage sites and on all sacred festival days,
this [Jāpya] is the greatest merit for bathing, giving, and recitation.
May all sentient beings become practitioners of austerity and celibacy;
having honored them all, one should feed them according to the prescribed rite.
Whatever great merit those possess— the perfection of the qualities of auspicious glory—
even greater than that is the merit arising from the recitation of the six-syllable mantra.
Even if all sentient beings were each to become a Sugata,
and someone were to honor all those Sugatas with offerings according to the prescribed rites;
Whatever great merit there may be from the glorious qualities of the True Dharma that bestows all aims,
the merit arising from the recitation of the six-syllable mantra exceeds even that.
And even if one were to honor the Sugatas with offerings according to the prescribed rites,
the merit arising from the recitation of the six-syllable mantra would be even greater than that.
The merit arising from the recitation of the six-syllable mantra is so exceedingly great that it cannot be measured even by all the omniscient ones.
How can the entirety [of merit] be measured by a single person?
Such is the exceedingly great merit arising from the recitation of the six-syllable mantra.
Having heard this which is proclaimed by all the Victors, I was filled with joy;
I desired to obtain this six-syllable vidyā for the welfare of the world.
For this is the supreme dharma, the means for accomplishing the qualities of perfect awakening;
it is subtle, future, unmanifest, and the excellent heart-essence of Lokeśvara.
All the perfections, all bathing in sacred fords, vows, and so forth—
all these are causes for the attainment of the mantra of great knowledge.
For when this accomplishment of the mantra of great knowledge is attained,
then one shall obtain the glorious qualities of the accomplishment of all great knowledges.
Thus, this supreme heart-mantra of Lokeśvara, the Lord of the World, is skilled in great skillful means for the welfare of the three worlds.
Thus, this great vidyā-mantra, which is the means for achieving perfect enlightenment,
has been declared by the lords of sages to be an incalculable and vast merit.
Regarding the cause for attaining this great six-syllable vidyā,
in the past, while wandering through all the buddha-fields, I too took refuge in all the Buddhas.
Having honored him with hospitable offerings and ritual services, he made this request for a boon.
Nowhere did they find this Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), the means for attaining the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, even from the presence of any Sugata.
Then, eager to attain this very knowledge, I departed from there and came with great joy to the world-system Sukhāvatī.
There, having beheld Amitābha seated in the assembly from afar,
I paid homage with palms joined and approached him while remaining at a distance.
Having bowed at the lotus-feet of that Teacher, the Lord of Munis, in the city,
he entered his dwelling while gazing [at them], his face smeared with falling tears.
Having seen that, the Blessed One, the Teacher, the omniscient one, knowing my mental aspiration and looking at me who had taken refuge in him, instructed me thus:
"Kutraputra, desiring the six-syllable vidyā, you have come here; what is this that you wish to speak before me? Tell me this if you so desire.
Having heard these words commanded by the Lord of Jinas, I was filled with faith.
Having bowed once more at his lotus feet, I addressed him thus:
O Blessed One, I desire the great vidyā of six syllables;
may you therefore fulfill this wish of my heart.
O Blessed One, wherever I am throughout all the world-systems in every direction,
Wandering here, I have come to obtain the six-syllable vidyā.
I have wandered everywhere throughout the buddha-fields of all the Buddhas, zealously searching for this vidyā.
Having taken refuge in all the Buddhas as well,
he worshipped them with offerings according to the prescribed rites, honoring them with faith and joy.
From no single Lord of Sages have I received this Great Knowledge; nor has even this six-syllable mantra been heard by me.
O Blessed One, O Teacher, please look upon me who has come to you for refuge as if I were your own son, and deign to establish me in the Dharma.
O Blessed One, be my protector, my sustainer, my refuge, and my ultimate resort; be my kinsman, friend, well-wisher, teacher, guru, lord, and the one who brings about my welfare.
O Blessed One, grant me the vision of the Dharma that perceives all objects;
like the moon, extinguish my great affliction and the heat of the fire.
Show me the path to enlightenment, which leads to the city of the Perfectly Awakened One;
grant me the treasury of Dharma, which bestows the bliss and glory of the True Dharma.
Establish me in the auspicious Dharma; impel me toward perfect Nirvana.
Thus, although he was repeatedly entreated by me in many ways,
Amitābha, the Lord of Jinas, nevertheless looked toward Lokeśvara.
Having seen that, the Great Being Lokeśvara arose;
with palms joined in reverence, he bowed to that King of Dharma and spoke as follows.
"Blessed One, with what intention do you command me? Carrying your command upon my head, I shall certainly act as you have instructed."
When this had been spoken by the Lord of the World, the Blessed One Amitaprabha,
having gazed upon Lokeśvara of great supernormal knowledge, gave this instruction:
Behold, noble son, this Padmottama, lord of sages,
who has come here to obtain the great vidyā of six syllables.
This Teacher, who is the Lord of Sages, the Perfectly Awakened One, and the Tathāgata,
has come here desiring the knowledge that bestows benefit upon the beings of the world.
Therefore, O son of good family, give this Great Queen Jagaddhīti to this seeker of the welfare and purity of all sentient beings, who is clear-minded through faith and devotion.
When the Lord of Sages had thus instructed him, Lokeśvara, the sovereign of the world,
beheld that Jina Abhitābha and spoke as follows.
"Blessed One, how can I give this six-syllable vidyā to him here without showing him the maṇḍala and without having conferred initiation?"
This Great Vidyā should not be given to a monk who has not been consecrated,
nor to one who is free from passion, nor to a wicked person, nor to a heretic of evil nature.
This great vidyā, which accomplishes the qualities of auspicious glory, should be given to one who is of excellent character,
full of faith, and a seeker of the Mahāyāna vow.
To the Bodhisattva who understands, who desires the welfare of all sentient beings,
who is clear in faith and devotion, and who accomplishes the virtues of the True Dharma.
O Blessed One, although he is intent upon the vow of the conduct of awakening for the sake of bringing benefit to all sentient beings, even toward this Sugata, the Arhat, he acts inappropriately.
If you have compassion, then consecrate him even after showing him the mandala;
thereafter, by your command, I shall grant it to him who is well-pleased.
Having heard what was thus reported by that Lokeśa,
Amitābha, the Lord of Sages, spoke to Lokeśa in this way:
"Noble son, I have explained that method for bestowing the vidyās,
which has been fully proclaimed in various ways by all the Lords of Sages."
The Guru prepares the maṇḍala using powders of coral, rubies, emeralds, as well as powders of gold and silver.
Likewise, having prepared a maṇḍala with flower powders, fragrant powders, and small tubes at a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should cause the consecration (abhiṣeka) to be bestowed.
If these qualities do not exist in one who wanders through various lands,
then even for one who possesses a noble station, is poor, yet possesses right-mindedness— [these qualities are essential].
The preceptor, having meditated in his mind upon the mandala characterized by mudrās,
or having bestowed the consecration of the holy conch, should transmit the vidyā.
O son of good family, by this procedure,
the six-syllable great vidyā should be given to this faithful person who is well-disposed.
Having heard this instruction imparted by Amitābha,
I arose joyful and stood before Lokeśvara.
Having joyfully prostrated at his lotus feet with palms joined in reverence, and gazing upon that Lord of the World, he made this request with great devotion:
O Blessed One, I have come here for refuge to you, the Blessed One;
grant me the six-syllable great vidyā for the welfare of the world.
By means of which I, having rescued all sentient beings from the ocean of existence and joined them to the path to enlightenment, may cause them to attain perfect nirvana.
Therefore, may you grant me that sovereign of all vidyās which accomplishes perfect awakening, for I seek the state of a perfectly awakened one throughout this entire world of sentient beings.
Thus entreated by me, that Lord of the World was pleased and bestowed upon me the Great Vidyā, reciting the six-syllabled mantra.
The Praṇava at its beginning, the lotus at its end,
and the seed-syllable *hṛd*— this is the six-syllabled mantra, renowned as the "Siddhā."
Having joyfully received the great lore that had been bestowed upon him,
he gave to that teacher of the world a necklace of pearls as a sacrificial fee.
Taking that pearl necklace as his sacrificial fee,
the Lord of the World presented it before the Fully Awakened Amitābha.
The Lord of Sages, Amitābha, having accepted that garland and being moved by my devotion, placed it before me and gave it to me.
Having accepted that garland bestowed by him, and being awakened,
he offered it there by presenting it to the community of disciples.
There, having meditated upon the glorious Lokeśvara exactly as he was taught by the Teacher, they recite this great mantra with concentrated minds.
Then all the hosts of obstacles and even the wicked hosts of Māra,
their souls overwhelmed with terror, flee to the ends of the quarters.
The earth, together with the oceans, mountains, and waters, shook in its sixfold manner;
a rain of flowers fell, and everywhere there was an auspicious festival.
Then, having received permission from the glorious Teacher, Lokeśvara, the Lord of the World, I bowed at his feet and, filled with joy, departed for my own hermitage.
Thus, by wandering through all the stages with extreme hardship,
this [attainment] of Lokeśvara has been reached by me through the power of Amitābha.
O son of noble family, this six-syllable great vidyā is difficult to obtain;
it was not obtained by any of the Sugatas, nor was it obtained by any of the Jinas.
Thus was it commanded by the Lord of Sages, Padmottama, in my presence;
and I too have heard this great means for the welfare of the world.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, that son of the Jina,
Viṣkambhin, gazing upon the Blessed One, spoke as follows:
"Blessed One, where shall I obtain this vidyā that brings welfare to the world, and how, from whom, and in what manner? It behoves you to instruct me in this."
Blessed are those pure-souled ones, meritorious and fortunate,
who recite this vidyā, hear it, and even meditate upon it.
And those who uphold [this], proclaim it, or even contemplate it with their minds—
all those great beings are the locus of the excellent qualities of auspicious glory.
Then the Blessed One, beholding Viṣkambhin, the one of great intelligence, [spoke].
"In this way, may these great beings come to exist," he thus ordained.
Furthermore, O son of good family, whoever should have this vidyā— the means for achieving perfect enlightenment—
copied, or should themselves copy it, or should even preserve it once it has been copied;
For by him indeed have the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dharma been caused to be written, as well as having been written and preserved.
And whoever, having fashioned stupas made of gold and jewels containing the jewel-like relics of all the Buddhas, should constantly worship them with joy;
Whatever great merit they possess, even more abundant and superior,
is the fruit of the six-syllable Vidyārājñī and the one-syllable [mantra].
Whoever should constantly recite with joy and faith this six-syllable vidyā, which accomplishes perfect enlightenment and is a mine of auspicious glory and excellent qualities—
He possesses inconceivable glory and great supernormal knowledge; he is the master of all perfections, and he shall also attain all dhāraṇīs and all meditative absorptions.
The master of all sciences, the Teacher, the sovereign lord of all phenomena,
the Arhat, the conqueror of Māra, he shall be the bearer of the welfare and purpose of all beings.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Munis,
the Bodhisattva Viṣkambhin was filled with joy; having heard it,
that Bodhisattva Viṣkambhin spoke thus to the Lord of Munis.
"Blessed One, where should I go where this six-syllable mantra exists? I must certainly be sent there by you, my teacher, in every way."
Having thus heard what was said by him, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
looked at Viṣkambhin and commanded him once again as follows.
"Noble son, there is only one who knows the six-syllable mantra;
he resides in the city of Vārāṇasī, constantly reciting it."
Having himself maintained [the practice] and having respectfully instructed others as well,
he— his self liberated through meditative concentration and absorption— dwells for the welfare of the world.
Having heard this which was taught by the Teacher, the Bodhisattva Viṣkambhin was filled with joy and spoke thus to that Teacher:
"Blessed One, I shall go there where the Teacher dwells;
I am eager even to see him in the great city of Vārāṇasī."
Seeing Viṣkambhin, the Great Being, thus filled with longing, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages, looked at him and gave this instruction:
Go, O son of noble family, if you so desire; worship that true guru who resides in the great city of Vārāṇasī, possessing this great vidyā.
That teacher, whose self is perfectly pure, a preacher of the Dharma who knows the self,
possesses great supernormal knowledges like a fully awakened Buddha, moving about as if he were a mass of merit.
A stūpa composed of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), like a beautiful body moving about,
he is a speaker of truth, one of virtuous conduct, and the bearer of the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings.
Resplendent like a wish-fulfilling gem, bestowing the accomplishment of all aims,
he is the King of Dharma, the sustainer of the world, and the lord capable of uplifting the world.
If, upon seeing that knower of the self, one censures him due to a lack of discernment,
[one is like all other sacred sites compared to the Ganges, or like all other seats of enlightenment compared to the Bodhimaṇḍa].
O son of good family, you must not view him otherwise;
having seen that Dharma-preacher, you must harbor no doubt.
The great-souled practitioner of yoga, whose three spheres are completely purified.
If, having seen that knower of the self, you revile him through lack of discernment,
you will indeed fall from the stage of a Buddha and even descend into the lower realms.
For he, whose self is purified by yoga, is free from conceptual construction and has conquered his senses;
though appearing as one who follows no conduct, smeared with filth, and clothed in impure rags.
He was engaged in worldly postures, relying upon the life of a householder;
he had entered into union with his capable wife and possessed both daughters and sons.

Nevertheless, that practitioner of yoga, who possesses great supernormal knowledge, who is purified by the six-syllable mantra, and who is like Samantabhadra, should be venerated by you with reverence.
Having heard what was thus instructed by the Blessed One, Viṣkambhin was awakened;
and looking upon the Blessed One, he spoke as follows.
O Blessed One, exactly as commanded by you, the Teacher, so shall it be;
having performed that and remaining in refuge, I shall honor him with great reverence.
"O Blessed One, I am going there to obtain the six-syllable vidyā;
it behoves you now to grant me your permission."
Then the Blessed One gave this permission and blessing to that Bodhisattva: "Go; may your purpose be accomplished."
Having received permission from the Lord of Sages, Viṣkambhin was filled with joy;
bowing with palms joined at the lotus-feet of the Buddha, he then set forth and traveled on.
Accompanied by many bodhisattvas who dwell in the sublime abodes,
as well as by monks, noble disciples, naked ascetics, and lay devotees.
By householders, by those observing vows, by brahmins and others, by the people of the city, by merchants, by caravan leaders, by guild-masters, and by the great folk;
Together with various offerings for worship, there were also diverse flowers of every season,
both those born in water and those grown on land.
All fragrant substances and sweet-smelling incenses,
all articles of adornment and various kinds of garments.
Banners, parasols, canopies, flags, and fans;
yak-tail whisks, brightly blazing jewel-lamps, and large drums.
All the substances of the elements, all the jewels in their entirety,
all medicinal herbs and the like, and all delicious objects of enjoyment.
In this manner, taking other objects and all his requisites as well, he went to Vārāṇasī with great enthusiasm.
Having arrived there, Viṣkambhin saw that Dharma-preacher;
bowing from afar with palms joined in reverence, he approached him with joy.
There, filled with joy, he went before the Dharma-preacher;
bowing with palms joined at his lotus-like feet and gazing upon him, he spoke thus:
Venerable Kauśalya, have you [renounced] even your sense faculties,
as well as all possessions and even your kinsmen and friends?
May you also know that purpose for which I have come here to the refuge of your Teacher; for that purpose, may you be gracious to me.
Having thus made his request in the presence of the Teacher, that son of the Sugata, Viṣkambhin,
whose nature is well-restrained, performed an offering in due order.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites with all offerings of worship, garments, and pure, beautiful robes;
and having adorned [the site] with banners, parasols, canopies, flags, fans, and so forth, he held a great festival accompanied by songs and instrumental music.
Then, before him, there appeared all kinds of materials and implements,
including various minerals and collections of gems, as well as objects of enjoyment and medicinal herbs.
Having placed all these before him, he prepared them;
then he performed prostrations with the eight limbs and circumambulations.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, he gazed upon the Teacher, the preacher of the Dharma, and with a very serene countenance, he made this request with great devotion:
O Venerable True Guru, Teacher Dharmashrigunashagara,
may you please fulfill the desire of my heart.
Those who always listen to the Dharma, having taken refuge in you—
the gods, as well as the asuras, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras— [do so].
Even the Garuḍas, the Nāgas, and the Vidyādharas and others,
as well as the Kumbhāṇḍas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, and Piśācas.
The Siddhas, the Sādhyas, the planets, all the stars, and the hosts of Apsarases;
the lords of all the worlds, as well as the Brahmins and the great seers.
As well as the self-restrained, the practitioners of yoga, the mendicants, and those who lead the holy life.
There were also bhikṣuṇīs, weavers, those observing vows, and lay devotees (upāsakas).
There were also non-Buddhist heretics, followers of Śiva, and devotees of Viṣṇu who practiced austerities;
as well as kings, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, guild-leaders, and great merchants.
The citizens, caravan leaders, merchants, and artisans—
as well as all other people— were likewise possessed of pure intentions.
May those meritorious great beings, who are the refuge of auspiciousness, glory, and excellent virtues—
bodhisattvas possessing the great superknowledges— become attainers of awakening.
And those who resort to you and have come for refuge—
may they all become pure-souled and attainors of enlightenment.
Merely by the sight of you, all sins,
even the most terrible ones, are destroyed without remainder.
All the perfectly awakened ones situated in the ten directions know you,
as do all the bodhisattvas and all the arhats who are practitioners of yoga.
Even the gods, such as Brahmā and Śakra, who are lords of all worlds,
always and in every way devote themselves [to him], desiring great merit.
Blessed are all those people who, having drunk the nectar of the Dharma, remain devoted to it, having attained the glory and virtues of the True Dharma.
This Vārāṇasī on earth is a great ground, a field of merit.
Smeared with the dust of your feet, she becomes exceedingly purified.
Therefore, O Venerable One, may you, the Teacher, look upon me with compassion;
sprinkle me with the nectar of merit and sustain me like your own son.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that wise Dharma-preacher,
even as he beheld the Great Being Viṣkambhin, spoke to him in this way:
O sons of noble family, do not give rise to regret here in my presence;
why would you wish for affliction within existence, which is the means for attaining the bliss of the true Dharma?
"How many, O venerable ones, are the afflictions that pertain to the experience of saṃsāra?"
These are the incidental [teachings] concerning the origin of beings, which accomplish the qualities of the true Dharma.
And those who fully comprehend this great six-syllable vidyā are not defiled by the afflictions, even while moving within the phenomena of saṃsāra.
Just as gold from the Jambu river is never defiled by impurities,
so it is for one who possesses this six-syllable great vidyā within their body.
"Even as he wanders through saṃsāra, his body is not defiled by the afflictions.
Having heard this instruction from him, Viṣkambhin was comforted;
bowing to that Dharma-preacher, he made this request.
O True Guru, grant the eye of Dharma to me whose path is lost;
O Lord of the World, satisfy me with the nectar-essence of the Dharma.
Plant for me the seed of the wish-fulfilling tree of perfect enlightenment upon this tree;
make for me a dwelling place for the jewels of the qualities of the true Dharma.
Make my body an abode for the prosperity of auspiciousness, glory, and happiness;
make it an indestructible foundation of virtue, well-established, and supported by the Bull.
Make me pure in soul, with the three spheres completely purified;
grant me the great vidyā that accomplishes the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
The six-syllable mantra, which is the support for the qualities of the glory of the True Dharma, exists for the welfare of the world.
By means of which I may quickly attain the excellent jewel of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment and rescue the world of beings from the great ocean of saṃsāra.
May I set in motion the light of the Wheel of Dharma within the abode of existence;
may I liberate the entire world from the bonds of affliction in the six realms of rebirth.
May I cause the entire world to hear the well-spoken words of the perfectly awakened ones;
may I spread throughout the world the Great Vehicle, the supreme vow.
I would establish the entire world upon the path to enlightenment;
therefore, O Ocean of Compassion, please grant me the great vidyā of six syllables.
May he who gathers the wisdom of perfect enlightenment grant it for the welfare of the world,
having bestowed upon me this glorious six-syllable great vidyā.

He is the protector, the lord, the teacher, the instructor, the true friend, the bearer of the purpose of virtuous qualities; he is the refuge, the kinsman, the well-wisher, the master, the sovereign, the father, and the ultimate resort.
My husband, who is devoted to his island-home, is your refuge.
When he had thus made his request, that Dharma-preacher, having heard him and looking toward the Great Being Viṣkambhin, spoke as follows.
O son of noble family, this great state of all vidyās is difficult to attain;
it is indestructible by all Māras, possessing the unsurpassed essence of a vajra.
It brings great peace to the burning heat of all the fires of affliction;
it is the means for accomplishing the bliss of the flourishing of the true Dharma and the virtues of auspicious glory.
It brings about the welfare of all sentient beings, fulfills the accumulations for awakening,
is sublime and vast as the supreme of all dharmas, and purifies all lower realms.
It is the means for accomplishing the state of liberation and the perfection of inexhaustible gnosis;
it is the means for accomplishing the awakening that is the essence of the ten perfections and all dharmas.
It is the state longed for by all the worlds, including the gods;
it is the locus of the state of all dharmas, the great state of entry.
And those who, having received the consecration according to the rules from the deities residing in their respective families, always practice the noble vow.
Some, resorting to sacred fords and desiring liberation through the true Dharma,
worship those [deities] with devotion, meditating upon and reciting mantras.
Some [practice] in a speechless wilderness, in a cave, in a lonely forest,
in a sacred field, in a beautiful house, on a ritual seat, or even in a cemetery.
And some [practiced] at a shrine, in a monastery, in an assembly hall,
in a pavilion, in a garden, at the foot of a tree, or in a temple of Śiva and other deities.
Some, having taken refuge on the shore of the great ocean, on the banks of a river, or on the edge of a lake,
and likewise elsewhere in a sacred field, remain concentrated in meditation.
Having approached for refuge to the respective tutelary deities of their own lineages,
they meditate upon, propitiate, and worship them, and thus pray for perfect nirvāṇa.
They do not attain final liberation even after performing difficult austerities;
they merely go to the abodes of the deities worshipped by their respective families.
And those noble great beings, the Bodhisattvas who seek the auspicious,
having paid homage to the Three Jewels, give gifts with devotion.
Anointed with this merit, they shall become free from affliction;
possessing pure conduct and observance, they shall move about in perfect self-restraint.
Anointed with this merit and having purified the three spheres,
they shall undertake the vow of patience and move about for the welfare of the world.
Endowed with this merit and striving to accomplish the true Dharma,
they should exert great vigor and enthusiasm to achieve the welfare of all beings.
Freed from this merit, free from afflictions, and having conquered their senses,
they— established in yoga, meditation, and concentration— should remain composed in samādhi.
Pervaded by this nectar of merit, those stainless Arhats,
having maintained the vow for perfect enlightenment, would attain the supreme Buddhist discipline.
Illumined by these rays of merit, those who dwell in the four modes of conduct,
having attained the jewel of wisdom, may move about with perfect self-restraint.
By the power of this merit, may you all, being skilled in every means,
practice the auspicious conduct that brings about the welfare of all sentient beings.
Richly endowed with this merit, moving about according to their will,
may they fulfill the accumulation of all that is beneficial for the welfare of the world.
Illumined by this merit, possessing the great superknowledges and being mines of virtue,
they shall diligently establish the entire world on the path to enlightenment.
With their limbs consisting of this merit, they shall attain the supreme knowledge of the ultimate truth,
conquer the Māras, and fully realize perfect enlightenment.
Then those Sugatas, the Buddhas, having awakened and established the beings of the world in perfect restraint, proceeded to the state of supreme nirvana.
Thus, after a long time, those Buddhas, practicing the conduct of awakening,
fulfill all ten perfections in their proper sequence.
Having conquered all the hosts of Māra and abiding in the four divine abodes,
they attained supreme knowledge, reached perfect enlightenment, and entered final liberation.
Thus, even all the Victors, having performed such difficult essential tasks, attained awakening after a long time and reached perfect nirvāṇa.
He who, with a mind set on awakening, constantly meditates upon this glorious Mahāsarvavidyeśvarī of six syllables and recites the mantra of Lokeśvara, [attains his goal].
At that moment, with his self purified and the three spheres completely cleansed,
endowed with auspicious glory and happiness, he shall depart for Sukhāvatī.
Having arrived there, taking refuge in the Sage Amitābha,
and having drunk the nectar of the qualities of awakening, one should practice the vow of a bodhisattva.
Then, with a nature purified by conventional truth and eager for the welfare of all sentient beings,
the adept fulfills all the perfections in their proper sequence.
Having conquered their senses, they fulfill the accumulation of conventional dharmas;
serving as a support for the excellent qualities of meditative concentration, they have even conquered the hosts of Māra.
Having attained the ultimate truth, one shall fully realize perfect enlightenment;
then, having reached the state of a Buddha, one shall make the world consist of the Dharma.
Free from conceptual construction and pure in essence, he shall proceed to perfect nirvāṇa;
all yogas are great vidyās, the causes for attaining the ultimate reality.
This knowledge is the means for accomplishing the wisdom of the great awakening to the Dharma;
for it is like the cultivation of grain that protects one from the phenomena of saṃsāra.
Thus, this great vidyā is the protector of all the true Dharma;
it should be diligently [established] throughout the entire world upon the excellent earth.
Having ploughed and sown the grain, they carefully tend it;
yet when the sprout has emerged, it is swept away by the waters of rivers that have burst their banks.

When it has been thoroughly moistened by the streams of water from the clouds and has grown large, it then becomes fully developed; having threshed it on the surface of the ground in a threshing-floor, [one obtains the grain].
Having crushed it and brought it home, having dried it with the rays of the sun,
he then diligently split it apart with a mallet.
Just as one discards the husks and retains only the grain,
so too that very grain, when perfected, sustains the entire cycle of existence.
The fulfillment of the accumulations for attaining the true Dharma is the means of achieving enlightenment;
