likewise are all the great yogas and all the perfections.
All sciences and mantras are for the sake of attaining the true Dharma;
it is the most excellent among all yogic sciences and mantras as well.
This great vidyā-mantra is proven to be the means for attaining perfect enlightenment;
in this very way, the great vidyā accomplishes the purpose of all dharmas.
Without great merit, this sublime yoga cannot be attained by anyone; for rice without its husk never grows in a fertile field.
This great vidyā is not obtained by those devoid of merit in any way;
for as long as this vidyā, which accomplishes all aims, is not obtained.
One should diligently accomplish all meritorious deeds until this vidyā is obtained; once it is attained, one may disregard merit.
Having meditated upon this very Great Vidyā, one should recite the mantra of Lokeśvara;
when this Vidyā is accomplished, it brings about the attainment of all provisions.
Then, one should accomplish the activities of the True Dharma according to one's own wish by means of this;
for she, appearing in the form of rice, is the means for accomplishing the phenomena of cyclic existence.
All phenomena have the form of chaff; this is the cause for attaining this knowledge.
Thus is this most great Queen of Knowledge, the six-syllabled one.
Having meditated upon all the perfections, all the perfectly enlightened Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Victors, always bow down with devotion.
The Arhats, free from all afflictions, bow down after meditating upon this;
so too do all the gods, beginning with Indra, and the great sages, beginning with Brahmā.
All the planets beginning with the Sun, as well as the stars beginning with the Moon;
all the Siddhas and Sādhyas, the Vasus, and the hosts of Apsarases.
All the lords of the thirty-three gods, as well as all the vidyādharas,
the world-lords such as Viṣṇu and Brahmā, and the kumbhāṇḍas headed by Yama.
All the lords of the rākṣasas, as well as Varuṇa and the others who are the lords of the nāgas;
all the lords of the garuḍas, and all the sovereigns of the winds.
All the yakṣa lords, beginning with Śrīda, and all the yogins, beginning with Īśa.
And the lords of the Gandharvas and Kinnaras, as well as the sovereigns of all the worlds.
Having meditated upon, recollected, and even prostrated before this six-syllable queen of vidyās, which is eternally constant, they worship her with great reverence.
Whoever, out of reverence for this well-accomplished queen of vidyās,
always and incessantly honors her by meditating upon her, recollecting her, and bowing down to her;
All of them, with their limbs purified, liberated from all transgressions,
free from afflictions, and stainless in soul, proceeded to Sukhāvatī.
There, having taken refuge in the Teacher Amitaruci and always drinking the nectar of the Dharma, they shall move about for the welfare of the world.
Thus, having brought benefit to the world of living beings and being filled with joy,
those bodhisattvas of great supernormal powers shall become kings of the Dharma.
Then those pure-souled ones, having purified the three spheres,
became Arhats and, having attained awakening, reached the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Thus, this six-syllabled vidyā is renowned as most great;
for by its mere recollection, all sins are indeed destroyed.
Whoever constantly recites this, and whoever should touch his robe,
he too shall become a Mahāsattva, a Bodhisattva who is irreversible.
Whoever honors this with devotion, by that all the Jinas are honored;
together with their Saṅghas, they too are always honored with acts of veneration.
Thus, this most great [mantra], which bestows the wealth of all auspiciousness and virtuous qualities,
is renowned everywhere throughout all worlds as the "Six-Syllabled One."
The Mother who gives birth to the Buddhas is also that Prajñāpāramitā;
holding her hands joined in reverence, she bows down to this auspicious one.
Therefore, this Great Vidyā is the means for accomplishing the dharmas of saṃsāra;
it is venerated by the Lords of Munis, by the Bodhisattvas, and by all the gods.
Even the acquisition of her collection of names is difficult to attain;
recollection and hearing of them, moreover, cannot be obtained without merit.
Having heard what was thus commanded by him, Viṣkambhin was filled with joy;
joining his palms in reverence and bowing, he made this request to the Dharma-preacher.
O Venerable One, O True Guru, O Teacher, I have come to you for refuge;
therefore, may you grant me the Great Vidyā for the welfare of the world.
Thus entreated by him, that Dharma-preacher, looking on,
recollected Lokeśvara, meditated upon him, and remained there with thoughts fixed on that gift.
Then from the sky there issued a captivating, great voice:
"Grant this [mantra] to him who desires merit for the sake of the welfare of the world."
This steadfast great being, a bodhisattva and son of the Victors,
has come here desiring to know what is beneficial for all sentient beings.
"One whose soul is serene through faith and devotion, and who yearns for the knowledge of awakening—to him this great vidyā, renowned for its efficacy, should be given; let it be bestowed."
Hearing that great sound emerging from it, the Dharma-preacher stood there reflecting, "From where does this sound proceed?"
Once again, this great sound issued forth from the sky:
"Let it be given to him who is so well-pleased, who strives for the wisdom of perfect enlightenment."
"May this be given with faith to the Bodhisattva, the steadfast one, who seeks the glory and virtues of the True Dharma for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings."
Hearing that beautiful sound emerging, the Dharma-preacher,
reflecting on where this sound was coming from, should look about.
Having surveyed all directions and looking about with a wise mind,
his heart filled with wonder, he beheld him as he gazed into the sky.
One should visualize the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, whose radiance shines like the full moon of autumn, who is adorned with matted locks as bright as Amitābha, and who holds a lotus in his hand.
Having seen that Bodhisattva, the son of the Conqueror, absorbed in the sky—
the support of auspicious glory and excellent virtues, and the sun of the Dharma of perfect enlightenment—
Beholding this, he rose with a heart filled with joy and wonder;
having performed a prostration with the eight limbs, he stood with palms joined in reverence, lost in meditation.
Seeing that Dharma-preacher thus situated, with his senses withdrawn, that Lord of the Three Worlds addressed him and gave this instruction:
O noble sons, this one is diligent in accomplishing the wisdom of perfect enlightenment;
let this great vidyā of six syllables be bestowed upon him.
Having heard this instruction from that Teacher of the World,
the Dharma-preacher looked at him, bowed, and spoke as follows:
O Blessed One, Protector, Lord of Dharma, I bear your command upon my head.
May you grant this great lore to him; may you be well-pleased.
Having thus addressed Lokeśa, that Dharma-preacher then called upon Viṣkambhin and, looking at him, spoke as follows:
"Noble son, the Teacher of the World has granted his command to me as I am pleased;
I shall give you the Great Vidyā—take this six-syllable mantra."
Having thus instructed him according to the prescribed rite, that most righteous one, having declared its complete purity, bestowed the six-syllabled mantra upon that great soul.
The six-syllabled mantra, consisting of the Praṇava, the Maṇika, the Ja, and the Hṛdbīja,
is established as this Great Vidyā renowned as the Ṣadakṣarī.
Having bowed with palms joined, Viṣkambhin, filled with joy, received this six-syllable lore, the most excellent among all sciences, which had been bestowed by him.
At that moment, the earth, together with its mountains and oceans, shook in six ways;
a rain of flowers fell from all sides, and auspiciousness prevailed everywhere.
As soon as that knowledge was imparted, Viṣkambhin became prosperous;
he attained numerous accumulations of merit and meditative concentrations.
Then, with a deeply serene mind, he gave that sword along with a sacrificial fee to him.
With joy, he gave away the four continents filled with the seven precious jewels.
Seeing him, that Dharma-preacher of great supernormal knowledge and supreme righteousness,
having gazed upon the Great Being Viṣkambhin, spoke thus:
"Noble son, you are noble, not ignoble; you are a son of the Sugata, a bodhisattva ready for conversion. Therefore, I shall not accept your offering."
These are not even sufficient as a fee for a single syllable, much less for six syllables; nevertheless, I would still accept them from you.
Having heard that, Viṣkambhin, possessed of great supernormal knowledge, presented to his true guru a pearl necklace of pure luster and of immense value.
Seeing it thus presented, the Dharma-preacher took it,
returned it to him, and looking at it, spoke to him in this way:
"Noble son, having once again approached this Śākyamuni, the Lord of Munis and Teacher of the World, you should speak these words on my behalf: 'Homage!'"
Having heard what was thus instructed by the Teacher, he was comforted;
looking at Viṣkambhin with great serenity, he spoke as follows.
"Whatever you have commanded, that indeed I shall do.
Having thus informed him and bowed, he took up the pearl necklace.
Then, with a deeply serene mind, Viṣkambhin bowed with palms joined before the lotus-feet of that true guru and set forth, proceeding with joy.
Together with all those by whom his heart's desire had always been attained,
he proceeded to the Jetavana grove with great auspiciousness and great enthusiasm.
There, seeing from afar the Blessed One seated in the assembly, he joined his palms in reverence, prostrated himself, and quickly approached him.
Having approached there, he bowed with palms joined at the lotus-feet of that Teacher, the Guru of the World, and seeking refuge, gazed intently upon them.
There, the Blessed One, seeing Viṣkambhin arrived, looked upon him.
Having gazed upon his lotus-like face, which was exceedingly serene, he commanded as follows:
Welcome, noble sons! Is there any well-being in your bodies? Having attained your desired object, you have come here with a gracious mind.
When the Lord of Sages had thus instructed him, Viṣkambhin was filled with serene faith;
beholding the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, he made this report:
O Blessed One, through the power of your compassion, I have obtained the vidyā that accomplishes perfect awakening and bestows the purpose of the noble qualities of auspicious glory.
Today my birth has become fruitful; I am now a son of the Buddha.
Previously, I have attained the true path to enlightenment, which is auspicious, glorious, and dedicated to the welfare of the world.
O Blessed One, since you are the Teacher who upholds the welfare and benefit of all beings,
you ought to exhort me so that I may swiftly attain awakening.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
looked toward Viṣkambhin and commanded him once again as follows.
Blessed are you, noble son, a bodhisattva and son of the Victors,
who has attained the great vidyā that brings about the welfare of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, I shall give to you, for the welfare of the world, that Great Vidyā which was spoken by seventy-seven crores of perfectly awakened Buddhas.
Whoever [upholds] this dhāraṇī-mantra, which destroys all transgressions,
which is the support for auspiciousness, glory, and excellent virtues, and which accomplishes the state of perfect awakening—
Having undertaken [the practice] with a pure mind, being mindful, meditative, and composed,
and maintaining the vow for perfect enlightenment, one should recite it always with reverence.
He is liberated from all evils, his faculties are completely purified, and he is wise.
A Bodhisattva who has purified himself of all defilements shall be successful.
All the lords of sages, having beheld him constantly and at all times,
protect him even from wicked Māras as if he were their own son.
That heroic one, a great being of great zeal, shall be invincible against all hosts of obstacles in accomplishing the qualities of the true Dharma.
The Goddess Prajñāpāramitā, the mother of the Perfectly Awakened Ones,
also always beholds that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva with equanimity.
Lokeśvara, beholding him who is the abode of the qualities of Śrībhadraka,
shall protect him everywhere and at all times, enjoining him to the vow of awakening.
Then, having mastered the three qualities and maintaining the vow of the conduct of awakening, he gradually fulfilled the entire equipment for complete enlightenment.
Then, with his self thoroughly purified, free from afflictions, and with stainless faculties, that Arhat, having utterly conquered the Māras, shall attain the threefold awakening.
Then that Teacher of the Three Worlds, having made the entire world consist of Dharma and having joined everyone to the vow of enlightenment, shall attain perfect nirvana.
Thus, this most excellent vidyā, which accomplishes the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha,
should always be upheld and recited by you for the welfare of the world.
And those who, having heard this melodious recitation and exposition of the Great Vidyā, rejoice in it, bow down, and honor it with reverence;
May they all be free from blemish, with the three spheres completely purified;
may those born of the Sugata’s essence be devoted to honoring the Three Jewels and honor them.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order,
they shall attain the threefold enlightenment and reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Thus, all the Lords of the World, having upheld this most exalted vidyā,
have constantly recited it and taught it for the welfare of the world.
Thinking thus, you too should recite this vidyā for the welfare of the world; it is the means for awakening, the auspicious glory that brings about the accumulation of Dharma.
Having thus instructed Viṣkambhin, the wise and virtuous Bodhisattva, that Lord of Sages, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, [spoke as follows].
"Āya oṃ cale cūle cunde svāhā"— this nine-syllable supreme dhāraṇī, a vidyā-mantra, he himself uttered and bestowed.
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence, Viṣkambhin received that nine-syllable Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) personally bestowed by the Teacher and recited it with joy.
Having been held by Viṣkambhin and recited before the Teacher,
that Great Vidyā became fully accomplished for the welfare of the three worlds.
By the power of this knowledge, that Viṣkambhin, possessed of pure vision,
beheld even all the pores of Lokeśvara’s body.
Having seen them, Viṣkambhin was filled with joy and wonder:
"Aha! What a marvel! This great illusion is now being manifested by me."
Having meditated thus— that even all the worlds are contained within the Dharmakāya of the Lord of the World— he remained composed, with his senses perfectly stilled.
Then Viṣkambhin, his mind perfectly serene and fully awakened,
bowed down to the Blessed One and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke as follows:
O Blessed One, Lord of the three worlds, [speak] now regarding the refuge of all dharmas.
I see all things within the pores of the hair in the Self of the universe.
How many worlds are there within the pores of his body— he who is indeed the sovereign of all phenomena— for he is capable of displaying them all?
When he had thus entreated him, the All-Knowing Blessed One, beholding that Great Being Viṣkambhin, gave this instruction.
O son of noble family, understand this: even all the worlds within the three realms exist as a refuge consisting of Dharma, belonging to the Lord of the World.
Therefore, he is the Lord of the three worlds, the locus consisting of all phenomena,
the sovereign of all phenomena, the Teacher, and the supreme lord of all the world.
Thus this Bodhisattva, of great renown, the refuge of the virtues of Dharma and glory, possessing great supernormal knowledges, shines as a king of Dharma.
Having taken refuge in him, meditating upon him, recollecting him with a concentrated mind,
and even uttering his name, one ought to worship him at all times.
Those who, having taken refuge in him, always meditate upon him, remember him,
and even utter his name, worship him with concentrated minds.
They do not go to an evil rebirth, but indeed proceed only to a happy destination;
endowed with auspicious glory and virtues, they should always observe the poṣadha.
Purified by that merit, their faculties stainless and free from defilement,
they shall uphold the vow of the conduct of awakening and move about for the welfare of the world.
Then those repositories of the six virtues, having performed every auspicious rite and maintaining mindfulness of the Three Jewels, passed away at the end to the Land of Bliss.
Having gone there and taken refuge in Amitābha,
they shall always drink the nectar of the Dharma and practice the great vow.
Then, O Great Being, those Bodhisattvas, who are mines of virtue,
shall fulfill the entire equipment for perfect enlightenment in due order.
Exerting themselves in the practice for the sake of attaining perfect enlightenment in order to establish the welfare of all sentient beings,
these Arhats are pure in nature and dwell in the four sublime abodes.
Having conquered the wicked hosts of Māra, those of great supernormal powers and excellent fortune,
having attained the threefold awakening, shall reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard this and other such instructions from the Lord of Sages,
all the worlds, including the gods and others who were present in that assembly, were enlightened and rejoiced.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, being thoroughly gladdened,
looked toward the Blessed One and spoke again as follows:
"O Blessed One, the Lord of the three worlds, the Sovereign of the world, the Son of the Victor—why does he not yet arrive here? When will he come? Please instruct us."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
looked toward the Great Being Viṣkambhin and gave this instruction:
Noble son, that Bodhisattva Lokeśa, the Lord of the World,
is now proceeding here to bestow a prophecy upon Maheśa.
In order for me also to grant an audience and to show these assemblies,
you should first establish everyone in virtue and then proceed here to enter the religious life.
Having heard these instructions given by the Lord of Sages, Viṣkambhin was awakened;
looking upon him, he stood there with a heart filled with joy.
At that moment, in that monastery at Jetavana,
beings of various colors and great merit shone forth, illuminating everything with their radiance.
In that garden there were great kalpa-trees that grant all desired objects,
as well as trees with flowers of every season and trees bearing every kind of fruit.
Ponds filled with water purified by the eight qualities,
and delightful lotuses and other blossoming flowers, appeared.
Touched by those rays, all the people gathered in the assembly experienced a state of great wonder and bliss, their hearts filled with joy.
Seeing the signs of Subhadrā appearing everywhere—
the lakes, trees, and so forth— they stood there filled with wonder.
Having observed them, Viṣkambhin, filled with joy and wonder,
bowed to the Blessed One and again questioned him with palms joined in reverence.
"Blessed One, from where have these meritorious divine rays come? They possess various colors and auspicious lusters; it would be well for you to explain this."
When Viṣkambhin had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the All-Knowing, looked toward him and the entire assembly and spoke as follows.
That noble Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who presides over the three realms, desires to come here.
Then, emitting their exceedingly meritorious radiance from all sides, they were directed to illuminate this monastery and beautify it.
Now that Lord of the World, having rescued all sentient beings from the ocean of existence and established them on the excellent path to enlightenment, shall conduct himself here.
At that moment, having arrived there at the monastery illuminating it,
that Lokeśvara entered while gazing about.
Seeing him arrived, the Blessed One was filled with serene confidence; he welcomed him, saying, "Come, may it be well with you," and inquired after his welfare.
When the Lord of Sages had thus questioned him, Avalokiteśvara, having seen [him],
announced, "O Blessed One, I have come," and drew near.
There, having placed a divine golden lotus before that Lord of Sages, he performed prostration at his lotus feet.
Then that Lord of the Three Worlds, taking his place at the left side of that Teacher, the Guru of the World, made this report while looking [at him] in this manner:
O Blessed One, this lotus has been sent to you by the Blessed Amitābha,
and he also inquires after your well-being in every respect.
Beholding his body made of gold, the Blessed One was filled with joy;
taking him up and placing him at his left side, he spoke thus:
Blessed are you, noble son; having been rescued from the ocean of existence, how many sentient beings have you established upon the path to awakening?
Thus questioned by the Lord of Sages, the Son of the Jina, the Sovereign of the World,
looked upon the Blessed One and the assembly and spoke as follows.
O Blessed One, you know all that within the abode of existence—
those beings whom I have rescued and established in the conventional truth.
Having heard this which had been spoken, the Blessed One was greatly delighted; looking toward Lokeśvara, who possesses great super-knowledge, he commanded him as follows.
Excellent, excellent, O Mahāsattva, sovereign of the entire triple world!
You alone are the protector and lord of all sentient beings, who bears the welfare of others as his purpose.
Having surveyed all the worlds within the ocean of existence,
you have rescued all sentient beings and established them on the path to enlightenment.
Therefore, you are the Great Being, the sovereign of the entire triple world;
the Lord of the World, the protector of the world, and the master of the universe.
All undertakings, even those as desired, are accomplished;
may you always be victorious in your vow to uplift all sentient beings.
May all those wicked Māras, touched by this light, become pure in intention;
having approached for refuge, may they become practitioners of the path to enlightenment.
For all sentient beings who maintain the recollection of your name,
may there always be auspiciousness and freedom from affliction everywhere.
Having thus bestowed upon that great-souled Lokeśa various blessings that had been accomplished, the Blessed One observed a vow of silence.
At that moment, Maheśvara arrived there;
beholding the Blessed One, he approached him from the front.
It proceeded forth from the mouth of the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages.
Having taken refuge in the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages,
and having prostrated at his lotus feet, he made this request with palms joined in reverence.
O Blessed One,
Teacher of all things, I go for refuge to you; may you deign to grant me the vow of the Mahāyāna.
Having heard this request respectfully made by Maheśvara, the Blessed One commanded Maheśa in this manner.
Go, noble son, and entreat this Lord of the World, the Master of the Universe;
may this Lord of the World grant you the vow that accomplishes awakening.
Having heard these instructions from the lord of sages, Maheśvara joyfully went before Lokeśa and prostrated at his lotus feet.
Then Maheśvara, standing before that Lokeśa,
was pleased by the truthful accounts of his excellent qualities and spoke thus with palms joined in reverence.
"O Blessed One, I bow to you, the Lord Avalokiteśvara,
the bearer of the lotus, the Great Sovereign, and the one who brings supreme joy."
To him who is seated in the lotus posture, whose beautiful form is surrounded by the splendor of the lotus,
who holds a radiant lotus in his hand, and who grants consolation to the world.
To the one with excellent eyes like the earth, whose five eyes are completely purified;
who wears a crown of jewel-like Victors, adorned with the wish-fulfilling gem.
Having thus praised that Maheśāna, the illustrious Guṇākara,
and bowing once more at his lotus feet, he took refuge while gazing [upon him].
Seeing him established in such a state, the noble Avalokiteśvara,
gazing upon his face which was like a lotus in full bloom, spoke as follows.
"O Maheśa, what is the intention in your mind? What pleases you? I shall indeed fulfill that; tell me so before me."
Having heard this command from the Lord of the Universe, that Maheśvara, filled with joy, bowed again and, with palms joined in reverence, made this request.
"O Blessed One, Teacher of all, my mind desires enlightenment;
therefore, for the welfare of the world, grant me the prophecy of perfect awakening.
Having heard this request, Lokeśvara, the Lord of the World, [replied].
Having addressed that Īśāna and gazing upon him, he commanded as follows:
"You are fortunate, O Maheśāna, that you desire perfect awakening; therefore,
I shall grant you the vow which is the means for achieving perfect awakening."
Therefore, at the outset, one who has constantly established their intention upon perfect enlightenment should, with faith,
perform worship of the Three Jewels and give whatever is desired by those in need.
Then, being of pure conduct and having purified the three spheres,
one should observe the Poṣadha vow, which is endowed with the practice of the eight limbs.
Then, maintaining steadfastness and practicing the four divine abodes,
you should observe the vow of patience through the equalization of self and others.
Then, maintaining great enthusiasm for merit and practicing the means of the True Dharma,
you should conquer all hosts of evil ones and observe the conventional vows.
Then, having completely conquered the afflictions and being free from desire for delight in cyclic existence,
you should practice the vow of meditation after meditating upon the perfectly awakened Lord.
Then, having plunged into the ocean of the treatises of the True Dharma for the welfare of the world,
and having obtained the jewel of wisdom, you should practice the vow of the Mahāyāna.

Then, having taken up the jewel that is the means for accomplishing the True Dharma— which possesses the qualities of meditative concentration, dispels all faults, and awakens all sentient beings— one should bring about the welfare of the world.
Then, intent upon the practice for attaining the siddhis of the Śrīdhāraṇī and other [mantras],
and having maintained the vow for perfect enlightenment, you should proceed for the welfare of the world.
Then, endowed with glorious virtues and concentrated in the *Bhadracaryā*,
having brought all sentient beings under your influence, may you become a powerful King of Dharma.
Then, having conquered the hosts of Māra, free from afflictions and with stainless faculties,
may you become an Arhat who has attained perfect enlightenment and is a sovereign of the ten stages.
Then you shall become a Tathāgata, a Lord of Sages, possessed of great superknowledges;
the sovereign of all vidyās, the Teacher, the Protector of the World, and the Guide.
Renowned as Bhasmeśvara, the Lord of the entire triple world,
you shall become a perfectly awakened Buddha, a Sugata, the sovereign king of all dharmas.
When the world-system is opened, it shall become your buddha-field;
then you, O Blessed One, having made the entire world consist of the Dharma.
Having accomplished the task of the Sugata, may you attain the abode of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of the World, that Maheśvara was delighted; and having bowed to the Lord of the World, he withdrew to a solitary place.
Then the Great Queen Umā also went before Lokeśvara;
bowing with palms joined at his lotus-feet, she joyfully offered this hymn of praise.
"O Blessed One, I bow to you, Avalokiteśvara, the Great Lord,
the Sustainer of the World, the Giver of Life, the Great-Souled One."
To the one whose eyes support the earth, who holds the auspicious lotus,
who is surrounded by the glory of the lotus, and who brings about pure consciousness;
To the Lord who upholds the Dharma, the sovereign of the ten stages,
who is always established in the vehicle of perfect nirvāṇa.
Thus the great goddess Umā, being well-pleased, bowed again to that son of the Jina, Lokeśvara, and having made her request with palms joined in reverence, spoke as follows.
O Blessed One, having looked upon me, liberate me from this female state;
deliver me from dwelling in the impurities of the age and from dwelling in the womb.
Having rescued them from the ocean of existence, which is a turbulent sea due to the grasping of afflictions,
and having established them on the path to enlightenment, lead them to the state of the Sugata.
Having heard this request made by the Great Goddess,
that Lord of the World looked toward Umā-devī and commanded thus:
"Sister, O Great Goddess, if you desire liberation,
you should honor the Three Jewels and observe the Poṣadha vow."
Then, having attained perfectly pure merit, with the three spheres completely purified,
and endowed with the qualities of auspicious glory, may you go to Sukhāvatī at the end of your life.
There, having taken refuge in the Protector Amitābha and always drinking the nectar of the Dharma, may you attain the vow of perfect enlightenment.
Then, having fulfilled all the perfections in their proper order,
may you become the sustainer of the world, the lord of the world, and the sovereign of the ten stages.
Then, having attained perfect enlightenment, the Tathāgata, the Lord of Sages,
became known as Umeshvara— the Blessed One, the Fully Awakened One, the Victor.
The Lord of all vidyās, the Teacher, the Sovereign Lord of all dharmas.
The King of Dharma, Lord of the World, the mine of the qualities of the glory of the True Dharma,
the sovereign of all sentient beings, the Arhat, the Master of the entire triple world.
"O conqueror of Māra, possessor of great supernormal knowledge, you shall become a leader;
on the southern side of the Himavat mountains, there shall be your buddha-field."
"May even all these heretics become your disciples," having been thus instructed by Lokeśa, the Teacher of the World,
the goddess Umā, filled with great joy, withdrew to a secluded spot there.
Then that Blessed One, having surveyed all those present in the assembly and looking toward Viṣkambhin, addressed him with these words:
Behold, noble son, Queen Umā, who desires perfect awakening;
she has been prophesied for awakening by this Lokeśvara for the welfare of the world.
You too have taken refuge in this true Teacher;
having resolved upon the aspiration for perfect enlightenment, honor him always with devotion.
By the power of this merit, may the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas become mines of glorious virtues, with the three spheres completely purified.
Then, having celebrated the festival of the auspicious bull for all beings everywhere, may you,
endowed with the happiness of the glory of the Dharma, go at last to Sukhāvatī.
Having gone there, take refuge in the Sage Amitābha;
always drinking the nectar of the Dharma, proceed for the welfare of the world.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order and having attained the threefold enlightenment, you shall reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having heard this instruction from the Blessed One, all those people gathered in the assembly, headed by Viṣkambhin, were filled with joyful intent.
Having arisen and approached the lotus feet of Lokeśvara, the Lord of the World, they placed their joined palms together and prostrated themselves in due order.
The Lord of the World touched the heads of them all,
and having bestowed the blessing of the accomplishment of awakening, he gladdened their hearts.
Then the glorious Jagannātha, Āryāvalokiteśvara,
having gazed upon the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, spoke thus:
O Blessed One, I wish to go to my own hermitage in Sukhāvatī;
therefore, by granting me permission, please gladden my heart.
When he had thus entreated him, that All-Knowing One gave a divine jewel-lotus to that Lokeśa and instructed him in this way:
Go, noble son, and having presented this lotus before the Teacher, the Great Sage, inquire after the health of Nami in my name.
Having replied, "So be it," Lokeśvara, the son of the Victor,
bowed to the Blessed One and, looking toward the assembly, proceeded.
Then the Lord of the World set forth with those rays of merit, illuminating the world of beings as he went toward Sukhāvatī.
Then, having approached the Teacher whose radiance was unsurpassed,
he bowed with palms joined before his lotus-feet and presented that lotus to him.
Seeing that Lord of the World approaching,
the all-knowing Amitābha, the Teacher of the world, looked upon him and gave this instruction:
"Come, you have arrived; noble son, take refuge here.
All your tasks are accomplished; I hope all is well with you?"
How many beings have been uplifted by you, and from where?
You have shown us the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Lord of Sages.
Thus questioned by Amitābha, Lokeśvara, with palms joined in reverence,
reported his entire life story in this manner before the Teacher.
O Blessed One, having diligently observed all living beings submerged in all the worlds and even in all the hells.
Having rescued those who were clear-minded, having awakened them and dispelled their weariness,
and having established them on the path to enlightenment, he caused them to practice for the welfare of the world.
Having thus established all those beings as achievers of perfect enlightenment,
I first went to see the Perfectly Awakened One residing in the Jetavana monastery.
Having entered there, I beheld that [deity] seated in the assembly of the Lord of Munis,
as well as the entire assembly and those disciples and sons of the Conquerors.
Having approached before Śākyamuni, the teacher of the world,
and having placed a lotus before him, he paid homage and took his seat.
There, Maheśvara was sent forth before the Blessed Ones;
he was prophesied by me for enlightenment, and Somā was likewise prophesied.
Likewise, all the worlds, having relied upon that assembly,
were entertained by me and established in the vow of the equipment for awakening.
Then, having obtained permission from that lord of sages, I approached you, filled with joy and eager for the sight of you all.
Therefore, that Blessed One sends this jeweled lotus with his greetings to you, and he also inquires after your well-being.
Having heard what was thus announced by that Lokeśa,
Amitābha, the Teacher of the World, rejoiced and was filled with joy.
Then Amitaprabha, having beheld that Lokeśvara, honored him and rejoiced, saying: "Excellent! You are blessed, O virtuous son!"
Thus, that Lord of the World, the son of the Victorious One who possesses great superknowledge,
should practice while maintaining the vow that brings about the welfare of all sentient beings.
Thus ends the chapter on the instruction for the prophecy of enlightenment concerning the Goddess Umā, the Great Sovereign who establishes all sentient beings upon the path to enlightenment.
18. The Section on the Entire Assembly of Beings Returning to Their Respective Abodes, Delighted by the Zeal to Hear the True Dharma.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, being thus delighted, bowed down to the Blessed One and, with palms joined, spoke as follows:
O Blessed One, today that Lord of the World has been seen by me;
therefore, my self is now purified, and I have also attained the True Dharma.
Today the fulfillment of my birth has been achieved and my heart's desire is perfected;
my hope is fully realized, and may I attain perfect awakening.
Furthermore, Blessed One, I now desire to hear the excellent renown of the specific virtues of this great-souled Lokeśvara.
Therefore, you ought to provide instruction and encouragement for the minds of all sentient beings who practice the vow of perfect enlightenment.
When Viṣkambhin had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the All-Knowing, beholding that Great Being, gave him this instruction:
Excellent! Listen attentively, O great being, noble son; with a concentrated mind, I shall proclaim in brief the true renown of the virtues of Lokeśa.
It is impossible for me to measure the extent of the merit and virtues of the great-souled Lokeśvara, which are immeasurable and incalculable.
For example, it is possible for me to calculate the precise weight in palas of every single mountain in all the worlds.
Having reduced the entire earth, including its mountains, to the size of a single atom of dust,
I am indeed able to calculate their number and measure.
I am able to count the number of drops of water in all the oceans and in all the rivers as well.
I am able to calculate the number of leaves for all trees, for every plant that grows upon the earth.
But it is not possible for me to calculate the supreme, immeasurable, and incalculable mass of merit of this Lord of the World.
May all sentient beings always serve and honor all the perfectly awakened Buddhas, together with their Saṅghas, with every kind of requisite and with the utmost respect.
Whatever great merit there may be for them in accomplishing the qualities of the glory of awakening,
the magnanimity arising from the worship of Lokeśvara is even greater than that.
When that Lord of the Three Worlds, the Bodhisattva of great supernatural power,
endowed with all meditative absorptions, acts for the welfare of the world;
Such is the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Bodhisattva of great supernatural power;
perfected in all meditative absorptions, there is no one like him in the three realms.
Just as I previously beheld the greatness of the qualities of this Samādhi belonging to the Lord of the Three Realms, which surpasses that of all the sons of the Victors.

Long ago, there was a Teacher, the Tathāgata Krakucchanda— the sovereign of all vidyās, the King of Dharma, the Arhat, the Sugata, the Jina. At that time, I was a Bodhisattva named Dānaśūra, who bore the welfare of others as his purpose.
He was devoted to the teaching of the true Dharma of that Teacher, the Lord of Munis.
At that same time, the leader Krakucchanda also dwelt here in this Jetavana monastery together with his assembly of monks.
Then, all the Brahmins headed by Brahmā and the lords of the thirty gods headed by Śakra, joyfully came to drink the nectar of the Dharma from that lord of sages.
All the lords of the worlds as well— the lords of the Daityas, the lords of the Rākṣasas,
the Gandharvas, the Kinnaras, the Yakṣas, the lords of the Nāgas, and the lords of the Garuḍas— [were present].
All the planets beginning with the Sun, the stars beginning with the Moon, the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, the Rudras, and all the Vidyādharas as well;
Kings, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, ministers, counselors, and common people;
merchants, caravan leaders, guild-masters, and great men.
The citizens of the city and the countryside, as well as others dwelling in the land—
all of them, having approached him and honored him in due order.
Having bowed to that Lord of Munis, Krakucchanda, those many great beings, the Bodhisattvas, remained seated in the assembly, absorbed in meditative concentration.
They performed the ritual of the body of samādhi before the Sage Krakucchanda.
When the Bodhisattva named Samantabhadra, possessed of great supernatural power, entered the meditative absorption known as Dhvajodgata;
Then that Bodhisattva Lokeśvara, possessed of great supernatural power,
entered the meditative absorption known as Vikiriṇa.
When the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the son of the Conqueror,
attained the samādhi known as "The Beautiful Eye of the Full Moon."
Then that Lord of the World, the Son of the Victor endowed with great supernormal knowledge,
attained the samādhi known as the "Excellent Sun-Eye."
When Samantabhadra, the son of the Victor endowed with great superknowledge,
entered that samādhi known as "Variegated," [the world was transformed].
Then Lokeśvara, the son of the Victor and possessor of great superknowledge,
entered the meditative absorption known as Gaganagañja.
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra entered the samādhi called Sarvākārakara, which produces all forms.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Lokeśvara also entered the samādhi known as Indramati.
When the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the mine of virtues,
attained the concentration called Indrarāja, [the world was transformed].
Then that Bodhisattva Guṇākara, the Lord of the World,
entered the samādhi known as "Profound as the Ocean."
When the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, possessed of great vigor,
attained the samādhi known as Siṃhavijṛmbhita (The Lion’s Yawn).
Then the Bodhisattva Lokeśvara, possessed of great vigor, entered the meditative absorption known as Siṃhavikrīḍita.
When the wise Bodhisattva Samantabhadra attained the samādhi known as Varadāyaka (the Bestower of Boons),...
Then the world-wandering Bodhisattva Subuddhimān attained that samādhi which completely dries up the Avīci hell.
When the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the wise one,
opened them up, he revealed even all the pores of his skin.
Then the Bodhisattva Lokeśvara, the wise one,
opened all his pores without exception.
Then Samantabhadra, beholding that Lokeśa of great supernatural power, bowed with palms joined and, gazing upon him, spoke thus:
Excellent! You are blessed in the world, O Lord of the World, since you possess such eloquence;
there is no one at all in the worlds who possesses a wisdom equal to your meditative concentration.
In this way, when there was a contest of meditative concentration with other great beings and bodhisattvas of great supernatural power,
that very Lokeśvara emerged victorious.
Then all those Bodhisattvas of great supernormal knowledge, being filled with serene faith,
bowed down to that Lokeśa of great supernormal knowledge and spoke thus:
Excellent! You are blessed in the world, O Lord of the World, since you possess such eloquence;
there is no one at all in the world who is as powerful through the perfection of meditative concentration as you are.
Then that Blessed One, having seen all those sons of the Sugata, addressed them in their presence and, looking upon them, gave this instruction:
Noble sons, this eloquence of the Lord of the World, Lokeśa— which you yourselves are even now beholding here— is indeed very slight.
Such is the exceedingly great eloquence of this Lord of the World that it does not exist at all in anyone, even among all the lords of sages.
Thus, the exceedingly great eloquence of that Lord of the World was recounted by the Sage-King Krakucchanda, as I have heard it.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, having been awakened,
gazed upon the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, and spoke thus:
O Blessed One, please instruct us upon that king of Mahāyāna sūtras which is called the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the source of all excellence.
Having heard which, may we all proceed with our minds pervaded by the fragrance of the flavor of the Dharma through the means of accomplishing the qualities of perfect enlightenment.
Having heard that, the Blessed One also commanded the great-minded Viṣkambhin: "Excellent! Listen with a concentrated mind; I shall speak of that."
Those who shall hear this well-spoken Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra,
even their most terrible sins shall all be exhausted.
It is certain that the ten unwholesome evils and even the five heinous crimes will be destroyed without remainder.
When the Lord of Sages had thus instructed him, Viṣkambhin was filled with joy;
looking toward the Blessed One, he spoke once more as follows:
O Blessed One, Teacher of All-Knowledge, may we understand how that evil committed by one who has exhausted [the merit of] the *Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra* is destroyed.
Having heard that, the Blessed One, observing Viṣkambhin who had been awakened as well as the people gathered in the assembly, commanded thus:
"Noble son, there exists that ford which is both stained and utterly stainless,
fashioned by the Lords of Sages on the southern side of Mount Sumeru."
Just as even a white garment thrown into the water of the Mala-tīrtha becomes blue,
so too one who is touched by that water becomes blue, even if they were previously pure.
Just as even a blue garment thrown into perfectly pure water becomes white,
so too shall even a sinful soul become pure when touched by that water.
Thus, whoever delights in this supreme sūtra of the Mahāyāna,
even if they are defiled by the true Dharma, they will quickly become afflicted by the afflictions.
Even one who has been stained by great evil, if they rejoice upon hearing this supreme Mahāyāna sūtra, shall become free from afflictions and abide in the presence of auspiciousness.
Just as Indra, possessing a hundred mouths, having emerged from his own abode,
burns all grasses, shrubs, creepers, and trees born upon the earth.
Likewise, this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the most excellent of all sūtras,
swiftly burns away even all transgressions without exception.
Those who, having heard this well-spoken king of Mahāyāna sūtras,
rejoice and delight in it, shall always honor it with devotion.
May they all become stainless beings, with faculties pure and free from afflictions—
bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who shall never turn back.
Having heard this supreme and most excellent king of all Mahāyāna sūtras, ordinary people of evil intent will certainly not rejoice in it.
And those who, having heard this most supreme king of Mahāyāna sūtras, rejoice in it and always devote themselves to it with reverence;
Blessed are all those persons who have purified the three spheres;
free from afflictions and stainless in nature, may they become sons of the Sugata.
And at the time of their death, twelve Sugatas, the Victors, will approach and, gazing upon them, shall grant this supreme boon:
Do not fear, noble son; for you have heard the *Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra*, and having rejoiced in it, you honor it with devotion and respect through acts of veneration.
With your self anointed by this merit, you shall not wander again in existence;
nor shall you ever be scorched by the torments of the fires of the afflictions.
Having enjoyed great happiness endowed with glorious virtues for as long as you live,
depart once more for Sukhāvatī in order to enjoy the nectar of the Dharma.
There, established in the refuge of the Jina Amitābha,
you should always drink the nectar of the Dharma and proceed in perfect self-restraint.
Then, with a stainless and pure self and the three spheres completely purified,
you should practice the vow of the conduct of awakening, which is the wealth for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Then, having fulfilled all the perfections in due order,
he becomes free from afflictions, an Arhat possessing the great superknowledges, and one who dwells in the four sublime abodes.
Having conquered all the hosts of Māra, with a mind unwavering from perfect enlightenment,
and having attained the threefold awakening, may you reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having heard this instruction given by all those Sugatas, they all,
expressing their mutual approval, bowed repeatedly to those Jinas.
Then, having recollected those Victors and having relinquished their life-breaths with concentrated minds,
they departed for Sukhāvatī together with those very Sugatas.
Having gone there and taken refuge in Amitābha,
they shall always drink the nectar of the Dharma and proceed toward the welfare of all beings.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for perfect enlightenment in due order,
they become free from afflictions, pure in essence, and completely purified in the three spheres.
Having conquered all the hosts of Māra and abiding in the four divine abodes,
they shall attain the threefold awakening and reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Thus, the merit arising from the *Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra* is even greater—
immeasurable and incalculable— it is the means for accomplishing the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
If you all, having understood this, desire perfect enlightenment,
then listen to this well-spoken king of Mahāyāna sūtras.
"Rejoice with devotion, honoring [the teaching] always with respect.
Having heard these words and others spoken by the Lord of Sages, all those present in the assembly said, "So be it," and being thus enlightened, they rejoiced.
Then all those members of the assembly, including Brahmā and the other great sages,
as well as Śakra and the other lords of the gods, and even the sovereigns of all the worlds—
Gandharvas, kiṃnaras, rākṣasas, siddhas, sādhyas,
celestial nymphs, vidyādharas, lords of the daityas, lords of the nāgas, and even the garuḍas—
And the mahoragas, O lord of daityas, as well as the lords of nāgas and the garuḍas too.
And the mahoragas from the southwest, the lords of spirits with auspicious intentions,
as well as yogins, ascetics, heretics, and practitioners of austerity.
The king of brahmins and all the others, as well as the humans, were propitiated;
having circumambulated him three times with joy, they joined their palms in reverence.
Having bowed to the Blessed One and his Saṅgha, they went each to their own abode.
Thus ends the section on the departure of each member of the assembly to their respective abodes, filled with joy and enthusiasm for hearing the true Dharma.
19. The Chapter on the Exposition of the Training and Restraint.
Then Ānanda, having risen and gone before the Blessed One, bowed with palms joined at his lotus-feet and, looking up at him, spoke thus:
O Blessed One, Teacher, it behoves you to fully teach the training and the restraint of the vows to us, your monks who lead the holy life.
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, that lord of sages, looking toward the venerable Ānanda, gave this instruction:
(265) Listen well, Ānanda! I shall explain in brief the training and the restraint that governs the celibate monks.
Those beings who are pure in nature, having gone forth into the hermitage of the Jina,
desire to maintain the restraint of the training as the means for achieving nirvāṇa.
First, having gazed upon that delightful pure field and sat down upon their own seats, they should remain composed, absorbed in meditation.
Celibates should never dwell in a place that is crowded with ashes, bones, hair, mud, refuse, and impurities.
One should never associate with monks of immoral conduct; neither conversation nor dwelling together with them should ever be undertaken.
One should not eat together with monks of immoral conduct, nor should one do anything at all with them; one should neither stay with them, nor go with them, nor play with them anywhere.

It should be bestowed upon one who has received full ordination, and not through a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturthakarma*); furthermore, this means for accomplishing the True Dharma must not be given to those of evil nature.
For those of evil character and corrupt nature are defilers of the Buddha's teaching;
they are devoted to the conduct of Māra, and their faculties are infested by the serpents of the afflictions.
Their dwelling must not be established within the Buddhist hermitage;
their residence should be provided far away, outside the hermitage grounds.
One should never engage in conversation with those of immoral conduct; for them, the property of the Saṅgha is not permitted, nor do they deserve it anywhere at all.
For them, there exists no practice of the conduct of an Arhat;
how then could there be the means for attaining perfect enlightenment, which brings about the welfare of all sentient beings?
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, that son of the Jina,
Ānanda, gazed upon the Sovereign of Munis and spoke as follows.
"Blessed One, at what time will monks who are immoral and deceitful become worthy of offerings in the hermitage of the Sugata, O Leader?"
When Ānanda had thus questioned him, the Blessed One, the All-Knowing Victor, looked toward Ānanda and instructed him once again as follows.
When three hundred years have passed since my complete parinirvāṇa,
there will be monks of immoral conduct who are skillful within the hermitage of the Sugata.
There, all those monks— of corrupt conduct and evil intent—
sitting together in the monastery, would practice the life of householders.
Accompanied by their wives, sons, daughters, brothers, kinsmen, and relatives,
they may wander about, heedless, enjoying pleasures according to their desire.
Having brought away all the requisites of the monastic communities by means of injustice,
and having made them their own property, they will turn them into their private dwellings.
Having taken up whatever they desire and having enjoyed their objects of pleasure as they wish,
they may move about confidently in the pursuit of the means for maintaining their households.
They would discharge excrement and urine even in the precincts belonging to the Saṅgha,
and they would vomit phlegm and saliva, and cast away their refuse everywhere.
Those of wicked intellect will not understand the ripening of these karmas;
like the insane, being difficult to tame and devoted to evil, they will act accordingly.
Those who discharge phlegm and other secretions in the precincts belonging to the Saṅgha shall become, it is said, needle-mouthed pretas in the Śālāṭavī forest.
Those who discharge feces, urine, and other waste in a monastic residence belonging to the Saṅgha shall become worms born of excrement and urine in Vārāṇasī.
Having stolen items such as tooth-sticks, and having caused harm to the Lord or to what belongs to the Saṅgha.
Those who steal and consume red rice, frogs, fish, and other aquatic creatures, as well as those who take and eat the property belonging to the Saṅgha,
shall become great pretas with needle-like mouths and bellies the size of mountains.
Those who, having prepared food, drink, and so forth, consume them, as well as those who consume what belongs to the Saṅgha,
shall be born into low families and be cooks with impaired faculties.
Falling from there, they are born as those who are lame, hunchbacked, or ugly-faced;
their limbs may be afflicted by leprosy and other diseases, and they may become carriers of putrid corpses.
When they stood there and moved slowly upon the ground holding a staff,
then all their flesh would disappear.
Thus, having performed actions leading to the states of woe, you shall experience various sufferings for many years and go to the hells.
And those greedy ones who consume the land belonging to the Saṅgha—
those wicked ones, their souls afflicted by defilements, shall go to the Raurava hell.
There, one should place heated iron balls into their mouths;
by these, even their palates, lips, hearts, and bellies will be completely consumed.
Their throats, hearts, bellies, intestines, and all their bodily parts will be consumed by fire;
yet even when thus dead, they shall live again as experiencers of their karma.
Seized by the guardians of Yama, they shall be cast into a terrible hell;
and by the power of their own karma, their tongues shall become exceedingly large.
There, the Yama-kiṃnaras plow their tongues with hundreds of plows;
thus they endure various sufferings for many years.
Having eaten and died, they would indeed go again to heaven in a jar of fire;
and there, a very large tongue would emerge for them as well.
Even if hundreds of thousands of needles were to pierce them, those kinnaras would not die; nevertheless, they will remain in suffering for a long time.
Then the Kinnaras of Yama will cast them into a pit of fireless flames;
even there, though dead, they shall not remain, for they are consumers of their own karma. Then the Kinnaras, having lifted them up, will cast them into the river of the hungry ghosts (preta-nadī).
There too, for many years, you shall experience various sufferings.
Having experienced [the results], they will remain afflicted by suffering for a very long time, consuming their karma.
Thus, as they wander perpetually in hell for three kalpas of years,
the ripening of that karma will finally be exhausted for them after a long time.
Having passed away from there, they are born in Jambudvīpa in a state of great suffering;
impoverished and blind from birth, they possess defiled intentions.
Thus, having experienced many sufferings throughout many births,
and always tormented by the fire of the afflictions, they shall wander in the ocean of existence.
Therefore, Ānanda, all the requisites and all the materials belonging to the Saṅghas must be protected with great effort.
(Gkv 268) One must never, even for a moment, consume any property belonging to the Saṅgha;
no one at all is able to cause the property of the Saṅgha to decay.
For indeed, any property belonging to the Saṅgha is not to be enjoyed through improper means;
like a blazing fire, the property of the Saṅgha is something that must not be touched, for it is burning.
It is like a mountain, always assailed and indestructible like a diamond;
it is as harmful as unwholesome poison and resembles the edge of a sharp sword.
Indeed, it is possible to equalize a disharmony of the humors by means of mantras and medicinal herbs;
however, no one can pacify the sin of stealing property belonging to the Saṅgha.

Thinking thus, those who desire the bliss of the glory of perfect enlightenment in this saṃsāra must protect the property belonging to the Saṅgha with effort; it must always be protected with reverence.
Having understood this thus, and having maintained the mind of awakening with equanimity,
one should undertake the vows of training and strive to guard them perfectly.
One who desires to protect the training must protect the mind with effort;
it is impossible to protect the training without protecting the fickle mind.
Untamed rutting elephants do not cause such agony here as that which the elephant of the mind causes once it is liberated [from restraint] in the Avīci hell and other realms.
If the elephant of the mind is bound on all sides by the protection of mindfulness,
all fear has set and constant well-being has arrived.
Tigers, lions, elephants, bears, and all wicked enemies;
all the guardians of hell, as well as ḍākinīs and rākṣasas.
All these become bound through the binding of the single mind;
all these become tamed through the taming of the single mind.
For all fears, even those immeasurable sufferings,
arise solely from the mind of all beings wandering in existence.
By whom were the weapons fashioned all around in hell?
By whom was the floor of glowing iron made, and from where did those women arise?
All this evil arises from the mind within the abode of existence;
therefore, there is nothing more terrifying than the mind in the three worlds.
If the perfection of generosity consisted in making the world free from poverty, why is the world still poor today, given that it was so for the Protectors of the past?
When one generates the thought of relinquishing all possessions toward all beings together with the Buddha, that is the perfection of giving; therefore, it is indeed the mind itself.
Where could fish and other creatures be taken so that they might not kill those who delight in them?
But when the mind of non-violence is attained, that is considered the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
How could they ever kill wicked people who are like the sky?
But when the mind of anger is killed, all enemies are slain.
Where would there be enough leather to cover the entire earth? Yet, with just the leather of a single sandal, the whole world is covered.
External phenomena can never be warded off in that same way;
one's own mind alone must be restrained—what is the use of warding off anything else?
Even with both speech and body, that fruit is not attained by one of dull vision;
whereas for one who is sharp, even a single moment of mind can result in such states as Brahmanhood and the like.
All recitations and austerities, even those performed over a long period of time,
do not succeed at all if they are done with a dull mind distracted by other thoughts.
To destroy suffering and attain happiness, they wander pointlessly in the sky.
Those by whom this entire essence of the Dharma— the secret mind— has not been cultivated,
therefore must always make their own minds well-established and well-guarded.
Having abandoned the vow of guarding the mind, what is the use of many other ascetic vows?
Just as one standing amidst the restless carefully protects a wound.
Thus, one situated among wicked people should protect the mind with great effort;
just as one who has experienced even a slight pain from a wound protects that wound with care, so should one guard the mind.
Is the mind not strong when terrified by the impact of the Saṃghāta mountains?
For one who dwells by this very method of abiding, even among wicked people, [the mind remains firm].
Even in the midst of women, a firm ascetic does not falter.
May gains perish, may prosperity, honor, body, and life perish;
may everything else, even skillfulness, perish—but may the mind of no one ever perish.
The mind alone must always be guarded, for it is the means for attaining the wisdom of perfect enlightenment;
one should protect both mindfulness and situational awareness with every effort.
Just as a man overwhelmed by disease is incapable of all activities,
so too a mind distracted by these two is incapable of accomplishing awakening.
For one whose mind lacks clear comprehension, that which has been heard, reflected upon,
and cultivated does not remain in memory, just as water does not stay in a jar with a crack.
Even many who are learned, and even those devoted to faith and diligence,
become defiled by transgressions through the fault of lack of clear comprehension.
Even those who have accumulated merits go to an evil rebirth, robbed by the thief of non-attentiveness that follows the theft of mindfulness.
This very host of thieves that are the afflictions assumes the guise of a savior;
having found an opportunity, it robs one of one's well-being and destroys both one's good rebirth and life itself.
Therefore, mindfulness should never be removed from the gateway of the mind;
even if it has departed, it should be reinstated by recollecting the suffering caused by evil.
For those fortunate ones who act with reverence, even through the fear of their preceptor’s instruction,
mindfulness becomes easy to cultivate by living in the company of their teacher.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess unimpeded vision everywhere;
this entire world of living beings always stands before them.
Having meditated thus, one should always remain endowed with shame, reverence, and fear;
in this way, the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) will arise for him again and again.
Clear comprehension then arises and does not depart again once it has come,
when mindfulness stands guard at the gateway of the mind for the sake of protection.
First of all, this mind must be constantly established in such a way that one should always remain like a senseless log of wood.
One should never cast fruitless glances;
rather, the gaze should always be directed downward, as if one were constantly looking inward.
For the sake of resting the gaze, one should occasionally look toward the directions,
merely observing the light while looking about as a form of welcome.
At the beginning of the path, for the sake of perceiving danger, one should repeatedly look in the four directions;
having rested, one gazes about, even turning back to look behind.
Whether advancing or retreating, having first ascertained what lies ahead and behind,
one should act after having understood the task at hand in all circumstances.
Having first enjoined the action by thinking, "The body must be maintained in this way," one should then repeatedly observe in the interim, "How is the body positioned?"
Having restrained the wild elephant of the mind with every effort, one whose mind is fixed on the Dharma is bound to the great pillar so that he is not released.
One should thus examine the mind, asking "Where does it abide?",
so that one never abandons the yoke of meditative concentration for even a single moment.
If one is unattached during times of fear, festivals, and so forth, one may act as one pleases; for it has been stated that equanimity toward moral discipline is appropriate at the time of giving.
Having understood what one has begun to do, one should not think of anything else;
rather, with an inner self absorbed in that very task, one should first bring it to completion.
For in this way all is well done; otherwise, neither will come to pass, and the affliction of lack of clear comprehension will surely increase.
When various kinds of idle chatter increase in many ways and all manner of curiosities arise, one should destroy the longing that has come upon them.
If, while kneading clay or cutting grass, edible fruit should come into one's hand,
one should remember the training of the Tathāgata and, becoming afraid at that very moment, let it go.
When one wishes to move or even wishes to speak,
one should first examine one's own mind and then act with steadfastness and reason.
When one perceives that one's own mind is either attracted or repelled,
then one should neither act nor speak, but remain like a piece of wood.
When the face is haughty or mocking, filled with pride and intoxication, and accompanied by excessive derision, the mind becomes deceitful.
When there appears the semblance of self-exaltation and the disparagement of others,
accompanied by insults and agitation, then one should remain like a piece of wood.
When the mind seeks gain, honor, or fame, or when it seeks attendants, or when it seeks service, then one should remain like a piece of wood.

When one wishes to speak with anger— whether out of harshness toward the interests of others, a desire for one's own self-interest, or even a longing for social status— one should remain as motionless as a log of wood.
When [the opponent] is intolerant, timid, arrogant, talkative,
or obstinately attached to his own position, then one should remain like a log of wood.
Thus, observing that the mind is either afflicted or engaged in fruitless endeavors,
the hero should always firmly restrain it by means of its antidote.
It was perfectly certain, serene, steadfast, full of respectful reverence,
modest, apprehensive, tranquil, and solely intent upon the propitiation of others.
Indeed, this arising of afflictions and so forth is unimpeded by the mutually contradictory desires of fools; thus, [the Buddha] was filled with compassion for them.
One should always maintain the mind, like a magical creation, under one's own control and that of sentient beings, regarding all blameless things as being like a magical emanation.
Remembering again and again that this excellent moment has been obtained after a long time,
one should hold such a mind steady and unshakable, like Mount Sumeru.
Dragged here and there by greed and by those greedy for its flesh, why does the body not act otherwise to provide a remedy in this situation?
Having fixed the intellect upon the body by means of the support of going and coming,
one should perform actions according to one's desire for the sake of accomplishing all aims.
Thus having brought his own self under control, he should always have a smiling face;
he should abandon the contraction of the brow into a frown, and be the first to speak as a friend to the world.
He should not suddenly throw down stools or other items upon hearing a sound; he should not slam a door, for he should always delight in silence.
Just as a crane, a cat, or a thief, moving silently and with great composure,
achieves their desired goal, so too should the ascetic always conduct himself.
One who is always a disciple to all should receive upon his head the instruction of those skilled in exhorting others and who offer assistance unasked.
One should utter words of praise for all well-spoken words; seeing one who performs meritorious deeds, one should gladden them with hymns of praise.
One should hear of his virtues when he is absent and continue to hear of them with satisfaction;
and when one's own qualities are being spoken of, one should cultivate the recognition of those virtues [in the speaker].
For all undertakings are for the sake of satisfaction, yet that is difficult to obtain even with mental efforts;
therefore, one should enjoy the happiness of contentment through the virtues produced by the labor of others.
In this case, there is no loss whatsoever, and there is great happiness in the next life;
whereas through hatred, there is the suffering of displeasure, and great suffering in the next life as well.
One should speak with words that are placed with confidence, whose meaning is clear, which are pleasing to the mind,
pleasant to the ear, rooted in compassion, and uttered in a soft and gentle tone.
One should always look upon sentient beings with an upright gaze, as if drinking them in with one's eyes;
for by relying upon these beings, one shall attain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.

Great merit arises from that which is produced through constancy and through the application of remedies; likewise, it arises toward those who provide qualities or assistance, and toward those who are suffering.
One should always be endowed with diligence and be self-reliant;
one should not grant any opportunity to anyone in any undertakings.
The perfections, beginning with generosity, become increasingly superior;
one should not abandon a superior [perfection] for the sake of another, except in the case of the bridge of conduct.
Having understood this, one should always be diligent in the interests of others;
for a compassionate person who perceives the welfare of others, even that which is prohibited may be performed if it is done unknowingly.
Having shared [his food] with those who have fallen into misfortune, the helpless, and those established in vows,
he should eat a moderate amount and discard three robes outside.
One should not afflict the body that serves the True Dharma for the sake of other ends;
for in this very way, one shall swiftly fulfill the hopes of sentient beings.
Therefore, one should not sacrifice one's life for someone whose intention is impure and lacks compassion;
however, it may be sacrificed for one whose intention is equal [to one's own], for in this way one does not fall away from the path.
One should not speak of the Dharma to one who lacks respect, who is unwell, or whose head is wrapped;
nor to one with an umbrella, a staff, or a weapon, nor to one whose head is covered.
One should not [teach] that which is profound and vast to those who are limited, nor to women in the absence of a man;
one should practice equal reverence toward all phenomena, whether inferior or superior.
One should not employ a recipient of the vast Dharma in inferior teachings,
nor should one entice them with sūtras and mantras while causing them to abandon proper conduct.
The discarding of tooth-sticks and saliva is not permitted; it is undesirable whether in water or on ground used for enjoyment, and the discharge of urine and so forth is likewise censured.
One should not eat with the mouth full, nor with noise, nor with the face stretched out; one should not sit with the feet dangling, nor rub the arms together.
One should not share a vehicle, a bed, or a seat with another woman;
having seen or heard anything that causes lack of confidence among the people, he should avoid it all.
One should not point at anything with a single finger, but rather respectfully with the right hand;
one should likewise indicate even the path using the entire hand.
One should utter some sound with a slight agitation for nine days;
however, one must perform the *acchatādi* rite, otherwise the ritual would remain uncompleted.
One should lie down on the bed of the Lord’s nirvāṇa in the desired direction,
being fully conscious and mindful of rising easily, and this must necessarily be done beforehand.
The conduct of Bodhisattvas is said to be immeasurable;
one should, for now, certainly practice that conduct which purifies the mind.
Day and night, three times a day, one should practice the Three Sections;
by means of the resolve for awakening and the intention of the Victors, one should completely purify all remaining downfalls.
Whatever states one enters, whether by one's own volition or under the influence of others,
one should diligently train in the instructions pertaining to those very states;
for there is nothing whatsoever that is not to be learned by the sons of the Conquerors.
There is nothing that is not merit for one who dwells as such;
whether indirectly or directly, he performs no other action than that which is for the benefit of sentient beings.
For the sake of sentient beings alone, one should dedicate everything toward enlightenment;
and one should never abandon a spiritual friend, even for the sake of one's own life.
One who upholds the vow of a bodhisattva and is skilled in the meaning of the Mahāyāna—
this, in brief, is the defining characteristic of clear comprehension.
Having repeatedly examined the state of one's body and mind,
that from which one is restrained, that wherein one is engaged, and that very thing [to which one is directed].
Therefore, for the sake of protecting the minds of the world, one should observe and practice the training.
All this well-conducted behavior— generosity and the worship of the Sugatas—
which has been performed throughout thousands of eons, anger destroys it all.
There is no evil equal to hatred, and no austerity equal to patience;
therefore, one should cultivate patience with effort through various methods.
When the seed of hatred resides in the heart, the mind finds no tranquility; it does not enjoy joy or happiness, nor does it attain sleep or steadfastness.
Even those who have taken refuge with him and honor him with wealth and respect desire to kill that master, for he is ill-favored by his own hatred.
Even friends are repelled by him; he gives nothing and is not served. In short, there is nothing by which an angry person may remain at ease.
He who, perceiving anger as an enemy, destroys it through persistent effort because it produces such sufferings as these, shall be happy both in this world and the next.
Therefore, having destroyed the power of anger through the majesty of the Three Jewels,
one should understand patience and cultivate it with effort by means of various methods.
Enemies do not go to destruction even by killing them throughout one's entire life;
however, he who destroys anger alone has slain all enemies.
Even by attaining only a small degree of perfection, one is always filled with joy; even in the midst of dejection, there is no loss of what is desired, for one's wholesome qualities do not diminish.
If there is a remedy, what is the use of despondency in that case?
If there is no remedy, what is the use of despondency in that case?
Suffering, injury, harshness, and ill-repute are undesirable for oneself or for those dear to one; for an enemy, it is the opposite.
Happiness is obtained only with great difficulty, whereas suffering is present without effort;
since liberation from suffering is achieved through external hardship, one must make the mind firm.
The Lords of Sages have declared that the field of sentient beings is the field of the Victors.
Having propitiated these [goddesses], all the perfectly awakened ones have attained final liberation.
Since both sentient beings and the Victors are the source from which the Buddha-dharmas arise,
what logic is there in having as much reverence for the Victors as one does not for ordinary beings?
This entire world has been made their own by those whose very nature is compassion; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, these beings who appear before us are none other than the Protectors themselves—what else could they be?
This alone is the propitiation of the Tathāgata; this alone removes the suffering of the world;
this alone is the accomplishment of one's own welfare. Therefore, practice this very thing.
Since both the hell-wardens and those who possess compassion derive their power from that [the Bodhisattva],
one should therefore serve sentient beings just as a servant serves a fierce king.
What could an angry king do that would cause the suffering of hell,
which is experienced precisely through the mental distress caused to living beings?
What could a gratified king give that would be equal to Buddhahood—
that which is experienced through bringing joy to sentient beings?
Let alone the future Buddhahood arising from the propitiation of sentient beings!
In this world as well, the patient person attains good fortune, fame, and stability.
One who is patient, while wandering through cyclic existence, attains a pleasing appearance, joy, health, long life, and the state of happiness enjoyed by a universal monarch.
Thus one should be patient, for through patience one is established in vigor;
indeed, without vigor there is no merit, just as there is no movement without wind.
What is vigor? It is enthusiasm for the wholesome. What is said to be its opposite? Laziness, contemptible power, despondency, and self-deprecation.
Laziness arises from the sleep of relishing the pleasure of non-activity, from craving for one's own basis, and from a lack of revulsion toward the suffering of saṃsāra.
Therefore, having abandoned laziness and maintained vigor with a concentrated mind,
one should practice the vow of the conduct of awakening, which brings about the welfare of all sentient beings.
For diligence is indeed a treasury containing all the jewels of virtue; by means of the great raft of diligence, one crosses over all calamities.
There is nothing to be conceived in this world that one who is established in and mounted upon diligence would not attain here.
That by which, amidst horses, elephants, chariots, and infantry, and in the midst of a tumultuous clash of iron arrows, javelins, and swords,
one slays the enemies and attains unsurpassed victory— that, indeed, is the prowess of a great warrior manifested here.

Having crossed, by their valor, oceans that are terrifying with the breaking of waves agitated by masses of towering water tossed by swarms of sea-monsters— as if they were mere puddles in a cow’s hoofprint— these heroes acquire the wealth of priceless jewels of virtue.

Having taken up the precepts— which possess the power of a counterforce against the fierce-bodied serpents of passion and the like— mortals endowed with vigor stand upon the most beautiful slopes of Mount Sumeru, possessing minds as stainless as those of the virtuous.
Together with the hosts of gods and siddhas, the bodhisattvas dwell in happiness.
That serenity which other gods dwelling in celestial palaces in the sky experience, free from all dualities,
is the splendor resulting from the firm application of vigor for the sake of producing an utterly vast fruit.

Thinking thus, one should always maintain enthusiasm in the accomplishment of perfect awakening and practice the vow of the conduct of enlightenment for the sake of establishing the welfare of all sentient beings.
Likewise, remembering the discourse on heedfulness, you should make yourself light;
yet you must remain prepared for the arrival of work as before, and be ready in every respect.
