Just as a tuft of cotton comes under the control of the wind's coming and going, so too should one come under the control of enthusiasm; in this way, supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is perfected.
Having thus increased one's enthusiasm, one should establish the mind in meditative concentration;
for a person whose mind is distracted stands within the fangs of affliction.
Through seclusion of body and mind, distraction cannot arise;
therefore, having abandoned the world, one should avoid discursive thoughts.
The world is not abandoned because of affection, nor due to thirst for gain and the like;
therefore, a wise person, when renouncing these, should reflect in this way.

Knowing that one who is well-yoked with calm abiding and insight brings about the destruction of the afflictions, one should first seek calm abiding; and that is attained through a delight that is independent of the world.
For whom could there be affection for things that are impermanent,
when one shall not see a beloved again for thousands of births?
Not seeing [the truth], he falls into discontent and does not abide in meditative concentration;
even upon seeing it, he is not satisfied, and as before, thirst continues to afflict him.
He does not see things as they truly are; he falls away from spiritual urgency and is consumed by that grief through his longing for union with what is dear.
Through constant preoccupation with that [worldly life], one's short lifespan passes away in vain again and again;
through such impermanent friends, the eternal Dharma is lost.
One who associates with fools will certainly go to a miserable rebirth;
since association with the dissimilar is not desired, what can be gained from the company of fools?
In one moment they become friends, and in another moment they become enemies;
ordinary people are difficult to please and become enraged even at occasions for joy.
If they do not listen, those who are provoked go to a miserable rebirth;
envy arises from the superior or equal, and pride from praise for the inferior self.
Since resentment arises from dispraise, when could there ever be benefit from a fool?
Self-exaltation, disparagement of others, and talk of delighting in cyclic existence—such things are inevitably unwholesome; they constitute the foolishness of a fool.
Thinking thus, the wise ascetic, having abandoned association with the foolish, should flee far from fools; and one who has encountered them should propitiate them with pleasant words.
One should not pursue intimacy with others, but remain like a neutral ascetic;
one should always dwell alone, happy and with an unafflicted mind.
Taking only the essence of the Dharma from the flowers like a bee taking honey,
he should wander everywhere as if he were a stranger, even among those with whom he is unacquainted.
Thus, the ascetic mahāsattva, free from desire for the pleasures of saṃsāra and attached to the true bliss of samādhi, should dwell with his mind fixed on awakening.
Having overcome the hosts of enemies that are the afflictions, the heroes attain the state of the glory of perfect enlightenment;
they bestow the gift of the factors of awakening upon the virtuous, for they proclaim meditation to be the cause therein.
Having torn asunder all the accumulations of defects such as passion, which serve as the sole cause for the continuous stream of births,
those men whose minds are like space— who regard a clod of earth and gold as equal— become the very causes of virtue.
Having utterly conquered the host of enemies that are the afflictions— the destroyers of the power of virtue— and having attained the mark [of mastery],
he has obtained the glory of perfect enlightenment, which consists of supreme qualities and is difficult for others to attain.
That kings, free from the fear of enemies, exercise sovereignty over sentient beings through wisdom—
regarding that, all those lords of men declare meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to be its sole cause, a treasury of all virtues.

Constantly producing the illumination of wisdom that pierces through the darkness of delusion on all sides, that sun of the Perfectly Awakened One is the cause for heroic men; therein, this samādhi is preeminent.
Thinking thus and composing oneself for the sake of abandoning the obscuration of afflictions,
one should draw the mind away from the wrong path, establish it in meditative concentration, and practice.
Having established this equipment within meditative concentration, one should practice.
Indeed, this entire preparation is for the sake of wisdom for the benefit of the world;
therefore, one should generate wisdom out of a desire for the cessation of suffering.
Conventional truth and ultimate truth—these two are considered the two truths.
Reality is that which is beyond the scope of the intellect; it is called the recollection of the intellect.
In this regard, the world is seen to be twofold: the yogi and likewise the ordinary person. Among these, the ordinary world is sublated by the world of the yogi.
Even yogins are surpassed by those of progressively higher intellectual distinction;
this is illustrated by an example accepted by both parties for the sake of the task at hand, without further analysis.
Entities are perceived by the world and are also conceptualized as being real; however, there is no dispute between yogis and the world regarding the fact that these are like an illusion.
Thinking thus, the wise ascetic, realizing that everything is fashioned by illusions,
should attain the jewel of wisdom and move about for the welfare of the world.
The form of a man devoid of the wealth of wisdom is like a painting—beautiful in appearance but lacking substance within.
For one endowed with intelligence, the desired fruit arises through vigor; indeed, vigor devoid of intelligence is an enemy that leads to one's own destruction.

Those who know declare that power of wisdom to be that by which a person knows their own past lives, separated by many births, as well as their future family, name, and lineage, including the middle, the end, and even the beginning.
In the world of mortals, the Buddha, having shattered the great mass of defilements and darkness,
creates the light of wisdom and constantly strikes down the multitude of faults in men.
He is the director of the senses and knows the minds of others even beyond them in every way;
moreover, they proclaim wisdom—which is the cause for the constant birth of the most excellent virtue—to be the primary factor therein.
Even when deeply submerged in an ocean of tasks in the midst of battle, preeminent men attain victory through the power of wisdom; therefore, wisdom is indeed the cause of all that is auspicious.
By the power of wisdom alone do the Victors conquer the terrible and most wicked army of Māra;
by the excellence of wisdom people shine forth, for wisdom is indeed proclaimed as the mother of the Victors.
Therefore, let wisdom alone be cultivated, for it accomplishes all virtues and goals;
those men who lack wisdom appear like lamps at dawn.
These six perfections alone are the treasure-trove of the jewels of the qualities of heaven and liberation for men on this earth.
Knowing this, a person intent on accomplishing their own welfare should always apply firm and swift effort toward them.
For this, Ānanda, is the supreme restraint of training for those who course in awakening; it has been prescribed by me and should be maintained until the attainment of awakening.
Those who, having adopted this supreme conduct with the aspiration for perfect enlightenment,
abide in the refuge of the Three Jewels and act for the welfare of the world;
They were the repositories of auspicious glory and virtues, possessed of moral discipline and pure faculties;
they dwelt in the fragrance of patience and gentleness, ever enthusiastic and benevolent in their intentions.
Free from afflictions, pure in nature, great beings, and discerning; possessed of wisdom, endowed with the great superknowledges, they are arhats and practitioners of the holy life.
"Having attained the threefold enlightenment, they shall reach the abode of the Perfect Buddhas.
Having heard this which was taught in the treatise, Ānanda was fully awakened.
Having gazed upon the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, he spoke thus:
"O Blessed One, regarding that which has been commanded by you as the means for attaining the state of a Perfectly Awakened One:
those who, having undertaken the restraint of the trainings, always practice in what is virtuous."
They alone are fortunate and blessed, skilled in the training and the vows of restraint;
being oriented toward discipline, they are the upholders of the treasury of the True Dharma.
The sons of the Conquerors, possessing the great superknowledges, being Arhats with stainless faculties,
become Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, who have attained awakening.
For them alone there shall always be constant good fortune in all places,
characterized by unwavering enthusiasm for accomplishing the true Dharma, free from calamity and free from agitation.
May there always be well-being for those who, abiding in refuge in the Three Jewels, practice for the welfare of the world, accomplishing the excellence of the qualities of awakening.
Having heard this which is called "Ānanda," that Blessed One, with joy,
looked toward the Venerable Ānanda and commanded him thus.
In this very way, may their constant practice for the sake of attaining perfect awakening surely become endowed with the virtues of the glory of the Dharma within the abode of existence.
Having thus fully understood this truth, you have all been awakened;
having paid homage to the Three Jewels, proceed for the welfare of the world.
If you always act by taking up what I have thus spoken,
you will surely attain perfect awakening and reach the state of a fully enlightened Buddha.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, all the members of the Saṅgha replied,
"So be it," and being thus enlightened, they rejoiced.
Then all those members of the Saṅgha, headed by Ānanda, with joyful hearts,
bowed at the feet of the Lord of Sages and departed for their respective abodes of meditation.
The Blessed One, having observed that they had all taken refuge in the abode of meditation,
went and sat within the meditation chamber, remaining absorbed in meditative concentration.
Thus has it been fully related to me by my teacher Śāṇavāsin;
having heard what was thus told by him, I have heard it—rejoice at this, O King!
O Great King, having caused the subjects to hear [the Dharma] and awakening them,
and having incited them toward the zeal of honoring the Three Jewels, protect them.
Likewise, O King, if this [kingdom] is always endowed with righteousness, prosperity, and virtue,
it will certainly be auspicious, energetic, and free from fear on all sides.
You too, having fulfilled the equipment for awakening in due order,
and having conquered the hosts of Māra, shall become an Arhat, attain awakening, and become a Victor.
Having heard this instruction from the Teacher, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, replied, "So be it," and rejoiced.
Thus ends the chapter on the summary of the training and the vows.
20. The Declaration of the Fruit:
Then once more, that king of kings, King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence, bowed to the Arhat Upagupta, looked upon him, and spoke as follows.
Venerable sir, please explain by what means this Lokanātha became renowned by the name Avalokiteśvara.
When the king had thus made his request, that arhat, the great-minded ascetic,
looked upon the great king Aśoka and instructed him as follows:
Listen, O highly fortunate King, to how it was told to me by my teacher;
I shall relate it to you exactly so, and having heard it, become enlightened.
The worlds, consisting of the six states of existence and resting within the realms of the threefold universe—
among them, those who are suffering, wicked, and tormented by the fire of the afflictions.
The Lord of the World gazed upon them all with a compassionate eye;
because of that, he became renowned throughout the three worlds as Avalokiteśvara.
Whichever sentient beings are beheld by the Lord of the World with a compassionate gaze,
they all shall become free from stain and pure in intention.
Even those who should hear the name of this Lord of the Three Worlds with reverence shall be freed from transgressions, devoid of afflictions, and possess pure faculties.
Even one who has fallen into the fire of suffering, if they should worship the Lord of the World while recollecting him,
then that Great Being will look upon them with a compassionate gaze.
Then, suddenly liberated from that fire of suffering,
with his faculties purified and his self cleansed, he shall possess a mind intent on perfect awakening.
Even while being swept away by the river, whoever cries out while remembering the Lord of the World—
then that Bodhisattva shall look upon him with a gaze of compassion.
Then the river shall grant a ford to him who seeks to cross;
having then crossed over quickly, he, devoted to righteousness, shall remain mindful.
And when merchant caravans, seeking jewels, embark upon the great ocean in ships and proceed in due order with great enthusiasm;
There, the ship, driven by the winds of the Kali age and tossed about, would swiftly be brought near the island of the Rākṣasīs.
Then, the Greatly Steadfast One, having recollected them, should bow to Lokeśvara;
at that time, Lokeśvara gazes upon all of them with a compassionate eye.
Then, those dark winds, being appeased, shall not blow;
thereafter, this ship, together with the merchant caravan, shall proceed safely to the Mine of Jewels.
There, all those merchants, having obtained jewels and being filled with joy,
returned safely; they arrived quickly and rejoined their own city in well-being.
If by chance a misfortune should occur while they are staying at the waters of all the holy fords,
those who have purified their souls, having died there, shall go to Sukhāvatī.
And whoever, though wicked and condemned to death, having been seized by executioners, should remember the Lord of the World in fear and, having meditated upon him, utter even his name; |||
Then the Lord of Passion shall look upon him with a compassionate gaze;
consequently, all those slayers will not be able to kill him.
If, having been thwarted by fate, he dies after abandoning his sinful refuge,
being pure in intention and purified in soul, he shall go to Sukhāvatī.
All the yakṣas, gandharvas, kumbhāṇḍas, and rākṣasas as well,
the kinnaras, garuḍas, nāgas, bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
They would not even be able to look upon one who is devoted to Lokeśvara, who meditates on him, who maintains mindfulness of him, and who utters his name.
And whoever, though bound with fetters and placed in a prison,
should remain mindful of Lokeśvara, meditate upon him, or even utter his name;
At that moment, the Lord of the World shall look upon him with a compassionate gaze;
then, released from bondage, he shall become one who delights in the Dharma.
Whether in a forest or even in a house that is beset by thieves and bandits, one who remembers the Lord of the World, meditates upon him, bows to him, or even utters his name, [is protected].
At that moment, may the Lord of the World look upon him with a compassionate eye;
then all those rogues and thieves shall turn their backs and depart.
And whoever is a patient, always afflicted, with a body overwhelmed by the disease of leprosy—
having remembered and meditated upon the Lord of the World, he should bow and recite even His name.
At that very moment, may the Lord of the World look upon him with a compassionate gaze;
then he shall be freed from disease, healthy, and his faculties restored through nourishment.
One whose intention is pure and whose self is purified should possess the mind set on perfect enlightenment;
if by chance misfortune should occur, having abandoned this body which is the locus of suffering,
one with a pure intention and a purified self shall go to Sukhāvatī.
Whoever is impoverished, suffering, wretched, helpless, and without refuge—
by recollecting Lokeśvara, meditating upon him, bowing to him, and even uttering his name;
At that moment, may the Lord of the World look upon him with a compassionate gaze;
then he shall become a virtuous person, endowed with glory and auspicious faculties.
And whoever, even in the midst of battle, surrounded by enemies,
should remember the Lord of the World, meditate upon him, bow down, and recite his name;
At that moment, may the Lord of the World look upon him with a compassionate gaze;
then, having completely conquered his enemies, he shall obtain and enjoy the glory of victory.
And whoever, even when houses, gardens, or hermitages are burning,
remembers the Lord of the World, meditates upon him, and utters his name with reverence;
At that time, may the Lord of the World look upon him with a compassionate gaze;
then that mass of fire will suddenly be extinguished and become tranquil.
In dispute or in strife, or even when insulted by wicked people,
one should remember the Lord of the World, meditate upon him, and utter his name while bowing.
At that moment, the Teacher of the World shall look upon him with a compassionate gaze;
then, being victorious over all, he shall establish them under his own power.
And whoever, scorched by the fire of the afflictions, with senses and mind agitated,
should remember the Lord of the World, meditate upon him, bow down, or even utter his name;
At that moment, the Great Being should look upon him with a compassionate gaze;
then he shall become a wise one of auspicious faculties, his nature auspicious and free from afflictions.
He who is childless and desires the jewel of a son should go for refuge to that Lokeśvara;
remembering him and meditating upon him, he should worship according to his ability while reciting the names.
Then that Lord of the three worlds shall look upon him with a compassionate gaze and grant him a jewel of a son, a being of great courage who is beloved by the world.
To one who requests a daughter, the Lord of the World would give a virtuous daughter, beautiful as Lakṣmī, with auspicious faculties, beloved by all beings, charming, and faithful.
One seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; one seeking wealth obtains wealth;
and even one seeking a kingdom obtains a kingdom, provided they possess devotion to the Lord of the World.
One who desires wealth obtains wealth; one who desires qualities obtains qualities;
one who desires objects of enjoyment obtains enjoyment; and one who desires a home obtains a home.
In this way, one who possesses devotion to Lokeśa shall obtain all other things and every kind of requisite, exactly as desired.
Therefore, he was proclaimed by all the Dharma-kings and lords of sages as "Āryāvalokiteśvara, the Lord of the Three Worlds."
Thus, for those who cultivate devotion to Lokeśvara, the merit is even greater—
immeasurable and incalculable— and it accomplishes the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Thus has it been taught in every way by all the Sugatas;
and it is likewise praised by all the Bodhisattvas possessed of great supernormal powers.
Thinking thus, O Great King, always take refuge in the Protector of the World and worship him with faith and joy.
For one who possesses devotion to the Lord of the World, there is no sin whatsoever.
Nor is there fear of wicked afflictions, nor is there ever any obstacle to true happiness.
All the hosts of wicked Māras will always be destroyed on every side,
and even the messengers of Yama and others shall flee with their faces turned away.
And for those who possess devotion to Lokeśa, inexhaustible and incalculable streams of merit increase incessantly, day and night.
Through the power of this merit, he obtains the True Dharma;
and through the power of that True Dharma, the Perfectly Awakened One is seen before him.
Then, through the power of the Buddha, the thought of awakening is easily obtained;
and by means of the thought of the vow for awakening, one practices the conduct of awakening.
Having gradually fulfilled the equipment for perfect enlightenment in due order,
and having utterly conquered all afflictions as well as the hosts of the four māras;
Having attained mastery in all respects and being endowed with the qualities of the dhāraṇīs,
one becomes a lord of the ten stages and shall fully realize perfect enlightenment.
Thinking thus, the Greatly Wise One, Lokeśvara, the Son of the Victor,
should always be venerated by the virtuous who desire the state of a Perfect Buddha.
Those who always and constantly worship Lokeśvara, the Lord of the World,
for them there is indeed no fear whatsoever, anywhere or at any time.
Upon beholding him, Brahmā and the other great seers, as well as Śakra and the other lords of the gods— even the sovereigns of all the worlds— would protect him.
Even the fires would protect this person who is permeated by devotion to the Lord of the World;
so too would all the *pretas*, such as Dharmarāja and others, as well as all the night-stalkers (*niśācara*).
For Varuṇa and all the kings, as well as all the hosts of Vāyu,
all the Yakṣas headed by Śrīda, and even all the lords of the Bhūtas [were there].
All the planets beginning with the Sun, the stars beginning with the Moon, all the Siddhas and Sādhyas, as well as the Rudras and the Vidyādharas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra and all the others, as well as all the Gandharvas, and the Kumbhāṇḍas such as Virūḍhaka and the rest, shall always be his constant followers and protect him.
All the lords of the nāgas, beginning with Virūpākṣa, as well as the Garuḍas,
and all the yakṣas, headed by Kuvera, [did so] with great respect.
All the kinnaras, such as Drumādi, all the asuras, such as Vemacitra,
and even all the piśācas shall protect him who is composed in meditative concentration.
All the hosts of Mothers, together with the lords of their youthful retinues; all the Bhairavas, and even all the hosts of Mahākālas.
The entire assembly of Ḍākas and Ḍākinīs, as well as all the Kāpālikas and all the Vaitāḍikas, having seen him, moved about with great reverence.
Likewise, the accomplished yogis, free from conceptual construction and having conquered their senses,
shall see from afar and protect him who has taken refuge in Lokeśvara.
The heroes, Vajrapāṇi and the others, are the accomplishers of the purpose of all mantras.
Having observed him, they should protect that one who practices devotion to the Lord of the World.
Ascetics and heretics as well, forest-dwellers and celibate students, Vaiṣṇavas and Śaivas, those who bear the sectarian marks and those who observe vows— [all these were there].
Even from afar, seeing one who is devoted to the Lord of the World,
they should bow down, join their palms in reverence, and praise him with great respect.
The Arhats and the monks, seeing him from afar, were filled with joy; having honored him by saying, "You are blessed," they would offer their congratulations.
Śrāvakas, mendicants, those observing vows, and lay devotees alike,
upon seeing that illustrious one from afar, would bow down with bodies deeply inclined.
And all those great beings, the Bodhisattvas, sons of the Conquerors,
having propitiated him with gifts of boons, would act for the welfare of the world.
And even the Pratyekabuddhas, having seen that one who is destined for enlightenment and having observed him, would comfort him and urge him toward the excellent restraint.
Even all the perfectly awakened ones, seeing him who has attained the state of a perfectly awakened one, rejoice and, establishing him in the true Dharma, lead him forward until the end of existence.
Thus, the majesty of the qualities of the True Dharma of this Great-Souled Lord of the World, the Sustainer of the Universe, is praised by all the Buddhas.
Realizing that the merit arising from the worship of Lokeśvara is thus exceedingly great, those who desire awakening should always rejoice in it and listen to it.
All these well-spoken jewels of the Mahāyāna sūtras are heard even by those who, in the degenerate age of the five corruptions, listen with faith.
They shall never, under any circumstances, go to an evil rebirth;
always born in happy states, they become practitioners of auspicious conduct.
Always remaining in refuge with Lokeśa, the Teacher of the World,
they should worship him until the end of existence, having meditated upon him, recited his name, and remembered him.
Anointed with this merit, those who are the abodes of auspicious glory and excellent virtues,
having enjoyed the attainment of happiness through the true Dharma, shall go to Sukhāvatī.
He who causes this entire world to hear it, awakening them, does not go to an evil destiny; indeed, he goes only to a happy state.
With a self purified by this merit, a refuge for the excellent qualities of auspicious glory,
and having enjoyed the attainment of the bliss of the true Dharma, may he go to Sukhāvatī.
And whoever, even in this age of Kali, being indifferent to their own life,
should sit in the midst of an assembly and speak these well-spoken sūtras;
He too, whose self is purified by this merit, shall never go to an evil rebirth; always born in a happy state, he will be a refuge for auspicious glory and excellent virtues.
Bringing about the welfare of all sentient beings by accomplishing the true Dharma itself,
and having enjoyed happiness accompanied by pure enthusiasm, one shall go to Sukhāvatī.
There, may all remain in refuge under the Teacher Amitaruci;
having always drunk the nectar of the Dharma, may they practice the vow of awakening.
Then, having fulfilled the equipment for enlightenment in due order,
they shall all become Lords of the World and masters of the ten stages.
Then those Bodhisattvas, sons of the Victors, with pure souls,
shall become Great Beings endowed with the threefold supernormal knowledges and auspicious faculties.
Having conquered all afflictions and the hosts of Māra, the Arhats, free from defilement,
attain the threefold enlightenment and reach the state of a Perfect Buddha.
Whoever joyfully writes down this King of Sūtras of the Veda and Mahāyāna has,
by that act, written down all the sublime teachings of the Mahāyāna.
Whoever has had this well-spoken king of sutras written down has thereby had all the wisdom of the well-spoken Mahāyāna written down.
Or by whomsoever this has been written and installed according to the rules,
having placed it in a pure location or within the home, it should always be worshipped with the articles of worship.
By that, all the Arhats and Jinas, as well as the Pratyekabuddhas together with their Saṅghas and the Bodhisattvas, truly become honored.
And whoever, having personally upheld this, should also instruct others,
constantly cultivating it through mindfulness, meditation, and even with joyful devotion;
All the lords of sages, the Pratyekabuddhas, the Victors,
the Arhats, and the Bodhisattvas will be pleased and grant him his heart's desire.
And whoever, having duly honored both this instructor and all the disciples as well, should satisfy them with food offerings;
By that [merit], all the perfectly awakened ones, as well as the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, monks, yogins, and those who lead the holy life, [are honored].
And all the bodhisattvas, as well as those who observe vows and ascetics,
should always be honored with food and remain thoroughly satisfied.
What is the use of saying more? All the Buddhas, the lords of sages;
all the goddesses who are the perfections (pāramitās); and all the assemblies of the sons of the Conquerors—[are likewise present].
Constantly observing them with a compassionate gaze and rejoicing in them, they should provide protection everywhere and bestow boons for the welfare of the world.
All the world-protectors, as well as all the gods and dānavas,
having provided protection, shall grant boons to those who accomplish the true Dharma.
Kings, too, having always provided protection for them and expressed their approval,
shall protect them with impartiality, fulfilling their every wish.
Their ministers as well— along with their councilors, attendants, servants, armies, and officials— should always act for their benefit.
May all the Vaiśyas be sustainers of all interests and dear to their friends; may all the guild-leaders and great merchants be doers of good.
Even enemies would become servants, and the wicked would come to have benevolent intentions;
likewise, all other people as well would possess minds of loving-kindness.
Beasts, birds, and even all insects and living creatures shall not be hostile toward them; rather, they shall be proclaimers of their welfare.
Thus, in all worlds, for those who accomplish the True Dharma,
there shall always be freedom from calamity, auspicious enthusiasm, and constant good fortune.
Thus, considering that the merit arising from devotion to the Lord of the World is most excellent in this world,
always remember and worship him, the Protector of the Three Worlds.
Those who, having taken refuge in him, remain composed in meditation,
and who always worship him with faith, even by uttering his name;
May the Three Jewels always remain well-pleased with them;
and having looked upon them with a compassionate gaze, may they always perform virtuous deeds.
Having heard this teaching as it was instructed by the monk Upagupta,
King Aśoka, awakened, broke into a loud roar of joy.
The entire assembly, having heard this, was deeply pacified;
responding with "So be it," they were awakened and offered their joyful approval.
Then all those people, having risen up filled with joy,
bowed to that Arhat Upagupta and departed for their respective homes.
From that time forward, that king, constantly remembering the Lord of the World,
meditating upon him and uttering his name, protected his subjects while remaining devoted to him.
Then, in the realm of that lord of men, there was always an absence of calamities and a flourishing of auspicious energy on all sides.
Having heard what was thus instructed by Jayaśrī,
Jinaśrīrāja— self-knowing and awakened— rejoiced together with his assembly.
Then that Jayashri, the son of Sugata, possessing great supernormal knowledge,
surveyed all the assemblies and again gave this instruction:
Whoever would cause this king of sūtras to be turned even in the Kali age—
whether he speaks it, hears it, causes others to hear it, or propagates it;
May all these perfectly awakened ones, always beholding them there with eyes of compassion, grant them well-being throughout the cycle of existence.
May all the goddesses of the perfections (pāramitā-devī), always bestowing auspiciousness upon them there,
fulfill the equipment for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) for the welfare of the world.
May all the Bodhisattvas, as well as the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Yogins, always bestow auspiciousness upon them.
May Brahmā, the world-protectors, and all the great ṛṣis always bestow auspiciousness there upon all of them.
May the clouds rain in due season, may the earth be rich with crops, and may there certainly be an abundance of food, free from calamities and full of great vitality.
May cows yielding abundant milk, trees laden with flowers and fruit, and medicinal herbs endowed with potency and vigor always flourish there in abundance.
May all living beings be healthy and long-lived; may they possess all necessary resources, be endowed with prosperity, and conduct themselves with auspiciousness.
May the king be most righteous, and may the ministers follow the path of policy;
may all people abide in virtuous conduct and accomplish the Dharma.
May there be no one of evil conduct, a thief, a wicked person, or a deceiver; may there be no one who is poor, unfortunate, wretched, or arrogant with pride and conceit.
May all beings, acting with equanimity and possessing the purity of the three spheres,
and guarding the vows of their respective families, act for the welfare of the world.
May all beings, possessing auspicious intentions and practicing the vow of perfect enlightenment,
always move toward what is virtuous after having paid homage to the Three Jewels.
Having heard what was thus declared by Jayaśrī, all those belonging to the Saṅgha,
having requested, "So be it," were delighted and rejoiced.
Thus ends the King of Sutras, the *Śrīmadāryāvalokiteśvaraguṇakāraṇḍavyūha*, spoken by Jayaśrī as requested by Jinaśrīrāja.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
May there be auspiciousness!
